POOL.h: Male satin bowerbirds build a stick structure called a bower and decorate it almost entirely with blue objects.
POOL.b: Near towns they collect bottle caps, pegs and straws to impress females. They even paint the inner walls with a mix of chewed plants and saliva.
POOL.m: Around Australian homes, a missing blue peg may have been taken by a hopeful bowerbird.

POOL.h: Almost every snowflake has six sides or six arms.
POOL.b: This comes from the way water molecules bond together as they freeze, forming a hexagonal pattern. The endless variety of shapes depends on the temperature and humidity each crystal meets as it falls.
POOL.m: Simple rules, applied in slightly different conditions, can create endless variety.

POOL.h: The box jellyfish has no brain, yet it has 24 eyes.
POOL.b: They sit in four clusters around its bell, and some even have lenses that can form images. Box jellyfish use them to steer around obstacles and find their way through murky coastal water.
POOL.m: Found in northern Australian waters, box jellyfish are why many tropical beaches have stinger nets and vinegar stations.

POOL.t: A westerly comes from the west
POOL.h: Winds are named for the direction they blow from.
POOL.b: A westerly blows from the west towards the east, and a sea breeze blows in from the sea. That is why Sydney’s famous “southerly buster” brings a sudden rush of cool air up from the south.
POOL.m: Knowing this makes weather forecasts much easier to read.

POOL.h: The Venus flytrap can count.
POOL.b: Its trap snaps shut only when trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds, which avoids wasting energy on raindrops or debris. After about five touches, it starts making digestive enzymes.
POOL.m: Even without a brain, living things can make surprisingly careful decisions.

POOL.h: Young sunflowers track the Sun across the sky.
POOL.b: During the day the stem grows faster on one side, turning the bud from east to west, and at night it swings back. Once mature, most face east permanently, which warms the flowers and attracts more bees.
POOL.m: Plants move more than we realise, just too slowly for us to notice.

POOL.h: The Wollemi pine was known only from fossils until 1994.
POOL.b: That year a national parks officer on a bushwalk found living trees in a remote gorge in Wollemi National Park, north-west of Sydney. Fewer than 100 adult trees grow in the wild, and their location is kept secret.
POOL.m: Major discoveries can still happen close to big cities. During the 2019–20 bushfires, firefighters worked specially to save the grove.

POOL.t: Why the Blue Mountains look blue
POOL.h: The Blue Mountains get their colour from eucalyptus trees.
POOL.b: Eucalypts release oils into the air, and the tiny droplets scatter blue light, giving the distant ridges a soft blue haze. The effect is strongest on warm, still days.
POOL.m: A landscape’s character can come from something invisible in its air.

POOL.t: Gum trees are built for bushfire
POOL.h: Many eucalypts are built to survive bushfire.
POOL.b: Buds hidden under their thick bark sprout new leaves after a fire, which is why blackened trunks turn fuzzy green within weeks. Some species also regrow from a woody swelling at their base called a lignotuber.
POOL.m: Fire has shaped Australian plants for millions of years, and many rely on it to regenerate.

POOL.t: The world’s biggest plant is a seagrass
POOL.h: The largest known plant on Earth is a seagrass in Western Australia.
POOL.b: In 2022, scientists found that a meadow in Shark Bay covering about 200 square kilometres is a single plant that spread by cloning itself. It is estimated to be at least 4,500 years old.
POOL.m: Seagrass meadows shelter marine life and store carbon, so protecting them helps the climate.

POOL.h: In seahorses, it is the male that gives birth.
POOL.b: The female places her eggs in a pouch on the male’s belly, where he fertilises and carries them for a few weeks. He then releases the tiny, fully formed young, sometimes hundreds at a time.
POOL.m: Nature has far more variety in parenting roles than we tend to assume.

POOL.h: Every clownfish matures first as a male.
POOL.b: They live in small groups led by a single breeding female, who is the largest fish. If she dies, the biggest male changes sex and takes her place.
POOL.m: Some fish can change sex during life, a trait found in hundreds of species.

POOL.t: Dolphins sleep with half a brain
POOL.h: Dolphins sleep with one half of their brain at a time.
POOL.b: One hemisphere rests while the other stays alert, so they can keep surfacing to breathe and watch for danger. They often close the eye opposite the sleeping half.
POOL.m: Sleep is so vital that even animals that can never fully switch off have found a way to get it.

POOL.h: Honeybees tell each other where food is by dancing.
POOL.b: In the “waggle dance”, the angle of the dance shows the direction of the food relative to the Sun, and the length of the waggle shows the distance. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding it.
POOL.m: Complex communication does not require words, or even a large brain.

POOL.h: There are roughly 20 quadrillion ants on Earth.
POOL.b: A 2022 study estimated that is about 2.5 million ants for every person. Together they outweigh all the world’s wild birds and wild mammals combined.
POOL.m: Small creatures, in vast numbers, quietly run many of Earth’s ecosystems.

POOL.h: Some termites in the Northern Territory build compass-aligned mounds.
POOL.b: Magnetic termite mounds are thin, flat wedges that point roughly north to south. Their broad sides catch the gentle morning and afternoon sun, while the narrow edge faces the harsh midday heat.
POOL.m: It is natural climate control, and engineers study mounds like these to design cooler buildings.

POOL.t: The numbat eats 20,000 termites a day
POOL.h: A numbat can eat up to 20,000 termites a day.
POOL.b: This striped marsupial from Western Australia uses a long, sticky tongue to lick them out of shallow soil tunnels. Unusually for a marsupial, it is active by day, matching the termites’ timetable.
POOL.m: The numbat is endangered, and fox control has been key to its recovery.

POOL.t: A shark that may live 400 years
POOL.h: The Greenland shark may live for around 400 years.
POOL.b: A 2016 study dated tissue in the eyes of these slow-growing Arctic sharks and estimated the oldest was at least 270 years old, and possibly far older. That makes it the longest-lived vertebrate known.
POOL.m: Some sharks alive today were born before Captain Cook reached Australia.

POOL.h: Corals get most of their food from tiny algae living inside them.
POOL.b: When the water gets too warm, corals expel these algae and turn white, which is called bleaching. If high temperatures last too long, the corals can starve and die.
POOL.m: Even a small rise in sea temperature, held for weeks, can damage an entire reef.

POOL.h: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm.
POOL.b: The name depends on where it forms: hurricanes in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific, typhoons in the north-west Pacific, and cyclones in the South Pacific and Indian Ocean. In the Southern Hemisphere they spin clockwise.
POOL.m: One weather system, three names: geography, not strength, decides the label.

POOL.h: The coldest air temperature reliably recorded on Earth is minus 89.2°C.
POOL.b: It was measured in 1983 at the Soviet (now Russian) Vostok Station, high on the Antarctic ice sheet. Satellites have detected even colder surface temperatures in parts of East Antarctica.
POOL.m: Antarctica’s extremes make it a natural laboratory for studying Earth’s climate.

POOL.t: The biggest flower has no leaves
POOL.h: The world’s largest single flower has no leaves, stem or roots.
POOL.b: Rafflesia arnoldii, from the rainforests of Sumatra and Borneo, can grow about a metre across. It lives as a parasite inside a vine and smells like rotting meat to attract flies.
POOL.m: Plants do not all make their own food: some survive entirely by stealing it.

POOL.h: Birds are living dinosaurs.
POOL.b: They descend from small feathered theropods, the same group that includes Tyrannosaurus and Velociraptor. When you watch a magpie or an emu, you are seeing a dinosaur lineage that survived the mass extinction 66 million years ago.
POOL.m: Dinosaurs never entirely disappeared: around 10,000 species of them are still flying around.

POOL.h: A bar-tailed godwit once flew 13,560 km without stopping.
POOL.b: In 2022, a young bird tagged in Alaska flew to Tasmania in about 11 days, without eating, drinking or landing. Godwits make similar journeys to Australia and New Zealand each year.
POOL.m: Protecting migratory birds means protecting wetlands across many countries.

POOL.h: Butterflies taste with their feet.
POOL.b: Sensors on their legs detect chemicals when they land. This helps females check whether a plant is the right food for their caterpillars before laying eggs.
POOL.m: Animals sense the world in ways that can be very different from our own.

POOL.h: The wood frog can freeze solid and survive.
POOL.b: In North American winters, around two thirds of its body water turns to ice and its heart stops beating. It floods its cells with glucose as a natural antifreeze and thaws back to life in spring.
POOL.m: Researchers study it for ideas on preserving human organs for transplant.

POOL.h: Victoria is home to one of the world’s biggest earthworms.
POOL.b: The giant Gippsland earthworm averages about a metre long and can stretch much further. It lives in deep, moist burrows, and you can sometimes hear it gurgling as it moves underground.
POOL.m: It is found nowhere else on Earth and is threatened by soil disturbance.

POOL.h: There have been no recorded deaths from funnel-web spider bites since antivenom was introduced in 1981.
POOL.b: The antivenom is made using venom milked from spiders, some caught by the public and handed in to the Australian Reptile Park. First aid is a pressure immobilisation bandage and calling 000.
POOL.m: A dangerous animal becomes far less deadly when good first aid and treatment are close at hand.

POOL.t: Cane toads were brought in on purpose
POOL.h: Cane toads were introduced to Australia deliberately.
POOL.b: In 1935, about 100 toads were brought from Hawaii to Queensland and bred, and thousands of their young were released to eat beetles damaging sugar cane. They did little to control the beetles, and their descendants have spread across much of northern Australia.
POOL.m: Fixes that ignore the whole ecosystem can create bigger problems than the ones they solve.

POOL.t: A tree older than the pyramids
POOL.h: Some living trees were already growing when the Great Pyramid was built.
POOL.b: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California known as Methuselah is more than 4,800 years old. Its exact location is kept secret to protect it.
POOL.m: Harsh, slow-growing conditions can produce the longest lives.

POOL.h: Canada has the longest coastline of any country.
POOL.b: Including its thousands of islands, it runs for more than 200,000 kilometres. That is several times the length of Australia’s mainland coast.
POOL.m: Coastline length depends on how finely you measure, a puzzle known as the coastline paradox.

POOL.t: France has the most time zones
POOL.h: France covers more time zones than any other country.
POOL.b: Thanks to overseas territories in the Pacific, the Caribbean and the Indian Ocean, it spans 12 time zones. Russia, the largest country by area, has 11.
POOL.m: Old empires left long shadows on the map, from territories to time zones.

POOL.t: The lake holding a fifth of fresh water
POOL.h: Lake Baikal in Siberia holds about a fifth of the world’s unfrozen fresh surface water.
POOL.b: It is the deepest lake on Earth, reaching about 1,640 metres, and one of the oldest, at around 25 million years. It holds more water than all five North American Great Lakes combined.
POOL.m: A single lake can be one of the planet’s most valuable natural resources.

POOL.h: The shores of the Dead Sea are the lowest land on Earth.
POOL.b: They lie more than 430 metres below sea level and drop further each year as the water level falls by about a metre annually. Its water is so salty that people float with ease.
POOL.m: The Dead Sea is shrinking mainly because the water that once fed it is used upstream.

POOL.t: The smallest country in the world
POOL.h: The smallest country in the world is smaller than many city parks.
POOL.b: Vatican City covers about 0.44 square kilometres inside Rome. It has its own flag, post office and passports, but a population of only a few hundred.
POOL.m: Sovereignty is about recognition and law, not size.

POOL.h: Most Australians live within about 50 km of the coast.
POOL.b: The country is roughly the size of the mainland United States, yet much of its interior is very sparsely populated. Australia is also one of the most urbanised nations on Earth, with most people living in a handful of coastal cities.
POOL.m: A map of land area says little about where people actually live.

POOL.t: Australia’s lowest point is a lake
POOL.h: Australia’s lowest point is a lake that is usually dry.
POOL.b: Kati Thanda–Lake Eyre in South Australia sits about 15 metres below sea level. It fills completely only rarely, and when it does, pelicans and other waterbirds flock there from far away.
POOL.m: Outback ecosystems are built around rare booms, not steady conditions.

POOL.h: Some of the cleanest air on Earth is measured in north-west Tasmania.
POOL.b: The Cape Grim station samples winds that have crossed thousands of kilometres of Southern Ocean. Its records, going back to 1976, help scientists track global changes in the atmosphere.
POOL.m: Clean baseline air lets scientists measure the whole planet’s atmosphere, not just local pollution.

POOL.h: A hill in New Zealand has one of the world’s longest place names.
POOL.b: Its Māori name, usually shortened to Taumata, runs to 85 letters. It tells of Tamatea, an ancestor said to have played his flute there to a loved one.
POOL.m: Place names can carry whole stories, not just labels.

POOL.h: Nobody can say for certain whether the Nile or the Amazon is longer.
POOL.b: Both are roughly 6,400 to 7,000 kilometres long, and the answer depends on where you decide each river begins and ends. Most references list the Nile first.
POOL.m: Even simple-sounding facts can depend on definitions.

POOL.h: The Amazon carries more water than any other river.
POOL.b: It delivers roughly a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers pour into the oceans. Its outflow is so strong that fresh water pushes far out into the Atlantic.
POOL.m: The Amazon basin’s health affects rainfall and climate well beyond South America.

POOL.t: Africa is bigger than it looks
POOL.h: Africa is about 14 times bigger than Greenland, even though many maps make them look similar.
POOL.b: The familiar Mercator projection, created in 1569 for sailors, stretches areas more and more towards the poles. It is great for navigation but badly distorts size.
POOL.m: Every flat map distorts something, so it pays to know which trade-off a map has made.

POOL.t: The loneliest place in the ocean
POOL.h: The most remote spot in the ocean is called Point Nemo.
POOL.b: It lies in the South Pacific about 2,700 km from the nearest land. Space agencies use the area as a graveyard for old spacecraft, and at times the nearest humans are astronauts on the International Space Station.
POOL.m: Remoteness is relative: sometimes the closest people are overhead, not on Earth.

POOL.h: About 7,000 languages are spoken in the world today.
POOL.b: Yet more than half the world’s population speaks one of just 23 of them. Around 40 per cent of all languages are endangered, many with fewer than 1,000 speakers.
POOL.m: When a language disappears, a unique way of seeing the world goes with it.

POOL.h: Papua New Guinea has more languages than any other country.
POOL.b: Around 840 are spoken there, more than a tenth of the world’s total. Rugged mountains, valleys and forests kept communities apart for thousands of years, letting languages develop separately.
POOL.m: Geography does not just shape landscapes, it shapes how people speak.

POOL.h: Mandarin Chinese has the most native speakers, but English has the most speakers overall.
POOL.b: Only about 400 million people speak English as a first language, yet around 1.5 billion speak it in total. For most of them it is a second language.
POOL.m: English is now mostly spoken by non-native speakers, which shapes how it is used worldwide.

POOL.h: Before 1788, more than 250 distinct languages were spoken across Australia.
POOL.b: Counting dialects, there were around 800 varieties. Many place names, such as Parramatta, Wagga Wagga and Uluru, come from First Nations languages, and communities today are working to revive them.
POOL.m: Place names are a daily reminder of the languages that shaped the land first.

POOL.h: Only two countries in the world are doubly landlocked.
POOL.b: Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan are surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries, so reaching the sea means crossing at least two borders. Liechtenstein sits between Switzerland and Austria.
POOL.m: Access to the sea has shaped trade, and history, for thousands of years.

POOL.t: The country with the highest low point
POOL.h: Lesotho is a country completely surrounded by South Africa.
POOL.b: It is also the only independent country lying entirely above 1,000 metres. Its lowest point is about 1,400 metres above sea level, the highest lowest point of any nation.
POOL.m: High altitude gives Lesotho cold winters and snow, unusual for southern Africa.

POOL.t: The longest border in the world
POOL.h: The border between Canada and the United States is the longest international border in the world.
POOL.b: It runs for about 8,900 kilometres, including the long land border with Alaska. For about 2,000 km in the west, it follows a straight line along the 49th parallel.
POOL.m: Many borders are drawn by treaty on a map, not by rivers or mountains.

POOL.t: Two islands, almost a day apart
POOL.h: Two islands less than 4 km apart are nearly a full day apart in time.
POOL.b: Big Diomede belongs to Russia and Little Diomede to the United States, with the International Date Line running between them. In winter, the sea between them can freeze over.
POOL.m: The date line is an agreed convention, not a physical feature.

POOL.t: The first country to see New Year
POOL.h: Kiribati is the first country to welcome each New Year.
POOL.b: Its Line Islands sit in the UTC+14 time zone, the earliest on Earth. In 1995, Kiribati shifted the International Date Line so the whole country would share the same calendar day.
POOL.m: Countries can, and do, redraw the invisible lines that organise time.

POOL.t: The peak farthest from Earth’s centre
POOL.h: The point on Earth farthest from its centre is not the top of Everest.
POOL.b: Because Earth bulges at the equator, the summit of Chimborazo in Ecuador is about 2 km further from the centre than Everest’s peak, even though it is lower above sea level.
POOL.m: The answer to “highest” depends on what you measure from.

POOL.h: Australia’s highest mountain is not Kosciuszko.
POOL.b: Mount Kosciuszko, at 2,228 metres, is the highest on the mainland. But Mawson Peak, an active volcano on Heard Island in the sub-Antarctic, rises to about 2,745 metres, the highest peak on Australian territory outside Antarctica.
POOL.m: Australia’s external territories stretch from the Indian Ocean to Antarctica.

POOL.t: The Sahara is mostly not sand
POOL.h: The Sahara is roughly the size of the United States.
POOL.b: Yet only about a quarter of it is covered in sand dunes. Most of it is rocky plateaus, gravel plains and mountains, some of which occasionally see snow.
POOL.m: Deserts are defined by lack of rain, not by sand.

POOL.h: Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth.
POOL.b: A desert is defined by low precipitation, not heat, and much of the Antarctic interior receives very little snow each year. Yet its ice sheet holds about 70 per cent of the world’s fresh water.
POOL.m: If all of Antarctica’s ice melted, sea levels would rise by many tens of metres.

POOL.h: Nepal has the only national flag that is not a rectangle or square.
POOL.b: It is made of two stacked triangular pennants, bearing a Moon and a Sun. Nepal’s constitution sets out the exact geometric steps for drawing it.
POOL.m: Symbols are designed with remarkable care when they represent a nation.

POOL.t: The world’s highest seat of government
POOL.h: Bolivia has two capitals.
POOL.b: Sucre is the constitutional capital, while the government sits in La Paz, which at about 3,600 metres is the highest seat of government in the world. Visitors often need a few days to adjust to the thin air.
POOL.m: Altitude affects everything there, from breathing to the temperature at which water boils.

POOL.t: Alaska is the most eastern state
POOL.h: Alaska is the northernmost, westernmost and easternmost US state.
POOL.b: Its Aleutian Islands stretch so far that some cross the 180° meridian into the Eastern Hemisphere. By that measure, parts of Alaska are further east than Maine.
POOL.m: Directions on a round planet can defy common sense.

POOL.t: Reno is west of Los Angeles
POOL.h: Reno, Nevada, is further west than Los Angeles.
POOL.b: California’s coast slants eastward as it heads south, so LA lies further east than most people picture. Our mental maps tend to straighten out real coastlines.
POOL.m: Checking a map often beats trusting your sense of direction.

POOL.h: Sailing through the Panama Canal from the Atlantic to the Pacific, you travel south-east.
POOL.b: The Isthmus of Panama bends in an S shape, so the canal’s Pacific end is actually further east than its Atlantic end.
POOL.m: Geography rarely matches the neat assumptions in our heads.

POOL.t: Ecuador is named after the equator
POOL.h: Ecuador is simply Spanish for “equator”.
POOL.b: The line passes just north of the capital, Quito, where a monument marks the “Middle of the World”. The equator also crosses 12 other countries, from Brazil and Kenya to Indonesia.
POOL.m: Even a country’s name can be a geography lesson.

POOL.t: Greenland’s name was a sales pitch
POOL.h: Greenland was named to attract settlers.
POOL.b: According to Icelandic sagas, Erik the Red chose the name in the 980s, reasoning that people would be more willing to go to a land with an appealing name. Today about 80 per cent of the island is covered by ice.
POOL.m: Marketing is far older than advertising agencies.

POOL.h: Australia moves about 7 centimetres north each year.
POOL.b: It rides on one of the fastest-moving continental plates. The drift adds up, so a new official datum released in 2017, GDA2020, shifted the country’s map coordinates by about 1.8 metres to keep GPS positions accurate.
POOL.m: The ground beneath us is slowly moving, and modern navigation has to account for it.

POOL.t: The world’s largest lake is a “sea”
POOL.h: The world’s largest lake is called a sea.
POOL.b: The Caspian Sea covers about 370,000 square kilometres, larger than Germany, and is bordered by five countries. Its water is salty, but only about a third as salty as the ocean.
POOL.m: What we call something is not always what it is.

POOL.h: The world’s biggest waterfall is underwater.
POOL.b: Beneath the Denmark Strait, between Greenland and Iceland, cold dense water plunges about 3,500 metres down the seafloor. Its flow dwarfs that of any waterfall on land.
POOL.m: Some of Earth’s largest features are hidden beneath the waves.

POOL.t: The countries with the most neighbours
POOL.h: China and Russia each share land borders with 14 countries.
POOL.b: That is more than any other nation. China’s neighbours range from North Korea and Vietnam to Afghanistan and Kazakhstan.
POOL.m: More neighbours means more trade, but also more borders to manage.

POOL.t: Singapore has grown by a quarter
POOL.h: Singapore has grown about 25 per cent bigger since the 1960s.
POOL.b: By reclaiming land from the sea, it has expanded from roughly 580 to more than 720 square kilometres. Parts of Changi Airport and the Marina Bay area sit on land that was once water.
POOL.m: When land runs out, some countries build more of it.

POOL.h: About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level.
POOL.b: Dykes, dunes and pumping stations keep the water out, and much of this land was reclaimed from lakes and the sea. The lowest point is almost 7 metres below sea level.
POOL.m: With planning and engineering, people can live safely where nature would put water.

POOL.h: K’gari, formerly Fraser Island, is the largest sand island in the world.
POOL.b: It stretches about 120 km along the Queensland coast. Remarkably, rainforest grows in its sand, and it has around 100 freshwater lakes.
POOL.m: K’gari is World Heritage-listed, recognised as a natural wonder of global importance.

POOL.h: Switzerland has four national languages.
POOL.b: German, French, Italian and Romansh are all recognised, though Romansh is the first language of less than 1 per cent of people. Swiss coins use the Latin name Helvetia, which favours none of them.
POOL.m: A shared identity does not require a single shared language.

POOL.h: Australia has no official language in law.
POOL.b: English is the national language in practice. In the 2021 Census, more than a fifth of Australians spoke a language other than English at home.
POOL.m: Diversity of language is part of everyday Australian life.

POOL.h: Western Australia has a lake that is naturally bubblegum pink.
POOL.b: Lake Hillier, on Middle Island off the coast near Esperance, gets its colour from salt-loving microalgae and bacteria. The pink stays even when the water is scooped into a glass.
POOL.m: Tiny organisms can transform an entire landscape.

POOL.h: One of the world’s longest fences stretches across Australia.
POOL.b: The Dingo Fence runs about 5,600 km through Queensland, New South Wales and South Australia. It was built to keep dingoes out of sheep-grazing land in the south-east.
POOL.m: Human barriers reshape ecosystems, often in ways no one planned.

POOL.h: In a 1999 study, people who scored lowest on tests of logic and grammar greatly overestimated how well they had done.
POOL.b: Later researchers argue part of the pattern is a statistical artefact, and most people misjudge themselves somewhat. The effect is real but smaller than internet memes suggest.
POOL.m: Feeling confident is not evidence of skill. Seek outside feedback, especially in areas where you are new.

POOL.t: You hunt for proof you’re right
POOL.h: People tend to search for, notice and remember information that supports what they already believe.
POOL.b: This confirmation bias is one of the most consistently demonstrated findings in psychology. It shapes everything from medical diagnoses to online arguments.
POOL.m: Before deciding, ask yourself: what evidence would change my mind, and have I actually looked for it?

POOL.t: Easy to recall feels more likely
POOL.h: We judge how common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
POOL.b: In a classic 1973 study, people guessed more English words start with K than have K as the third letter. The reverse is true, but first letters are simply easier to search.
POOL.m: Vivid news stories distort your sense of risk. Check real statistics before worrying about rare dangers.

POOL.t: Everything takes longer than you think
POOL.h: In a 1994 study, students predicted they would finish their thesis in about 34 days on average.
POOL.b: It actually took about 56. Even their “worst case” estimates were too optimistic, a pattern called the planning fallacy.
POOL.m: Base estimates on how long similar past projects really took, not on how this one feels.

POOL.h: People value things more when they have built them themselves.
POOL.b: In studies published in 2012, participants were willing to pay more for storage boxes they had assembled than for identical pre-built ones, and valued their own clumsy origami almost as much as expert work.
POOL.m: Effort creates attachment. Be careful when judging your own projects, and involve others to build their buy-in.

POOL.h: In a famous 1990 experiment, students given a university coffee mug asked roughly twice as much to sell it as other students would pay to buy it.
POOL.b: Simply owning an object makes it feel more valuable. Economists call this the endowment effect.
POOL.m: When selling or decluttering, ask what you would pay for the item today if you didn’t already own it.

POOL.h: People keep investing in failing plans because of what they have already spent.
POOL.b: We finish bad films, hold losing shares and stay in doomed projects to avoid “wasting” past effort. But money and time already spent are gone whatever you decide next.
POOL.m: Judge every choice by its future costs and benefits only. The past is spent either way.

POOL.h: In a 1981 study, people facing a disease expected to kill 600 mostly chose a plan that “saves 200 people”.
POOL.b: When the identical plan was described as “400 people will die”, most rejected it. Only the wording changed, a result known as the framing effect.
POOL.m: Reframe important decisions both ways, as gains and as losses, and see whether your choice survives.

POOL.t: The decoy that steers your choice
POOL.h: Adding a clearly worse option can shift people toward a nearby better one.
POOL.b: Researchers documented this “decoy effect” in 1982. It is why a medium drink priced just below the large one makes the large look like a bargain.
POOL.m: When a menu or price list feels designed, ask which option exists only to make another look good.

POOL.h: A famous 2000 study found shoppers were far more likely to buy jam from a display of 6 flavours than one of 24.
POOL.b: It launched the idea that too much choice paralyses us. But a 2010 review of many studies found the average effect was close to zero.
POOL.m: Choice overload happens in some situations, not all. Be wary of neat stories built on one study.

POOL.t: Willpower may not be a fuel tank
POOL.h: The popular theory of “ego depletion” said self-control runs out like fuel after use.
POOL.b: Many studies seemed to support it. But a 2016 replication across 23 labs and over 2,000 people found almost no effect.
POOL.m: Don’t count on a “willpower tank” theory. Designing your environment beats relying on self-control.

POOL.h: A 2010 study claimed standing in expansive “power poses” for two minutes changed hormone levels and risk-taking.
POOL.b: Larger follow-up studies failed to reproduce the hormone effects, and one of the original authors publicly said she no longer believed them. Some people may still feel slightly more confident.
POOL.m: A famous finding is not proof. Look for findings that have been independently replicated.

POOL.h: Stanford studies from the 1960s and 70s found children who waited longer for a second treat did better years later.
POOL.b: A larger, more diverse 2018 replication found the link was much weaker, and shrank further once family background was taken into account.
POOL.m: Self-control matters, but circumstances shape behaviour more than a single childhood test can reveal.

POOL.h: The 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment was stopped after six days, supposedly because ordinary students became cruel guards.
POOL.b: Later-released recordings and interviews show researchers encouraged the guards to be tough. Many psychologists now see it as a demonstration of expectations, not proof of human nature.
POOL.m: Famous studies can be wrong. Situations matter, but so do the instructions and pressure people receive.

POOL.t: Most people obeyed to the end
POOL.h: In Stanley Milgram’s 1960s obedience studies, about 65% of participants in the main version kept giving what they believed were 450-volt shocks when instructed.
POOL.b: The shocks were fake and the “victim” was an actor. A partial 2009 replication found similar willingness, up to the point it tested.
POOL.m: Ordinary people can do harmful things under authority. Knowing this makes it easier to be the one who refuses.

POOL.t: Wrong answers, because everyone else said so
POOL.h: In Solomon Asch’s 1950s experiments, people judged which line matched another in length.
POOL.b: When actors in the group gave obviously wrong answers, about 75% of participants went along at least once. Alone, people almost never made mistakes.
POOL.m: Just one other dissenting voice sharply reduced conformity in Asch’s studies. Be that voice when it counts.

POOL.h: After an event, people overestimate how predictable it was.
POOL.b: Studies since the 1970s show that once people learn an outcome, they misremember their earlier predictions as more accurate. This hindsight bias makes the past look obvious and past decisions look foolish.
POOL.m: Write predictions down before outcomes are known. Judge decisions by the information available at the time.

POOL.h: In 1920, psychologist Edward Thorndike noticed that army officers who rated a soldier highly on one quality tended to rate him highly on all of them.
POOL.b: This halo effect means attractive or confident people are often assumed to be smarter and kinder too.
POOL.m: In hiring and judging, score qualities separately and independently, ideally before meeting the person.

POOL.h: When people memorise a list, they recall the first and last items best and forget the middle.
POOL.b: Early items get more rehearsal, while the latest ones are still fresh in mind. Psychologists call this the serial position effect.
POOL.m: Put your most important points at the start and end of a talk, meeting or email.

POOL.h: In the 1880s, Hermann Ebbinghaus memorised nonsense syllables and tested himself over weeks.
POOL.b: He found most forgetting happens quickly, within the first hours and days, and then levels off. A 2015 replication produced a very similar curve.
POOL.m: If you want to keep something, review it soon after learning it, before the steep drop.

POOL.t: One word can change a memory
POOL.h: In a 1974 study, people watched a car crash film.
POOL.b: Those asked how fast the cars “smashed” into each other gave higher speed estimates than those asked about cars that “hit”. A week later, the “smashed” group was more likely to remember broken glass that never existed.
POOL.m: Memory is reconstructed, not replayed. Leading questions can quietly rewrite what witnesses believe they saw.

POOL.h: Researchers asked students to record their memories of the 11 September 2001 attacks the next day, and of an ordinary event.
POOL.b: Over the following months, both memories changed by similar amounts. But confidence in the dramatic memory stayed high.
POOL.m: Feeling certain about a memory is not proof it is accurate. Keep records of what really matters.

POOL.h: The popular “21 days to form a habit” idea comes from a 1960 self-help book, not research.
POOL.b: A 2010 University College London study found new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, ranging from 18 to 254 days.
POOL.m: Don’t quit at week three. Expect a couple of months, and know that missing one day barely matters.

POOL.h: Plans phrased as “If situation X happens, then I will do Y” make people far more likely to follow through.
POOL.b: A 2006 review of 94 studies found these implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals. They link a cue to an action in advance.
POOL.m: Turn vague goals into specific triggers, like “When I pour my morning coffee, I’ll write for ten minutes.”

POOL.h: In a 1973 study, preschoolers who enjoyed drawing were promised a certificate for doing it.
POOL.b: Later, in free time, they drew less than children who had not expected a reward. Being paid for something you already love can make it feel like work.
POOL.m: Protect activities you do for joy. Praise effort and interest rather than attaching rewards to everything.

POOL.h: Psychologist John Gottman identified four conflict habits linked to relationship breakdown: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling.
POOL.b: In his research, contempt, such as eye-rolling or mockery, was an especially strong warning sign. Each has a healthier alternative, like complaining about a behaviour rather than attacking character.
POOL.m: How you argue matters more than whether you argue. Watch for contempt above all.

POOL.t: How you react to good news matters
POOL.h: A 2004 study found that how partners respond to each other’s good news predicts relationship quality.
POOL.b: Enthusiastic, curious responses were linked to more satisfying relationships. Dismissive or distracted replies, even when not hostile, were linked to worse ones.
POOL.m: When someone shares a win, ask questions and show real excitement. It builds connection.

POOL.h: The Harvard Study of Adult Development began following young men in 1938 and has continued for over 80 years, later adding their families.
POOL.b: Its directors report that warm, close relationships were among the strongest predictors of health and happiness in later life. Wealth and fame were far less important.
POOL.m: Invest in friendships and family. Relationships appear to be a long-term health habit, not a luxury.

POOL.t: Dunbar’s number is shakier than it sounds
POOL.h: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar proposed in the 1990s that humans can maintain about 150 stable relationships, based on primate brain size.
POOL.b: It became famous in business and pop science. A 2021 reanalysis using updated data found the estimate could plausibly range from a handful to several hundred.
POOL.m: Social limits exist, but there is no magic number. Focus on the quality of your connections.

POOL.h: A 2003 study compared organ donor consent across Europe.
POOL.b: In Austria, where people are donors unless they opt out, consent was nearly universal. In neighbouring Germany, where people must opt in, it was about 12%. Most people simply keep whatever option is preselected.
POOL.m: Check the defaults in your super, subscriptions and settings. Doing nothing is still a choice.

POOL.h: In a 1990 Stanford study, people tapped out well-known songs like “Happy Birthday” on a table and predicted listeners would name about half of them.
POOL.b: Listeners guessed just 3 out of 120. Once you know something, it is hard to imagine not knowing it.
POOL.m: When explaining, assume less background than feels necessary and test your explanation on a newcomer.

POOL.h: Since a 1977 study, research has shown that statements heard repeatedly are rated as more believable.
POOL.b: A 2015 study found this “illusory truth effect” works even when people already know the correct answer. Familiarity is easily mistaken for accuracy.
POOL.m: A claim you’ve seen many times isn’t more likely to be true. Check the source, not the frequency.

POOL.t: Black came up 26 times in a row
POOL.h: In 1913, at the Monte Carlo Casino, a roulette ball reportedly landed on black 26 times in a row.
POOL.b: Gamblers bet heavily on red, sure it was “due”. But each spin is independent, and the belief otherwise is called the gambler’s fallacy.
POOL.m: Past random outcomes do not change future odds. Streaks in chance events are not signals.

POOL.t: A small blunder can make you likeable
POOL.h: In a 1966 study, people listened to a recording of a highly skilled quiz contestant.
POOL.b: When he clumsily spilled coffee at the end, listeners rated him more likeable. The same blunder made an average contestant seem less likeable. Psychologists call this the pratfall effect.
POOL.m: If you are clearly competent, admitting a small mistake can make you more relatable, not less respected.

POOL.h: Daniel Kahneman described flight instructors who believed praise made pilots worse and shouting made them better.
POOL.b: In reality, an unusually good landing is usually followed by a more average one, and a bad one by a better one. This regression to the mean happens regardless of feedback.
POOL.m: Extreme results tend to be followed by ordinary ones. Don’t credit or blame your reaction for the change.

POOL.h: In a 1999 study, people counted basketball passes in a short video.
POOL.b: About half failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit walking through the scene. When focused on one task, we can miss something obvious right in front of us.
POOL.m: Attention is narrow. When driving or doing risky tasks, a “quick glance” at your phone matters.

POOL.t: Your brain listens for your name
POOL.h: In a noisy room you can tune into one conversation, yet still catch your name spoken elsewhere.
POOL.b: Researchers named this the cocktail party effect in the 1950s. In a 1959 study, about a third of people noticed their own name in a message they were told to ignore.
POOL.m: Using someone’s name is a genuine way to grab attention. Use it sparingly and sincerely.

POOL.t: Small yeses lead to bigger ones
POOL.h: In a 1966 study, homeowners were asked to put a large, ugly “Drive Carefully” sign on their front lawn.
POOL.b: Only about 17% agreed. But among those who had earlier agreed to a tiny request, about 76% said yes. This is the foot-in-the-door technique.
POOL.m: Start big goals, and big requests, with a small first step. Also notice when others use this on you.

POOL.h: In the 1880s, French engineer Maximilien Ringelmann found people pulled less hard on a rope as more joined in.
POOL.b: Later studies confirmed this “social loafing” in shouting, clapping and teamwork. When individual effort is hidden, people tend to coast.
POOL.m: Give each team member clear, visible responsibilities so that everyone’s contribution counts.

POOL.h: Putting feelings into words can dial them down.
POOL.b: A 2007 brain imaging study found that labelling emotional images with words, such as “angry”, reduced activity in the amygdala, a region involved in emotional reactions. This is called affect labelling.
POOL.m: When upset, try naming the exact feeling. It can create a little distance and help you think clearly.

POOL.h: A runaway trolley will kill five people unless you pull a lever to divert it, killing one.
POOL.b: Philosopher Philippa Foot raised the scenario in 1967, and Judith Jarvis Thomson later named it. Most people say they would pull the lever, but far fewer would push a person off a bridge to stop it.
POOL.m: Our moral intuitions care about how harm happens, not just how many people are affected.

POOL.h: If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship?
POOL.b: The puzzle appears in Plutarch’s writing, nearly 2,000 years ago. Thomas Hobbes later added a twist: what if someone rebuilt a ship from all the old planks?
POOL.m: The same question applies to you. Your body and beliefs change constantly. What makes you still you?

POOL.t: Would you plug into the machine?
POOL.h: In 1974, philosopher Robert Nozick imagined a machine that could give you any experiences you wanted, perfectly simulated, for life.
POOL.b: Most people say they would not plug in. Nozick argued this shows we value more than pleasant feelings: we want to actually do things and be connected to reality.
POOL.m: If pleasure alone isn’t the goal, ask what real achievements and relationships you want your life to contain.

POOL.h: John Rawls proposed a test for fairness in 1971.
POOL.b: Design society’s rules without knowing who you will be in it: rich or poor, healthy or sick, talented or not. From behind this “veil of ignorance”, he argued, people would choose to protect the worst off.
POOL.m: A handy fairness check: would you still accept this rule if you didn’t know which side of it you’d land on?

POOL.h: In Plato’s Republic, Glaucon tells of the Ring of Gyges, which makes its wearer invisible.
POOL.b: He asks whether anyone would stay just if they could never be caught. Plato used the story to ask whether we are good only because we fear the consequences.
POOL.m: Character is what you do when no one is watching. It’s a useful question to ask yourself honestly.

POOL.t: Achilles can never catch the tortoise
POOL.h: The Greek philosopher Zeno of Elea argued that swift Achilles can never overtake a tortoise with a head start.
POOL.b: Each time he reaches where it was, it has moved a little further. Modern mathematics resolves it: infinitely many ever-smaller steps can add up to a finite distance and time.
POOL.m: Paradoxes are useful. Puzzles that seem absurd have pushed thinkers towards deep ideas about infinity.

POOL.h: A donkey stands exactly between two identical piles of hay and starves because it cannot choose.
POOL.b: The puzzle is named after the 14th-century philosopher Jean Buridan, but it does not appear in his surviving writings. A similar idea appears much earlier in Aristotle.
POOL.m: Waiting for the perfect choice can cost more than picking a good option and moving on.

POOL.t: “I think, therefore I am” was first French
POOL.h: René Descartes first wrote his famous line in French, as “je pense, donc je suis”, in his 1637 Discourse on the Method.
POOL.b: The Latin “cogito, ergo sum” appeared in his later Principles of Philosophy. He was searching for one thing he could not possibly doubt.
POOL.m: Doubting everything can be a method. Descartes used it to find a firm foundation for knowledge.

POOL.t: You can’t get an “ought” from an “is”
POOL.h: Scottish philosopher David Hume noticed that writers often slide from describing how things are to claiming how they ought to be.
POOL.b: In his Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), he argued facts alone cannot prove moral conclusions. This became known as the is–ought problem.
POOL.m: “That’s how it’s always been done” describes a fact. It doesn’t prove it’s the right way.

POOL.t: Australia’s black swans broke a proverb
POOL.h: For centuries in Europe, a “black swan” was a figure of speech for something impossible.
POOL.b: Then in 1697, Dutch explorer Willem de Vlamingh’s crew saw black swans in Western Australia. The story became a classic illustration of the problem of induction: no number of observations can prove a general rule.
POOL.m: Past experience is not proof about the future. Stay open to the case you haven’t seen yet.

POOL.t: A three-page paper that shook philosophy
POOL.h: For centuries, many philosophers defined knowledge as a justified, true belief.
POOL.b: In 1963, Edmund Gettier published a paper of about three pages showing cases where someone has a justified true belief by pure luck. Philosophers still debate how to fix the definition.
POOL.m: Being right for the wrong reasons is not the same as knowing. Check how you reached a conclusion.

POOL.h: Australian philosopher Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who knows every physical fact about colour but has lived only in a black-and-white room.
POOL.b: When she first sees red, does she learn something new? Jackson argued yes, though he later changed his mind.
POOL.m: Knowing about something is not the same as experiencing it. Some knowledge only comes firsthand.

POOL.h: Stoic philosophers such as Seneca recommended imagining setbacks in advance: losing money, health or status.
POOL.b: The practice is often called premeditatio malorum, the “premeditation of evils”. The aim was not gloom but preparation, so misfortune would not catch them off guard.
POOL.m: Briefly picturing what could go wrong makes you calmer, better prepared and more grateful for what you have.

POOL.t: Would you ruin your shoes to save a child?
POOL.h: In 1972, Melbourne-born philosopher Peter Singer asked: if you saw a child drowning in a shallow pond, would you wade in, even if it ruined your expensive shoes?
POOL.b: Almost everyone says yes. Singer argued that distance should not change the duty, so we should also help people dying of poverty far away.
POOL.m: A useful test of your values is whether they still hold when the person in need is out of sight.

POOL.h: Today “epicurean” suggests luxury, but Epicurus taught that the pleasant life was a simple one.
POOL.b: He valued friendship, modest food and freedom from fear and pain. His school, founded in Athens around 306 BCE, was called the Garden.
POOL.m: Happiness often comes from reducing wants, not endlessly adding pleasures.

POOL.h: The Cynic philosopher Diogenes lived in a large ceramic jar in Athens and rejected comfort and convention.
POOL.b: Ancient accounts say Alexander the Great offered to grant him any wish. Diogenes replied that Alexander could stand out of his sunlight.
POOL.m: Needing little makes you hard to buy or intimidate. Freedom can come from wanting less.

POOL.h: The most famous philosopher of ancient Athens left no writings of his own.
POOL.b: Everything we know about Socrates comes from others, mainly his student Plato, the historian Xenophon and the playwright Aristophanes. Scholars still debate which of Plato’s views are really Socrates’.
POOL.m: Ideas can outlive their authors through others. Much of Socrates survives only because of his students.

POOL.h: Aristotle argued that most virtues sit between two vices.
POOL.b: Courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, and generosity between stinginess and wastefulness. The right point is not a simple average but depends on the person and situation.
POOL.m: When a strength starts to cause problems, you may have pushed it to an extreme. Look for balance.

POOL.h: In his 1929 book The Thing, writer G.
POOL.b: K. Chesterton imagined a reformer who finds a fence across a road and wants it removed because he sees no use for it. Chesterton’s reply: go away and find out why it was put there first. Only then can you decide whether to take it down.
POOL.m: Before scrapping a rule or routine, find out what problem it was meant to solve.

POOL.h: In Daoist philosophy, wu wei means “non-action” or “effortless action”.
POOL.b: It does not mean laziness but acting in harmony with the natural flow of things, without forcing. The Daodejing praises water, which is soft and yielding yet overcomes the hard and strong.
POOL.m: Sometimes the best results come from easing off, not pushing harder.

POOL.h: An early Buddhist text compares pain to being struck by an arrow.
POOL.b: Most people then add a second arrow: worry, resentment and dwelling on the pain. The first arrow may be unavoidable, but the second is our own reaction, the text suggests.
POOL.m: You can’t always avoid setbacks, but you can avoid piling extra suffering on top of them.

POOL.h: “Never attribute to malice that which is adequately explained by stupidity.” The saying is credited to Robert J.
POOL.b: Hanlon, who submitted it to a 1980 joke book of Murphy’s Law variations. Similar ideas appear much earlier, including in Goethe’s 1774 novel The Sorrows of Young Werther.
POOL.m: When someone lets you down, assume a mistake or oversight before assuming bad intent. You will usually be right, and calmer.

POOL.t: Kant wouldn’t lie to a murderer
POOL.h: Immanuel Kant argued that lying is always wrong.
POOL.b: In a 1797 essay, he accepted the hardest case: you should not lie even to a murderer asking where your friend is hiding. Many readers find this conclusion shows the limits of strict rules.
POOL.m: Moral principles are useful, but testing them against extreme cases reveals where they may break.

POOL.h: Jeremy Bentham, founder of utilitarianism, asked that his body be preserved after his death in 1832.
POOL.b: His skeleton, dressed in his own clothes and topped with a wax head, is on public display at University College London. His real preserved head is stored separately.
POOL.m: Bentham wanted to be useful even after death. His philosophy measured everything by its consequences.

POOL.h: In Greek myth, Sisyphus is condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever, only to watch it roll down again.
POOL.b: In 1942, Albert Camus argued the struggle itself can give life meaning. He concluded: “One must imagine Sisyphus happy.”
POOL.m: Meaning may come from how we engage with repetitive tasks, not from finishing them.

POOL.h: Two suspects each do better by betraying the other, yet both end up worse off if both betray.
POOL.b: The dilemma was developed at the RAND Corporation in 1950. In Robert Axelrod’s later computer tournaments, a simple strategy called “tit for tat”, which starts by cooperating, performed best.
POOL.m: In repeated relationships, start by cooperating, respond fairly and be quick to forgive.

POOL.t: The Meditations were a private diary
POOL.h: Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor, never meant the Meditations for publication.
POOL.b: He wrote them in Greek as personal notes, probably during military campaigns. The title was added later, and the work is often described as addressed “to himself”.
POOL.m: Some of history’s most quoted advice was written as self-reminders. Journaling can help you think like a philosopher.

POOL.h: The Stoic teacher Epictetus was born into slavery around 50 CE, and his name means “acquired”.
POOL.b: He later gained his freedom and founded a school. He wrote nothing himself: his student Arrian recorded his teachings.
POOL.m: His focus on what we can control came from real experience of having very little control.

POOL.t: How many grains make a heap?
POOL.h: One grain of sand is not a heap, and adding a single grain never seems to turn a non-heap into a heap.
POOL.b: Yet a million grains clearly is one. This is the sorites paradox, from the Greek word for heap, first posed in ancient Greece.
POOL.m: Many real concepts, like “tall” or “old”, have blurry edges. Arguing over the exact line can miss the point.

POOL.h: A straw man argument attacks a weaker, distorted version of someone’s view instead of what they actually said.
POOL.b: It is easy to knock over, like a figure stuffed with straw. It feels like winning but avoids the real disagreement.
POOL.m: Before disagreeing, restate the other person’s view so well that they agree with your summary.

POOL.t: Attack the argument, not the person
POOL.h: An ad hominem fallacy, Latin for “to the person”, dismisses an argument by attacking the person who made it.
POOL.b: A cousin is “tu quoque” (“you too”): rejecting advice because the adviser doesn’t follow it. A smoker who warns against smoking can still be right.
POOL.m: The truth of a claim doesn’t depend on who says it. Judge the reasoning and evidence.

POOL.h: A false dilemma presents only two options when more exist: “You’re either with us or against us.” It pressures people into choosing an extreme.
POOL.b: Real situations usually allow middle grounds, combinations or entirely different paths.
POOL.m: When offered only two choices, ask: what are the other options nobody has mentioned?

POOL.t: After this, therefore because of this
POOL.h: The Latin phrase “post hoc ergo propter hoc” names the mistake of assuming that because one thing followed another, the first caused it.
POOL.b: You wore lucky socks and your team won. Sequence alone does not prove cause.
POOL.m: Before crediting a cause, ask what else changed and whether the result would have happened anyway.

POOL.h: Someone claims no Scotsman puts sugar on porridge.
POOL.b: Shown a Scotsman who does, they reply, “No true Scotsman puts sugar on porridge.” Philosopher Antony Flew named this move, which protects a claim by redefining terms to exclude counterexamples.
POOL.m: If a claim can never be proven wrong because the goalposts keep moving, it isn’t saying much.

POOL.h: The appeal to nature fallacy assumes that anything natural is good or safe, and anything artificial is bad.
POOL.b: But arsenic, snake venom and poison mushrooms are natural, while vaccines and eyeglasses are not. Whether something is natural says little about whether it helps or harms.
POOL.m: Judge products and choices by evidence of their effects, not by labels like “natural”.

POOL.t: You are taller in the morning
POOL.h: You are roughly a centimetre taller when you wake up than when you go to bed.
POOL.b: During the day, gravity squeezes fluid out of the soft discs between your vertebrae, and they plump up again while you lie down at night. Astronauts in orbit can grow several centimetres for the same reason.
POOL.m: Your height is not a fixed number, so measure it at the same time of day if you want to compare.

POOL.t: Babies have more bones than adults
POOL.h: A newborn has roughly 270 to 300 bones, while an adult has 206.
POOL.b: Many of a baby’s bones start as separate pieces that fuse as the child grows, including parts of the skull, spine and pelvis. The soft gaps in a baby’s skull, called fontanelles, close over the first couple of years.
POOL.m: Growing up is partly a process of bones joining together.

POOL.t: Your smallest bone is in your ear
POOL.h: The smallest bone in your body is the stapes, deep in your middle ear, and it is only about 3 millimetres long.
POOL.b: Shaped like a stirrup, it passes sound vibrations from the eardrum to the fluid-filled inner ear. Without it, hearing would be badly muffled.
POOL.m: Some of the body’s most important parts are also its tiniest.

POOL.t: Each eye has a hole in its vision
POOL.h: Every eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, because there are no light-sensing cells there.
POOL.b: You never notice it because your brain fills in the gap using the surrounding scene and the view from your other eye.
POOL.m: What you “see” is partly a guess your brain makes, not a perfect recording.

POOL.t: Your eyes see the world upside down
POOL.h: The lens of your eye projects an upside-down image onto the retina, just as a camera lens does.
POOL.b: Your brain flips and interprets the signal so the world looks the right way up. You never experience the raw, inverted image at all.
POOL.m: Perception is an interpretation, and the brain does a huge amount of work you never notice.

POOL.h: A familiar smell can bring back a memory from decades ago in an instant.
POOL.b: Smell signals travel very directly to brain areas involved in emotion and memory, such as the amygdala and hippocampus, rather than taking the longer route most other senses use. That is why a scent can feel so vivid and emotional.
POOL.m: Scents are powerful memory cues, so linking a smell to a moment can help you remember it.

POOL.t: Most of flavour is really smell
POOL.h: Much of what we call taste is actually smell.
POOL.b: Your tongue detects only a few basic tastes, while aromas rising from food in your mouth to the back of your nose provide most of the rich detail. This is why food tastes bland when you have a blocked nose.
POOL.m: To enjoy food fully, slow down and breathe, because your nose is doing much of the tasting.

POOL.h: The famous map showing sweet at the tip and bitter at the back is a myth.
POOL.b: It grew from a misreading of a 1901 German study, and in fact every region of the tongue with taste buds can detect all the basic tastes. Sensitivity varies only slightly from place to place.
POOL.m: Even diagrams printed in textbooks for decades can be wrong, so check the original source.

POOL.h: In 1908, Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda identified the savoury taste he called umami.
POOL.b: He traced it to glutamate in kombu seaweed broth. Scientists later found dedicated taste receptors for it, and umami is now accepted alongside sweet, sour, salty and bitter.
POOL.m: The savoury depth of tomatoes, parmesan and mushrooms is a real, distinct taste.

POOL.t: Your body is paralysed when you dream
POOL.h: During REM sleep, when most vivid dreaming happens, your brain switches off most of your voluntary muscles.
POOL.b: This temporary paralysis stops you from acting out your dreams. Your eyes and breathing muscles keep working, which is how REM sleep got its name: rapid eye movement.
POOL.m: Sleep is not the brain switching off but a carefully controlled state.

POOL.h: Sleep is not one continuous state but a series of cycles, each lasting roughly 90 minutes.
POOL.b: Each cycle moves through lighter sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep, and most adults go through about four to six cycles a night. Deep sleep dominates early in the night, while REM grows longer towards morning.
POOL.m: Waking at the end of a cycle, rather than in deep sleep, can help you feel less groggy.

POOL.t: Your brain cleans itself while you sleep
POOL.h: Sleep appears to help your brain wash away waste.
POOL.b: In a 2013 study in mice, the spaces between brain cells widened during sleep, letting fluid flush out waste products much faster than during waking hours. Researchers are still working out exactly how this applies to humans.
POOL.m: Sleep is maintenance time, not wasted time.

POOL.h: An Australian and New Zealand study found that staying awake for about 17 to 19 hours impaired performance roughly as much as a blood alcohol level of 0.05%.
POOL.b: Longer periods without sleep produced impairment similar to higher alcohol levels. Tired people also have brief “microsleeps” they may not notice.
POOL.m: A long day followed by a long drive is a genuine safety risk, so rest first.

POOL.t: Your body clock is not quite 24 hours
POOL.h: Your internal body clock runs on a cycle slightly longer than 24 hours for most people.
POOL.b: Daylight, especially morning light, resets it each day and keeps it in step with the sun. This is why a cycle of light and dark matters so much for good sleep.
POOL.m: Getting outside in the morning helps set your body clock for the day ahead.

POOL.h: The brain itself has no pain receptors, so it cannot feel being touched or cut.
POOL.b: This is why surgeons can operate on some patients while they are awake and talking. Headaches come from surrounding structures, such as blood vessels, nerves and the membranes around the brain.
POOL.m: The organ that registers all your pain feels none of its own.

POOL.h: The human brain contains roughly 86 billion neurons, according to a 2009 study that counted them by dissolving brain tissue into countable nuclei.
POOL.b: The older figure of 100 billion was a rough estimate that had never been properly counted. Each neuron can connect to thousands of others.
POOL.m: Even a widely repeated number deserves checking, because someone eventually has to count.

POOL.t: The small brain holding most neurons
POOL.h: Your cerebellum, the small wrinkled structure at the back of your brain, holds about 80% of your neurons.
POOL.b: It makes up only around a tenth of the brain’s mass. It helps coordinate movement, balance and timing, and plays roles in learning and thinking too.
POOL.m: Size is a poor guide to importance, in brains as elsewhere.

POOL.t: London cabbies grow their memory centre
POOL.h: A famous 2000 study found that London taxi drivers had a larger rear hippocampus, a region vital for spatial memory, than non-drivers.
POOL.b: The longer they had driven, the bigger it tended to be. Drivers must memorise thousands of streets to pass a test called “the Knowledge”.
POOL.m: Your brain physically adapts to what you practise, even in adulthood.

POOL.t: Nerve signals can outpace a race car
POOL.h: The fastest nerve signals in your body travel at about 120 metres per second, roughly 430 km/h.
POOL.b: They race along nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty insulating layer called myelin. Signals in thin, uninsulated fibres can crawl along at around a metre per second.
POOL.m: Fast signals and spinal reflexes let you pull your hand off a hot stove before the pain fully registers.

POOL.t: Two metres of DNA in every cell
POOL.h: If you stretched out the DNA from a single one of your cells, it would be about 2 metres long.
POOL.b: It is packed into a nucleus far narrower than a human hair by winding around proteins like thread on spools. You have trillions of cells, each carrying this tightly folded code.
POOL.m: Nature solved an extreme storage problem long before engineers did.

POOL.h: Humans have only about 20,000 protein-coding genes, far fewer than the 100,000 some scientists once predicted.
POOL.b: That is roughly the same number as a mouse. Genes that code for proteins make up only around 1 to 2% of our DNA, while some of the rest helps control when genes switch on.
POOL.m: Complexity comes less from the number of genes than from how they are used.

POOL.h: Even identical twins, who share almost exactly the same DNA, have different fingerprints.
POOL.b: Fingerprint ridges form in the womb and are shaped by tiny differences in position, pressure and growth. Even the ten prints on your own fingers all differ from each other.
POOL.m: Genes set the blueprint, but development adds details that make everyone unique.

POOL.h: Your body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells.
POOL.b: A 2016 study estimated about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in a typical adult. The long-quoted claim that bacteria outnumber us ten to one was based on an old rough estimate.
POOL.m: You are an ecosystem, and most of those microbes live peacefully in your gut.

POOL.t: Red blood cells live about four months
POOL.h: A red blood cell lives for about 120 days before it is recycled.
POOL.b: To keep up, your bone marrow makes roughly two million new red blood cells every second. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, which leaves more room for oxygen-carrying haemoglobin.
POOL.m: Your body is constantly rebuilding itself, even while you sit still.

POOL.t: Your heart beats 100,000 times a day
POOL.h: At around 70 beats a minute, your heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day.
POOL.b: Over a long life, that adds up to more than 2.5 billion beats. It rests only in the brief pause between each beat.
POOL.m: A small effort, repeated for decades, becomes something enormous, as your heart shows.

POOL.t: Your heart has its own pacemaker
POOL.h: Your heartbeat starts inside the heart itself, in a small cluster of cells called the sinoatrial node.
POOL.b: It fires electrical signals on its own, while nerves and hormones only speed it up or slow it down. This is why a transplanted heart can beat even though its nerves were cut.
POOL.m: The heart does not wait for orders from the brain to keep you alive.

POOL.t: Your stomach survives its own acid
POOL.h: Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid strong enough to have a pH of around 1.5 to 3.5.
POOL.b: It avoids digesting itself thanks to a thick layer of protective mucus. The cells lining it are also replaced every few days.
POOL.m: Constant renewal is one of the body’s best defences.

POOL.h: The liver can regrow to near its full size even after up to about two-thirds of it is removed.
POOL.b: This remarkable ability makes living-donor transplants possible, where a healthy person gives part of their liver. Both the donor’s and the recipient’s portions grow back within months.
POOL.m: Few organs can repair themselves so completely, making the liver a standout exception.

POOL.t: Muscles can only pull, never push
POOL.h: Every muscle in your body works by contracting, which means it can only pull.
POOL.b: To move a joint back and forth, muscles work in opposing pairs. Your biceps bends your elbow and your triceps straightens it again.
POOL.m: Every push you make is really a clever arrangement of pulls.

POOL.h: You cannot tickle yourself because your brain predicts the sensation.
POOL.b: When you move, your cerebellum forecasts what you will feel and dampens the response. Experiments in the late 1990s found that adding a delay between a person’s movement and a robotic touch made it feel more ticklish.
POOL.m: The brain constantly filters out predictable signals so surprises stand out.

POOL.t: Your pupils widen when you think hard
POOL.h: Your pupils widen slightly when you concentrate hard, not just when the light is dim.
POOL.b: Psychologists in the 1960s found pupil size rose as mental tasks got harder, then shrank once the answer was found. It is one of the few visible signs of mental effort.
POOL.m: Thinking hard is real physical work, and your eyes quietly show it.

POOL.h: The famous 37 °C figure was popularised by German physician Carl Wunderlich in the 1800s.
POOL.b: Modern studies suggest the average is a little lower, around 36.6 °C. Temperature also varies between people and rises and falls through the day.
POOL.m: “Normal” in the body is usually a range, not a single number.

POOL.t: Goosebumps are a leftover from fur
POOL.h: Goosebumps are a reflex inherited from our hairier ancestors.
POOL.b: Tiny muscles at the base of each hair contract when you are cold or feel a strong emotion, pulling the hairs upright. In furry animals this traps a warmer layer of air or makes them look bigger, like a cat’s puffed-up tail.
POOL.m: Some of your body’s reactions are left over from a time when they were far more useful.

POOL.h: Your eyes jump several times a second in quick movements called saccades.
POOL.b: During each jump, your brain suppresses the blurry image so you never notice the motion. Try watching your own eyes move in a mirror and you will not see them shift.
POOL.m: Your smooth view of the world is carefully edited by your brain.

POOL.h: The cornea, the clear front window of your eye, has no blood vessels.
POOL.b: Instead, it takes in much of its oxygen directly from the air. Having no blood vessels keeps it perfectly transparent so light can pass through clearly.
POOL.m: Some tissues trade a blood supply for clarity.

POOL.h: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in the human body.
POOL.b: It is made mostly of mineral crystals and contains no living cells, so once it is lost it cannot regrow. Bone, by contrast, is living tissue that repairs itself.
POOL.m: The hardest part of you is also one of the few that cannot heal.

POOL.t: About 1 in 12 men is colour blind
POOL.h: Around 1 in 12 men and about 1 in 200 women of Northern European descent have red-green colour blindness.
POOL.b: The genes for red and green light receptors sit on the X chromosome. Men have only one X, so a single faulty copy is enough to affect them.
POOL.m: A colour-coded chart may be unreadable for a noticeable share of your audience.

POOL.t: Wrinkly fingers are controlled by nerves
POOL.h: Fingers wrinkle in water because nerves signal blood vessels to narrow, not simply because skin soaks up water.
POOL.b: Fingers with damaged nerves often do not wrinkle at all. One idea is that the wrinkles improve grip on wet objects, though studies disagree.
POOL.m: Even something that seems passive can be an active response from your nervous system.

POOL.h: Charles Darwin wrote that blushing is “the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions.” In 1872 he noted that a blush cannot be produced at will, and linked it to thinking about what others think of us.
POOL.b: Scientists still debate why it evolved.
POOL.m: Blushing may signal to others that you care about their opinion.

POOL.h: In 1901, Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner discovered that human blood comes in different groups.
POOL.b: Mixing incompatible blood caused clumping, which explained why many early transfusions failed. His work made transfusions far safer and earned him a Nobel Prize in 1930.
POOL.m: One careful observation has since helped save many millions of lives.

POOL.h: Time can matter more than the amount you save.
POOL.b: At a hypothetical 7% annual return, compounding monthly, someone investing $200 a month from 25 to 35, then stopping, would have about $281,000 at 65. Someone investing the same monthly amount from 35 to 65 would contribute three times as much but end with about $244,000.
POOL.m: Compound growth rewards time. The earliest dollars do the heaviest lifting.

POOL.t: Small fees take a big bite
POOL.h: A 1% yearly fee can quietly eat about a quarter of your final balance over 30 years.
POOL.b: $10,000 growing at 7% a year becomes about $76,000, but at 6% it becomes about $57,000. The fee compounds against you, just as returns compound for you.
POOL.m: When comparing investments or super funds, fees deserve close attention.

POOL.h: At 3% inflation, money loses about half its buying power in roughly 23 years.
POOL.b: The notes in your wallet stay the same, but what they can buy shrinks each year. Economists call confusing face value with real value the “money illusion”.
POOL.m: Cash kept idle for decades quietly loses value, even if the number never changes.

POOL.h: By November 1923, one US dollar was worth about 4.2 trillion German marks.
POOL.b: During Weimar Germany’s hyperinflation, prices could double in days, and workers were paid more than once a day so they could spend before prices rose again. Some people burned banknotes for heat because they were cheaper than firewood.
POOL.m: Trust in money can collapse fast when governments print it to cover debts.

POOL.h: Hungary in 1946 suffered the worst hyperinflation ever recorded.
POOL.b: At its peak, prices doubled roughly every 15 hours. The government printed a 100 quintillion pengő note, the highest face value of any banknote ever issued, before replacing the currency with the forint.
POOL.m: Hyperinflation can wipe out a lifetime of savings in weeks.

POOL.t: The first coins came from Lydia
POOL.h: Some of the earliest known coins were made in the kingdom of Lydia, in modern Turkey, around the 7th century BCE.
POOL.b: They were stamped lumps of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver. The stamp guaranteed their weight, so people no longer had to weigh metal for every trade.
POOL.m: Money works best when people trust it without checking every time.

POOL.h: On the Pacific island of Yap, giant stone discs called rai served as money, some taller than a person.
POOL.b: Large stones often stayed in place while ownership passed from one family to another by shared agreement. One stone, lost at sea during transport, was reportedly still counted as wealth.
POOL.m: Money is really a shared record of who owns what, much like a modern bank balance.

POOL.h: Records of debts and interest were kept in ancient Mesopotamia long before coins were invented.
POOL.b: Babylon’s Code of Hammurabi, from around 1750 BCE, even set maximum interest rates on loans of grain and silver. Clay tablets recorded who owed what to whom.
POOL.m: Credit and trust came first, and coins were a later convenience.

POOL.h: The famous Dutch tulip bubble of 1637 is often told as a tale of national ruin.
POOL.b: Historians such as Anne Goldgar have found little evidence of widespread bankruptcies, and trading involved a fairly small group of merchants. Many popular details came from moralising pamphlets and a colourful 1841 book.
POOL.m: Famous stories about financial madness can be exaggerated too, so check the sources.

POOL.h: In 1720, shares in Britain’s South Sea Company rose from about £128 to around £1,000 within months, then collapsed.
POOL.b: Many investors were ruined, and Isaac Newton reportedly lost a large sum. A parliamentary inquiry later exposed bribery of officials.
POOL.m: Even brilliant people can be swept up when everyone around them is buying.

POOL.h: After the Wall Street Crash of 1929, the Dow Jones index fell by about 89% from its peak by mid-1932.
POOL.b: It did not return to its 1929 high until November 1954, about 25 years later. The crash helped trigger the Great Depression.
POOL.m: Markets can recover, but sometimes the wait is far longer than anyone expects.

POOL.h: When Australia planned its switch to decimal currency, the government proposed calling the new unit the “royal”.
POOL.b: The name was so unpopular that it was dropped in favour of the dollar. Decimal currency arrived on 14 February 1966, helped by a cartoon mascot called Dollar Bill.
POOL.m: Public opinion can reshape even the name of a country’s money.

POOL.h: In 1988, Australia issued the world’s first polymer banknote, a $10 note marking the Bicentenary.
POOL.b: It was developed by the Reserve Bank of Australia with the CSIRO to beat counterfeiters. Many countries, including Canada, the UK and New Zealand, now use polymer notes.
POOL.m: An Australian innovation now sits in wallets around the world.

POOL.t: The day the dollar left gold
POOL.h: On 15 August 1971, US President Richard Nixon ended the right of foreign governments to swap US dollars for gold.
POOL.b: This broke the Bretton Woods system set up in 1944. Since then, major currencies have been backed by trust in governments and central banks, not by metal.
POOL.m: Modern money is valued by confidence, not by gold in a vault.

POOL.t: Most money is created by banks
POOL.h: Most money today is not notes and coins but bank deposits, created when banks make loans.
POOL.b: The Bank of England explained this plainly in 2014: when a bank lends, it creates a new deposit in the borrower’s account. Physical cash is only a small share of the money supply.
POOL.m: Money is mostly numbers on ledgers, and lending is what makes most of them.

POOL.h: Gresham’s law says that when two forms of money have the same face value, people hoard the more valuable one and spend the other.
POOL.b: When silver coins were debased, people kept the purer old coins and spent the new ones. It is named after Thomas Gresham, a 16th-century English financier.
POOL.m: People respond to hidden value, even when official prices say two things are equal.

POOL.t: Every choice has a hidden price
POOL.h: The true cost of anything includes what you give up to get it.
POOL.b: Economists call this opportunity cost. An evening spent scrolling may cost nothing in dollars, but it costs the next best thing you could have done with that time.
POOL.m: Before deciding, ask “compared to what?”, because the best choice depends on the alternatives.

POOL.t: A dollar isn’t always a dollar
POOL.h: We tend to treat money differently depending on where it came from or what we label it for.
POOL.b: Economist Richard Thaler called this “mental accounting”. A tax refund or a win may feel like “free money” and get spent more easily than wages, though every dollar is equally valuable.
POOL.m: Treating all money as the same pool leads to better decisions.

POOL.h: People tend to overvalue immediate rewards compared with later ones, even when waiting pays much more.
POOL.b: Economists call this present bias. It helps explain why saving, exercising and other long-term plans are so easy to postpone.
POOL.m: Automating good choices, like savings transfers, removes the daily battle with present bias.

POOL.t: The dressing gown that cost a fortune
POOL.h: The French philosopher Denis Diderot received a splendid new dressing gown and soon felt his old belongings looked shabby beside it.
POOL.b: He replaced one item after another, and later wrote an essay regretting it. The term “Diderot effect” describes how one purchase can trigger a spiral of others.
POOL.m: Before buying an upgrade, consider what else it might make you want.

POOL.h: In a famous 2001 study, people bidding for sports tickets offered far more when told they would pay by credit card rather than cash.
POOL.b: Handing over cash feels like a loss, while tapping a card barely registers. Researchers call this the “pain of paying”.
POOL.m: If you are trying to spend less, make payments feel more real.

POOL.h: A price of $9.99 feels noticeably cheaper than $10, even though the difference is one cent.
POOL.b: Our brains read numbers from left to right and give the first digit extra weight. Researchers call this the left-digit effect.
POOL.m: Round prices up in your head to see what you are really paying.

POOL.h: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith described a pin factory where ten workers, each doing one step, could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day.
POOL.b: A single worker doing everything alone, he said, might struggle to make even twenty. This division of labour is a key source of productivity.
POOL.m: Specialising and cooperating can multiply what people achieve.

POOL.t: When a measure becomes a target
