POOL.h: Economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that a statistic used as a target tends to lose its value as a measure.
POOL.b: Anthropologist Marilyn Strathern later summed it up: “When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” People learn to hit the number instead of the goal.
POOL.m: Watch what a target rewards, not just what it was meant to measure.

POOL.h: In 1902, French authorities in Hanoi paid a bounty for each rat tail handed in.
POOL.b: People began cutting off tails and releasing the rats to breed, and some were suspected of farming rats. Historians use it as a classic example of a perverse incentive.
POOL.m: Incentives shape behaviour, sometimes in ways the designer never intended.

POOL.t: When a higher price boosts demand
POOL.h: Some luxury goods become more desirable as their price rises, because a high price signals status.
POOL.b: These are called Veblen goods, after economist Thorstein Veblen. He coined the term “conspicuous consumption” in his 1899 book The Theory of the Leisure Class.
POOL.m: Sometimes we buy the price tag, not the product, so ask who you are really buying it for.

POOL.h: In 1968, ecologist Garrett Hardin argued that shared resources, like pastures, are doomed to overuse.
POOL.b: Economist Elinor Ostrom later studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems where communities managed shared resources well for centuries. In 2009 she became the first woman to win the economics Nobel.
POOL.m: Local rules and trust can protect shared resources without either privatisation or government control.

POOL.t: Trade helps even the less efficient
POOL.h: David Ricardo showed in 1817 that two countries can both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything.
POOL.b: Each should focus on what it gives up least to produce, its comparative advantage. His example used English cloth and Portuguese wine.
POOL.m: Focus your time where your advantage is greatest, even if you could do everything yourself.

POOL.t: The first company to sell shares
POOL.h: The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, is often called the first company to offer shares to the public.
POOL.b: Investors could buy and sell its shares in Amsterdam, which helped create one of the world’s first stock exchanges. It became one of the most powerful trading companies in history.
POOL.m: The idea of owning a slice of a business changed how the world funds big ventures.

POOL.t: All the world’s gold in one cube
POOL.h: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube roughly 22 metres on each side.
POOL.b: That is more than 200,000 tonnes, packed small because gold is extremely dense. Almost all of it still exists, as jewellery, bars, coins and electronics.
POOL.m: Rarity is part of what has made gold a store of value for thousands of years.

POOL.h: The word dollar traces back to a silver coin minted in Joachimsthal, a valley in Bohemia, in the 1500s.
POOL.b: The coin was called a “Joachimsthaler”, shortened to “thaler”. The word spread to become the Dutch “daler” and the English “dollar”.
POOL.m: Even a modern currency name carries centuries of history.

POOL.h: Harry Markowitz showed in 1952 that combining different investments can lower risk without necessarily lowering expected returns.
POOL.b: When some assets fall, others may hold steady or rise. His portfolio theory earned him a share of the 1990 economics Nobel.
POOL.m: Spreading risk is not just folk wisdom: it has a mathematical basis.

POOL.h: In a 1975 study, Robert Cialdini’s team asked students to chaperone young offenders on a zoo trip.
POOL.b: Only about 17% agreed. But when first asked to volunteer two hours a week for two years, which everyone refused, about half then agreed to the zoo trip.
POOL.m: A refused big request makes a smaller one feel like a concession. Notice when a ‘compromise’ was the plan all along.

POOL.t: The power of a free drink
POOL.h: In a 1971 study by Dennis Regan, a stranger either bought participants a Coke or did not.
POOL.b: Later he asked them to buy raffle tickets. Those who had received the drink bought about twice as many, even when they did not particularly like him.
POOL.m: Small unasked-for gifts create a strong urge to repay. Free samples work for a reason.

POOL.h: In 1968 Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson told teachers that certain pupils were about to ‘bloom’ intellectually.
POOL.b: The pupils had been picked at random, yet some showed bigger gains, especially the youngest. Later research found teacher expectation effects are real but usually modest.
POOL.m: How you expect someone to perform can nudge how they perform. Expect good things, deliberately.

POOL.h: In the 1920s and 30s, studies at the Hawthorne Works factory near Chicago seemed to show workers improved whenever conditions changed, simply because they were being watched.
POOL.b: Later reanalyses found the original evidence was much weaker than the legend. Being observed can still change behaviour.
POOL.m: When tracking anything, from sleep to spending, remember that watching it may change it.

POOL.h: In the 1960s Martin Seligman and Steven Maier found animals that could not escape an unpleasant situation often stopped trying later, even when escape became easy.
POOL.b: Decades on, they concluded the brain’s default is passivity, and that a sense of control is what has to be learned.
POOL.m: Small wins that prove your actions matter can rebuild the drive to keep trying.

POOL.h: Psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied people so absorbed in an activity that time seemed to vanish, a state he called flow.
POOL.b: It tends to happen when a task’s challenge closely matches your skill, with clear goals and quick feedback. Too easy brings boredom, too hard brings anxiety.
POOL.m: To enjoy work more, adjust the difficulty: stretch yourself slightly, but not to breaking point.

POOL.h: In a 1975 study, Duncan Godden and Alan Baddeley had divers learn word lists either on a beach or about 6 metres underwater.
POOL.b: Divers recalled noticeably more when tested in the same place they had learned. Surroundings act as cues that help memories come back.
POOL.m: If you’re stuck recalling something, picture where you were when you learned it.

POOL.h: In 1966 Roger Brown and David McNeill read out definitions of rare words, such as a navigation instrument (a sextant).
POOL.b: People stuck on the word could often guess its first letter and number of syllables. Memory often retrieves a word’s outline before the whole thing.
POOL.m: If a word is stuck, stop straining. It often pops up later once you relax.

POOL.t: Why your teens and twenties stick
POOL.h: Ask older adults to recall memorable events and a cluster appears from roughly ages 10 to 30.
POOL.b: Psychologists call it the reminiscence bump. One explanation is that this period is packed with firsts and with forming an identity, and new experiences are easier to remember.
POOL.m: Novelty makes time memorable at any age. New experiences keep later years from blurring together.

POOL.h: Most adults cannot recall events from before about age three or four, a pattern called childhood amnesia.
POOL.b: Babies do learn and remember, but those early memories rarely last into adulthood. Some ‘earliest memories’ are actually built later from photos and family stories.
POOL.m: A vivid early memory may be partly reconstructed. Treat it as a story you tell, not a recording.

POOL.h: In 1973 William Chase and Herbert Simon showed chess players a board for five seconds.
POOL.b: A master recalled far more pieces from real game positions than a beginner did. With pieces placed randomly, the master’s advantage mostly vanished, because experts remember meaningful chunks, not more raw detail.
POOL.m: Expertise is built on recognisable patterns. Practise with real examples, not isolated facts.

POOL.h: In a 1977 study, people who judged whether words described themselves later remembered more of them than people who judged the words’ meaning or sound.
POOL.b: Linking information to yourself creates richer connections in memory. Psychologists call this the self-reference effect.
POOL.m: When learning something new, ask how it relates to your own life. It will stick better.

POOL.h: People generally remember pictures better than words.
POOL.b: In a 1973 study by Lionel Standing, people shown 10,000 pictures over five days could still pick out most of them from new images. Images seem to be stored in a richer, more distinctive way than words.
POOL.m: Sketch a quick diagram or picture alongside notes you want to remember.

POOL.h: In 1933 German psychologist Hedwig von Restorff found that an item which stands out from a list, such as one number among words, is remembered better than the rest.
POOL.b: This isolation effect is why highlighting and bold text work, but only when used sparingly.
POOL.m: If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out. Make only the key point distinctive.

POOL.t: Defending a choice you never made
POOL.h: In a 2005 study, people picked the more attractive of two face photos.
POOL.b: Through sleight of hand, researchers sometimes handed them the photo they had rejected. Most did not notice, and many explained why they preferred it, even citing features only the rejected face had.
POOL.m: Our reasons are often invented after the choice. Hold explanations of your own preferences lightly.

POOL.h: In a 1998 study, a researcher asked passers-by for directions.
POOL.b: Midway, two men carrying a door walked between them, and the researcher was swapped for a different person. About half the people did not notice they were now talking to someone else.
POOL.m: We see far less than we think. Don’t assume someone noticed something just because it was in front of them.

POOL.h: In 1935 John Ridley Stroop showed that naming the ink colour of a word is slow when the word spells a different colour, such as ‘RED’ printed in blue.
POOL.b: Reading is so automatic for adults that it gets in the way. The test is still widely used in research.
POOL.m: Well-practised habits run on autopilot and can override your intentions. Change the cue, not just your resolve.

POOL.h: In the McGurk effect, reported in 1976, a video shows lips saying ‘ga’ while the audio says ‘ba’.
POOL.b: Many people hear ‘da’, a blend of the two. Knowing about the trick does not stop it, because the brain merges sight and sound to decide what was said.
POOL.m: Seeing a speaker’s face really does help you hear, which is why noisy calls are easier with video on.

POOL.h: You learn a new word or buy a new car, then start seeing it everywhere.
POOL.b: Linguist Arnold Zwicky named this the frequency illusion in 2005, and it is also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon. The thing hasn’t become more common: you have simply started noticing it.
POOL.m: Seeing something often is not evidence that it is becoming more common.

POOL.h: In a 1980 study, Neil Weinstein found students rated themselves more likely than classmates to enjoy good events, like owning a home, and less likely to suffer bad ones, like illness.
POOL.b: Most people show this optimism bias, which cannot be true for everyone at once.
POOL.m: Optimism helps motivation, but buy the insurance and wear the seatbelt anyway.

POOL.h: In a 1975 study, Ellen Langer gave office workers lottery tickets, letting some choose their own.
POOL.b: When later asked to sell them back, those who had chosen wanted over four times as much on average. Picking the ticket felt like it improved their odds, though it could not.
POOL.m: Feeling in control of chance is an illusion. Luck-based games don’t reward your choices.

POOL.h: When calm, we underestimate how much hunger, anger or tiredness will change our choices.
POOL.b: Economist George Loewenstein called this the hot-cold empathy gap. It is why people shop hungry, vow to skip dessert while full, or send messages they regret when upset.
POOL.m: Make important decisions when calm, and plan ahead for the ‘hot’ moments you know will come.

POOL.h: Psychologists Daniel Gilbert and Timothy Wilson found people overestimate how intensely and how long they will feel after events such as a break-up or a job rejection.
POOL.b: They called this the impact bias. We tend to overlook our own ability to cope and make sense of things.
POOL.m: Before dreading an outcome, remember you have adapted to hard things before and likely will again.

POOL.h: Economist Herbert Simon coined the word ‘satisficing’ in 1956 for choosing the first option that meets your standards.
POOL.b: In a 2002 study, Barry Schwartz and colleagues found people who always hunt for the best option, called maximisers, reported less happiness and more regret than satisficers.
POOL.m: For everyday choices, set your criteria, pick the first option that meets them, and stop looking.

POOL.h: In a 1978 study, Ellen Langer’s team asked to cut in line at a photocopier.
POOL.b: A plain request worked about 60% of the time. Adding ‘because I’m in a rush’ raised it to about 94%. Even the empty reason ‘because I have to make copies’ got about 93%.
POOL.m: People respond to the shape of a reason, especially for small requests. Give real reasons, and question hollow ones.

POOL.h: In a 2008 hotel study, a card saying most guests reused their towels boosted reuse more than a card urging guests to help the environment.
POOL.b: Saying most guests who had stayed in that same room reused towels worked better still. We look to people like us to decide what to do.
POOL.m: To encourage a habit, show that others are already doing it, rather than complaining that few do.

POOL.h: In a 1993 Princeton study, students rated how comfortable they were with campus drinking habits, and how comfortable they thought the average student was.
POOL.b: Most rated themselves less comfortable than others. Privately doubting while assuming everyone else approves is called pluralistic ignorance.
POOL.m: If you have doubts in a group, voice them. Others may be quietly thinking the same thing.

POOL.h: In a 1977 Stanford study, students were asked to walk around campus wearing a sign saying ‘Eat at Joe’s’.
POOL.b: Those who agreed guessed most others would agree too, while those who refused guessed most would refuse. We assume our own choices are more common than they are.
POOL.m: Your view may feel like common sense only because it is yours. Ask, rather than assume, what others think.

POOL.h: In the early 1970s Henri Tajfel split schoolboys into groups based on trivial things, such as preferring paintings by Klee or Kandinsky.
POOL.b: Even with meaningless labels and no contact, the boys tended to give more rewards to their own group. It takes very little to create ‘us’ and ‘them’.
POOL.m: Group loyalty can sneak into judgement. Ask whether you’d decide the same way if the labels were swapped.

POOL.h: In 1954 psychologist Gordon Allport proposed that contact between groups reduces prejudice, especially when people have equal status and shared goals.
POOL.b: A 2006 review of over 500 studies found contact was generally linked with less prejudice, even when conditions were not ideal.
POOL.m: Getting to know people from different backgrounds, as equals working together, is one of the best ways to break down stereotypes.

POOL.h: In 1971, after schools in Austin, Texas were desegregated, Elliot Aronson designed lessons where each child held one piece of the material and the group needed every piece.
POOL.b: Cooperation replaced competition. Studies reported students liked each other more and showed less prejudice.
POOL.m: When groups clash, give them a shared task that nobody can complete alone.

POOL.h: In 1898 Norman Triplett noticed cyclists rode faster when racing others than when riding alone against the clock.
POOL.b: He tested children winding fishing reels and found many worked faster alongside another child. Later research showed company helps with easy or practised tasks but can hurt with hard, unfamiliar ones.
POOL.m: Practise new skills privately, then perform familiar ones in front of others.

POOL.h: In a 1950 study of student housing at MIT, researchers found residents were far more likely to be friends with next-door neighbours than with people a few doors away.
POOL.b: Those living near stairways and letterboxes made more friends. Simple proximity shapes who we get close to.
POOL.m: Want new friends? Put yourself where the same people pass by regularly.

POOL.h: In studies published in 2018, strangers chatted and then rated how much they liked their partner, and how much they thought their partner liked them.
POOL.b: People consistently underestimated how much they were liked. Researchers called this the liking gap, and it lingered for months between new university roommates.
POOL.m: After an awkward-feeling conversation, go easy on yourself. The other person probably enjoyed it more than you think.

POOL.h: In a 1949 paper, psychologist Bertram Forer described giving students a ‘personalised’ personality profile.
POOL.b: Everyone got the same text, assembled largely from horoscopes, yet on average they rated its accuracy about 4.3 out of 5. Vague, flattering statements feel personal, which is called the Forer or Barnum effect.
POOL.m: If a description seems to fit you perfectly, check whether it would fit almost anyone.

POOL.h: At a 1906 country fair in Plymouth, England, about 800 people guessed the weight of an ox.
POOL.b: Francis Galton found the middle guess was within about 1% of the true weight of 1,198 pounds (about 543 kg). Averaged together, independent guesses cancelled out individual errors.
POOL.m: Group judgement works best when people guess independently, before hearing each other’s views.

POOL.h: In a 2008 study, Elizabeth Dunn and colleagues gave people $5 or $20 to spend by that evening.
POOL.b: Those told to spend it on someone else or on charity reported feeling happier than those told to spend it on themselves. The amount made little difference.
POOL.m: A small gift or a shout for someone else can lift your mood more than a treat for yourself.

POOL.h: In 1986 James Pennebaker asked students to write for 15 minutes a day, over four days, about upsetting experiences.
POOL.b: Compared with students writing about neutral topics, they made fewer visits to the health centre in the following months. Hundreds of studies followed, generally finding modest benefits.
POOL.m: Writing privately and honestly about a difficult experience can help you make sense of it.

POOL.h: In a 2014 study, Katherine Milkman and colleagues let people listen to gripping audiobooks only while at the gym.
POOL.b: At first, gym visits rose compared with a control group, though the effect faded after a holiday break. Pairing a guilty pleasure with a chore makes the chore easier to start.
POOL.m: Save a favourite podcast or show for the task you tend to put off.

POOL.h: Researchers found Google searches for ‘diet’ and gym visits jump at the start of a new week, month or year, and after birthdays.
POOL.b: In 2014 they named this the fresh start effect. Landmarks on the calendar help people feel they can leave past failures behind.
POOL.m: You don’t need to wait for New Year. Any Monday, birthday or first of the month can be a restart.

POOL.h: In a 2006 study, some café customers got a 10-stamp loyalty card and others got a 12-stamp card with two stamps already filled.
POOL.b: Both needed 10 coffees, but the head-start group finished faster. People speed up as a goal feels closer, known as the goal-gradient effect.
POOL.m: Break big goals into stages so you always feel near the next finish line.

POOL.t: Much of your day is habit
POOL.h: In a 2002 diary study, Wendy Wood and colleagues found about 43% of people’s daily actions were done almost every day in the same place, usually while thinking about something else.
POOL.b: These habits are triggered by context rather than by conscious decisions.
POOL.m: To change a habit, change the cues around it: move the biscuits, put the running shoes by the door.

POOL.h: In Plato’s Euthyphro, Socrates asks: is something pious (good) because the gods love it, or do the gods love it because it is pious?
POOL.b: If the first, goodness seems arbitrary; if the second, goodness exists independently of the gods. Philosophers still debate it.
POOL.m: Ask whether a rule is right because an authority says so, or whether the authority says so because it is right.

POOL.h: Aristotle’s word for the good life was eudaimonia, often translated as ‘happiness’ but closer to ‘flourishing’.
POOL.b: For him it was not a passing mood but a whole life lived well, using reason and practising the virtues. It is something you do, not just something you feel.
POOL.m: Aim for a life that goes well overall, not just for a string of pleasant moments.

POOL.h: Aristotle argued we are not born virtuous, nor against it.
POOL.b: We become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave acts, just as builders become builders by building. Character, for him, forms through practice until good actions become second nature.
POOL.m: Want to be more patient or generous? Act that way repeatedly, even before it feels natural.

POOL.h: Aristotle described three kinds of friendship: those based on usefulness, those based on pleasure, and those based on admiring each other’s character.
POOL.b: The first two fade when the benefit or fun ends. The third is rarer and slower to form, but far more lasting.
POOL.m: Enjoy all kinds of friends, but invest time in the few who make you a better person.

POOL.h: Followers of Epicurus summed up his teaching as a ‘four-part cure’: don’t fear the gods, don’t worry about death, what is good is easy to get, and what is terrible is easy to endure.
POOL.b: The formula survives in writing by Philodemus in the first century BCE.
POOL.m: Much anxiety comes from fears that shrink when examined calmly.

POOL.h: Marcus Aurelius often imagined looking down on the world from a great height: crowds, cities, wars and weddings, all brief and small.
POOL.b: The French scholar Pierre Hadot called this exercise ‘the view from above’. It shrinks daily irritations down to size.
POOL.m: When something feels huge, picture it from space. Most worries look very different from there.

POOL.h: The Stoics recommended adding a mental reserve clause to plans: ‘I will sail, unless something prevents me.’ Seneca describes the wise person acting this way.
POOL.b: You commit fully to the effort while accepting that the outcome is not entirely in your hands.
POOL.m: Adding ‘if nothing gets in the way’ to your plans makes disappointment easier to bear.

POOL.h: The Stoic Hierocles pictured each person at the centre of a series of circles: self, family, relatives, fellow citizens and finally all humanity.
POOL.b: He urged people to draw the outer circles inward, treating relatives like family and strangers like relatives.
POOL.m: Try extending a little more care to the next circle out, like treating a colleague as you would a friend.

POOL.h: The Greek philosopher Pyrrho, who travelled to India with Alexander the Great’s army, taught that we should suspend judgement on questions we cannot settle.
POOL.b: He and his later followers, the Pyrrhonian sceptics, held that this led to ataraxia, a peaceful state of mind free from worry.
POOL.m: Not every question needs a firm opinion. Sometimes ‘I don’t know’ is the calmest honest answer.

POOL.h: The Greek sophist Protagoras declared that ‘man is the measure of all things’.
POOL.b: Plato took this to mean that things are as they appear to each person: the wind is cold to the one who feels cold. It is an early statement of relativism.
POOL.m: Two people can genuinely experience the same situation differently. Start there before arguing about who is right.

POOL.h: In the Phaedrus, Plato compares the soul to a charioteer driving two winged horses.
POOL.b: One is noble and obedient, the other unruly and driven by appetite, and reason, the charioteer, must steer them both. Much later psychology echoes his picture of a divided mind.
POOL.m: Feeling pulled in two directions is normal. The skill lies in steering, not in having no horses.

POOL.h: John Stuart Mill wrote in his Autobiography: ‘Ask yourself whether you are happy, and you cease to be so.’ He found happiness came most when aiming at something else, such as helping others or pursuing an art.
POOL.b: Chasing it directly tended to backfire.
POOL.m: Throw yourself into meaningful projects and relationships. Happiness often arrives as a side effect.

POOL.h: John Stuart Mill argued some pleasures are higher than others.
POOL.b: ‘It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied,’ he wrote, ‘better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.’ Those who know both kinds, he claimed, prefer the higher ones.
POOL.m: Easy pleasures are fine, but deeper ones, like learning and friendship, tend to repay their effort.

POOL.h: Asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius offered ‘shu’, often translated as reciprocity: do not impose on others what you would not want for yourself.
POOL.b: This negative form of the golden rule appears in the Analects, compiled by his followers.
POOL.m: Before acting, ask how you would feel on the receiving end.

POOL.t: Call things by their right names
POOL.h: Confucius taught that social order depends on the ‘rectification of names’.
POOL.b: If words do not match reality, he warned, affairs cannot succeed. A ruler should truly act as a ruler, and a parent as a parent, so that titles match the conduct they describe.
POOL.m: Say what you mean. Vague or misleading labels quietly cause confusion and conflict.

POOL.h: The Chinese philosopher Mencius argued that human nature is good.
POOL.b: Anyone who suddenly saw a child about to fall into a well, he said, would feel alarm and compassion, not to win praise but spontaneously. Such feelings are ‘sprouts’ of virtue that need cultivating.
POOL.m: Your good instincts are real. Like seedlings, they grow with attention and wither with neglect.

POOL.h: The Chinese philosopher Xunzi disagreed with Mencius, arguing that human nature is bad and goodness comes from deliberate effort.
POOL.b: He compared people to warped wood that must be steamed straight, or metal that must be sharpened. Learning, ritual and teachers do the shaping.
POOL.m: Whether or not you agree, good character is clearly built through practice and good influences.

POOL.h: The Daoist thinker Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering happily about.
POOL.b: On waking, he wondered: was he Zhuangzi who had dreamed of being a butterfly, or a butterfly now dreaming it was Zhuangzi? The story plays with how fixed our identity really is.
POOL.m: Holding your sense of self a little loosely can make change feel less threatening.

POOL.h: Zhuangzi tells of a huge, gnarled tree that carpenters ignored because its wood was useless.
POOL.b: Because nobody wanted it, it lived to an enormous age. Trees with good timber, by contrast, were cut down young.
POOL.m: Not everything must be productive. Some of life’s value lies in things no one can put a price on.

POOL.h: In a story by Zhuangzi, Cook Ding carves oxen so skilfully that his knife has stayed sharp for 19 years.
POOL.b: Rather than hacking, he follows the natural gaps between the joints. Ordinary cooks, he says, have to replace their knives every month.
POOL.m: Mastery often means working with the grain of a problem rather than forcing through it.

POOL.h: Around the 5th century BCE, the Chinese philosopher Mozi argued for ‘impartial care’: caring for other people’s families and states as you care for your own.
POOL.b: He believed most harm comes from favouring your own group. He also criticised lavish funerals and wars of conquest as wasteful.
POOL.m: Ask whether a decision would still seem fair if it affected someone you’ll never meet.

POOL.h: The Ming dynasty philosopher Wang Yangming taught the unity of knowledge and action.
POOL.b: Someone who claims to know they should respect their parents but never does, he argued, does not truly know it yet. Real knowledge shows itself in behaviour.
POOL.m: If you ‘know’ something is good for you but never do it, your knowledge may not be as deep as you think.

POOL.t: The blind men and the elephant
POOL.h: In an old Indian parable, several blind men each touch one part of an elephant.
POOL.b: One feels the trunk and says it’s like a snake, another feels a leg and says it’s like a pillar. The story appears in Buddhist, Jain and Hindu traditions, and Jain thinkers used it to show truth has many sides.
POOL.m: In a disagreement, you might each be describing a real part of a bigger picture.

POOL.h: Tradition says the Buddha grew up in luxury, then spent years in extreme self-denial, nearly starving himself.
POOL.b: He concluded that neither indulgence nor harsh asceticism led to wisdom. His path, the middle way, avoids both extremes.
POOL.m: When a habit swings between excess and punishing restriction, look for a sustainable middle.

POOL.h: Impermanence, anicca in the ancient Pali language, is one of the three marks of existence in Buddhist teaching.
POOL.b: Everything that arises, including feelings, bodies and circumstances, eventually passes away. Suffering, the teaching says, comes largely from clinging to what cannot last.
POOL.m: Good times and bad ones both pass. Enjoy the first fully and wait out the second.

POOL.h: In the Questions of King Milinda, the Buddhist monk Nagasena asks a Greek-descended king whether a chariot is its wheels, its axle or its pole.
POOL.b: None of them, the king admits. Nagasena says the self is similar: a convenient name for a changing collection of parts.
POOL.m: You are not fixed. Seeing yourself as a process makes change feel more possible.

POOL.h: The Charvaka school of ancient India rejected the afterlife, rebirth and anything that could not be perceived.
POOL.b: Its followers held that perception is the only reliable source of knowledge. Most of their own writings are lost, so we know them largely through their critics.
POOL.m: Asking ‘how could we know that?’ has a long history in every culture, not just the West.

POOL.h: In the Chandogya Upanishad, a father teaches his son Svetaketu by dissolving salt in water: the salt is invisible, yet present in every sip.
POOL.b: He repeats ‘tat tvam asi’, ‘you are that’, often understood to mean the individual self is one with ultimate reality. It is among Hinduism’s best-known sayings.
POOL.m: Seeing yourself as connected to something larger can soften both loneliness and self-importance.

POOL.h: The Persian philosopher Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, imagined a person created in mid-air, eyes covered, limbs apart, touching nothing.
POOL.b: Such a person, he argued, would still be aware of their own existence. He used this to argue the self is known directly, not through the body.
POOL.m: Your sense of being ‘you’ is so basic it is hard to doubt, a point Descartes reached centuries later.

POOL.h: The 11th-century thinker al-Ghazali argued that we never actually see fire cause cotton to burn.
POOL.b: We only see the burning follow the contact, again and again. His challenge anticipated David Hume’s famous doubts about causation by about 650 years.
POOL.m: Seeing two things happen together, even often, is not the same as knowing one causes the other.

POOL.h: The 12th-century Andalusian philosopher Ibn Rushd, known in Latin as Averroes, wrote such detailed commentaries on Aristotle that medieval European scholars simply called him ‘the Commentator’.
POOL.b: He argued that philosophy and religion, properly understood, do not contradict each other.
POOL.m: Deep engagement with other people’s ideas, even across cultures and centuries, is how thinking moves forward.

POOL.h: In his Muqaddimah, completed in 1377, Ibn Khaldun argued that dynasties rise on asabiyyah, a strong sense of group solidarity.
POOL.b: Over generations, comfort and luxury weaken it, and a newer, more united group takes over. He is often called a founder of sociology.
POOL.m: Teams, clubs and companies thrive on shared purpose. Comfort can quietly erode it.

POOL.h: The 10th-century philosopher al-Farabi was so respected in the Islamic world that he was called the ‘Second Teacher’, second only to Aristotle.
POOL.b: He wrote on logic, music and the ideal city, which he said should aim at the happiness of its citizens.
POOL.m: Good communities, like good lives, need a clear idea of what they are for.

POOL.t: The boy alone on an island
POOL.h: In the 12th century, Andalusian philosopher Ibn Tufayl wrote Hayy ibn Yaqzan, about a boy raised by a gazelle on an uninhabited island.
POOL.b: Through observation and reasoning alone, he works his way to deep truths about nature and God. It is often called one of the first philosophical novels.
POOL.m: Curiosity and careful thinking can take you remarkably far, even without teachers.

POOL.h: In his Confessions, written around 400 CE, Augustine wrote: ‘What then is time?
POOL.b: If no one asks me, I know. If I wish to explain it, I do not know.’ He concluded the past exists for us only as memory, and the future only as expectation.
POOL.m: Many everyday ideas that feel obvious turn slippery the moment you try to define them.

POOL.h: Around 524 CE, the Roman statesman Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy while imprisoned.
POOL.b: In it, Lady Philosophy reminds him that Fortune’s wheel always turns, and what Fortune gives, she can take away. True happiness, she argues, cannot depend on luck.
POOL.m: Build your sense of worth on what fortune cannot remove, like character and understanding.

POOL.h: Around 1120 the French scholar Peter Abelard compiled Sic et Non (‘Yes and No’), listing respected authorities who contradicted each other.
POOL.b: Rather than hiding the conflicts, he used them to train readers to reason. By doubting, he wrote, we come to inquiry, and by inquiry we perceive truth.
POOL.m: When experts disagree, don’t just pick a side. Use the disagreement to understand the question better.

POOL.h: The 12th-century Jewish philosopher Maimonides ranked charity in eight levels, with reluctant giving at the bottom.
POOL.b: Near the top, neither giver nor receiver knows the other. The highest level is helping someone become self-sufficient, through a loan, a partnership or a job.
POOL.m: The best help often builds independence rather than ongoing dependence.

POOL.h: The 17th-century French thinker Blaise Pascal argued that if God might exist, betting on belief costs little and could gain infinitely, while disbelief risks infinite loss.
POOL.b: Critics ask which god to bet on, and whether belief can simply be chosen. It is an early example of decision theory.
POOL.m: When outcomes are lopsided, weigh the size of what’s at stake, not just how likely it is.

POOL.t: The man who invented the essay
POOL.h: In the 1570s, Michel de Montaigne retired to a tower on his estate and began writing short pieces he called ‘essais’, meaning attempts.
POOL.b: He wrote about friendship, fear, cannibals and his own habits. His motto was ‘Que sais-je?’, meaning ‘What do I know?’
POOL.m: Writing honestly and curiously about your own experience is a way of thinking things through.

POOL.h: In his Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1689), John Locke argued the mind at birth is like ‘white paper’, with no ideas built in.
POOL.b: All knowledge, he said, comes from experience. Modern science suggests we are born with some tendencies, but experience still shapes us profoundly.
POOL.m: What you read, do and surround yourself with becomes part of your mind. Choose it with care.

POOL.h: David Hume wrote in 1739 that ‘reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions’.
POOL.b: He meant reason cannot set our goals by itself: it can only work out how to get what we already desire. Motivation, for Hume, starts with feeling.
POOL.m: Arguments rarely change minds on their own. Connect with what people actually care about.

POOL.h: In 1748 David Hume wrote that ‘a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence’.
POOL.b: Some claims deserve firm confidence, others only tentative belief, and some none at all. Carl Sagan later popularised a related line: extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence.
POOL.m: Hold beliefs with the strength the evidence supports, and adjust as new evidence arrives.

POOL.h: Immanuel Kant argued we must treat people always as ends in themselves, never merely as means.
POOL.b: Relying on a shopkeeper’s service is fine. Deceiving or manipulating someone to get what you want treats them as a mere tool, which he held is always wrong.
POOL.m: Ask whether the other person could knowingly agree to how you’re treating them.

POOL.h: In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill argued the only good reason to restrict someone’s freedom against their will is to prevent harm to others.
POOL.b: Their own good, he said, is not enough. People may be advised and argued with, but not forced.
POOL.m: Before trying to control someone’s choices, ask whether they are really harming anyone else.

POOL.t: Would you live it all again?
POOL.h: In The Gay Science (1882), Friedrich Nietzsche imagined a demon telling you that you must live your life again, exactly the same, an infinite number of times.
POOL.b: Would you curse the demon, or welcome the news? He offered it as a test of how fully you embrace your life.
POOL.m: If you’d dread repeating how you spend your days, that’s a signal to change something.

POOL.h: Jean-Paul Sartre described a café waiter whose movements are a little too precise, as if performing the role of waiter.
POOL.b: Sartre called hiding behind a role ‘bad faith’: pretending we have no choice when we do. For him, we are not fixed by nature but define ourselves through our choices.
POOL.m: ‘That’s just who I am’ can be an excuse. You’re freer to change than your roles suggest.

POOL.t: What makes a game a game?
POOL.h: Ludwig Wittgenstein asked what all games have in common: not winning, since some games have no winner, and not competition or skill either.
POOL.b: Instead, he said, games share overlapping similarities, like resemblances within a family. Many words work this way, without one neat definition.
POOL.m: Arguments over definitions often go nowhere. Look at how a word is actually used instead.

POOL.h: Philosopher Karl Popper argued that a scientific theory must be falsifiable: some possible observation must be able to show it is wrong.
POOL.b: A theory that can explain every possible outcome, he said, really explains nothing. He admired Einstein for making risky predictions that could have failed.
POOL.m: Be wary of any claim that no conceivable evidence could ever count against.

POOL.h: In 1952 Bertrand Russell imagined a tiny china teapot orbiting the Sun between Earth and Mars, too small for any telescope to see.
POOL.b: No one could disprove it, yet it would be absurd to expect others to believe it. The burden of proof, he argued, lies with whoever makes the claim.
POOL.m: If someone asks you to disprove their claim, it’s fair to ask for their evidence first.

POOL.h: In Leviathan (1651), Thomas Hobbes imagined life without any government, a ‘state of nature’.
POOL.b: It would be a war of every man against every man, he argued, and life would be ‘solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short’. People accept rules and authority to escape that fear.
POOL.m: Rules can feel irritating, but many solve real problems of trust. Ask what life would be like without them.

POOL.h: In 1980 John Searle imagined himself in a room, following a rulebook to answer messages in Chinese with Chinese symbols.
POOL.b: To outsiders he seems fluent, yet he understands no Chinese. He argued that following rules for symbols is not the same as understanding, a question now asked about AI.
POOL.m: Producing the right answer is not always proof of understanding, in machines or in people.

POOL.h: Derek Parfit imagined a teleporter that scans your body on Earth, destroys it and builds an exact copy on Mars.
POOL.b: Is the person on Mars really you? In Reasons and Persons (1984), he argued personal identity matters less than we think, and what matters is psychological connection and continuity.
POOL.m: Parfit found this freeing: caring less about a fixed self made him care more about others.

POOL.h: Two people drive home equally drunk: one gets home safely, the other hits a pedestrian who steps out.
POOL.b: Philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel called this moral luck: we judge people partly by outcomes they did not control. It remains a puzzle for any theory of blame.
POOL.m: When judging others, and yourself, consider the choices made, not just how things happened to turn out.

POOL.h: Philosophers use the principle of charity: interpret what someone says in its most reasonable form before judging it.
POOL.b: Donald Davidson argued we must assume others are mostly rational just to understand their words at all. It turns debates into shared problem-solving.
POOL.m: Assume the other person has a sensible point, then find it. You’ll understand, and persuade, far better.

POOL.h: A slippery slope argument claims one small step will inevitably lead to extreme results: ‘If we allow this, soon anything will be allowed.’ Sometimes such chains are real, but each link needs evidence.
POOL.b: Without it, the argument relies on fear rather than reasoning.
POOL.m: When warned that one step leads to disaster, ask how likely each step in between really is.

POOL.h: Citing an expert is often reasonable.
POOL.b: The fallacy is treating someone’s say-so as proof, especially outside their field: a famous physicist’s views on nutrition carry no special weight. Thomas Aquinas noted that an argument resting only on human authority is the weakest kind.
POOL.m: Ask whether an expert is speaking within their area, and whether other experts agree.

POOL.h: In logic, ‘begging the question’ does not mean ‘raising the question’.
POOL.b: It means an argument quietly assumes its own conclusion: ‘He’s trustworthy, because he told me he’s honest.’ The phrase comes from a Latin translation of a term used by Aristotle.
POOL.m: If an argument only works once you already agree with it, it hasn’t proven anything.

POOL.h: Ubuntu is a southern African philosophy often summed up in the Zulu saying ‘umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’: a person is a person through other people.
POOL.b: It sees identity and humanity as built through relationships and community. Archbishop Desmond Tutu helped make the idea known worldwide.
POOL.m: Your wellbeing is tied up with others. Small acts of care strengthen both them and you.

POOL.h: Mungo Man was buried beside a lake in western New South Wales around 40,000 years ago, his body sprinkled with red ochre.
POOL.b: It is one of the oldest known ritual burials anywhere in the world. In 2017, his remains were returned to Country at Lake Mungo.
POOL.m: Ceremony and care for the dead have extraordinarily deep roots on this continent.

POOL.h: At Madjedbebe, a rock shelter on Mirarr Country in Arnhem Land, archaeologists found stone tools, ground ochre and seed-grinding stones.
POOL.b: A 2017 study dated the oldest layers to about 65,000 years ago. It suggests people have lived in Australia for at least that long.
POOL.m: Aboriginal peoples belong to one of the oldest continuing cultures on Earth.

POOL.h: From at least the 1700s, fishing fleets from Makassar in Sulawesi sailed to northern Australia each year to collect trepang, or sea cucumber, for sale to China.
POOL.b: Yolngu people traded and worked with them. Makassarese words entered Yolngu languages, including ‘balanda’, meaning white people, from ‘Hollander’.
POOL.m: Australia was part of Asian trade networks long before British colonisation.

POOL.h: Tupaia, a priest and navigator from Ra’iatea, near Tahiti, joined James Cook’s Endeavour in 1769.
POOL.b: He drew a chart of more than 70 Pacific islands from memory. When the ship reached Aotearoa New Zealand, he acted as interpreter, because Māori could understand his language.
POOL.m: European explorers leaned heavily on the deep ocean knowledge of Pacific navigators.

POOL.h: About 3,000 years ago, the Lapita people sailed beyond the Solomon Islands into the open Pacific, reaching Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries.
POOL.b: Archaeologists trace them by their distinctive stamped pottery. They are ancestors of today’s Polynesians.
POOL.m: Some of history’s boldest voyages were made in canoes, without maps or compasses.

POOL.t: Sailing to Tahiti by the stars
POOL.h: In 1976, the double-hulled canoe Hōkūleʻa sailed about 4,000 km from Hawaiʻi to Tahiti without instruments.
POOL.b: Micronesian navigator Mau Piailug guided it using stars, ocean swells and birds. The voyage showed that Polynesian settlement could have come from skilled navigation, not lucky drifting.
POOL.m: Traditional knowledge can be tested and proven, not just remembered.

POOL.h: The First Fleet reached Botany Bay in January 1788, but Arthur Phillip found it unsuitable and moved to Port Jackson.
POOL.b: As the British were leaving, two French ships under La Pérouse sailed into Botany Bay. They stayed about six weeks, then disappeared at sea.
POOL.m: European rivals were watching the Pacific closely in the 1780s.

POOL.h: On 26 January 1808, officers of the New South Wales Corps marched on Government House and arrested Governor William Bligh, the same Bligh who had faced the mutiny on the Bounty.
POOL.b: The officers ran the colony until Britain sent Lachlan Macquarie to restore order.
POOL.m: Power in early Sydney rested on who controlled trade, especially rum.

POOL.h: Mary Reibey was transported to Sydney in 1792, as a teenager, for stealing a horse.
POOL.b: She later ran shipping, trading and property businesses and became one of the colony’s wealthiest people. Her portrait now appears on the Australian $20 note.
POOL.m: A convict record did not have to define a life in early Australia.

POOL.h: When gold was found in Victoria in 1851, the colony had about 77,000 people.
POOL.b: Ten years later, it had more than 500,000. The wealth that followed helped make ‘Marvellous Melbourne’ one of the richest cities in the world by the 1880s.
POOL.m: A single discovery can reshape a whole society within a decade.

POOL.t: Burke and Wills relied on help
POOL.h: In 1861, the Burke and Wills expedition became the first European party to cross Australia from south to north, but Burke and Wills died near Cooper Creek on the way back.
POOL.b: The only survivor of the final group, John King, lived because Yandruwandha people fed and sheltered him.
POOL.m: In the outback, local knowledge was the difference between death and survival.

POOL.t: A test set in Scottish Gaelic
POOL.h: From 1901, Australian immigration law let officials give an unwanted arrival a 50-word dictation test in any European language.
POOL.b: In 1934, Czech writer Egon Kisch, who spoke many languages, was tested in Scottish Gaelic and failed. The High Court later ruled Gaelic did not count.
POOL.m: Laws can look neutral on paper while being designed to exclude.

POOL.h: On 26 January 1938, while Sydney celebrated 150 years since British arrival, Aboriginal activists met at the Australian Hall to hold a Day of Mourning.
POOL.b: They called for full citizen rights and equality. It is recognised as one of the first major Aboriginal civil rights gatherings.
POOL.m: NAIDOC Week traces its roots to this protest.

POOL.h: In 1963, Yolngu people at Yirrkala sent petitions to federal parliament protesting a bauxite mine on their land.
POOL.b: The typed text, in Yolngu Matha and English, was surrounded by traditional bark painting. They were the first traditional documents recognised by the Commonwealth Parliament.
POOL.m: The Bark Petitions helped begin the long road to land rights in Australia.

POOL.h: In 1965, Charles Perkins and a group of University of Sydney students toured country New South Wales by bus.
POOL.b: They drew national attention to Aboriginal people being barred from swimming pools, clubs and shops, including in Moree. Perkins graduated from university the following year.
POOL.m: Shining a light on unfairness can shift a whole nation’s view.

POOL.h: On 26 January 1972, four Aboriginal men set up a beach umbrella on the lawns opposite Parliament House, now Old Parliament House, in Canberra and called it the Aboriginal Embassy.
POOL.b: It protested the lack of land rights. After being removed and re-established several times, the Tent Embassy has stood on the site continuously since 1992.
POOL.m: A simple symbol can carry a powerful message for decades.

POOL.t: The case that ended terra nullius
POOL.h: In 1992, the High Court ruled in the Mabo case that native title had survived British colonisation.
POOL.b: Eddie Koiki Mabo and other Meriam people from Mer, in the Torres Strait, had pursued the case for ten years. Mabo died a few months before the decision.
POOL.m: The ruling overturned the legal idea that Australia had belonged to no one.

POOL.h: In 1971, Neville Bonner became the first Aboriginal person to sit in the Australian Parliament, as a senator for Queensland.
POOL.b: He had very little formal schooling and had worked as a stockman and labourer. In 1979, he was named Australian of the Year.
POOL.m: Representation came late, but it began with determined individuals.

POOL.h: In 1893, New Zealand became the first self-governing country where women could vote in national elections.
POOL.b: Campaigners led by Kate Sheppard gathered nearly 32,000 signatures. The sheets were glued into a roll about 270 metres long and unrolled across the floor of Parliament.
POOL.m: Persistent, organised campaigning can change laws that seem fixed.

POOL.h: Around 1157 BC, under Pharaoh Ramesses III, the tomb builders of Deir el-Medina in Egypt stopped work because their grain rations were late.
POOL.b: They sat near the temples and refused to return until supplied. A scribe recorded it on what is now called the Turin Strike Papyrus.
POOL.m: Workers bargaining over pay is as old as organised labour itself.

POOL.t: The pharaoh with a false beard
POOL.h: Hatshepsut ruled Egypt as pharaoh for about 20 years in the 1400s BC.
POOL.b: Statues often show her with the ceremonial false beard worn by kings. After her death, many of her images were defaced, probably on the orders of her successor, Thutmose III.
POOL.m: Power could override tradition, but history could also be edited afterwards.

POOL.h: The ancient Olympic Games at Olympia are traditionally dated from 776 BC and continued for more than a thousand years.
POOL.b: Athletes competed naked, and winners received an olive wreath, not a medal. The games probably ended in the late 300s or 400s AD.
POOL.m: The modern Olympics revived one of the longest-running traditions in history.

POOL.h: Around 100 AD, Claudia Severa wrote to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina at Vindolanda, a Roman fort in northern England, inviting her to a birthday party.
POOL.b: The thin wooden tablet survived in waterlogged ground. Its closing lines are among the earliest known Latin handwriting by a woman.
POOL.m: Friendship looks much the same across nearly 2,000 years.

POOL.h: On a marble balustrade in Istanbul’s Hagia Sophia, someone carved Norse runes that include the name Halfdan, probably many centuries ago.
POOL.b: Scandinavians served Byzantine emperors as elite bodyguards known as the Varangian Guard. At least one visitor left his mark on the great church.
POOL.m: People have been leaving an ‘I was here’ for a very long time.

POOL.h: After a bloody war against Kalinga around 261 BC, the Indian emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhism and non-violence.
POOL.b: He had his principles carved on rocks and pillars across his empire. The lion capital from one pillar, at Sarnath, is now India’s national emblem.
POOL.m: Leaders can change course, and say so publicly.

POOL.h: Nalanda, in what is now Bihar in India, was a great Buddhist centre of learning from about the 5th century AD.
POOL.b: It drew students from as far away as China and Korea, and the Chinese monk Xuanzang studied there. It was sacked around 1200.
POOL.m: Hubs of international learning existed long before Europe’s universities.

POOL.h: Wu Zetian ruled China in her own name from 690 to 705 AD, founding her own Zhou dynasty.
POOL.b: She is the only woman in Chinese history to hold the title of emperor. Her government expanded the imperial exams, which chose officials by merit.
POOL.m: She crossed a barrier no other woman crossed in over 2,000 years of imperial China.

POOL.h: Between 1405 and 1433, Admiral Zheng He led seven great voyages for the Ming dynasty, reaching India, Arabia and East Africa.
POOL.b: His fleets carried tens of thousands of crew. One voyage brought a giraffe back to the emperor’s court, where it was welcomed as a lucky omen.
POOL.m: China had the means to dominate the oceans, then chose to turn inward.

POOL.h: Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple-building firm, was founded in 578 AD by craftsmen brought from the Korean kingdom of Baekje to build a Buddhist temple in Osaka.
POOL.b: It was run by the same family for over 1,400 years before becoming part of a larger company in 2006.
POOL.m: Specialist skills and careful succession can keep a business alive for centuries.

POOL.t: A university founded by a woman
POOL.h: According to tradition, in 859 AD Fatima al-Fihri used her inheritance to found a mosque in Fez, Morocco, which grew into the University of al-Qarawiyyin.
POOL.b: It is often described as the oldest existing, continually operating university in the world. Its library is among the oldest still in use.
POOL.m: One act of generosity can create an institution that outlasts empires.

POOL.h: Timbuktu, in Mali, was a great centre of scholarship from around the 1400s, and local families kept hundreds of thousands of manuscripts on law, astronomy and medicine.
POOL.b: In 2012, when armed groups occupied the city, librarians secretly moved most of them to safety in Bamako.
POOL.m: Africa has a rich written scholarly tradition that is often overlooked.

POOL.t: An African empire that minted coins
POOL.h: The Kingdom of Aksum, in today’s Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a major trading power in the early centuries AD.
POOL.b: It minted its own gold, silver and bronze coins. Under King Ezana in the 300s, it became one of the first states to adopt Christianity.
POOL.m: Ancient Africa had powerful states that traded with Rome, Arabia and India.

POOL.t: The traveller who outdid Marco Polo
POOL.h: Starting in 1325, the Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta travelled for nearly 30 years, reaching West Africa, India, the Maldives and China.
POOL.b: He covered roughly 120,000 km, far more than Marco Polo. His account, known as the Rihla, was written down after he returned home.
POOL.m: The medieval world was more connected than we often imagine.

POOL.h: The Mongol Empire ran a relay system called the Yam, with stations spaced along its roads.
POOL.b: Messengers could swap for fresh horses and carry urgent news a few hundred kilometres in a day. Officials carrying a metal pass called a paiza could use the stations.
POOL.m: Fast, reliable communication helped hold a vast empire together.

POOL.h: Around 1100 AD, Cahokia, near modern St Louis in the United States, was home to perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people.
POOL.b: Its largest earthwork, Monks Mound, is the biggest pre-Columbian earthen structure in the Americas. It was the largest city north of Mexico before European arrival.
POOL.m: Complex cities flourished in North America long before colonisation.

POOL.h: In 1545, the Spanish began mining Cerro Rico at Potosí, in today’s Bolivia, using forced Indigenous labour.
POOL.b: Its silver became Spanish dollars, which circulated from Europe to China. The Spanish dollar was even legal tender in the United States until 1857.
POOL.m: Global trade and money were shaped by one mountain, at great human cost.

POOL.h: In July 1518, a woman in Strasbourg began dancing in the street and would not stop.
POOL.b: Within weeks, dozens and possibly hundreds of people had joined in. Records show officials hired musicians, believing more dancing would cure it. The cause is still debated.
POOL.m: Stress and shared beliefs can produce strange behaviour across a whole community.

POOL.h: In 1714, Britain offered a prize for a way to find longitude at sea.
POOL.b: John Harrison, a self-taught carpenter and clockmaker, spent decades building clocks that kept accurate time on rolling ships. James Cook took a copy of Harrison’s design on his second voyage and praised it.
POOL.m: Better timekeeping made ocean navigation far safer.

POOL.h: Hokusai’s ‘The Great Wave off Kanagawa’, made around 1831, is a woodblock print, not a one-off painting.
POOL.b: Thousands of impressions were probably printed and sold cheaply. Hokusai was about 70 when he made it, and he signed some later works ‘old man mad about drawing’.
POOL.m: Some of the world’s most famous art was made to be affordable.

POOL.h: Vincent van Gogh made about 2,100 artworks, including around 860 oil paintings, in a career of only about ten years.
POOL.b: He began painting seriously in his late twenties. Many of his best-known works, such as ‘The Starry Night’, came in his last two years.
POOL.m: A short career can still leave an enormous body of work.

POOL.h: The Eiffel Tower was built for the 1889 World’s Fair in Paris and was given a permit to stand for 20 years.
POOL.b: Many artists protested it as ugly. It survived partly because Gustave Eiffel promoted its scientific uses, especially as a radio antenna.
POOL.m: Usefulness can save something that taste alone would have removed.

POOL.t: Beethoven could not hear the applause
POOL.h: Beethoven was almost completely deaf when his Ninth Symphony premiered in Vienna in 1824.
POOL.b: At the end, he was still facing the orchestra. According to later accounts, a singer turned him around so he could see the audience cheering and waving hats and handkerchiefs.
POOL.m: Great work can come from someone facing enormous obstacles.

POOL.t: The Four Seasons came with poems
POOL.h: When Vivaldi published ‘The Four Seasons’ in 1725, each concerto was paired with a sonnet, possibly written by Vivaldi himself.
POOL.b: The music follows the poems closely, with birdsong, a barking dog, a summer storm and people slipping on ice. It is an early example of music telling a story.
POOL.m: Listening with the poems in mind reveals details you might otherwise miss.

POOL.h: Handel composed ‘Messiah’ in about 24 days in 1741.
POOL.b: It premiered at a charity concert in Dublin in 1742. Organisers asked women not to wear hooped dresses and men to leave their swords at home, so more people could fit inside.
POOL.m: Ambitious work can be done quickly when skill and preparation meet.

POOL.h: Mozart wrote his first symphony in London in 1764, aged about eight, while touring Europe with his family.
POOL.b: By then he had already performed for royalty in several countries. He wrote more than 600 works before his death at 35.
POOL.m: Early talent flourishes with intense training and opportunity.

POOL.h: The didgeridoo, known to Yolngu people as the yidaki, comes from northern Australia.
POOL.b: It is traditionally made from a eucalyptus branch hollowed out by termites. Players use circular breathing, inhaling through the nose while pushing air out through the mouth, to keep the drone going without a break.
POOL.m: Nature and human skill work together in this ancient instrument.

POOL.h: Across Australia, many Aboriginal peoples hold songlines: routes across the land recorded in song, story, dance and art.
POOL.b: A songline can describe waterholes, landmarks and paths over hundreds of kilometres, crossing many language groups. Knowing the song means knowing the way.
POOL.m: Oral traditions can store precise, practical knowledge for thousands of years.

POOL.h: Some of the oldest known musical instruments are flutes carved from bird bones and mammoth ivory, found in caves in southern Germany.
POOL.b: They are roughly 35,000 to 40,000 years old. One nearly complete flute, made from a griffon vulture’s wing bone, has five finger holes.
POOL.m: Music has been part of human life for as long as we have made art.

POOL.h: At the 1889 Paris World’s Fair, the composer Claude Debussy heard a Javanese gamelan orchestra, with its layered gongs and metal keyed instruments.
POOL.b: He was deeply impressed. Echoes of its shimmering sound and unusual scales appear in later works such as his piano piece ‘Pagodes’.
POOL.m: Cross-cultural encounters often spark new directions in art.

POOL.h: The tune of ‘Happy Birthday to You’ comes from ‘Good Morning to All’, a song for young children published in 1893 by American sisters Mildred and Patty Hill.
POOL.b: The birthday words appeared later. In 2015, a United States court ruled that long-running copyright claims over the song were invalid.
POOL.m: Some of the world’s most-sung music started as a simple classroom tool.

POOL.t: Silent Night began with a guitar
POOL.h: ‘Silent Night’ was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria.
POOL.b: Priest Joseph Mohr wrote the words, and teacher Franz Xaver Gruber composed the melody, which was first sung with guitar accompaniment. It has since been translated into hundreds of languages.
POOL.m: A modest village song can travel the whole world.

POOL.h: The first Academy Awards were held in 1929 at a private dinner in Hollywood, with about 270 guests.
POOL.b: The winners had been announced three months earlier, and the presentation took about 15 minutes. ‘Wings’, a silent war film, won the top award.
POOL.m: Institutions that seem grand today often started small.

POOL.h: On 28 December 1895, the Lumière brothers held one of the first public film screenings for a paying audience, in the basement of a Paris café.
POOL.b: They showed ten short films, each under a minute long. Stories of viewers fleeing from a filmed train are probably exaggerated.
POOL.m: Cinema began as a novelty before it became an art form.

POOL.h: ‘Raja Harishchandra’, released in 1913 by Dadasaheb Phalke, is regarded as India’s first full-length feature film.
POOL.b: It was silent, and every role, including the queen, was played by men, because acting was not considered respectable for women. India’s highest film honour is named after Phalke.
POOL.m: One pioneer helped launch one of the world’s biggest film industries.

POOL.t: The first animated feature was Argentine
POOL.h: The first known animated feature film, ‘El Apóstol’, was made in Argentina in 1917 by Quirino Cristiani.
POOL.b: It was a political satire made with cut-out figures. The only known copies were later destroyed in a fire, so it can no longer be seen.
POOL.m: Film history is fragile, and many early works are lost forever.

POOL.h: Miguel de Cervantes and William Shakespeare are both recorded as dying around 23 April 1616, and UNESCO chose that date for World Book Day.
POOL.b: Yet they did not die on the same day. Spain used the Gregorian calendar and England the older Julian one, about ten days apart.
POOL.m: Dates can mislead when calendars differ.

POOL.h: In 1623, seven years after Shakespeare died, two of his fellow actors published a collection of his plays now called the First Folio.
POOL.b: About 18 of them, including ‘Macbeth’ and ‘The Tempest’, had never been printed before. Without it, they might have been lost.
POOL.m: Friends and colleagues can preserve a legacy that would otherwise vanish.

POOL.t: A Christmas Carol in six weeks
POOL.h: Charles Dickens wrote ‘A Christmas Carol’ in about six weeks in late 1843, partly because he needed money.
POOL.b: Its first printing of 6,000 copies sold out within days. The story helped shape modern Christmas, with its emphasis on family, feasting and generosity to the poor.
POOL.m: One short book can influence how a whole culture celebrates.

POOL.t: A book written on a bet
POOL.h: Dr Seuss wrote ‘Green Eggs and Ham’ after his publisher bet him he could not write a book using only 50 different words.
POOL.b: He succeeded, and it became one of the best-selling children’s books ever. His earlier ‘The Cat in the Hat’ used 236 different words.
POOL.m: Tight limits can spark creativity rather than restrict it.

POOL.h: J.R.R.
POOL.b: Tolkien, a professor of Old English, began inventing languages as a young man, including the Elvish tongues Quenya and Sindarin. He later explained that his stories were made to give the languages a world to live in, rather than the other way around.
POOL.m: A deep passion for one thing can grow into something much larger.

POOL.h: Rotokas, spoken by a few thousand people on Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, has one of the smallest alphabets in the world, with only 12 letters.
POOL.b: Hawaiian uses just 13, including the ʻokina, a mark for a glottal stop. English, by comparison, has 26.
POOL.m: Languages can be rich and expressive with very few sounds.

POOL.t: A village name made for tourists
POOL.h: The Welsh village often shortened to Llanfairpwll has a 58-letter full name.
POOL.b: It was lengthened in the 1860s, reportedly to attract visitors travelling on the new railway. The name roughly describes the local church, a whirlpool and a nearby red cave.
POOL.m: A clever name can put a small place on the map.

POOL.h: On La Gomera, in Spain’s Canary Islands, people use Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish that can carry across deep valleys for kilometres.
POOL.b: It is taught in local schools. UNESCO recognised it as intangible cultural heritage in 2009.
POOL.m: Communities adapt language to suit their landscape.

POOL.t: Where the word kangaroo comes from
POOL.h: The word ‘kangaroo’ comes from ‘gangurru’, a Guugu Yimithirr word from the Cooktown area of Queensland, recorded by James Cook’s crew in 1770.
POOL.b: It referred to a particular large grey kangaroo. Words like ‘koala’ and ‘boomerang’ come from Dharug, a Sydney language.
POOL.m: Everyday Australian English carries words from many First Nations languages.

POOL.h: In 1887, the Polish eye doctor L.
POOL.b: L. Zamenhof published a guide to Esperanto, a language designed to be easy to learn and to help different peoples understand each other. Its grammar has no irregular verbs. It remains the most widely spoken constructed language.
POOL.m: A shared language was seen as a path to reducing conflict.

POOL.h: Most Icelanders do not have family surnames.
POOL.b: Instead, they take a name from a parent’s first name, such as Jónsdóttir (Jón’s daughter) or Ólafsson (Ólafur’s son). People are addressed by first name, and even the phone directory has been ordered that way.
POOL.m: Naming customs reveal how a society thinks about family and identity.

POOL.h: Auslan, the sign language of Australia’s Deaf community, comes from British and Irish sign languages.
POOL.b: American Sign Language descends from French Sign Language instead. So Deaf Australians and Deaf Britons usually understand each other more easily than either does an American signer.
POOL.m: Sign languages have their own histories and families, just like spoken ones.

POOL.h: Early sushi was a way to preserve fish.
POOL.b: Fish was packed in fermenting rice for months, and the rice was often thrown away. Over time the process shortened, and in the early 1800s Edo, now Tokyo, developed fast, fresh nigiri sushi sold at street stalls.
POOL.m: Many famous dishes began as practical ways of storing food.

POOL.h: The word ‘ketchup’ probably comes from ‘kê-tsiap’, a fermented fish sauce from southern China.
POOL.b: British traders brought the idea home around 1700, making ketchups from mushrooms, walnuts and oysters. Tomato ketchup took off in the United States in the 1800s.
POOL.m: Foods travel and transform, sometimes keeping only their name.

POOL.h: The lamington, a sponge cake dipped in chocolate and rolled in coconut, is named after Lord Lamington, Governor of Queensland from 1896 to 1901.
POOL.b: It was most likely created in Queensland during his time there, though its exact inventor remains uncertain.
POOL.m: Everyday foods can carry quiet pieces of history.

POOL.h: The word ‘Anzac’ is protected by Australian law, and using it commercially needs permission.
POOL.b: Anzac biscuits are an exception, as long as they stay close to the traditional recipe and are not called ‘cookies’. The oat and golden syrup biscuit is closely linked with the First World War.
POOL.m: Words can carry such meaning that a nation chooses to protect them.

POOL.h: The Chiko Roll was created by Frank McEncroe, a boilermaker, and first sold at the Wagga Wagga Show in 1951.
POOL.b: Inspired by the Chinese egg roll, it was designed to be eaten with one hand at football games and outdoor events. It became a classic of Australian takeaway shops.
POOL.m: Good food ideas often come from solving a simple, practical problem.

POOL.t: A dessert named after an Australian
POOL.h: Peach Melba was created in London in the 1890s by chef Auguste Escoffier to honour Australian soprano Nellie Melba.
POOL.b: Melba toast is named after her too. She was born Helen Porter Mitchell and took her stage name from her home city, Melbourne.
POOL.m: Australian performers were international stars well over a century ago.

POOL.h: In 1973, the Australian Government paid $1.3 million for Jackson Pollock’s ‘Blue Poles’ for its planned national gallery, then a record price for a modern American painting.
POOL.b: Many people were outraged at the cost. Today it is considered one of the National Gallery of Australia’s most valuable and famous works.
POOL.m: Bold decisions in art can look very different decades later.

POOL.t: A school mural started a movement
POOL.h: In 1971, at Papunya, west of Alice Springs, teacher Geoffrey Bardon encouraged senior men to paint a mural on the school wall.
POOL.b: Their Honey Ant Dreaming design helped spark the Western Desert art movement. Painting soon moved onto boards and canvas, and it is now celebrated worldwide.
POOL.m: Contemporary Aboriginal art grew from ancient designs meeting new materials.

POOL.t: A celebrated painter who started late
POOL.h: Anmatyerre artist Emily Kame Kngwarreye began painting on canvas in the late 1980s, when she was in her late seventies.
POOL.b: In roughly eight years she produced more than 3,000 works. She represented Australia at the 1997 Venice Biennale and is one of the country’s most celebrated artists.
POOL.m: It is never too late to begin, or to excel.

POOL.t: David came from a rejected block
POOL.h: Michelangelo carved his statue of David from a tall block of marble that other sculptors had started and abandoned decades earlier.
POOL.b: He was only 26 when he began, and finished in 1504. The statue stands about 5.17 metres tall.
POOL.m: Where others see failure, a skilled eye can see potential.

POOL.h: Rodin’s ‘The Thinker’ was first designed around 1880 as a small figure for ‘The Gates of Hell’, a huge bronze doorway inspired by Dante’s ‘Inferno’.
POOL.b: It was meant to show the poet looking down on his creation. Later enlarged, it became a symbol of thought itself.
POOL.m: Artworks can take on meanings their makers never planned.

POOL.h: Many of the famous moai of Rapa Nui, often pictured as giant heads, actually have full torsos below ground.
POOL.b: The best-known examples, on the slopes of the Rano Raraku quarry, were gradually buried by soil over centuries. Excavations have revealed carvings on their backs.
POOL.m: What we see on the surface is not always the whole story.

POOL.h: Of Frida Kahlo’s roughly 140 paintings, about 55 are self-portraits.
POOL.b: After a bus accident at 18 left her badly injured, she began painting while recovering in bed, using a mirror fixed above her. Her work blends Mexican folk art, personal experience and rich symbolism.
POOL.m: Art can grow out of hardship and long hours alone.

POOL.h: In 1856, 18-year-old chemist William Perkin was trying to make the malaria drug quinine from coal tar.
POOL.b: Instead, he produced a vivid purple dye, later called mauve. It was the first commercially successful synthetic dye, and it made purple clothing affordable for ordinary people.
POOL.m: Failed experiments can lead to world-changing discoveries.

POOL.h: In the ancient Mediterranean, the prized dye called Tyrian purple came from sea snails, and thousands of snails were needed for a small amount of dye.
POOL.b: Its huge cost made it a mark of power. In Rome, the right to wear certain purple garments was restricted by law.
POOL.m: Rarity and cost, not just beauty, give colours their meaning.

POOL.h: Egyptian blue, made by heating sand, a copper source and lime, is the oldest known synthetic pigment, first produced around 5,000 years ago.
POOL.b: Its recipe was later lost. Modern scientists found it gives off invisible infrared light when lit, which helps them detect faint traces on ancient artworks.
POOL.m: Ancient chemistry was surprisingly sophisticated.

POOL.t: Tango was born in port cities
POOL.h: Tango developed in the late 1800s in working-class neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo, on either side of the Río de la Plata.
POOL.b: It blended European, African and local traditions. In 2009, UNESCO listed it as intangible cultural heritage shared by Argentina and Uruguay.
POOL.m: Great art forms often grow from mixed, immigrant communities.

POOL.h: In 2018, UNESCO added the reggae music of Jamaica to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
POOL.b: Growing out of ska and rocksteady in the late 1960s, reggae is known for its offbeat rhythm and songs about justice, love and faith. Bob Marley helped carry it around the world.
POOL.m: A small island can shape music far beyond its shores.

POOL.h: The stories of Aladdin and Ali Baba do not appear in any known early Arabic manuscript of ‘One Thousand and One Nights’.
POOL.b: French translator Antoine Galland added them in the early 1700s, after hearing them from Hanna Diyab, a Syrian storyteller visiting Paris.
POOL.m: Famous stories often have surprising, hidden contributors.

POOL.t: The first author known by name
POOL.h: Enheduanna, a high priestess in the Mesopotamian city of Ur around 2300 BC, is often considered the first author in history known by name.
POOL.b: She wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna. She was the daughter of Sargon of Akkad, founder of one of the first empires.
POOL.m: The first writer we know by name may well have been a woman.

POOL.t: The chess queen was once weak
POOL.h: Chess grew from the Indian game chaturanga, around the 6th century.
POOL.b: For centuries, the piece beside the king was an adviser that could move only one square diagonally. In late 15th-century Europe, it became the powerful queen we know, making games much faster.
POOL.m: Rules evolve, and one change can transform a whole game.

POOL.t: Tarot began as a card game
POOL.h: Tarot cards first appeared in northern Italy in the 1400s for a trick-taking game, later called tarocchi, played with an extra suit of picture cards.
POOL.b: Using them for fortune-telling only became popular in France in the late 1700s. Tarot card games are still played in parts of Europe.
POOL.m: Objects often gain meanings far from their original purpose.

POOL.h: From 1912 to 1948, the Olympics awarded medals for painting, sculpture, architecture, literature and music inspired by sport.
POOL.b: Founder Pierre de Coubertin himself won a gold medal for literature in 1912 under a pen name. The contests were later dropped, partly because entrants were professionals.
POOL.m: The Olympics once treated art and sport as partners.

POOL.h: LEGO was founded by Danish carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen, who began making wooden toys in the early 1930s.
POOL.b: The name comes from the Danish ‘leg godt’, meaning ‘play well’. The company began making plastic bricks in 1949, and patented the modern interlocking design in 1958.
POOL.m: A simple, well-designed idea can last for generations.

POOL.t: Kabuki was started by a woman
POOL.h: Kabuki theatre is traced to Izumo no Okuni, a woman who performed new dances in Kyoto around 1603.
POOL.b: Women’s troupes became hugely popular, but in 1629 authorities banned women from the stage. Since then, male actors called onnagata have played female roles.
POOL.m: Traditions that seem timeless were often shaped by specific rules and events.

POOL.t: A king who loved to dance
POOL.h: Louis XIV of France was a keen dancer who performed in court ballets as a young man, famously appearing as the rising sun in 1653.
POOL.b: In 1661, he founded the Royal Academy of Dance. That is one reason ballet’s basic terms, like plié and jeté, are French.
POOL.m: Royal patronage turned a court pastime into a disciplined art.

POOL.h: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the world’s largest mud-brick building.
POOL.b: Rain wears away its surface, so each year the town joins a festival called the Crépissage to replaster it with fresh mud. The current building dates from 1907.
POOL.m: Some buildings survive because a whole community keeps caring for them.

POOL.h: Fortune cookies are almost unknown in China.
POOL.b: Researchers have traced them to crackers from around Kyoto, brought to California by Japanese immigrants in the early 1900s. Chinese restaurants in the United States later made them their own.
POOL.m: Many ‘traditional’ foods are really products of migration.

POOL.h: Every late autumn, Korean families and neighbours gather for kimjang, making large batches of kimchi to last through winter.
POOL.b: The shared work passes on recipes and strengthens community ties. UNESCO listed kimjang as intangible cultural heritage in 2013.
POOL.m: Food traditions are as much about people as about ingredients.

POOL.h: In 2017, UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo, or pizza maker, to its list of intangible cultural heritage.
POOL.b: The skills include kneading, stretching and spinning the dough, then baking it in a wood-fired oven. They are passed down through families and workshops in Naples.
POOL.m: Everyday crafts can be treasured as much as grand monuments.

POOL.t: A joyful festival for the dead
POOL.h: During Mexico’s Día de Muertos, around 1 and 2 November, families build altars called ofrendas with photos, candles, marigolds and the favourite foods of loved ones who have died.
POOL.b: It is a joyful remembrance rather than a sad one, blending Indigenous traditions with Catholic feast days.
POOL.m: Remembering the dead can be a celebration of life.

POOL.h: Every August, the town of Buñol in Spain holds La Tomatina, where thousands of people throw overripe tomatoes at each other for about an hour.
POOL.b: It began in 1945, reportedly after a scuffle in the town square. The town now limits numbers with tickets.
POOL.m: Odd local events can grow into global traditions.

POOL.h: Around Lunar New Year, hundreds of millions of people in China travel home to be with family.
POOL.b: The travel season, called chunyun, lasts about 40 days and involves billions of trips. It is often described as the largest annual human migration on Earth.
POOL.m: Family ties can move whole nations.

POOL.h: Thailand’s traditional new year, Songkran, is held in mid-April, in the hottest part of the year.
POOL.b: People traditionally pour water gently over the hands of elders and over Buddha images as a blessing. Today it is also famous for huge, joyful street water fights.
POOL.m: Traditions can become playful while keeping their original meaning.

POOL.h: Kintsugi is a Japanese technique of repairing broken pottery with lacquer mixed with powdered gold or silver.
