POOL.b: Instead of hiding the cracks, it highlights them. It reflects the idea that damage and repair are part of an object’s history, not something to disguise.
POOL.m: Flaws and repairs can add to beauty and meaning.

POOL.h: ‘Ka Mate’, the haka famously performed by New Zealand’s All Blacks, was composed around 1820 by the Ngāti Toa chief Te Rauparaha.
POOL.b: It celebrates his escape from enemies while hiding in a kūmara pit. Haka are performed on many occasions, including welcomes, funerals and celebrations.
POOL.m: Haka is a living tradition, not just a sporting ritual.

POOL.t: A picture that spread Christmas trees
POOL.h: Decorated Christmas trees were a German custom.
POOL.b: In 1848, the Illustrated London News printed a picture of Queen Victoria, Prince Albert and their children around a decorated tree. Albert was German, and the image helped make the tradition popular across Britain and beyond.
POOL.m: One widely shared image can spread a tradition.

POOL.h: The Parthenon in Athens, built between 447 and 432 BC, is full of subtle curves.
POOL.b: Its base rises slightly in the middle, and its columns swell a little and lean inward. These refinements may correct optical illusions that make long straight lines appear to sag.
POOL.m: Great design sometimes bends the rules to look right.

POOL.t: A ribbon cut by a horseman
POOL.h: At the opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge in 1932, before Premier Jack Lang could cut the ribbon, Francis de Groot rode up on horseback and slashed it with his sword.
POOL.b: He belonged to a group who believed a royal representative should open the bridge. The ribbon was retied and cut again.
POOL.m: Even carefully planned ceremonies can take unexpected turns.

POOL.h: Melbourne’s Royal Exhibition Building was built for the 1880 International Exhibition.
POOL.b: In 1901, it hosted the opening of the first Parliament of Australia. In 2004, it became the first building in Australia to be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List.
POOL.m: A single building can witness the birth of a nation.

POOL.h: Diwali, celebrated by Hindus, Sikhs, Jains and some Buddhists, usually falls in October or November.
POOL.b: Homes are lit with small oil lamps called diyas, and many families make rangoli, colourful patterns on the floor. It celebrates the victory of light over darkness.
POOL.m: Shared festivals can bring together different faiths and communities.

POOL.t: Penicillin grew on a forgotten dish
POOL.h: In 1928, Alexander Fleming returned from holiday to find mould growing on a bacteria culture, with a clear ring around it where the bacteria had died.
POOL.b: Over a decade later, Adelaide-born Howard Florey and Ernst Chain turned the mould’s chemical into a working medicine.
POOL.m: Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize, and antibiotics changed medicine forever.

POOL.t: Teflon came from an empty cylinder
POOL.h: In 1938, DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett opened a cylinder of gas he was using in refrigerant research, and nothing came out.
POOL.b: Cutting it open, he found a slippery white powder had formed inside. It was polytetrafluoroethylene, later sold as Teflon.
POOL.m: Some of the most useful materials were found by chemists who investigated a failure instead of throwing it away.

POOL.t: The glue that was too weak
POOL.h: In 1968, 3M scientist Spencer Silver made an adhesive that stuck lightly and peeled off cleanly, but nobody knew what to do with it.
POOL.b: Years later, colleague Art Fry used it to stop bookmarks falling out of his church hymn book. Post-it Notes went on sale in 1980.
POOL.m: An invention can wait years for the right problem to come along.

POOL.h: In November 1895, German physicist Wilhelm Röntgen noticed a screen across his lab glowing while he worked with a cathode-ray tube wrapped in black card.
POOL.b: He called the unknown rays X-rays. Within weeks he had imaged the bones of his wife’s hand, and in 1901 he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
POOL.m: He chose not to patent X-rays, so hospitals around the world could start using them almost at once.

POOL.h: When Dmitri Mendeleev published his periodic table in 1869, he left gaps for elements nobody had found yet and predicted what they would be like.
POOL.b: Gallium was discovered in 1875 and germanium in 1886, and both closely matched his predictions.
POOL.m: A good theory does not just explain what we know. It predicts what we will find.

POOL.h: Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes, for physics in 1903 and chemistry in 1911.
POOL.b: She handled radium and polonium so closely that her notebooks are still radioactive today, and they are kept in lead-lined boxes in Paris.
POOL.m: Early researchers had little idea how dangerous radiation could be.

POOL.h: Absolute zero, minus 273.15 °C, is the point where particles have the least possible motion.
POOL.b: The laws of physics say it can never quite be reached. Even so, laboratories have cooled atoms to within a billionth of a degree of it.
POOL.m: Cold is really the absence of heat energy, and there is a floor to how low it can go.

POOL.h: When lightning strikes sand or dry soil, it can melt the grains into hollow, branching tubes of natural glass called fulgurites.
POOL.b: They trace the path the electricity took into the ground and can be more than a metre long.
POOL.m: A lightning strike can leave behind a glassy fossil of itself.

POOL.h: In 1927, Professor Thomas Parnell at the University of Queensland poured heated pitch into a sealed funnel, then cut the stem open in 1930.
POOL.b: The pitch looks like a brittle solid but is actually a very thick liquid. A drop falls roughly once a decade, and watchers keep missing the moment.
POOL.m: It is recognised as the world’s longest-running laboratory experiment, and it shows solids and liquids are not always what they seem.

POOL.h: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes learned that at noon on midsummer the Sun shone straight down into a well at Syene in Egypt, while at Alexandria it cast a shadow of about 7 degrees.
POOL.b: Knowing the distance between the two cities, he calculated Earth’s circumference and got surprisingly close.
POOL.m: With a shadow and careful reasoning, an ancient scholar measured the whole planet.

POOL.t: The man who weighed the world
POOL.h: In 1798, Henry Cavendish hung lead balls from a delicate twisting wire and measured the tiny pull of gravity between them and larger weights.
POOL.b: From that faint attraction he worked out Earth’s density, about 5.5 times that of water, and so its mass.
POOL.m: Gravity between everyday objects is incredibly weak, but careful measurement can still reveal it.

POOL.h: In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a 67-metre pendulum from the dome of the Panthéon in Paris.
POOL.b: Over the day, the direction of its swing slowly turned. The pendulum was not changing course: the floor beneath it was turning with the Earth.
POOL.m: It was the first simple, visible demonstration of Earth’s rotation.

POOL.h: Around 1801, Thomas Young shone light through two narrow slits and saw stripes of light and dark on a screen, a pattern only waves make.
POOL.b: Much later, physicists fired electrons one at a time through two slits and found they still built up the same striped pattern.
POOL.m: At the smallest scales, particles and waves are not as separate as common sense suggests.

POOL.t: A shell bouncing off tissue paper
POOL.h: In 1909, researchers working with New Zealand-born physicist Ernest Rutherford fired tiny alpha particles at thin gold foil.
POOL.b: Most passed straight through, but a few bounced back. Rutherford said it was like firing a large artillery shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you.
POOL.m: The experiment revealed that every atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre.

POOL.t: The flask that ended a myth
POOL.h: People once believed life could arise on its own from rotting matter.
POOL.b: Around 1859, Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long, curved swan necks that let in air but trapped dust. The broth stayed fresh unless the neck was broken off.
POOL.m: Microbes come from other microbes, an idea that underpins hygiene and food safety today.

POOL.t: Frog legs led to the battery
POOL.h: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani saw frog legs twitch when touched with metal and decided animals held a special electricity.
POOL.b: Alessandro Volta suspected the metals instead, and in 1800 he stacked zinc and copper discs between salty cardboard to build the first battery.
POOL.m: A scientific argument between two rivals gave us the volt and portable electricity.

POOL.h: Plants need nitrogen, and most of the air is nitrogen, but plants cannot use it in that form.
POOL.b: In the early 1900s, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch developed a way to turn it into ammonia for fertiliser. Researchers estimate this now helps feed around half the world’s population.
POOL.m: One industrial chemical reaction quietly supports billions of meals every day.

POOL.h: In 1907, Belgian-born chemist Leo Baekeland in New York combined phenol and formaldehyde under heat and pressure to make Bakelite.
POOL.b: Earlier plastics were based on plant materials, but this one was made entirely from laboratory chemicals. It was soon shaped into radios, telephones and electrical fittings.
POOL.m: Bakelite launched the age of plastics, for better and for worse.

POOL.t: A Nobel Prize from sticky tape
POOL.h: In 2004, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester used ordinary sticky tape to peel graphite into thinner and thinner flakes.
POOL.b: They isolated graphene, a sheet of carbon just one atom thick, and won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
POOL.m: Graphene is extremely strong and conducts electricity well, yet it was found with a remarkably cheap method.

POOL.h: In 1957, American engineers Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes sealed two plastic sheets together, trapping air bubbles, hoping to sell a textured wallpaper.
POOL.b: It flopped, as did an attempt at greenhouse insulation. It finally took off as protective packaging for delicate goods such as computers.
POOL.m: A failed product can succeed brilliantly once it finds the right job.

POOL.t: Superglue was set aside at first
POOL.h: In 1942, Harry Coover was searching for a clear plastic for gun sights and found a chemical that stuck to everything, so he put it aside.
POOL.b: In 1951 it resurfaced during other research, and this time its stickiness was seen as the point. It went on sale in 1958.
POOL.m: Whether something is a flaw or a feature depends on the problem you are solving.

POOL.h: Seismologists now mostly use the moment magnitude scale rather than Charles Richter’s 1935 scale, which struggled with very large quakes.
POOL.b: Each whole number step means roughly 32 times more energy released. So a magnitude 7 releases about 1,000 times the energy of a magnitude 5.
POOL.m: Small differences in magnitude numbers hide enormous differences in power.

POOL.h: On 28 December 1989, a magnitude 5.6 earthquake struck Newcastle in New South Wales.
POOL.b: It killed 13 people and caused billions of dollars in damage, even though the quake itself was only moderate. Soft ground and older buildings made the effects far worse.
POOL.m: Australia sits in the middle of a tectonic plate, but it still has earthquakes, and building standards matter.

POOL.h: Tiny zircon crystals from the Jack Hills in Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, the oldest known pieces of Earth.
POOL.b: Chemical clues inside them suggest liquid water may have existed on the surface within a few hundred million years of the planet forming.
POOL.m: Grains smaller than a grain of sand can rewrite the story of the early Earth.

POOL.h: Stromatolites are layered mounds built slowly by microbes that trap and bind sediment.
POOL.b: Living examples grow in Hamelin Pool at Shark Bay, Western Australia, while fossil ones in the Pilbara are around 3.5 billion years old, among the earliest evidence of life on Earth.
POOL.m: Some of the planet’s oldest kinds of life are still at work on the Western Australian coast.

POOL.h: In 1912, German scientist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined and had slowly drifted apart, pointing to matching coastlines and fossils.
POOL.b: Many geologists dismissed him because he could not explain how continents moved. Evidence from the sea floor in the 1960s showed he was largely right.
POOL.m: A correct idea can be rejected for decades if nobody can explain how it works.

POOL.h: Rain slowly dissolves minerals from rocks, and rivers carry them to the ocean.
POOL.b: When seawater evaporates, the water leaves but the salts stay behind. Over hundreds of millions of years, this has built up to about 3.5% salt, mostly sodium chloride.
POOL.m: The sea is salty because it is where the land’s dissolved minerals end up.

POOL.t: The longest mountain range is underwater
POOL.h: The mid-ocean ridge system winds around the globe for about 65,000 km, almost all of it hidden beneath the sea.
POOL.b: It forms where tectonic plates pull apart and rising molten rock creates new ocean floor. Iceland is one of the few places where it rises above the waves.
POOL.m: Much of Earth’s volcanic activity and new crust forms out of sight on the ocean floor.

POOL.t: Water that stays liquid below zero
POOL.h: Very pure, still water can be cooled well below 0 °C without freezing, because ice crystals need something to start forming around, like a speck of dust.
POOL.b: A bottle of this supercooled water can turn to slush within seconds when it is tapped or opened.
POOL.m: Freezing is not automatic at 0 °C. It needs something to get it started.

POOL.h: Living things take in carbon, including a little radioactive carbon-14.
POOL.b: After death, the carbon-14 decays, halving roughly every 5,730 years, so measuring what remains reveals age. Beyond about 50,000 years too little is left, which is why dinosaur bones are dated by other methods.
POOL.m: Willard Libby’s method won the 1960 Nobel Prize and transformed archaeology, within its limits.

POOL.h: Around 300 BCE, Euclid proved there are infinitely many prime numbers.
POOL.b: Suppose there were a last one: multiply all the primes together and add 1. The result cannot be divided evenly by any prime on the list, so there must be another prime that was missed.
POOL.m: It is one of the oldest and most elegant proofs in mathematics, and it is still taught today.

POOL.h: In 1202, Leonardo of Pisa, later known as Fibonacci, posed a puzzle about breeding rabbits whose answer is the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and so on, with each number the sum of the two before.
POOL.b: The same book helped popularise Hindu-Arabic numerals in Europe.
POOL.m: His bigger legacy may be the digits 0 to 9 that we now use every day.

POOL.h: Any flat map can be coloured with just four colours so that no neighbouring regions share one.
POOL.b: Mathematicians suspected this from 1852 but only proved it in 1976, when Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken used a computer to check a huge number of cases.
POOL.m: It was the first major theorem proved with a computer’s help, which sparked debate about what counts as a proof.

POOL.t: A margin note that took centuries
POOL.h: Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat wrote in the margin of a book that he had a marvellous proof of a theorem, but the margin was too small to contain it.
POOL.b: Mathematicians tried for centuries to prove it. Andrew Wiles finally succeeded in 1994, using maths Fermat never had.
POOL.m: Some simple-looking problems need entire new branches of mathematics to crack.

POOL.t: A strip with only one side
POOL.h: Give a paper strip a half twist and tape its ends together, and you get a Möbius strip, described in 1858.
POOL.b: It has only one side and one edge. Cut it along the middle and, instead of two loops, you get one longer loop.
POOL.m: Everyday objects can hide surprising geometry, and a whole branch of maths called topology studies it.

POOL.h: The ancient Babylonians counted in base 60, and their system passed into astronomy and timekeeping.
POOL.b: Sixty divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30, which made fractions easy to work with. It also shaped our 360-degree circle.
POOL.m: Our clocks still carry a counting system from ancient Mesopotamia, about 4,000 years old.

POOL.h: Welsh mathematician Robert Recorde introduced the equals sign in 1557, tired of writing ‘is equal to’ over and over.
POOL.b: He chose two parallel lines because, as he put it, no two things can be more equal. His lines were much longer than the ones we use today.
POOL.m: Even the simplest maths symbols were invented by someone trying to save effort.

POOL.h: A Babylonian clay tablet called Plimpton 322, written around 1800 BCE, lists sets of whole numbers that fit the rule for right-angled triangles.
POOL.b: That is more than 1,000 years before Pythagoras was born. The theorem carries his name, but others clearly knew the pattern earlier.
POOL.m: Famous names often attach to ideas that are much older.

POOL.h: Isaac Newton himself told the story of watching an apple fall in a garden, which set him wondering why things always fall straight towards the ground.
POOL.b: The detail of it bouncing off his head was added later. The apple helped him think about gravity reaching as far as the Moon.
POOL.m: The real story is about curiosity, not a bump on the head.

POOL.h: In 1783, the Montgolfier brothers sent a sheep, a duck and a rooster up in a hot-air balloon at Versailles, watched by King Louis XVI.
POOL.b: The animals landed safely after about eight minutes. Two months later, the first people made a free balloon flight over Paris.
POOL.m: Early aviators tested whether the upper air was safe to breathe before risking human lives.

POOL.h: William Lawrence Bragg grew up in Adelaide and, with his father William Henry Bragg, worked out how to use X-rays to reveal the arrangement of atoms in crystals.
POOL.b: Father and son shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics, when Lawrence was just 25.
POOL.m: X-ray crystallography later helped reveal the structure of DNA and countless medicines.

POOL.h: In the 1850s, Scottish-born newspaper printer James Harrison in Geelong, Victoria, built one of the first practical mechanical ice-making machines, using the cooling effect of evaporating ether.
POOL.b: He later tried shipping frozen meat to Britain, but the attempt failed when the ice melted.
POOL.m: Refrigeration went on to transform Australia’s economy by letting meat and dairy reach distant markets.

POOL.h: Gold is so malleable it can be beaten into leaf less than a ten-thousandth of a millimetre thick.
POOL.b: At that thinness, light passes through it and looks greenish. Gilders use such leaf to cover frames, domes and book edges with very little metal.
POOL.m: A tiny amount of gold can cover a large area, which is why gilding has been used for thousands of years.

POOL.h: In 1842, Christian Doppler predicted that the pitch of a wave changes when its source moves towards or away from you.
POOL.b: In 1845, Dutch scientist Christophorus Buys Ballot tested it with musicians playing a steady note on a moving train while listeners with trained ears judged the pitch.
POOL.m: The same effect explains passing sirens and lets astronomers measure how fast stars are moving.

POOL.t: The sea is blue by itself
POOL.h: Water itself is very faintly blue.
POOL.b: It absorbs red light slightly more than blue, which is invisible in a glass but obvious through metres of water. That is why deep, clear water still looks blue even under a grey sky.
POOL.m: The colour of the ocean comes largely from the water itself, not only from the sky above it.

POOL.h: In 2007, astronomers combing through old data from the Parkes radio telescope in New South Wales found a single, extremely bright radio burst lasting just a few milliseconds.
POOL.b: It came from far beyond our galaxy. It was the first known fast radio burst, and many more have been detected since.
POOL.m: One of astronomy’s big modern puzzles was first spotted in Australian data.

POOL.t: The Parkes signals from a microwave
POOL.h: For years, the Parkes telescope picked up strange, short radio bursts nicknamed perytons.
POOL.b: In 2015, astronomer Emily Petroff and colleagues traced them to staff opening the site’s microwave oven door before it had finished, which released a brief burst of radio waves.
POOL.m: Good science rules out ordinary explanations before claiming an extraordinary one.

POOL.h: Many Aboriginal peoples see an emu in the Milky Way, formed not by stars but by dark dust lanes, with its head at the Coalsack beside the Southern Cross.
POOL.b: How the emu appears through the year was linked to real emu behaviour, such as when to collect eggs.
POOL.m: Aboriginal astronomy wove the night sky into practical knowledge of seasons and food.

POOL.h: Many Aboriginal cultures across Australia tell of the Pleiades star cluster as sisters pursued across the sky by a man, often linked to stars in Orion.
POOL.b: Ancient Greek myth tells a strikingly similar tale of seven sisters chased by the hunter Orion.
POOL.m: People on opposite sides of the world looked at the same stars and told remarkably similar stories.

POOL.h: On 29 November 1967, WRESAT, a satellite built in Adelaide, lifted off from Woomera in South Australia.
POOL.b: That made Australia one of the first handful of countries to launch a satellite from its own territory. WRESAT studied the upper atmosphere and radiation from the Sun.
POOL.m: The South Australian desert once put Australia near the front of the space age.

POOL.h: In 1971, a British Black Arrow rocket lifted off from Woomera and placed the Prospero satellite into orbit.
POOL.b: Remarkably, the government had already cancelled the program, so Black Arrow never flew again. Prospero kept sending signals for years afterwards.
POOL.m: Woomera was a key testing ground for Britain’s rocket program after World War II.

POOL.h: In 1979, the falling US space station Skylab broke up over Western Australia, scattering debris near Esperance.
POOL.b: The local shire issued NASA a $400 fine for littering. It went unpaid for 30 years, until an American radio host raised the money in 2009.
POOL.m: Space hardware has to come down somewhere, which is why re-entries are now planned much more carefully.

POOL.h: In 1969, a meteorite broke apart over Murchison in Victoria.
POOL.b: Scientists found it contained amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, and tiny dust grains that formed around other stars before our Sun even existed.
POOL.m: Some ingredients of life are made in space and delivered to planets by falling rocks.

POOL.t: A giant crater in the Kimberley
POOL.h: In remote northern Western Australia lies Wolfe Creek Crater, about 880 metres across, blasted out when an iron meteorite struck the ground.
POOL.b: The local Jaru people know it as Kandimalal and have their own stories of its making. It is one of the best-preserved impact craters on Earth.
POOL.m: Impacts have shaped Earth’s surface, though erosion hides most of the evidence.

POOL.t: Hammer and feather on the Moon
POOL.h: In 1971, Apollo 15 commander David Scott dropped a geologist’s hammer and a falcon feather at the same time on the Moon.
POOL.b: With no air to slow the feather, both hit the ground together, in front of a live television audience back on Earth.
POOL.m: It confirmed Galileo’s idea that, without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate.

POOL.h: In 1970, after an oxygen tank exploded on Apollo 13, Jack Swigert radioed ‘Houston, we’ve had a problem here’, and Jim Lovell repeated ‘Houston, we’ve had a problem’.
POOL.b: Neither said the famous film version, ‘Houston, we have a problem’. The crew used their lunar module as a lifeboat and returned safely to Earth.
POOL.m: Calm teamwork under pressure turned a near-disaster into one of NASA’s finest moments.

POOL.h: On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
POOL.b: It was a polished metal sphere about 58 cm wide with four long antennas, and radio operators around the world could tune in to its simple beeping signal.
POOL.m: That small beep started the space race.

POOL.h: On 16 June 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova launched aboard Vostok 6.
POOL.b: She orbited Earth 48 times in almost three days, more time in space than all American astronauts had logged up to then combined. She had been a textile worker and amateur parachutist.
POOL.m: She was just 26, and it would be 19 years before another woman flew in space.

POOL.h: In 1984, Sydney-born oceanographer Paul Scully-Power flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger, studying the oceans from orbit.
POOL.b: He was the first Australian-born person in space. Adelaide-born Andy Thomas later flew on four Shuttle missions and lived aboard the Russian space station Mir.
POOL.m: Australians have a small but real place in the history of human spaceflight.

POOL.h: Mercury’s days are hot enough to melt lead, yet its poles hold water ice, even though it is the closest planet to the Sun.
POOL.b: Deep craters there never see sunlight, so they stay far below freezing. NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft confirmed the ice in 2012.
POOL.m: Permanent shadow can keep ice frozen even close to the Sun.

POOL.h: Jupiter is the largest planet, yet it spins the fastest, turning once in just under 10 hours.
POOL.b: The rapid spin makes it noticeably wider at the equator than from pole to pole, and helps stretch its clouds into colourful bands.
POOL.m: Size does not slow a planet down, and Jupiter’s spin shapes both its form and its weather.

POOL.t: Saturn’s rings are thinner than paper
POOL.h: Saturn’s main rings stretch about 280,000 km across, yet they are typically only around 10 metres thick.
POOL.b: They are made of countless chunks of ice and rock, from dust grains to boulders. Relative to their width, they are far thinner than a sheet of paper.
POOL.m: Some of the most striking sights in space are also incredibly delicate.

POOL.h: Every 13 to 16 years, Earth lines up with the plane of Saturn’s rings.
POOL.b: Seen exactly edge-on, the thin rings almost vanish in small telescopes. Galileo was baffled in 1612 when the ‘ears’ he had seen on Saturn seemed to disappear.
POOL.m: Our changing viewing angle can make even huge features seem to come and go.

POOL.h: Neptune has the fastest winds measured on any planet, reaching around 2,000 km/h, faster than the speed of sound on Earth.
POOL.b: Scientists are still working out how such a cold, distant world, receiving so little sunlight, drives such violent weather.
POOL.m: Planetary weather can be powered by a planet’s inner heat, not just by sunlight.

POOL.h: In 1781, William Herschel spotted Uranus with a homemade telescope, the first planet discovered in recorded history.
POOL.b: He wanted to name it Georgium Sidus, meaning George’s Star, after King George III. Astronomers eventually settled on Uranus, the Greek god of the sky.
POOL.m: The discovery doubled the size of the known solar system overnight.

POOL.h: In 1930, Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old in Oxford, suggested the name Pluto for the newly found world, after the Roman god of the underworld.
POOL.b: Her grandfather passed the idea on to astronomers, who chose it unanimously. Its first two letters also honoured Percival Lowell, who had searched for it.
POOL.m: Anyone can contribute to science, even from the breakfast table.

POOL.h: When NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015, it revealed a huge, pale, heart-shaped region.
POOL.b: Its western lobe, called Sputnik Planitia, is a vast plain of frozen nitrogen that slowly churns and renews its surface, a little like a lava lamp.
POOL.m: Even small, distant, frozen worlds can be geologically active.

POOL.h: Ceres, about 940 km across, is the largest object in the asteroid belt and the first to be found, in 1801.
POOL.b: It was called a planet for decades, then an asteroid, and since 2006 a dwarf planet. NASA’s Dawn spacecraft found bright salt deposits in its craters.
POOL.m: Labels in astronomy change as we learn more, even when the object itself does not.

POOL.t: The asteroid belt is mostly empty
POOL.h: Films show spaceships dodging tightly packed rocks, but asteroids in the main belt are usually hundreds of thousands of kilometres apart.
POOL.b: Spacecraft cross it without steering around anything. All the belt’s asteroids together add up to only a few percent of the Moon’s mass.
POOL.m: Space is so vast that even a crowded region is overwhelmingly empty.

POOL.t: The rock that ended the dinosaurs
POOL.h: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid roughly 10 km wide struck what is now Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater, around 180 km across.
POOL.b: Dust and gases blocked sunlight and triggered a mass extinction that wiped out the non-bird dinosaurs.
POOL.m: Mammals, and eventually humans, rose in the world that was left behind.

POOL.t: The blast that flattened a forest
POOL.h: In 1908, something from space exploded in the air above Tunguska in Siberia, flattening around 80 million trees over roughly 2,000 square kilometres.
POOL.b: No crater was found, because the object, probably a small asteroid or comet, burst apart before reaching the ground.
POOL.m: Events like this are why space agencies track near-Earth objects and test ways to deflect them.

POOL.t: A moon bigger than a planet
POOL.h: Jupiter’s moon Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, about 5,270 km wide and bigger than the planet Mercury.
POOL.b: It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, and it probably hides a salty ocean beneath its icy crust.
POOL.m: What makes something a moon is what it orbits, not how big it is.

POOL.h: Jupiter’s moon Io is the most volcanically active body in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes, some throwing plumes hundreds of kilometres high.
POOL.b: Jupiter’s gravity constantly squeezes and flexes it, heating its interior, much as bending a paperclip back and forth makes it warm.
POOL.m: Gravity can do more than hold things in orbit. It can melt rock.

POOL.h: Neptune’s largest moon, Triton, circles the planet in the opposite direction to Neptune’s spin.
POOL.b: It is the only large moon in the solar system to do this, so scientists think it was captured from the Kuiper Belt, the icy zone beyond Neptune. It even has geysers.
POOL.m: A moon’s orbit can reveal where it came from.

POOL.t: A Martian moon on borrowed time
POOL.h: Mars’s moon Phobos orbits so close that it circles the planet about three times a day, and it is slowly spiralling inward.
POOL.b: In roughly 30 to 50 million years, it is expected to either crash into Mars or be torn apart into a ring.
POOL.m: The solar system is still changing, just on timescales far longer than a human life.

POOL.t: Mars’s moons are Fear and Dread
POOL.h: American astronomer Asaph Hall discovered Mars’s two small moons in 1877 and named them Phobos and Deimos, Greek for fear and dread.
POOL.b: In myth, they were sons of Ares, the Greek counterpart of Mars, who went with him into battle. Both are small and lumpy, like potatoes.
POOL.m: Astronomers often borrow from mythology, keeping ancient stories alive in the sky.

POOL.h: The leading explanation for the Moon’s origin is that a Mars-sized body, often called Theia, collided with the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.
POOL.b: Debris thrown into orbit gradually clumped together to form the Moon. Apollo rocks, strikingly similar to Earth’s, support the idea.
POOL.m: Our Moon may exist thanks to a colossal collision early in Earth’s history.

POOL.t: The Moon rang like a bell
POOL.h: In 1969, after Apollo 12 astronauts left the Moon, mission controllers crashed their discarded lunar module ascent stage into the surface.
POOL.b: Seismometers the crew had set up recorded vibrations lasting nearly an hour. The Moon’s dry, fractured rock carried the shaking far longer than rock on Earth would.
POOL.m: Moonquake recordings helped scientists work out what lies inside the Moon.

POOL.h: Astronauts on Apollo 11, 14 and 15 left panels of special reflectors on the Moon.
POOL.b: Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at them and time the return flash, which takes about 2.5 seconds. That measures the Moon’s distance to within a few millimetres.
POOL.m: These measurements revealed the Moon’s slow drift away from Earth and have tested Einstein’s theory of gravity.

POOL.h: In September 1859, a huge solar storm struck Earth.
POOL.b: Auroras were seen as close to the equator as the Caribbean, and telegraph systems sparked, shocked operators and in some cases kept working with their batteries disconnected. It is named after astronomer Richard Carrington, who saw the flare.
POOL.m: A storm that size today could seriously disrupt satellites, GPS and power grids.

POOL.t: A star that would swallow Mars
POOL.h: Betelgeuse, the red star in Orion, is a red supergiant.
POOL.b: If it replaced our Sun, its surface would reach beyond the orbit of Mars. It is expected to explode as a supernova, though probably not for many thousands of years.
POOL.m: Big, bright stars live fast and die young compared with small, steady stars like our Sun.

POOL.h: Sirius, in the constellation Canis Major, is the brightest star in the night sky.
POOL.b: It is about 8.6 light-years away and roughly 25 times more luminous than the Sun. Ancient Egyptians watched for its first dawn appearance each year as a sign the Nile flood was near.
POOL.m: Stars have been used as calendars for thousands of years.

POOL.h: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
POOL.b: Found in 1846, it only completed its first full orbit since its discovery in July 2011.
POOL.m: Some cycles are longer than a human life. Astronomers work across generations.

POOL.h: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds look like detached pieces of the Milky Way, but they are separate, smaller galaxies close to our own.
POOL.b: They lie about 160,000 and 200,000 light-years away and are best seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Aboriginal peoples told stories about them long before Magellan sailed.
POOL.m: From a dark Australian sky, you can see other galaxies without any telescope.

POOL.h: At the centre of the Milky Way sits Sagittarius A*, a black hole about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.
POOL.b: Astronomers proved it was there by tracking stars whipping around an invisible object over decades. The work earned a share of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.
POOL.m: Even when we cannot see something, its effect on its neighbours can reveal it.

POOL.t: The woman who measured the universe
POOL.h: In 1912, Henrietta Swan Leavitt, employed at Harvard to study photographic plates, showed that pulsing stars called Cepheids brighten and dim at a rate linked to their true brightness.
POOL.b: By comparing true and apparent brightness, astronomers could finally work out distances to faraway stars.
POOL.m: Her discovery became the measuring stick Edwin Hubble used to show the universe is expanding.

POOL.h: Until the 1920s, many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe and that fuzzy spirals were clouds within it.
POOL.b: In 1924, Edwin Hubble found Cepheid stars in the Andromeda ‘nebula’ and showed it was far too distant to be part of our galaxy.
POOL.m: In one discovery, the known universe grew from a single galaxy to countless.

POOL.h: In 1925, Cecilia Payne showed in her PhD thesis that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
POOL.b: Leading astronomers assumed stars had a make-up similar to Earth’s, and she was persuaded to describe her result as almost certainly not real.
POOL.m: She was right, and her thesis is now considered one of the most important in astronomy.

POOL.h: In 1967, Cambridge PhD student Jocelyn Bell Burnell noticed a strange, perfectly regular radio pulse in her telescope data.
POOL.b: Half jokingly, the team labelled it LGM-1, for little green men. It turned out to be the first known pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star.
POOL.m: Careful attention to an odd bit of data led to a major discovery.

POOL.h: When the Hubble Space Telescope reached orbit in 1990, its images were blurry.
POOL.b: Its main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape by about 2 micrometres, roughly one-fiftieth the width of a human hair. In 1993, astronauts fitted corrective optics, like glasses for the telescope.
POOL.m: Hubble went on to become one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.

POOL.h: In January 1610, Galileo pointed his small telescope at Jupiter and saw four points of light that shifted position night after night.
POOL.b: He realised they were moons orbiting Jupiter. Today they are called the Galilean moons: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
POOL.m: It showed that not everything in the heavens circles Earth, weakening the old Earth-centred view.

POOL.h: In November 1572, a brilliant new star appeared in the constellation Cassiopeia, for a time outshining Venus before fading over many months.
POOL.b: Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe measured it carefully and showed it lay far beyond the Moon. We now know it was a supernova.
POOL.m: It challenged the ancient belief that the heavens beyond the Moon never change.

POOL.t: A supernova seen from the south
POOL.h: In February 1987, a star exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and it was visible to the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.
POOL.b: Detectors on Earth caught a burst of ghostly particles called neutrinos a few hours before the light arrived.
POOL.m: It was the closest supernova seen in nearly 400 years and confirmed how massive stars die.

POOL.t: Comet tails can lead the way
POOL.h: A comet’s tail does not stream behind it like smoke from a train.
POOL.b: Sunlight and the solar wind push its gas and dust away from the Sun, so as a comet heads back out of the inner solar system, its tail actually leads the way.
POOL.m: Sunlight and the solar wind exert real pressure on everything they touch.

POOL.h: Each Voyager spacecraft carries a gold-plated record with sounds and images of Earth, including spoken greetings in 55 languages, music ranging from Bach to Chuck Berry, and instructions for playing it.
POOL.b: The project was led by astronomer Carl Sagan.
POOL.m: It is a time capsule that may outlast almost every other human-made object.

POOL.t: Earth as a pale blue dot
POOL.h: In 1990, at Carl Sagan’s urging, Voyager 1 turned its camera back from about 6 billion km away and photographed Earth.
POOL.b: Our planet appeared as a tiny speck, less than a pixel wide, caught in a band of scattered sunlight.
POOL.m: The image became a powerful reminder of how small and fragile our shared home is.

POOL.h: At the International Space Station’s height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground.
POOL.b: Astronauts float because the station and everyone in it are constantly falling towards Earth, while moving sideways so fast that they keep missing it.
POOL.m: An orbit is simply a fall that never hits the ground.

POOL.h: Everything we can see, from stars to people, makes up only around 5% of the universe’s contents.
POOL.b: Roughly 27% is dark matter, detected by its gravity, and about 68% is dark energy, which appears to be speeding up the universe’s expansion.
POOL.m: Most of the universe is made of things scientists still cannot directly explain.

POOL.t: A planet around a Sun-like star
POOL.h: In 1995, Swiss astronomers Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found a planet orbiting the star 51 Pegasi.
POOL.b: It was a giant like Jupiter but circled its star in just four days, a kind of planet nobody had expected. They shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
POOL.m: Thousands of planets around other stars have since been found, showing planetary systems are common.

POOL.h: Valles Marineris on Mars stretches about 4,000 km, roughly the width of Australia, and plunges up to about 7 km deep.
POOL.b: Unlike the Grand Canyon, it was not mainly carved by a river but formed as the Martian crust cracked and pulled apart.
POOL.m: Mars holds some of the most dramatic landscapes in the solar system.

POOL.h: The air pressure on the surface of Venus is about 90 times that on Earth, similar to being about 900 metres under the sea.
POOL.b: Soviet Venera landers were built like submarines, and in 1970 Venera 7 sent the first data ever received from another planet’s surface.
POOL.m: Venus shows how a runaway greenhouse effect can make a planet hostile.

POOL.h: At Tidbinbilla, near Canberra, giant dishes form one of NASA’s three Deep Space Network sites, along with California and Spain.
POOL.b: The sites are spread around the globe so that, as Earth turns, at least one can always stay in contact with distant spacecraft.
POOL.m: Spacecraft across the solar system rely on Australian soil to phone home.

POOL.h: In December 2020, a capsule from Japan’s Hayabusa2 spacecraft parachuted into the Woomera area of South Australia.
POOL.b: It carried samples collected from the asteroid Ryugu. Scientists later found amino acids and other organic material in the tiny grains.
POOL.m: Australia’s vast, empty outback makes an ideal landing site for precious space samples.

POOL.t: The first spacewalk nearly went wrong
POOL.h: In March 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his spacecraft for about 12 minutes.
POOL.b: His suit ballooned in the vacuum so much that he could not fit back through the hatch. He had to let air out of his suit to squeeze inside.
POOL.m: Early spaceflight relied on improvisation as much as planning.

POOL.t: Earthrise changed how we saw home
POOL.h: On 24 December 1968, Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders photographed Earth rising over the Moon’s horizon.
POOL.b: He and his crewmates were the first people to orbit the Moon and see our whole planet as a globe. The photo, Earthrise, is often credited with inspiring the environmental movement.
POOL.m: Seeing Earth from afar made its fragility suddenly visible.

POOL.h: In the late 1970s, the outer planets lined up in a way that happens only about once every 175 years.
POOL.b: Voyager 2 used this to fly past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, using each planet’s gravity to slingshot on to the next.
POOL.m: Gravity assists let small spacecraft reach distant worlds without enormous amounts of fuel.

POOL.t: Moths that navigate by the stars
POOL.h: Bogong moths can steer by the night sky.
POOL.b: Each spring, billions fly up to 1,000 km from south-eastern Australia to cool caves in the Australian Alps. A 2025 study found they use the pattern of the stars and the Milky Way to hold their course.
POOL.m: Bogong moths are the first insects shown to use the stars for long-distance navigation.

POOL.t: The frogmouth is not an owl
POOL.h: The tawny frogmouth looks like an owl but is not one.
POOL.b: It is more closely related to nightjars, and it catches insects with its wide beak rather than grabbing prey with its feet. By day it freezes on a branch, looking remarkably like a broken stump.
POOL.m: Looking alike is not the same as being related.

POOL.h: Male platypuses carry a venomous spur on each hind leg.
POOL.b: The venom is not deadly to people, but it causes intense pain that can last for days and resists ordinary painkillers. Males produce more of it in the breeding season, which suggests it is mainly used against rival males.
POOL.m: Venomous mammals are rare, and Australia is home to one of the best known.

POOL.h: The blue-ringed octopus is only about the size of a golf ball.
POOL.b: Its bite carries tetrodotoxin, which can paralyse the muscles used for breathing, and there is no antivenom. People have survived when given rescue breathing until the toxin wears off.
POOL.m: In rock pools, look but never pick up a small octopus, however pretty.

POOL.t: A jellyfish smaller than a fingernail
POOL.h: One of the most dangerous jellyfish in Australian waters can be about a centimetre across.
POOL.b: Irukandji jellyfish are nearly transparent, and a sting that feels mild at first can trigger severe pain, vomiting and dangerously high blood pressure within about half an hour.
POOL.m: Tropical stinger season warnings apply even when you cannot see anything in the water.

POOL.h: The leafy seadragon is covered in frond-like flaps that make it look like drifting seaweed.
POOL.b: It lives only in southern Australian waters and is the marine emblem of South Australia. Like seahorses, the male carries the eggs, attached under his tail.
POOL.m: Some of Australia’s strangest animals live just off its southern coast.

POOL.h: The pistol shrimp snaps its claw so fast that it creates a collapsing bubble of water.
POOL.b: The collapse makes one of the loudest sounds in the ocean and a tiny flash of light. The shock stuns small prey nearby.
POOL.m: Colonies of snapping shrimp are loud enough to interfere with navy sonar.

POOL.h: Mantis shrimp strike with one of the fastest punches in the animal kingdom.
POOL.b: Their club-like limbs accelerate so quickly that they create collapsing bubbles in the water, and they can crack snail shells and even aquarium glass. Engineers study their clubs to design tougher materials.
POOL.m: Nature’s toughest designs often come from animals only a few centimetres long.

POOL.h: Geckos climb glass using millions of microscopic hairs on their toes.
POOL.b: Each hair splits into even finer tips that get so close to a surface that weak forces between molecules hold them there. Changing the angle of the toe breaks the grip instantly.
POOL.m: Researchers have copied gecko feet to make reusable dry adhesives.

POOL.t: Sloths have gardens in their fur
POOL.h: Sloths move so slowly that algae grows in their fur, giving them a greenish tint.
POOL.b: Their fur also hosts moths and other small creatures. Most sloths climb down only about once a week to go to the toilet, a risky trip for such a slow animal.
POOL.m: A slow life can become a home for a whole community of other species.

POOL.h: Elephants communicate with deep rumbles too low for human ears to hear.
POOL.b: These infrasound calls can travel several kilometres through the air and the ground. Elephants may pick up the vibrations through sensitive nerve endings in their feet and trunks.
POOL.m: A savanna that seems quiet to us may be full of elephant conversations.

POOL.h: Lions, tigers, leopards and jaguars can roar but cannot purr continuously.
POOL.b: Cheetahs, cougars and house cats purr but cannot roar. The difference comes largely from the structure of the voice box and a small bone in the throat.
POOL.m: Even within one family of animals, small anatomical changes create very different voices.

POOL.h: The Arctic tern makes the longest known migration of any animal.
POOL.b: It breeds in the Arctic and spends the southern summer near Antarctica, flying tens of thousands of kilometres a year. Because it follows summer, it sees more daylight than almost any other creature.
POOL.m: Over a lifetime of about 30 years, one tern may fly the distance to the Moon and back about three times.

POOL.h: Chameleons change colour mostly to communicate and control their temperature, not to hide.
POOL.b: Their skin contains tiny crystals that reflect different colours as the skin stretches or relaxes. Males flash bright colours to warn rivals or attract females.
POOL.m: A popular explanation can be partly true and still miss the main point.

POOL.h: Flamingos are not born pink.
POOL.b: Chicks hatch grey or white and gain their colour from pigments in the algae and small crustaceans they eat. In zoos, keepers add these pigments to the food, or the birds slowly fade.
POOL.m: You really can be coloured by what you eat, if you are a flamingo.

POOL.h: A starling murmuration has no leader.
POOL.b: A 2008 study found each bird tracks about seven of its nearest neighbours, matching their speed and direction. Thousands of these small adjustments produce the huge, rippling shapes that move across the evening sky.
POOL.m: Complex group behaviour can come from simple rules followed by everyone.

POOL.h: Most land plants live in partnership with fungi around their roots.
POOL.b: The fungi spread fine threads through the soil and pass water and nutrients to the plant. In return, the plant feeds the fungi with sugars made by photosynthesis.
POOL.m: Healthy soil is not just dirt. It is a living trading network.

POOL.h: Some species of bamboo can grow close to a metre in a single day.
POOL.b: Bamboo is a giant grass, not a tree, and a new shoot reaches its full height within a few months. It then spends the following years hardening rather than growing taller.
POOL.m: Fast growth and lasting strength are often two separate stages.

POOL.t: A plant with only two leaves
POOL.h: Welwitschia grows just two leaves in its entire life, and they never stop growing.
POOL.b: This desert plant from Namibia and Angola can live for over 1,000 years. Its leaves split and fray in the wind, so old plants look like a tangled heap.
POOL.m: In harsh places, patience can be a better strategy than speed.

POOL.h: Many banksias keep their seeds locked in woody cones for years.
POOL.b: The cones often open only after the heat of a bushfire, releasing seeds onto freshly cleared, ash-rich ground. This means the next generation starts when there is less competition.
POOL.m: Many Australian plants do not just survive fire. They depend on it.

POOL.h: The boab tree of the Kimberley stores water in its swollen trunk to survive the long dry season.
POOL.b: Boabs can live for many centuries. One hollow boab near Derby in Western Australia is known as the Prison Boab Tree.
POOL.m: Aboriginal people have long used boabs for food, water and medicine.

POOL.h: The Queensland lungfish can gulp air using a single lung.
POOL.b: Fossils show it has changed remarkably little in about 100 million years. It lives in only a few rivers in south-east Queensland and is protected by law.
POOL.m: Some living species are windows into what life looked like in the age of dinosaurs.

POOL.h: The last known thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, died at Hobart’s Beaumaris Zoo in 1936.
POOL.b: It was a striped, dog-like marsupial that once lived across mainland Australia and New Guinea. Bounties paid for killing thylacines helped push the species to extinction.
POOL.m: Just 59 days earlier, Tasmania had finally given the species legal protection.

POOL.h: Grey-headed flying foxes can travel tens of kilometres in a night to feed.
POOL.b: As they move between trees, they carry pollen and seeds across long distances. Many eucalypts and rainforest plants rely on them for pollination, especially at night.
POOL.m: Noisy bats in a park may be doing essential work for the bush.

POOL.h: The wedge-tailed eagle is Australia’s largest bird of prey.
POOL.b: Its wingspan can reach about 2.3 metres, and it often soars on thermals high above open country. Pairs may use and rebuild the same huge stick nest for many years.
POOL.m: Wedge-tails are now protected across Australia after decades of being culled as pests.

POOL.h: Female superb fairy-wrens sing to their eggs before they hatch.
POOL.b: The chicks learn a note from this call and use it when begging for food. Cuckoo chicks spend less time in the egg and learn the note poorly, so parents can spot the imposters by their call.
POOL.m: Learning can begin before birth, even in birds.

POOL.h: About three quarters of animals in the deep open ocean can make their own light.
POOL.b: Called bioluminescence, it is used to attract prey, find mates and confuse predators. Most of the light is blue, the colour that travels furthest through seawater.
POOL.m: The largest habitat on Earth is dark, but it is far from unlit.

POOL.h: Every night, huge numbers of small fish, squid and plankton rise hundreds of metres towards the ocean surface to feed.
POOL.b: Before dawn they sink back into the dark to hide from predators. It is thought to be the largest migration of animals on Earth, happening every day.
POOL.m: The ocean’s daily commute helps carry carbon from the surface into the deep sea.

POOL.h: When a whale dies and sinks to the seabed, it becomes a feast called a whale fall.
POOL.b: Sharks and scavengers strip the flesh, then worms and bacteria feed on the bones for years or even decades. Some species are found almost nowhere else.
POOL.m: In nature, even an ending can support new life for a long time.

POOL.h: Humpback whale songs spread across oceans like popular tunes.
POOL.b: Researchers found new songs from eastern Australia moving east across the South Pacific to French Polynesia over about two years. Male humpbacks in a region all sing the same song, and it keeps changing.
POOL.m: Culture, in the form of shared learned behaviour, is not unique to humans.

POOL.h: A fluffy cumulus cloud can hold around 500 tonnes of water.
POOL.b: That water is spread through a huge volume as tiny droplets, each light enough to be held up by rising air. Bigger storm clouds hold far more.
POOL.m: Something can look light and still carry enormous weight.

POOL.h: Falling raindrops are not shaped like teardrops.
POOL.b: Small ones are nearly round, and larger ones flatten on the bottom as air pushes against them, looking more like a hamburger bun. Very big drops break apart as they fall.
POOL.m: Even familiar symbols can be based on a mistake.

POOL.h: Lightning flashes around the world roughly 40 to 50 times every second.
POOL.b: Most strikes happen over land in the tropics, where warm, moist air rises fastest. Only a fraction reach the ground, and most stay within or between clouds.
POOL.m: At any moment, thousands of thunderstorms are active somewhere on Earth.

POOL.h: The Morning Glory cloud rolls over the Gulf of Carpentaria most springs.
POOL.b: It is a tube-shaped cloud that can stretch for hundreds of kilometres and often appears at dawn near the Queensland town of Burketown. Glider pilots travel there to ride the rising air in front of it.
POOL.m: Some weather is so reliable and spectacular that it becomes a tourist event.

POOL.h: Mushrooms are more closely related to animals than to plants.
POOL.b: Fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight, and their cell walls contain chitin, the same material found in insect shells. Genetic studies place fungi and animals on the same main branch of life.
POOL.m: The world is not neatly split into plants and animals.

POOL.h: Australia’s ghost fungus glows a soft green in the dark.
POOL.b: It grows on dead and dying trees in forests across southern Australia, often in autumn. The light is made by a chemical reaction inside the fungus, a kind of bioluminescence.
POOL.m: On a dark forest walk after rain, switching off your torch can reveal a hidden light show.

POOL.h: A tropical fungus can take over the behaviour of carpenter ants.
POOL.b: Infected ants climb onto a leaf, clamp down with their jaws and die in a spot ideal for the fungus. It then grows a stalk from the ant’s head to rain spores on the ants below.
POOL.m: Parasites can shape the behaviour of their hosts in startling ways.

POOL.t: A brainless blob that plans routes
POOL.h: A slime mould called Physarum polycephalum can find the shortest route through a maze.
POOL.b: In a 2010 experiment, researchers placed food on a map in the pattern of the towns around Tokyo, and the slime mould grew a network strikingly similar to the real rail system. It has no brain at all.
POOL.m: Efficient solutions can emerge from simple growth, without any planning.

POOL.h: A lichen is not a single organism.
POOL.b: It is a fungus living together with algae or bacteria that make food from sunlight. The fungus provides shelter and moisture, which lets lichens grow on bare rock, tree bark and even gravestones.
POOL.m: Cooperation lets living things survive where neither partner could alone.

POOL.h: Tasmania is home to one of the tallest flowering plants on Earth.
POOL.b: A mountain ash nicknamed Centurion, in the state’s south, stands about 100 metres tall. Only a yellow meranti in Borneo has been measured slightly taller, and a few conifers, such as California’s coast redwoods, grow taller still.
POOL.m: Australia’s forests hold some of the tallest trees on the planet.

POOL.t: An octopus thinks with its arms
POOL.h: About two thirds of an octopus’s neurons are in its arms, not its brain.
POOL.b: Each arm can taste, touch and make simple decisions on its own, even reaching for food without instructions from the brain. The brain sets goals while the arms handle the details.
POOL.m: Intelligence does not have to live in one central place.

POOL.h: The kakapo of New Zealand is the world’s heaviest parrot, and it cannot fly.
POOL.b: It feeds at night, climbs trees and waddles through the forest. With so few left, every kakapo has a name and is closely monitored by conservation workers.
POOL.m: Islands without mammal predators produced birds that no longer needed to fly.

POOL.h: Rats make high-pitched chirps when they are tickled, too high for us to hear.
POOL.b: Neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found they would chase the researcher’s hand to be tickled again. Scientists now use these sounds to study positive emotions in animals.
POOL.m: Play and joy seem to run deeper in the animal kingdom than once thought.

POOL.h: A tiger’s stripes are not just in its fur.
POOL.b: Its skin underneath is striped too, so a shaved tiger would still show its pattern. No two tigers share exactly the same stripes, which lets researchers identify individual tigers from camera trap photos.
POOL.m: Nature gives each tiger its own built-in ID card.

POOL.h: Polar bears have black skin under their white-looking fur.
POOL.b: Each hair is actually transparent with a hollow core, and it appears white because it scatters sunlight, much like snow does. Their thick fur and a layer of fat, rather than the dark skin, do most of the work of keeping them warm.
POOL.m: What we see is often about how light behaves, not the true colour of a thing.

POOL.t: A giraffe’s neck, a human count
POOL.h: A giraffe has seven bones in its neck, the same number as a human.
POOL.b: Each one is simply much longer, up to about 25 centimetres. Almost all mammals share this count of seven, whatever the length of their neck.
POOL.m: Evolution tends to stretch existing parts rather than add new ones.

POOL.t: The frog that births by mouth
POOL.h: The gastric-brooding frog of Queensland swallowed its fertilised eggs.
POOL.b: The young developed in the mother’s stomach, which stopped producing acid, and she then gave birth to them through her mouth. Both known species disappeared in the 1980s.
POOL.m: When a species is lost, we may also lose knowledge we never had the chance to learn.

POOL.t: Everest would vanish in the trench
POOL.h: The deepest known point in the ocean is Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.
POOL.b: It lies about 10,900 metres below the surface. If Mount Everest were placed in it, its summit would still be more than 2 km underwater.
POOL.m: Far more people have stood on Everest’s summit than have visited Challenger Deep.

POOL.h: Russia stretches across eleven time zones.
POOL.b: When people in Kaliningrad, on the Baltic Sea, are finishing dinner, people in Kamchatka, on the Pacific, are waking up to the next day. The country covers more than one ninth of Earth’s land.
POOL.m: Russia is so wide that its east and west live almost half a day apart.

POOL.h: China is about as wide as the continental United States, yet it officially uses a single time zone.
POOL.b: All clocks follow Beijing time, so in the far western region of Xinjiang the sun can rise very late by the clock. Many people there informally use a local time two hours behind.
POOL.m: Time zones are political decisions as much as geographic ones.

POOL.h: Istanbul sits on both Europe and Asia.
POOL.b: The Bosphorus Strait runs through the middle of the city, dividing its European and Asian sides, and bridges and tunnels link them. Locals can commute between continents every day.
POOL.m: The line between continents is sometimes just a short ferry ride.

POOL.t: A border through the living room
POOL.h: In the towns of Baarle-Hertog and Baarle-Nassau, the Belgium and Netherlands border zigzags through streets, shops and even houses.
POOL.b: There are dozens of small enclaves of one country inside the other. Traditionally, a home’s nationality is decided by where its front door sits.
POOL.m: Borders on a map can make for very strange everyday lives.

POOL.h: Pheasant Island, in a river between France and Spain, changes hands every six months.
POOL.b: It has been shared this way since the Treaty of the Pyrenees was signed there in 1659. Spain runs it for half the year and France for the other half.
POOL.m: Old peace deals can leave behind unusual arrangements that last for centuries.

POOL.h: Bir Tawil is a patch of desert between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims.
POOL.b: Two different border lines drawn in 1899 and 1902 mean each country claims a more valuable area instead, called the Hala’ib Triangle. Claiming Bir Tawil would weaken their case for it.
POOL.m: It is one of the few places on Earth’s land that no country claims.

POOL.t: Two New Years in one street
POOL.h: Tweed Heads in New South Wales and Coolangatta in Queensland sit side by side.
POOL.b: New South Wales uses daylight saving but Queensland does not, so in summer the twin towns are an hour apart. On New Year’s Eve, locals can celebrate midnight twice by crossing the border.
POOL.m: A time zone line can run down the middle of a single street.

POOL.h: Lord Howe Island changes its clocks by just 30 minutes for daylight saving.
POOL.b: The island, about 600 km off the New South Wales coast, is normally half an hour ahead of Sydney. In summer it moves to the same time as Sydney’s daylight saving.
POOL.m: It is one of very few places in the world to use a half-hour daylight saving shift.

POOL.h: A small group of towns on the Nullarbor uses its own unofficial time zone.
POOL.b: Around Eucla, near the Western Australia and South Australia border, locals set clocks 45 minutes ahead of Perth. It is known as Central Western Time.
POOL.m: Remote communities often solve practical problems in their own way.

POOL.h: Macquarie Island, about 1,500 km south-east of Tasmania, is made of rock from deep inside the Earth.
POOL.b: It is the only place where rocks from the mantle are being pushed above sea level. This made it a World Heritage site in 1997.
POOL.m: A remote Australian island lets geologists study rocks normally hidden kilometres below the seafloor.

POOL.t: Kata Tjuta is taller than Uluru
POOL.h: Near Uluru stands Kata Tjuta, a group of 36 rounded domes.
POOL.b: Its highest point rises about 546 metres above the surrounding plain, roughly 200 metres higher than Uluru. Its name comes from the local Anangu language and is often translated as ‘many heads’.
POOL.m: Both sites are sacred to the Anangu people, who jointly manage the national park.

POOL.h: Mount Augustus in Western Australia is about two and a half times the size of Uluru.
POOL.b: It rises around 700 metres above the surrounding plain and is roughly 8 km long. Because it is covered in scrub, it looks less dramatic than Uluru and gets far fewer visitors.
POOL.m: Fame is not always a good guide to size.

POOL.h: The national capital was once given its own piece of the coast.
POOL.b: Jervis Bay, on the New South Wales south coast, was transferred to the Commonwealth in 1915 so the capital would have access to the sea. It is now a separate Commonwealth territory, though ACT laws still apply there. It is home to a naval college and a national park.
POOL.m: Planners in the early 1900s imagined the capital needing its own port.

POOL.h: Many Australian capitals are named after British public figures.
POOL.b: Sydney honours Lord Sydney, a British home secretary, and Melbourne honours Lord Melbourne, a British prime minister. Brisbane was named after a governor of New South Wales, and Adelaide after the wife of King William IV.
POOL.m: Place names are often a snapshot of who held power when a town was founded.

POOL.h: Darwin is named after the naturalist Charles Darwin, who never went there.
POOL.b: In 1839, John Clements Wickham, who had sailed with Darwin on HMS Beagle, named the harbour Port Darwin in his honour. The town itself did not officially take the name Darwin until 1911.
POOL.m: Friendships can leave their mark on maps.

POOL.h: The name ‘Australia’ comes from Terra Australis, Latin for ‘southern land’.
POOL.b: Explorer Matthew Flinders promoted the name in the early 1800s, preferring it to New Holland. Governor Lachlan Macquarie used it in official reports from 1817, and it soon became standard.
POOL.m: A name that started as a guess on old maps ended up describing a real continent.

POOL.h: Tasmania was once called Van Diemen’s Land.
POOL.b: Abel Tasman named it in 1642 after Anthony van Diemen, the Dutch Governor-General of the East Indies, based in Batavia. It was renamed Tasmania in 1856, partly to leave behind its reputation as a harsh penal colony.
POOL.m: Renaming a place can be a way of trying to change its story.

POOL.h: No bridge crosses the main stream of the Amazon River.
POOL.b: Most of its length runs through thinly populated rainforest, and its banks flood and shift with the seasons. People and goods cross by boat and ferry instead.
POOL.m: Where a river is the main road, a bridge is less needed and much harder to build.

POOL.t: The deepest river in the world
POOL.h: The Congo River is the deepest river in the world.
POOL.b: In parts of its lower course it is more than 220 metres deep. The depth creates such strong currents that fish living in different parts of the river have become separate species.
POOL.m: A river can act as a barrier to life, not just a highway for it.

POOL.h: Many people assume rivers flow south, but the Nile flows north.
POOL.b: Rivers simply run downhill towards the sea, whatever the compass direction. The Nile rises in the highlands of east Africa and flows north to the Mediterranean.
POOL.m: Maps put north at the top, but water pays no attention to that.

POOL.t: A lake high in the Andes
POOL.h: Lake Titicaca sits about 3,800 metres above sea level on the border of Peru and Bolivia.
POOL.b: It is often called the highest navigable lake in the world, with ferries and boats crossing it. The Uros people live on floating islands made of reeds.
POOL.m: People have found ways to live well in some of the world’s most extreme settings.

POOL.t: A waterfall named for a pilot
POOL.h: The world’s tallest waterfall is named after an American pilot.
POOL.b: Angel Falls in Venezuela drops about 979 metres from a flat-topped mountain. It is named after Jimmie Angel, who landed his plane on top in 1937, though local Pemon people knew it long before.
POOL.m: In Venezuela it is also officially called Kerepakupai Merú, its Pemon name.

POOL.h: In Iceland you can snorkel in a gap between tectonic plates.
POOL.b: The Silfra fissure lies in the rift where the North American and Eurasian plates are slowly pulling apart. Its glacial water is so clear that divers can see for over 100 metres.
POOL.m: The plates here drift apart by about 2 cm a year, so the gap you swim in is slowly widening.

POOL.t: Why Australia is not an island
POOL.h: Greenland is the largest island in the world, while Australia is counted as a continent.
POOL.b: Geographers draw the line there partly because Australia sits on its own tectonic plate. Australia is more than three times the size of Greenland.
POOL.m: The line between an island and a continent is a convention, not a law of nature.

POOL.h: Indonesia is made up of about 17,000 islands, making it the world’s largest archipelagic country.
POOL.b: They stretch more than 5,000 km from east to west, wider than mainland Australia. Only a few thousand of the islands are inhabited.
POOL.m: A single country can span as much distance as a continent.

POOL.h: The Maldives is the lowest-lying country in the world.
POOL.b: It is made up of over a thousand coral islands in the Indian Ocean, and its highest natural point is only about 2.4 metres above sea level. Most of its land is lower still.
POOL.m: For low-lying island nations, rising sea levels are a threat to their existence.

POOL.h: Mongolia is the least densely populated independent country in the world.
POOL.b: It has only about two people for every square kilometre, and around half of its people live in the capital, Ulaanbaatar. Many others still live as nomadic herders.
POOL.m: Vast open land shapes a way of life that has lasted for centuries.

POOL.h: Reykjavik in Iceland is the most northerly capital of an independent country.
POOL.b: Wellington in New Zealand is the most southerly. Both cities sit close to the edge of major tectonic plates and have strong winds, earning Wellington the nickname ‘Windy Wellington’.
POOL.m: Capitals at the edges of the map share more than you might expect.

POOL.t: Places that have never seen rain
POOL.h: Parts of Chile’s Atacama Desert are among the driest places on Earth.
POOL.b: Some weather stations there have never recorded rain. The desert is shielded by the Andes to the east and a cold ocean current to the west, which stop moist air arriving.
POOL.m: Scientists test Mars rovers in the Atacama because it is so dry and lifeless.

POOL.h: The village of Mawsynram in north-east India receives about 11,800 millimetres of rain a year on average.
POOL.b: Most falls during the summer monsoon, when moist air from the Bay of Bengal is forced up the Khasi Hills. Locals use full-body umbrellas woven from bamboo and leaves.
POOL.m: Mountains shape rainfall more than almost anything else.

POOL.h: The world’s most widely used climate map was based on plants.
POOL.b: Around 1900, the climatologist Wladimir Köppen built on the idea that vegetation reflects local climate. His system groups places into zones such as tropical, arid, temperate and polar, using temperature and rainfall.
POOL.m: Plants were a natural record of climate long before we had weather stations everywhere.

POOL.t: The Tropic of Capricorn is moving
POOL.h: Rockhampton in Queensland has a monument marking the Tropic of Capricorn.
POOL.b: But the tropic slowly drifts because Earth’s tilt changes over time. It is currently moving north by about 15 metres a year, so the marker no longer sits on the line.
POOL.m: Even the lines on a globe are not fixed forever.

POOL.h: In Longyearbyen, on the Norwegian islands of Svalbard, the sun does not rise from late October to mid-February.
POOL.b: In summer it is the reverse, with the sun never setting for about four months. The town is one of the most northerly settlements in the world.
POOL.m: The further you go from the equator, the more extreme the seasons of light become.

POOL.h: Many medieval European maps put east at the top, not north.
POOL.b: East was where the sun rose, and many mapmakers placed the Garden of Eden there. That is where the word ‘orient’ comes from, meaning to face east.
POOL.m: Putting north at the top is a habit, not a rule.

POOL.h: Null Island is a fake island at 0 degrees latitude and 0 degrees longitude.
POOL.b: The point lies in the Gulf of Guinea, off west Africa, in open ocean. Mapping software often wrongly places data there when coordinates are missing, so errors pile up in one spot.
POOL.m: A missing value can quietly turn into a false location.

POOL.t: A fake town that became real
POOL.h: Agloe, New York, began as a made-up town on a 1930s map.
POOL.b: Mapmakers added it as a trap to catch anyone copying their work. Later, a real general store opened at the spot and was named Agloe, because that is what the map said.
POOL.m: A small error on a map can shape the real world.

POOL.t: The island that was never there
POOL.h: For over a century, maps showed Sandy Island in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia.
POOL.b: In 2012, Australian scientists on a research ship went to find it and found open ocean more than a kilometre deep. It had even appeared on Google Maps.
POOL.m: Even modern maps can repeat old mistakes until someone checks.

POOL.h: Argentina’s name comes from ‘argentum’, the Latin word for silver.
POOL.b: Early Spanish explorers heard stories of a mountain of silver inland and hoped the region held great riches. The great estuary on its coast, the Río de la Plata, also means ‘river of silver’.
POOL.m: Many place names record what explorers hoped to find, not what they found.

POOL.h: Venezuela’s name is usually traced to ‘little Venice’.
POOL.b: In 1499, European explorers saw houses built on stilts over the water of Lake Maracaibo and were reminded of the Italian city. The name was first used for the coastline and later for the whole country.
POOL.m: A single view from a ship can name a nation.

POOL.h: Egypt is mostly in Africa, but its Sinai Peninsula lies in Asia.
POOL.b: The Suez Canal is usually treated as the line between the two continents. That makes Egypt one of a handful of countries spread across two continents.
POOL.m: Continents are useful labels, but countries do not always fit neatly inside them.

POOL.h: Mount Everest is named after George Everest, a British surveyor general of India who never saw the mountain and objected to the honour.
POOL.b: He even pronounced his name ‘Eve-rest’. Locally it has long been known as Chomolungma in Tibetan and Sagarmatha in Nepali.
POOL.m: Official names often ignore older local ones.

POOL.h: K2, the world’s second-highest mountain, never got a proper English name.
POOL.b: In 1856, a British surveyor labelled the peaks of the Karakoram range K1, K2, K3 and so on. Most later received local names, but K2’s label stuck.
POOL.m: Sometimes a working label is simply too useful to replace.

POOL.h: Tristan da Cunha, in the South Atlantic, is often called the most remote inhabited island in the world.
POOL.b: Its nearest inhabited neighbour, St Helena, is more than 2,000 km away. A few hundred people live there, and it can only be reached by ship.
POOL.m: Communities can thrive even at the far edges of the map.

POOL.h: Salar de Uyuni in Bolivia is the largest salt flat in the world, covering about 10,000 square kilometres.
POOL.b: It is so flat that its height varies by less than a metre across its entire area. Satellites use it to calibrate their measurements.
POOL.m: After rain, a thin layer of water turns it into a vast mirror of the sky.

POOL.h: The Danube flows through or along ten countries, more than any other river.
POOL.b: It passes four capital cities: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. It rises in Germany’s Black Forest and empties into the Black Sea.
POOL.m: Rivers have linked peoples and trade across Europe for thousands of years.

POOL.h: The Murray is Australia’s longest river, running about 2,500 km.
POOL.b: It starts in the Australian Alps and forms much of the border between New South Wales and Victoria. The Murray-Darling Basin supplies water to a large share of Australia’s farms.
POOL.m: One river system supports a large part of the food grown in Australia.

POOL.h: Australia is the driest inhabited continent on Earth.
POOL.b: Only Antarctica, which counts as a desert because so little snow falls there, receives less precipitation. Much of Australia’s vast interior gets less than 250 millimetres of rain a year, and rivers there may flow only after rare heavy rain.
POOL.m: Water shapes where Australians live, farm and build.

POOL.h: The Australian Antarctic Territory covers about 42 per cent of Antarctica, the largest claim by any country.
POOL.b: It is about four fifths the size of mainland Australia. Under the Antarctic Treaty of 1959, territorial claims are put on hold and the continent is kept for peaceful purposes.
POOL.m: A treaty signed during the Cold War still governs a whole continent.

POOL.h: Between about 40 and 50 degrees south, strong westerly winds blow almost without interruption.
POOL.b: Sailors called them the Roaring Forties. Ships on the route from Europe to Australia used these winds to cross the Indian Ocean quickly.
POOL.m: Tasmania sits right in the Roaring Forties, which gives its west coast some of the cleanest air and wildest weather in Australia.

POOL.t: The Suez Canal has no locks
POOL.h: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, has no locks.
POOL.b: The Mediterranean and Red Sea are at nearly the same level, so ships sail straight through. The Panama Canal, by contrast, uses locks to lift ships about 26 metres over the land.
POOL.m: The simplest engineering solution depends on the ground you start with.

POOL.h: At its narrowest point, the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide.
POOL.b: On a clear day, you can see Morocco from southern Spain. The strait is the only natural link between the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean.
POOL.m: Two continents that feel worlds apart are within sight of each other.

POOL.h: Brazil shares a border with every country in South America except Chile and Ecuador.
POOL.b: That is ten neighbours in all, counting the French overseas region of French Guiana. Brazil also covers nearly half of the continent’s land area, and the Amazon rainforest makes up much of it.
POOL.m: Size brings neighbours, and neighbours bring shared rivers, trade and history.

POOL.h: Chile is about 4,300 km long but, on average, less than 200 km wide.
POOL.b: It stretches from the Atacama Desert in the north to the glaciers of Patagonia in the south. That gives it a remarkable range of climates in a single country.
POOL.m: Shape can matter as much as size when it comes to geography.

POOL.h: Proprioception is your sense of where your body parts are without looking.
POOL.b: Receptors in your muscles, tendons and joints constantly report their position and stretch to your brain. It is why you can touch your nose with your eyes closed or climb stairs in the dark.
POOL.m: Balance and coordination practice keeps this quiet sense sharp, which matters more as we age.

POOL.h: Your inner ear has three fluid-filled loops called semicircular canals that detect turning.
POOL.b: When you spin, the fluid starts moving with you. When you stop suddenly, it keeps swirling for a moment, so your brain is told you are still turning when you are not.
POOL.m: Dizziness after a ride is your balance system catching up, not something wrong with your eyes.

POOL.h: Your skin is the largest organ in your body, covering about 1.5 to 2 square metres in an adult.
POOL.b: It is constantly renewing itself: the outer layer is replaced from below about every month or so. Shed skin cells make up part of household dust.
POOL.m: Your skin is working all the time as a barrier, so it is worth looking after like any other organ.

POOL.t: Your gut is no tennis court
POOL.h: The inside of the small intestine was long said to have the surface area of a tennis court.
POOL.b: A 2014 study measured it more carefully and found the whole digestive tract has about 30 square metres, closer to half a badminton court.
POOL.m: Even well-known science facts get corrected when someone measures them properly.

POOL.t: The second brain in your gut
POOL.h: Your digestive tract has its own network of hundreds of millions of neurons, called the enteric nervous system.
POOL.b: It can manage digestion largely on its own, and it constantly exchanges signals with the brain through the vagus nerve.
POOL.m: The ‘gut feeling’ of butterflies when nervous is a real conversation between your gut and your brain.

POOL.t: Most serotonin lives in your gut
POOL.h: Serotonin is best known as a brain chemical linked to mood.
