POOL.b: Yet about 90% of the body’s serotonin is made in the gut, where it helps control how food moves through the intestines. Serotonin in the blood cannot cross into the brain.
POOL.m: Body chemicals often have several jobs in different places, so simple ‘happy chemical’ stories miss a lot.

POOL.h: Bone is living tissue.
POOL.b: Cells called osteoclasts break down old bone while osteoblasts lay down new bone, and in adults this remodelling replaces most of the skeleton over roughly a decade. Bones respond to load, growing denser where they are stressed.
POOL.m: Weight-bearing activity like walking and lifting helps tell your bones to stay strong.

POOL.h: The hyoid is a small U-shaped bone in your throat, just above the voice box.
POOL.b: It is the only bone in the body that does not connect to any other bone. Held in place by muscles and ligaments, it supports your tongue and helps you swallow and speak.
POOL.m: Speech relies on small, easily overlooked structures working together.

POOL.h: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
POOL.b: Its length is roughly a quarter of a person’s height, which is why forensic scientists can estimate height from a femur alone.
POOL.m: Bones carry a surprising amount of information about the person they belonged to.

POOL.h: The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the human body.
POOL.b: It is not mainly for sitting: it helps keep your body upright and powers climbing stairs, standing up and running. Its large size is linked to humans walking on two legs.
POOL.m: Strong glutes support everyday movements like getting out of a chair and climbing hills.

POOL.t: Blood vessels could circle the Earth
POOL.h: By one common estimate, all the blood vessels in an adult laid end to end would stretch about 100,000 kilometres.
POOL.b: That is enough to wrap around the Earth more than twice. Most of that length is made up of tiny capillaries.
POOL.m: Your heart pushes blood through an astonishing network every minute of your life.

POOL.h: An average adult has roughly 5 litres of blood, making up about 7 to 8% of body weight.
POOL.b: About half of it is plasma, a straw-coloured liquid that carries nutrients, hormones and waste. Most of the rest is red blood cells.
POOL.m: Blood is mostly a delivery liquid, which is why hydration affects so much of how you feel.

POOL.t: Hearing cells do not grow back
POOL.h: Your inner ear contains thousands of tiny hair cells that turn sound vibrations into nerve signals.
POOL.b: In humans, these cells do not regrow once they are destroyed. Damage from loud noise builds up over the years and is permanent.
POOL.m: Turning the volume down and using ear protection at loud events protects hearing you cannot replace.

POOL.h: A narrow passage called the Eustachian tube links your middle ear to the back of your throat.
POOL.b: When air pressure changes quickly, such as on a plane, it opens to even out the pressure on both sides of the eardrum. That brief equalising is the pop.
POOL.m: Swallowing or yawning helps open the tube, which is why it eases blocked ears on flights.

POOL.t: Why your recorded voice sounds odd
POOL.h: When you speak, you hear your voice through the air and also through vibrations in the bones of your skull.
POOL.b: Bone conduction adds deeper tones. A recording captures only the airborne sound, so it sounds higher and thinner than the voice you know.
POOL.m: The voice on the recording is the one everyone else hears, so there is no need to cringe.

POOL.h: Earwax is not dirt.
POOL.b: It traps dust, fights germs and keeps the ear canal moist. Skin in the canal slowly grows outwards, and jaw movements from talking and chewing help carry old wax towards the opening, where it falls away.
POOL.m: Poking things deep into your ears can push wax further in rather than clearing it.

POOL.h: Most people have a nasal cycle: one nostril is slightly more congested than the other, and they swap every few hours.
POOL.b: Tissue inside the nose swells and shrinks under control of the nervous system. You usually only notice it when you have a cold.
POOL.m: A blocked side that switches over is normal body rhythm, not always a sign of illness.

POOL.t: Night vision takes half an hour
POOL.h: When you walk from a bright room into darkness, your eyes need time to adjust.
POOL.b: The rod cells that handle dim light rebuild a light-sensitive pigment, and full dark adaptation takes around 20 to 30 minutes. A burst of bright light resets much of it.
POOL.m: For stargazing, give your eyes time in the dark and use a red light if you need to see.

POOL.t: Look sideways to see faint stars
POOL.h: The centre of your vision is packed with colour-sensing cone cells, which work poorly in dim light.
POOL.b: The rods that detect faint light are concentrated around the edges. Astronomers use ‘averted vision’, looking slightly to one side of a faint star so it appears brighter.
POOL.m: In the dark, glancing slightly away from something can help you see it better.

POOL.h: Only a tiny central patch of your retina, called the fovea, gives sharp, detailed vision.
POOL.b: It covers roughly the area of your thumbnail held at arm’s length. Your eyes constantly dart around, and the brain stitches the pieces into a seemingly clear scene.
POOL.m: Much of what you think you see clearly is your brain filling in the gaps.

POOL.h: In 1848, American railway worker Phineas Gage survived an iron rod passing through the front of his brain.
POOL.b: Friends reported his personality changed afterwards. His case became one of the first clues that particular brain regions shape behaviour, although later retellings exaggerated some details.
POOL.m: Who we are is closely tied to how our brain is physically wired.

POOL.h: In 1861, French doctor Paul Broca studied a patient who could understand speech but could say only one word, ‘tan’.
POOL.b: After the man died, Broca found damage in a region of the left frontal lobe. That area, now called Broca’s area, is linked to producing speech.
POOL.m: Much of what we know about the brain came from carefully studying individual patients.

POOL.t: The man who could not remember
POOL.h: In 1953, surgery to treat Henry Molaison’s severe seizures removed parts of his brain including much of both hippocampi.
POOL.b: Afterwards he could not form new lasting memories of events. Yet he steadily improved at a drawing task without recalling ever doing it.
POOL.m: Memory is not one system: knowing facts and learning skills use different parts of the brain.

POOL.h: In 1796, English doctor Edward Jenner tested whether infection with mild cowpox protected people against deadly smallpox.
POOL.b: It did. The word vaccine comes from the Latin vacca, meaning cow, in honour of this first vaccination method.
POOL.m: Many modern medical words carry the story of how the treatment was first discovered.

POOL.h: In the 1840s, Hungarian doctor Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that mothers in a Vienna ward staffed by doctors died far more often than in a ward run by midwives.
POOL.b: He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths fell dramatically. Many colleagues rejected his idea.
POOL.m: Good evidence can still take years to win over people, especially experts.

POOL.h: In 1854, London doctor John Snow mapped cholera deaths in Soho and found they clustered around a water pump on Broad Street.
POOL.b: He persuaded officials to remove its handle. His work helped show that cholera spreads through contaminated water, not bad air.
POOL.m: Simply plotting data on a map can reveal causes nobody could see before.

POOL.h: Before the 1840s, surgery was performed on patients who were fully awake, so surgeons prized speed above all.
POOL.b: In 1846, dentist William Morton gave a public demonstration of ether anaesthesia in Boston. Within months it was being used around the world.
POOL.m: Pain relief we take for granted is less than two centuries old.

POOL.h: In 1816, French doctor René Laennec needed to listen to a young woman’s heart but felt uncomfortable pressing his ear to her chest.
POOL.b: He rolled some paper into a tube and found the heartbeat sounded clearer. He went on to design a wooden stethoscope.
POOL.m: Useful inventions often start as a quick fix to an awkward everyday problem.

POOL.h: Melbourne surgeon Graeme Clark led the team that developed the multi-channel cochlear implant, first implanted in 1978.
POOL.b: The device turns sound into electrical signals that stimulate the hearing nerve directly. It has since helped hundreds of thousands of people hear.
POOL.m: Australian research has changed lives around the world.

POOL.h: Perth plastic surgeon Fiona Wood and scientist Marie Stoner developed a technique for spraying a patient’s own skin cells onto burns.
POOL.b: It helps wounds heal faster than waiting for grown sheets of skin. It became widely known after it was used on burns patients from the 2002 Bali bombings.
POOL.m: Faster healing of burns means less scarring and a quicker return to normal life.

POOL.h: While you are awake, a chemical called adenosine gradually builds up in your brain and creates sleep pressure.
POOL.b: Caffeine works by blocking adenosine receptors, so the tiredness signal cannot land. The adenosine is still there, which is why fatigue can hit once the caffeine wears off.
POOL.m: Coffee hides tiredness rather than removing it, and real rest is the only true fix.

POOL.h: Your brain releases the hormone melatonin as darkness falls, helping signal that it is night.
POOL.b: Bright light in the evening, especially blue-rich light, suppresses melatonin and can push your body clock later. Morning light does the opposite and helps set it earlier.
POOL.m: Dimmer evenings and bright mornings help your body clock keep good time.

POOL.t: Teenagers are wired to stay up
POOL.h: During adolescence, the body clock naturally shifts later, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until well into the night.
POOL.b: This is a biological change, not just a habit. It is one reason some schools have trialled later start times.
POOL.m: A teenager who cannot fall asleep early is often fighting their biology, not being lazy.

POOL.h: While you sleep, your brain replays and strengthens memories from the day.
POOL.b: Studies repeatedly find people remember newly learned material better after a night’s sleep than after the same hours awake. Deep sleep and REM sleep both seem to play a role.
POOL.m: Sleeping on new learning is part of studying, not time taken away from it.

POOL.h: Over the 1963 to 1964 New Year, American high school student Randy Gardner stayed awake for about 264 hours, roughly 11 days, for a science fair project.
POOL.b: Researchers watched him develop problems with mood, concentration, memory and perception. Record attempts like this are now discouraged because of the risks.
POOL.m: Even short-term sleep loss steadily chips away at how well your brain works.

POOL.t: That jolt as you drift off
POOL.h: Many people feel a sudden twitch or falling sensation just as they fall asleep.
POOL.b: It is called a hypnic jerk and is very common and harmless. Scientists are still not sure why it happens, though caffeine, stress and tiredness seem to make it more frequent.
POOL.m: An occasional jolt as you nod off is a normal quirk of falling asleep.

POOL.t: Lactic acid is not the villain
POOL.h: The muscle soreness that peaks a day or two after hard exercise is not caused by lactic acid.
POOL.b: Lactate clears from muscles within about an hour, and the body even uses it as fuel. Delayed soreness is linked to tiny strains in muscle fibres and the repair that follows.
POOL.m: Soreness after new exercise is part of adapting and usually eases as you get used to it.

POOL.h: Research suggests that when muscles grow through training, they gain extra nuclei inside their cells.
POOL.b: These seem to stick around even after a long break and muscle shrinks. That may help explain why regaining lost fitness is often faster than building it the first time.
POOL.m: Past training is rarely wasted, even if you have stopped for a while.

POOL.h: In a 2011 study, older adults who walked briskly three times a week for a year saw their hippocampus, a key memory region, grow by about 2%.
POOL.b: A comparison group doing stretching saw a small decline. Exercise raises chemicals that support brain cells.
POOL.m: Regular movement looks after your brain as well as your heart.

POOL.t: Built to run in the heat
POOL.h: Humans are unusually good at running long distances in hot weather.
POOL.b: We have millions of sweat glands and little body hair, so we can shed heat while moving. Some scientists think early humans used this to wear down prey by tracking it for hours.
POOL.m: Your ability to sweat freely is one of the most remarkable features of the human body.

POOL.h: Fresh sweat is almost odourless.
POOL.b: Body odour comes from bacteria on the skin breaking down sweat from apocrine glands, which are concentrated in places like the armpits. Most sweat comes from other glands and is mainly water and salt, used for cooling.
POOL.m: Keeping skin clean tackles body odour at its source: the bacteria.

POOL.h: A food calorie on overseas packaging is really a kilocalorie, and one is equal to about 4.2 kilojoules.
POOL.b: Australia uses kilojoules on its labels, so the numbers look about four times bigger. Both measure the same thing: the energy food provides.
POOL.m: Divide kilojoules by about 4.2 when comparing Australian labels with overseas calorie counts.

POOL.h: In 1747, Scottish naval surgeon James Lind gave sailors with scurvy different treatments.
POOL.b: Those given citrus fruit recovered remarkably fast. It is often called one of the first controlled clinical trials, though it took decades for the British navy to act on it fully.
POOL.m: Comparing treatments side by side remains the backbone of modern medicine.

POOL.h: In 1912, Polish biochemist Casimir Funk proposed that certain diseases were caused by missing ‘vital amines’ in food.
POOL.b: He called them vitamines. When it turned out many were not amines at all, the final ‘e’ was dropped, giving us the word vitamin.
POOL.m: Scientific names often preserve early guesses that later turned out partly wrong.

POOL.t: Polished rice and a missing vitamin
POOL.h: In the 1890s, Dutch doctor Christiaan Eijkman noticed chickens fed polished white rice developed a disease like human beriberi, while those fed unpolished rice did not.
POOL.b: The outer bran layers removed by polishing contained something vital, later identified as thiamine, vitamin B1. He shared a Nobel Prize in 1929.
POOL.m: Refining food can strip out nutrients that were doing important work.

POOL.h: Your body cannot digest dietary fibre, but your gut bacteria can.
POOL.b: They ferment it into short-chain fatty acids, which help nourish the cells lining the colon. Different fibres feed different microbes, so a varied diet supports a more varied gut community.
POOL.m: Eating a range of plant foods is a way of feeding the helpful bacteria inside you.

POOL.h: Taste bud cells live only about one to two weeks before being replaced.
POOL.b: That is why the numb, scalded feeling after hot soup fades within days. Your sense of taste can also change over time, which is part of why foods you disliked as a child may become favourites.
POOL.m: It is worth retrying foods you once disliked, because your taste really does change.

POOL.h: Researchers found that people vary widely in how strongly they taste bitterness.
POOL.b: So-called supertasters, often estimated at about a quarter of people, tend to have more of the tiny bumps that hold taste buds. They may find foods like black coffee and some green vegetables intensely bitter.
POOL.m: A fussy eater may genuinely be tasting something stronger than you are.

POOL.h: For some people, coriander tastes unpleasantly like soap.
POOL.b: A 2012 genetic study linked this to variation near a smell receptor gene called OR6A2, which picks up the aldehyde compounds found in coriander leaves. The genetic effect is modest, so genes are only part of the story.
POOL.m: Food dislikes can have a genetic basis, so they are not always just stubbornness.

POOL.h: Some people sneeze when they step into bright light.
POOL.b: It is called the photic sneeze reflex and runs in families. One idea is that signals from the eyes and nose travel along closely linked nerves, so a burst of light gets misread as a tickle.
POOL.m: An odd reflex can simply be a quirk of how your nerves are wired.

POOL.h: Eating something icy too quickly can trigger a sharp headache.
POOL.b: The cold on the roof of your mouth causes rapid changes in blood vessels there, and nearby nerves send pain signals that the brain reads as coming from the forehead. It passes within a minute.
POOL.m: Brain freeze is a harmless mix-up of nerve signals that fades on its own.

POOL.t: Your funny bone is a nerve
POOL.h: The funny bone is not a bone.
POOL.b: It is the ulnar nerve, which runs close to the surface behind the elbow with little padding. Knocking it presses the nerve against bone and sends a jolt of tingling down to your ring and little fingers.
POOL.m: That strange zap is a nerve telling you exactly where it runs.

POOL.t: Kidneys filter a bathtub a day
POOL.h: Your kidneys filter roughly 180 litres of fluid from your blood every day.
POOL.b: Almost all of it is reabsorbed, leaving only about one to two litres to leave the body as urine. They also balance salts and help control blood pressure.
POOL.m: Two fist-sized organs are quietly cleaning your blood around the clock.

POOL.h: Your two lungs are not identical.
POOL.b: The right lung has three lobes, while the left has only two and is slightly smaller, leaving room for the heart, which tilts to the left. Inside, hundreds of millions of tiny air sacs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide.
POOL.m: The body is full of small asymmetries that make everything fit together.

POOL.h: The main urge to breathe comes from rising carbon dioxide in your blood, not falling oxygen.
POOL.b: Sensors in your brainstem track it closely. That burning need to breathe when holding your breath is mostly carbon dioxide building up.
POOL.m: Your breathing is steered by chemistry, which is why slow breathing can change how you feel.

POOL.h: Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, two to three times faster than toenails.
POOL.b: A lost fingernail regrows in around six months, while a big toenail can take a year or more. Nails on your dominant hand tend to grow slightly faster.
POOL.m: Slow toenail growth is why damage to toenails stays visible for so long.

POOL.t: The twins who made transplants work
POOL.h: In 1954, surgeons in Boston led by Joseph Murray performed the first successful kidney transplant.
POOL.b: The donor and recipient were identical twins, so the body did not reject the new organ. Murray later shared a Nobel Prize for the work.
POOL.m: Transplants began with twins because rejection by the immune system was the biggest hurdle.

POOL.h: Before the 1920s, type 1 diabetes was usually fatal.
POOL.b: In 1921 in Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin, and in 1922 a 14-year-old boy named Leonard Thompson became the first person treated with it. Patients close to death recovered within weeks.
POOL.m: Many conditions that were once fatal are now managed thanks to research.

POOL.h: For centuries, doctors thought blood was made in the liver and used up by the body.
POOL.b: In 1628, English physician William Harvey showed that the heart pumps the same blood round and round the body in a loop. It overturned ideas that had stood since ancient Greece.
POOL.m: Careful measurement can overturn beliefs that have lasted for centuries.

POOL.h: The world’s first IVF baby, Louise Brown, was born in England in 1978.
POOL.b: Australia followed in 1980 with Candice Reed, born in Melbourne after work by a team from Monash University. Australian researchers went on to pioneer several key IVF techniques.
POOL.m: Many families today exist thanks to medical research done in Australia.

POOL.t: The barter economy that never was
POOL.h: Textbooks often say money replaced barter because swapping goods was clumsy.
POOL.b: Yet anthropologists have found no society that ran mainly on barter between neighbours. Communities more often relied on credit, gifts and informal debts, with barter used mostly between strangers.
POOL.m: Money is as much about trust and keeping track of what we owe each other as it is about swapping things.

POOL.h: In 1813, Governor Lachlan Macquarie tackled a coin shortage in New South Wales by punching the centres out of Spanish silver dollars.
POOL.b: The ring became the ‘holey dollar’, worth five shillings, and the small disc became the ‘dump’, worth fifteen pence. The holes also made the coins less useful elsewhere.
POOL.m: Governments have long used clever tricks to keep money circulating at home.

POOL.h: The Bank of New South Wales opened in Sydney in April 1817, with Governor Lachlan Macquarie’s support, becoming Australia’s first bank.
POOL.b: Before then, the colony relied on scarce coins and handwritten promissory notes. After merging with the Commercial Bank of Australia in 1982, it was renamed Westpac.
POOL.m: Some of today’s biggest banks trace their roots to the colony’s earliest days.

POOL.t: Money is named after a goddess
POOL.h: Ancient Rome minted coins at or near the temple of Juno Moneta on the Capitoline Hill.
POOL.b: Her title Moneta gave rise to the words ‘money’ and ‘mint’. The same root travelled through Latin and French into English.
POOL.m: Everyday words often carry thousands of years of history in them.

POOL.h: Medieval Italian money changers did business at benches or tables in the marketplace, called banco.
POOL.b: That gave us the word bank. ‘Bankrupt’ comes from the Italian banca rotta, meaning a broken bench, a phrase for a failed money-lending business.
POOL.m: Banking grew out of simple trust between traders in a busy market.

POOL.h: In 1494, Italian friar Luca Pacioli published the first widely read description of double-entry bookkeeping.
POOL.b: Every transaction is recorded twice, as a debit and a credit, so errors show up when the books do not balance. Businesses around the world still use the method today.
POOL.m: Recording where money comes from and where it goes is the basis of all good money management.

POOL.h: Isaac Newton spent his later years in charge of England’s Royal Mint.
POOL.b: He oversaw a huge recoinage and personally pursued counterfeiters and coin clippers, who shaved silver off the edges of coins. Grooved edges on coins helped reveal clipping.
POOL.m: The ridges on some coins today are a leftover from the fight against clipping.

POOL.h: The Bank of England was founded in 1694 to lend money to the government of William III, which needed funds to fight France.
POOL.b: Over time it became the model for central banks around the world, managing a nation’s currency and interest rates.
POOL.m: Central banks began as government lenders and grew into guardians of a nation’s money.

POOL.h: Banks lend out most of the money deposited with them, so they could never repay every customer at once.
POOL.b: If enough people fear a bank will fail and rush to withdraw, it can fail for that reason alone. This insight contributed to a Nobel Prize in 2022.
POOL.m: Deposit guarantees exist to stop fear itself from bringing down healthy banks.

POOL.h: Since 2008, Australia’s Financial Claims Scheme has protected deposits in authorised banks, building societies and credit unions up to a set limit per person per institution.
POOL.b: If one of these fails, the government steps in to repay covered savers.
POOL.m: Guarantees like this are a key reason people can keep savings in a bank with confidence.

POOL.h: Australia’s central bank functions were once handled by the Commonwealth Bank, which also served ordinary customers.
POOL.b: In 1960, the Reserve Bank of Australia began operating as a separate institution. It sets the cash rate and issues Australia’s banknotes.
POOL.m: Separating the central bank from everyday banking helps it focus on the whole economy.

POOL.h: In 1990, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand became the first central bank to adopt a formal inflation target.
POOL.b: It was given a clear goal and the independence to pursue it. Australia and many other countries soon followed with their own targets.
POOL.m: A clear, public goal makes it easier to hold decision-makers to account.

POOL.h: When a central bank raises interest rates, borrowing becomes more expensive and saving more rewarding.
POOL.b: People and businesses tend to spend less, which cools demand and eases pressure on prices. The effect takes time, often a year or more to fully show up.
POOL.m: Interest rate changes are slow-acting tools, so decisions today are aimed at the economy of tomorrow.

POOL.h: The Australian Bureau of Statistics tracks inflation by pricing a ‘basket’ of goods and services that households typically buy, from bread to rent to health care.
POOL.b: Changes in the total cost of that basket give the Consumer Price Index. The basket is updated as spending habits change.
POOL.m: Your own inflation rate may differ from the official one, depending on what you buy.

POOL.h: Deflation sounds pleasant, but steadily falling prices can hurt an economy.
POOL.b: People delay purchases while waiting for bargains, and debts become harder to repay in real terms. Japan struggled with low growth and falling prices for years after its asset bubble burst in the early 1990s.
POOL.m: A little steady inflation is generally considered healthier than prices that keep falling.

POOL.h: Economists once thought high inflation and high unemployment rarely happened together.
POOL.b: Then the oil shocks of the 1970s delivered both at once, a mix nicknamed stagflation. It forced a major rethink of how economies and central banks work.
POOL.m: Economic rules of thumb can break when the world changes.

POOL.h: People tend to think about money in dollar amounts rather than buying power, an effect called money illusion.
POOL.b: In a 1997 study, most people thought a worker given a 5% pay rise during 4% inflation would be happier than one given a 2% rise with no inflation, even though the second was better off in real terms.
POOL.m: Always compare pay rises and investment returns with inflation to see what they are really worth.

POOL.h: Albert Einstein is often quoted calling compound interest the eighth wonder of the world or the most powerful force in the universe.
POOL.b: Researchers have found no evidence he ever said anything of the kind. The quotes appear to have been attached to his name decades after his death.
POOL.m: Compound interest is powerful on its own merits, no famous endorsement needed.

POOL.h: When Benjamin Franklin died in 1790, he left 1,000 pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent to young tradespeople and left to grow for 200 years.
POOL.b: By the 1990s, the funds had grown to millions of dollars.
POOL.m: Given enough time, even modest sums can compound into something remarkable.

POOL.h: Compound interest means earning interest on your past interest.
POOL.b: The same force works against you when you borrow: unpaid interest on a debt gets added to the balance, and then that grows too. That is why balances left to roll over can swell faster than expected.
POOL.m: Compounding rewards patient savers and punishes lingering debt in exactly the same way.

POOL.h: The Superannuation Guarantee began in Australia in 1992, requiring employers to pay a set percentage of wages into workers’ retirement savings.
POOL.b: Before then, many workers had no super at all. The system has since grown into one of the largest pools of retirement savings in the world.
POOL.m: Money set aside automatically for decades can end up a major part of your retirement.

POOL.h: Australia’s income tax is progressive, charged in brackets.
POOL.b: Moving into a higher bracket only means the extra dollars above that threshold are taxed at the higher rate. The rest of your income is taxed exactly as before, so a pay rise never leaves you worse off in income tax.
POOL.m: Going up a tax bracket only affects the extra dollars, not your whole income.

POOL.t: What a tax deduction is worth
POOL.h: A tax deduction reduces the income you are taxed on, not your tax bill dollar for dollar.
POOL.b: So a $100 deduction saves you $100 multiplied by your marginal tax rate. A tax offset, by contrast, comes straight off the tax you owe.
POOL.m: Spending money just to get a deduction usually leaves you poorer overall.

POOL.t: Income tax paid for a war
POOL.h: The Australian federal government first taxed personal incomes in 1915, to help pay for the First World War.
POOL.b: Some states already had their own income taxes. During the Second World War, the Commonwealth took over income tax collection entirely.
POOL.m: Many taxes introduced as temporary measures end up lasting for generations.

POOL.h: Australia’s goods and services tax began on 1 July 2000, replacing a patchwork of older taxes including wholesale sales tax.
POOL.b: It is charged on most goods and services, with some exceptions such as basic food. The revenue goes to the states and territories.
POOL.m: GST is built into most prices you pay, which is why it is easy to forget it is there.

POOL.h: Since 1987, Australia has used dividend imputation.
POOL.b: When a company pays tax on its profits and then pays dividends, shareholders receive franking credits for the tax already paid. This stops the same profit being fully taxed twice, once as company profit and again as personal income.
POOL.m: Australian shares can be taxed differently from overseas ones because of franking credits.

POOL.h: In 1696, England introduced a tax based on the number of windows in a house, since windows were easy for assessors to count from the street.
POOL.b: Many owners bricked up windows to pay less. The tax lasted until 1851, and bricked-up windows can still be seen on old buildings.
POOL.m: People change their behaviour to avoid a tax, often in ways its designers never intended.

POOL.h: Around 1700, Russian Tsar Peter the Great introduced a tax on beards as part of his push to modernise Russia along European lines.
POOL.b: Men who wanted to keep their beards had to pay and carry a token proving it.
POOL.m: Taxes can be used to change behaviour, not just to raise money.

POOL.h: Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1789 that ‘in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes’.
POOL.b: He was not the first. Similar lines appear decades earlier, including in a 1726 work by English writer Daniel Defoe.
POOL.m: Famous sayings are often older than the famous person they are credited to.

POOL.t: Striking gas can hurt an economy
POOL.h: In 1977, The Economist coined the term Dutch disease.
POOL.b: After the Netherlands found huge natural gas reserves, its currency rose and other industries like manufacturing struggled to compete. The idea is often discussed in Australia during mining booms.
POOL.m: A boom in one industry can quietly squeeze others in the same economy.

POOL.h: Adam Smith’s ‘invisible hand’ is one of the most famous ideas in economics.
POOL.b: Yet Smith used the phrase only once in The Wealth of Nations and once in his earlier book on moral sentiments. He also wrote extensively about sympathy, fairness and the dangers of monopolies.
POOL.m: Famous thinkers are often more nuanced than the slogans attached to them.

POOL.h: Saving is sensible for one household, but if everyone saves more at once during a downturn, total spending falls.
POOL.b: Businesses sell less, cut jobs and incomes drop, so people may end up saving no more than before. John Maynard Keynes helped popularise the idea.
POOL.m: What makes sense for one person can play out very differently across a whole economy.

POOL.t: ‘In the long run we are all dead’
POOL.h: John Maynard Keynes wrote this line in 1923.
POOL.b: He was not dismissing the future. He was criticising economists who said problems would sort themselves out eventually, arguing that such advice was useless if people suffered badly in the meantime.
POOL.m: Famous quotes often mean something different once you read them in context.

POOL.h: In 1850, French economist Frederic Bastiat imagined a boy breaking a shop window.
POOL.b: Some might say it helps the economy by giving the glazier work. Bastiat pointed out the unseen cost: the shopkeeper now cannot spend that money on something else.
POOL.m: Look for the hidden costs, not just the visible activity, when judging whether something is good.

POOL.t: Why diamonds cost more than water
POOL.h: Water is essential to life yet cheap, while diamonds are unnecessary yet expensive.
POOL.b: Adam Smith puzzled over this. Economists later explained that price reflects the value of one more unit: water is abundant, so an extra litre is worth little, while diamonds are scarce.
POOL.m: Prices reflect scarcity at the margin, not how important something is overall.

POOL.h: In 1986, The Economist began comparing the price of a McDonald’s Big Mac around the world as a light-hearted guide to whether currencies are overvalued or undervalued.
POOL.b: It is based on purchasing power parity, the idea that the same item should cost roughly the same everywhere.
POOL.m: A simple comparison can make a complicated idea surprisingly easy to understand.

POOL.h: Economist Simon Kuznets developed early national income accounts for the United States in the 1930s, laying groundwork for GDP.
POOL.b: He warned that such measures could not tell us much about a nation’s welfare. GDP counts spending, not happiness, health or leisure.
POOL.m: A growing economy is not the same as people living better lives.

POOL.h: An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people outside a deal.
POOL.b: A factory’s pollution harms neighbours who never agreed to it. In 1920, economist Arthur Pigou suggested taxing such harms so that prices reflect their true cost.
POOL.m: The price you pay does not always include every cost your choice creates.

POOL.h: Moral hazard comes from the insurance world.
POOL.b: When people are protected from the full cost of a risk, they may take more of it. Insurers use excesses partly so that customers still have some reason to be careful.
POOL.m: Having a stake in the outcome tends to make people more careful.

POOL.h: In 1970, economist George Akerlof described how used car markets can break down when sellers know more than buyers.
POOL.b: Fearing a ‘lemon’, buyers offer less, so owners of good cars stop selling. Several journals rejected his paper, and it later helped win him a Nobel Prize.
POOL.m: Inspections, warranties and reviews exist to close the information gap between buyers and sellers.

POOL.h: Hawala is an ancient system for transferring money through a network of brokers, used for centuries across the Middle East, South Asia and Africa.
POOL.b: A broker in one city tells a partner elsewhere to pay out the money, and they settle up between themselves later.
POOL.m: Money can travel without anything physical moving, as long as people trust each other.

POOL.h: In 1989, Australia introduced HECS, with repayments tied to a graduate’s income rather than a fixed schedule.
POOL.b: Economist Bruce Chapman helped design it. Other countries, including England and New Zealand, later adopted income-contingent student loans of their own.
POOL.m: Australian policy ideas are sometimes copied around the world.

POOL.h: The Great Depression hit Australia hard because the country relied heavily on exports like wool and wheat, whose prices collapsed.
POOL.b: Unemployment climbed to around 30% in 1932. Many families went hungry and relied on food relief.
POOL.m: Economies that depend on a few exports can be badly exposed when world prices fall.

POOL.t: The land boom that broke Melbourne
POOL.h: In the 1880s, ‘Marvellous Melbourne’ enjoyed a wild land boom fuelled by easy credit.
POOL.b: When it collapsed, many banks and building societies failed or closed their doors in 1893. Victoria’s economy took years to recover.
POOL.m: Property booms built on easy credit can end with painful busts.

POOL.h: In 1969, Australian mining company Poseidon announced a nickel discovery in Western Australia.
POOL.b: Its shares soared from under a dollar to around $280 within months, dragging other mining stocks up with them. When the frenzy faded, prices collapsed and many investors lost heavily.
POOL.m: Excitement about a big discovery can push prices far beyond what the business is worth.

POOL.h: In the late 1990s, investors piled into internet companies, many with no profits.
POOL.b: The Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, then fell by about 78% over the next two and a half years. It took around 15 years to regain its peak.
POOL.m: A good idea, like the internet, can still be a bad investment at the wrong price.

POOL.h: On 19 October 1987, the Dow Jones index in the United States fell by about 22.6% in a single day.
POOL.b: The panic spread worldwide, and Australia’s share market fell about a quarter when it opened the next day. Many markets recovered within a couple of years.
POOL.m: Markets can fall sharply without warning, which is why timeframes matter for investing.

POOL.h: On 15 September 2008, US investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, turning a housing slump into a global financial crisis.
POOL.b: Australia was one of the few advanced economies to avoid a recession, helped by strong banks, government stimulus and demand for its resources.
POOL.m: When one big bank fails, the effects can spread through the entire financial system.

POOL.h: Scottish economist John Law persuaded France to adopt paper money and backed a company promising riches from French Louisiana.
POOL.b: Shares soared in 1719, then collapsed in 1720, ruining investors and damaging trust in paper money in France for decades.
POOL.m: Promises of fabulous riches from far away deserve extra scepticism.

POOL.h: In 1920, Charles Ponzi promised investors in Boston 50% returns in 45 days, supposedly from trading international postal reply coupons.
POOL.b: In reality, he paid early investors with money from new ones. The scheme collapsed within months, and his name became a byword for fraud.
POOL.m: If returns sound too good to be true and rely on new investors, walk away.

POOL.h: On 22 May 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, one of the first known purchases using the cryptocurrency.
POOL.b: At the time the coins were worth only about US$40. Their value later soared to a fortune.
POOL.m: Nobody knows the future value of what they spend today.

POOL.h: The first cash machine opened in 1967 at a Barclays bank in Enfield, London, designed by John Shepherd-Barron.
POOL.b: He wanted a six-digit code, but said his wife could only remember four. Four digits became the standard in many places.
POOL.m: Good design often means working with the limits of human memory.

POOL.h: For much of the Middle Ages, the Catholic Church condemned usury, which often meant charging any interest at all on loans.
POOL.b: Merchants found workarounds, such as disguising interest as fees or currency exchange charges. Attitudes gradually softened as trade expanded.
POOL.m: Views on what is fair in lending have changed a great deal over the centuries.

POOL.h: Roman emperors facing large bills often reduced the silver in their coins.
POOL.b: By the late third century, the denarius and its successor coins contained only a tiny fraction of the silver they once held. Prices soared as people lost faith in the money.
POOL.m: When money is quietly made worth less, prices eventually rise to catch up.

POOL.t: An emperor tried to freeze prices
POOL.h: In 301 AD, Roman Emperor Diocletian issued an edict setting maximum prices for over a thousand goods and wages.
POOL.b: Punishments for breaking it were severe. Goods reportedly disappeared from markets, and the edict was largely ignored within a few years.
POOL.m: Forcing prices down usually leads to shortages rather than cheaper goods.

POOL.t: A lottery built the Opera House
POOL.h: Most of the cost of the Sydney Opera House was paid for by the Opera House Lottery, which began in 1957.
POOL.b: As construction costs blew out far beyond early estimates, the lottery kept funding the project. The building opened in 1973.
POOL.m: Big public projects are often paid for in creative ways.

POOL.h: In 1992, Australia withdrew its 1 and 2 cent coins because they cost more to handle than they were worth.
POOL.b: Cash totals are now rounded to the nearest 5 cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
POOL.m: When a coin costs more to use than it is worth, it is time for it to go.

POOL.h: Australia replaced its $1 note with a coin in 1984 and its $2 note with a coin in 1988.
POOL.b: Coins cost more to make than notes but last for decades, while paper notes wore out quickly in everyday use.
POOL.m: Durable money can save the public money over time.

POOL.h: Most money today is fiat money: it has value because governments declare it legal tender and people trust it, not because it can be swapped for gold.
POOL.b: Fiat is Latin for ‘let it be done’.
POOL.m: The money in your wallet rests on collective trust in the system behind it.

POOL.h: The word credit comes from the Latin credere, meaning to believe or to trust.
POOL.b: When a lender gives you credit, they are trusting that you will pay it back. A credit rating is essentially a measure of that trust.
POOL.m: Every loan is a form of trust, and that trust is built through reliable repayments.

POOL.h: Once thought impossible, negative interest rates were used by the European Central Bank from 2014 and the Bank of Japan from 2016.
POOL.b: Banks were effectively charged for holding cash at the central bank. In Denmark, some homeowners were offered mortgages with slightly negative rates.
POOL.m: Even long-held economic assumptions can be overturned.

POOL.h: In 2009, Zimbabwe issued a 100 trillion dollar banknote during severe hyperinflation.
POOL.b: Prices were rising so fast that shops raised them several times a day. The country soon abandoned its own currency and used foreign ones such as the US dollar instead.
POOL.m: Stable money is something many countries cannot take for granted.

POOL.t: Wall Street had a real wall
POOL.h: Wall Street in New York is named after a wooden wall built by Dutch settlers in the 1650s, when the city was called New Amsterdam.
POOL.b: In 1792, 24 brokers signed the Buttonwood Agreement under a tree nearby, the beginnings of the New York Stock Exchange.
POOL.m: The world’s great financial centres often began with small, informal arrangements.

POOL.h: Economists Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi designed a plan where workers agree in advance to save part of their future pay rises.
POOL.b: Because saving comes from money they have not yet received, it feels painless. In one company, savings rates rose sharply over a few years.
POOL.m: Committing future money to saving is easier than giving up money you already have.

POOL.h: A 2013 study found Indian sugarcane farmers scored lower on thinking tests before harvest, when money was tight, than after it.
POOL.b: Researchers argued that financial worry takes up mental bandwidth, leaving less for other decisions.
POOL.m: Money stress can make everyday decisions harder, which is why a buffer helps.

POOL.h: In the 1840s, British investors poured money into hundreds of proposed railway lines, many poorly planned or duplicated.
POOL.b: Share prices collapsed in 1847 and many investors were ruined, yet the boom left Britain with much of the rail network it still uses.
POOL.m: A bubble can wipe out investors while still leaving behind something genuinely useful.

POOL.h: Studies by psychologists Leaf Van Boven and Thomas Gilovich found that people tend to get more lasting happiness from experiences, like trips and concerts, than from material purchases.
POOL.b: Experiences become part of our identity and are easier to share with others.
POOL.m: When choosing what to spend on, memories often outlast possessions.

POOL.h: In 1976, John Bogle launched one of the first index funds for ordinary investors.
POOL.b: It aimed to match the market rather than beat it, keeping costs low. Critics mocked it as ‘Bogle’s folly’, but index investing later became one of the most popular ways to invest.
POOL.m: Low costs and simplicity can beat trying to outsmart the market.

POOL.t: You understand less than you think
POOL.h: In a 2002 study at Yale, Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil asked people how well they understood everyday objects like zips, flush toilets and locks.
POOL.b: Most rated themselves fairly highly. Then they were asked to write a step-by-step explanation, and their ratings dropped sharply. The gap is called the illusion of explanatory depth.
POOL.m: Before arguing about how something works, try explaining it step by step. It is a quick, humbling test of what you really know.

POOL.h: In 1985, Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky studied basketball shooting and concluded the “hot hand” was an illusion.
POOL.b: For decades it was a textbook example of seeing patterns in randomness. In 2018, economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo found a subtle statistical bias in the original method. Reanalysed, the data showed a modest hot hand after all.
POOL.m: Even famous findings can be revised. Hold confident conclusions a little loosely, including debunkings.

POOL.h: In 1978, psychologists Pauline Clance and Suzanne Imes described the “impostor phenomenon” in high-achieving women who felt their success was luck and feared being found out.
POOL.b: Later research found the feeling is common across genders, jobs and ages. It is not a medical diagnosis, but a widely shared pattern of self-doubt.
POOL.m: If you feel like an impostor, you are in large company. Look at the evidence of your track record, not just the feeling.

POOL.h: Psychologist Gabriele Oettingen found that simply fantasising about a happy outcome can make people put in less effort.
POOL.b: Imagining success can feel a little like having achieved it. She developed a method called WOOP: name your Wish, picture the Outcome, identify the inner Obstacle, then make a Plan for it.
POOL.m: Dream about the goal, then deliberately picture what will get in the way and how you will handle it.

POOL.t: Five dollars is not always five dollars
POOL.h: In a classic 1981 study by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, most people said they would drive 20 minutes to save $5 on a $15 calculator.
POOL.b: Far fewer would make the same trip to save $5 on a $125 calculator. The saving was identical. We tend to judge changes relative to the starting amount, not in absolute terms.
POOL.m: When you weigh a saving or a cost, ask what it is worth in plain dollars, not as a share of the price.

POOL.t: When a word stops making sense
POOL.h: Repeat a word like “spoon” out loud over and over, and it soon starts to sound strange and empty.
POOL.b: This is called semantic satiation. The term was coined by psychologist Leon Jakobovits James in his 1962 doctoral thesis at McGill University. The effect usually fades within moments of stopping.
POOL.m: Familiar things can lose their meaning through sheer repetition, which is worth remembering for slogans and routines too.

POOL.t: Knowing does not break the illusion
POOL.h: In 1889, German psychiatrist Franz Carl Müller-Lyer published a drawing of two equal lines, one ending in inward arrowheads and one in outward “tails”.
POOL.b: The line with tails looks clearly longer. Even after measuring them and knowing the truth, most people still see the difference.
POOL.m: Knowing about a bias does not switch it off. Use rulers, checklists and data where it matters.

POOL.h: In 1952, British psychologist William Edmund Hick showed that the time it takes to choose grows with the number of options.
POOL.b: Ray Hyman confirmed it in 1953. The increase is not linear: doubling the options adds a roughly fixed amount of extra time. Designers call it Hick’s law.
POOL.m: Trim the choices you face daily, from menus to wardrobes, and simple decisions get faster.

POOL.t: Stress helps, up to a point
POOL.h: In 1908, Robert Yerkes and John Dodson found that mice learned a task faster with moderate electric shocks, but not with strong ones, especially when the task was hard.
POOL.b: Their result was later generalised into the idea that performance rises with arousal and then falls. The famous “inverted U” is a simplification, but the core pattern is widely seen.
POOL.m: A little pressure can sharpen you. For complex tasks, aim for calm focus rather than high stress.

POOL.h: In a 1998 study, Matthew Botvinick and Jonathan Cohen hid a person’s real hand and placed a rubber hand in view.
POOL.b: Both were stroked with a brush at the same time. After a few minutes many people felt the rubber hand was their own. Later studies found people react with a spike of alarm when the rubber hand is threatened.
POOL.m: Your sense of your own body is built by the brain from what you see and feel, and it can be fooled.

POOL.h: In 1901, sponge divers recovered a corroded lump of bronze from a shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
POOL.b: Inside were interlocking gears. The Antikythera mechanism, made roughly 2,000 years ago, could predict eclipses and track the Sun and Moon. Nothing of similar complexity is known for over a thousand years afterwards.
POOL.m: Ancient people were often more technically skilled than we assume.

POOL.h: On 15 January 1919, a huge tank of molasses burst in Boston’s North End.
POOL.b: A wave of about 8.7 million litres swept through the streets, crushing buildings. Twenty-one people died and around 150 were injured. Investigations blamed a poorly built tank, and the disaster helped tighten building rules.
POOL.m: Even harmless-sounding substances become dangerous in bulk. Safety rules are often written after a disaster.

POOL.t: The fire with few recorded deaths
POOL.h: The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 in a bakery on Pudding Lane.
POOL.b: Over four days it destroyed about 13,000 houses and old St Paul’s Cathedral. Only a handful of deaths were officially recorded. Historians think the true toll was higher, since the deaths of poorer people often went unrecorded.
POOL.m: Official records show what was counted, not always what happened.

POOL.h: In 1991, hikers in the Ötztal Alps, on the Austrian–Italian border, found a body in melting ice.
POOL.b: He turned out to be about 5,300 years old, and was named Ötzi. In 2001, an X-ray revealed a stone arrowhead in his shoulder, showing he had been shot. His body also carries more than 60 tattoos.
POOL.m: One well-preserved person can tell us more about daily life than a whole ruined city.

POOL.h: The eruption of Vesuvius that buried Pompeii was long dated to 24 August AD 79, based on copies of a letter by Pliny the Younger.
POOL.b: In 2018, archaeologists found a charcoal inscription there dated to mid-October. Together with autumn fruits found in the ruins, many experts now think the eruption happened in autumn.
POOL.m: Even well-known dates rest on evidence, and new evidence can move them.

POOL.t: The warship that sank at once
POOL.h: On 10 August 1628, the Swedish warship Vasa set off on her maiden voyage in Stockholm.
POOL.b: She sailed only about 1,300 metres before a gust tipped her over and she sank. She was top-heavy, with too little ballast for her heavy guns. Raised in 1961, she is now one of the best-preserved ships of her era.
POOL.m: Pressure to impress can override sound engineering. Test before you launch.

POOL.h: In July 1553, teenage Lady Jane Grey was proclaimed queen of England after the death of Edward VI.
POOL.b: Support quickly swung to his half-sister Mary, and Jane was deposed after about nine days. She was executed in February 1554. She had been placed on the throne largely by the ambitions of others.
POOL.m: Power handed to you by others can be taken away just as fast.

POOL.h: In 1900, Arthur Evans began uncovering clay tablets at Knossos on Crete, written in a script called Linear B.
POOL.b: For decades no one could read it. In 1952, Michael Ventris, an English architect and amateur, showed it was an early form of Greek. Most tablets turned out to be inventories and palace records.
POOL.m: Outsiders with fresh eyes sometimes solve what experts cannot.

POOL.h: On 6 May 1937, the German airship Hindenburg caught fire while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey.
POOL.b: It was destroyed in about half a minute, and the footage became famous. Yet 62 of the 97 people aboard survived. Thirty-six people died, including one member of the ground crew.
POOL.m: Dramatic images can make a disaster seem even worse than it was.

POOL.h: On 5 July 1841, Thomas Cook organised a train trip for about 500 people from Leicester to a temperance meeting in Loughborough, England.
POOL.b: Tickets cost a shilling and included travel and refreshments. The success led him to organise more trips, and his firm grew into one of the world’s best-known travel companies.
POOL.m: Many big industries began as one practical solution to a local need.

POOL.h: In 1676, Danish astronomer Ole Rømer noticed that eclipses of Jupiter’s moon Io came later than predicted when Earth was farther from Jupiter.
POOL.b: He reasoned the delay was the time light took to cross the extra distance. It was the first strong evidence that light travels at a finite speed.
POOL.m: Small, careful discrepancies in data can point to big discoveries.

POOL.h: In 1963, Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba noticed that a hot ice-cream mix froze before a cooler one.
POOL.b: He later published the observation with physicist Denis Osborne, and it became known as the Mpemba effect. Experiments since have given mixed results, and careful studies often find no effect. It depends heavily on the conditions.
POOL.m: A striking claim needs careful testing. Some famous effects shrink when you control the details.

POOL.h: Flick water onto a very hot pan and droplets can skate around for a long time instead of vanishing.
POOL.b: Above roughly 200 °C, the bottom of the drop turns to vapour instantly and the drop floats on that cushion. This is the Leidenfrost effect, described by German doctor Johann Leidenfrost in 1756.
POOL.m: Cooks use this as a test: when water drops glide like beads, a stainless steel pan is hot enough.

POOL.h: In 1827, Scottish botanist Robert Brown saw tiny particles from pollen grains jiggling constantly in water.
POOL.b: The motion puzzled scientists for decades. In 1905, Albert Einstein explained it as the particles being bumped by moving water molecules. Jean Perrin’s experiments confirmed this, helping prove atoms are real.
POOL.m: Everyday oddities can hide deep truths. Take small puzzles seriously.

POOL.t: The chemistry of a golden crust
POOL.h: The browning of toast, seared steak and roasted coffee comes mostly from the Maillard reaction.
POOL.b: It is named after French chemist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912. Sugars and amino acids react at high heat, creating hundreds of flavour compounds. It is different from caramelisation, which involves sugar alone.
POOL.m: Pat food dry before searing. While the surface is wet, it stays near 100 °C and browns poorly.

POOL.t: The woman who first tested CO2
POOL.h: In 1856, American scientist Eunice Foote filled glass cylinders with different gases and placed them in sunlight.
POOL.b: The one with carbon dioxide heated the most. She suggested more of it in the air would warm the planet. Her paper was read at a scientific meeting that year, three years before John Tyndall’s better-known work.
POOL.m: Important discoveries can be overlooked. Credit is not always given where it was first earned.

POOL.h: When Swedish astronomer Anders Celsius proposed his temperature scale in 1742, water boiled at 0 and froze at 100.
POOL.b: The scale was flipped soon after his death in 1744. The change is often credited to botanist Carl Linnaeus, though others proposed it too.
POOL.m: Conventions that feel natural today were often arbitrary choices.

POOL.h: Ancient Greeks noticed that amber rubbed with fur could attract light things like straw.
POOL.b: Their word for amber was ēlektron. In 1600, English physician William Gilbert used the Latin word “electricus” for this effect. In 1891, George Johnstone Stoney used “electron” for the basic unit of charge.
POOL.m: Many science words carry their history in their names.

POOL.t: A sonic boom follows the plane
POOL.h: A sonic boom is not a single bang made when a plane breaks the sound barrier.
POOL.b: It is a cone of pressure that trails the aircraft the whole time it flies faster than sound. People on the ground hear it as the cone sweeps past. This is why supersonic flights such as Concorde’s were mostly kept over the sea.
POOL.m: Many effects we imagine as one moment are really continuous processes.

POOL.h: Salt melts ice because salty water freezes at a lower temperature than pure water.
POOL.b: But ordinary salt works much less well in very cold weather, below about −10 °C. In theory, a salt solution can stay liquid to about −21 °C, but in practice it melts ice too slowly by then.
POOL.m: In a hard freeze, grit or sand for traction may help more than extra salt.

POOL.h: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in beads, taking dirt with it.
POOL.b: In the 1970s, German botanist Wilhelm Barthlott showed why: the leaf is covered in tiny waxy bumps, so water barely touches the surface. This “lotus effect” has inspired self-cleaning paints, glass and fabrics.
POOL.m: Nature often solves engineering problems first. Look to it for ideas.

POOL.h: Each autumn, monarch butterflies from eastern North America fly thousands of kilometres to forests in central Mexico.
POOL.b: No single butterfly makes the round trip. The return north takes several generations, yet the next autumn’s butterflies find the same forests.
POOL.m: Some journeys are too long for one lifetime, and only succeed as a team effort across generations.

POOL.h: At the start of the wet season, tens of millions of red crabs on Christmas Island migrate from the forest to the sea to breed.
POOL.b: Females release their eggs into the ocean in time with the tides and the phase of the Moon. Roads are closed, and special bridges and tunnels help the crabs cross.
POOL.m: Small changes, like a crab bridge, can let people and wildlife share the same space.

POOL.h: In the 1990s, divers off Amami Ōshima in southern Japan began spotting perfect circles, about 2 metres wide, in the sand.
POOL.b: In 2011 they found the maker: a male pufferfish just over 10 cm long. He spends days carving the pattern with his fins to attract a female, who lays her eggs in the centre.
POOL.m: Remarkable work can be done by the smallest makers. Some mysteries have simple, surprising answers.

POOL.t: The fish that shoots its prey
POOL.h: Archerfish, found in mangroves from India to northern Australia, spit jets of water at insects on leaves above the surface.
POOL.b: The insect falls and the fish eats it. They can hit targets more than a metre away, allowing for how light bends at the water’s surface.
POOL.m: Precision can be learned. Archerfish improve their aim with practice, much as we do.

POOL.h: Once a year, a few nights after a full moon in late spring, many corals on the Great Barrier Reef release eggs and sperm at the same time.
POOL.b: The water fills with drifting pink and white bundles. Scientists from James Cook University first documented this mass spawning in the early 1980s.
POOL.m: Timing can matter as much as effort. Coordinated action gives each tiny egg a better chance.

POOL.h: Emperor penguin fathers balance their single egg on their feet through the Antarctic winter for about two months.
POOL.b: They do not eat during this time and lose a large share of their body weight. To survive temperatures below −40 °C and fierce winds, they huddle together, slowly rotating so each bird takes a turn on the cold edge.
POOL.m: Taking turns in the hard spot is how a group gets through a hard season.

POOL.h: Australia’s green tree ants build nests by pulling living leaves together.
POOL.b: Workers form chains to bend the leaves into place. Others hold larvae in their jaws and use them like glue guns, since the larvae produce silk that binds the leaves.
POOL.m: Teamwork can turn simple parts into complex structures.

POOL.h: In the eastern United States, periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground, then emerge in their billions within a few weeks.
POOL.b: One idea is that the prime-number cycles make it hard for predators to sync with them, though this is still debated. In 2024, a particular 13-year group and 17-year group emerged in the same year for the first time since 1803, overlapping in only a small area.
POOL.m: Patience, and sheer numbers, can be powerful survival strategies.

POOL.h: In some forests, the crowns of neighbouring trees stop just short of touching, leaving a pattern of narrow gaps like cracks in a puzzle.
POOL.b: This is called crown shyness. Scientists are still unsure why it happens. Ideas include branches being worn back as trees sway in the wind, and trees sensing each other’s shade.
POOL.m: Even familiar sights, like a forest canopy, can still hold open questions.

POOL.t: Seashells at the top of Everest
POOL.h: The rock at the summit of Mount Everest is limestone that formed on an ancient seafloor, roughly 450 million years ago.
POOL.b: It contains fossils of small sea creatures. The seabed was lifted over 8 km by the slow collision of India with Asia, which is still pushing the Himalayas up today.
POOL.m: Given enough time, the ground beneath us can change beyond recognition.

POOL.h: The Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once one of the four largest lakes in the world.
POOL.b: From the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the rivers feeding it to grow cotton. By the 2010s it had lost most of its area, leaving fishing boats stranded in desert. A dam built in 2005 has helped the northern part recover.
POOL.m: Big environmental damage can happen within a single lifetime, and partial repair is still possible.

POOL.h: Beneath roughly a fifth of Australia lies the Great Artesian Basin, one of the largest underground water reserves in the world.
POOL.b: Water entering it along the Great Dividing Range moves very slowly and can be up to a couple of million years old by the time it surfaces. It has supported outback towns and stations for over a century.
POOL.m: The resources we cannot see still need looking after. Old water is slow to replace.

POOL.h: The Nullarbor Plain takes its name from Latin for “no tree”.
POOL.b: It stretches across the south of Western Australia and South Australia, and is one of the largest single slabs of limestone in the world. Its flat surface hides extensive caves beneath. The Trans-Australian Railway crosses it on a straight track of about 478 km.
POOL.m: A place name can be a simple description. Read names as clues.

POOL.h: Mount Wycheproof in north-west Victoria is often promoted as the smallest registered mountain in the world.
POOL.b: It stands about 148 metres above sea level but only about 43 metres above the surrounding plains. The town holds an annual race where people run up it carrying sacks of wheat.
POOL.m: What counts as big depends on the landscape around it.

POOL.h: The Canary Islands are named after dogs, not birds.
POOL.b: The name comes from the Latin Canariae Insulae, “islands of dogs”, recorded by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder, who described large dogs there. The canary bird was later named after the islands.
POOL.m: Word origins can run the opposite way to what seems obvious.

POOL.h: In Canada’s Bay of Fundy, the difference between high and low tide can reach about 16 metres, the largest in the world.
POOL.b: The bay’s shape and length make the water slosh in rhythm with the tides, amplifying them. Boats that float at high tide can sit on mud a few hours later.
POOL.m: When something repeats in step with its natural rhythm, small pushes can become huge effects.

POOL.t: Europe’s highest peak depends on a line
POOL.h: If the Caucasus Mountains count as part of Europe, the continent’s highest peak is Mount Elbrus in Russia, at 5,642 metres.
POOL.b: If not, it is Mont Blanc, on the French–Italian border, at about 4,800 metres. The border between Europe and Asia is a convention and has been drawn in different places.
POOL.m: Many “facts” depend on definitions. Ask how a category was drawn before comparing.

POOL.t: Most people live in the north
POOL.h: About nine in ten people on Earth live in the Northern Hemisphere.
POOL.b: Most of the world’s land lies north of the equator, including nearly all of Europe, Asia and North America. The south includes Australia, most of South America, southern Africa and parts of South-East Asia.
POOL.m: A map’s layout hides lopsided realities. The Southern Hemisphere is mostly ocean.

POOL.h: San Marino, surrounded by Italy, traces its founding to AD 301, when by tradition a stonemason named Marinus settled on Mount Titano.
POOL.b: It claims to be the oldest surviving republic in the world. Its constitution of 1600 is among the oldest written constitutions still in force.
POOL.m: Small states can be remarkably durable. Size is not the same as strength.

POOL.h: According to Aristotle, people mocked the early Greek thinker Thales of Miletus because his philosophy had left him poor.
POOL.b: So, reading the signs of a good harvest ahead, he paid small deposits in winter to secure the olive presses of Miletus and Chios. When the harvest came in, everyone needed a press, and he hired them out at whatever price he liked.
POOL.m: Knowledge often looks useless until the moment it is needed. Deep understanding of a field tends to pay off in ways others do not see coming.

POOL.t: The letter that broke a life’s work
POOL.h: In 1902, as German logician Gottlob Frege’s great work on the foundations of arithmetic was being printed, he received a letter from a young Bertrand Russell.
POOL.b: Russell asked about the set of all sets that are not members of themselves: is it a member of itself? Either answer leads to a contradiction, and Frege’s system collapsed. Frege added an appendix admitting the problem, which Russell later praised as a rare act of intellectual honesty.
POOL.m: Finding a flaw in your own thinking is painful but valuable. Owning a mistake openly earns more respect than defending it.

POOL.h: In 1688 Irish thinker William Molyneux asked John Locke a puzzle: if a person born blind learned to tell a cube from a sphere by touch, and then gained sight, could they tell which was which just by looking?
POOL.b: Both men guessed no. In 2011 a study of children in India treated for blindness from birth found they could not immediately match shapes they had touched to shapes they saw, though they learned to within days.
POOL.m: Our senses need experience to work together. Much of what feels obvious to us was learned, not given.

POOL.h: In his Pensées, published in 1670 after his death, Blaise Pascal wrote that all of humanity’s unhappiness comes from one thing: not knowing how to sit quietly in a room.
POOL.b: In a 2014 study led by Timothy Wilson, many volunteers left alone with their thoughts for about 15 minutes chose to give themselves a mild electric shock rather than simply sit. About two thirds of the men and a quarter of the women pressed the button.
POOL.m: Being alone with your own mind is a skill. A few minutes of quiet without a screen each day is worth practising.

POOL.h: In 1851 German philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer told a parable about porcupines on a cold winter’s day.
POOL.b: They huddle together for warmth, but their quills prick each other, so they move apart, then grow cold and draw close again. Eventually they find a distance where they are warm enough without getting hurt. Sigmund Freud later borrowed the image to describe human closeness.
POOL.m: Every relationship needs its own comfortable distance. Too close and too far can both hurt.

POOL.h: In 1961 political thinker Hannah Arendt attended the Jerusalem trial of Nazi official Adolf Eichmann for The New Yorker.
POOL.b: Her 1963 book argued that he seemed less a monster than a thoughtless careerist following orders and chasing promotion, and she called this “the banality of evil”. Historians have since found Eichmann was more committed to Nazi ideas than he appeared at trial, but her warning about thoughtlessness still resonates.
POOL.m: Great harm does not need great villains. Stopping to think about what you are asked to do is a moral act in itself.

POOL.h: Around 1078 Anselm of Canterbury argued that God is “that than which nothing greater can be conceived”, and that such a being must exist, since existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind.
POOL.b: A monk named Gaunilo of Marmoutier replied that the same logic would prove a perfect island exists somewhere. Centuries later, Immanuel Kant objected that existence is not a quality that makes something greater.
POOL.m: If an argument could prove anything at all, it proves nothing. Test reasoning by trying it on a silly example.

POOL.h: Socrates is often quoted as saying “I know that I know nothing”, but that neat line does not appear in Plato’s writings.
POOL.b: In Plato’s Apology, Socrates says he is wiser than a man who thinks he knows things only because he does not think he knows what he does not know. The snappy version is a later paraphrase.
POOL.m: Real wisdom is knowing where your knowledge runs out. Saying “I don’t know” is a strength, not a failure.

POOL.t: You cannot step in the same river twice
POOL.h: The Greek thinker Heraclitus of Ephesus, writing around 500 BCE, is famous for saying you cannot step into the same river twice.
POOL.b: That exact phrase comes from Plato’s paraphrase. A surviving fragment puts it more subtly: different waters flow over those who step into the same rivers. The river stays a river precisely because it keeps changing.
POOL.m: Things can keep their identity while constantly changing. That includes you, your relationships and your city.

POOL.h: In Philosophical Investigations, published in 1953, Ludwig Wittgenstein imagined everyone carrying a box holding something they call a “beetle”.
POOL.b: Nobody can look into anyone else’s box, so the thing inside could differ or even be empty. Yet the word “beetle” still works in conversation. Wittgenstein’s point was that words for inner experiences get their meaning from shared use, not from private objects.
POOL.m: When a word like “stress” or “fine” comes up, ask what the other person actually means. Shared words can hide very different experiences.

POOL.t: The Night Watch was cut down
POOL.h: Rembrandt finished his huge militia portrait in 1642, but in 1715 it was moved to Amsterdam’s town hall and trimmed on all sides to fit the wall.
POOL.b: The biggest strip came off the left side, removing two militiamen and a child. Its famous name came later too: darkened varnish made the daytime scene look like night.
POOL.m: Even masterpieces get altered by practical decisions. What we see today is not always what the artist made.

POOL.h: Johannes Vermeer of Delft, who died in 1675, left only about 35 paintings that experts agree are his.
POOL.b: He died in debt and was largely forgotten for nearly two centuries. French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger revived his reputation in the 1860s, and works like Girl with a Pearl Earring are now world famous.
POOL.m: A small body of careful work can outlast a large one. Quality can matter more than quantity.

POOL.t: The Last Supper began flaking early
POOL.h: Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper in Milan in the 1490s, on the wall of a monastery dining hall.
POOL.b: Instead of true fresco on wet plaster, he experimented with paint on dry plaster so he could work slowly. The paint began flaking within decades. The wall survived a 1943 bombing behind sandbags, and a restoration lasting about 21 years ended in 1999.
POOL.m: A clever shortcut can carry hidden costs. Proven methods exist for a reason, even when new ones look better.

POOL.h: Tchaikovsky wrote the 1812 Overture in 1880 to mark Russia’s defence against Napoleon, complete with church bells and cannon fire.
POOL.b: He told his patron Nadezhda von Meck it was “very loud and noisy” and written without much love. It became one of his most performed pieces anyway.
POOL.m: Creators are not always the best judges of their own work. Share things even when you have doubts about them.

POOL.t: A piece with no notes played
POOL.h: On 29 August 1952, pianist David Tudor sat at a piano in Woodstock, New York, and played nothing for four minutes and 33 seconds.
POOL.b: John Cage’s piece 4′33″ asks the audience to notice the sounds already around them: rain, rustling, coughs. Cage had earlier visited a soundproof chamber at Harvard and still heard sounds, which convinced him true silence does not exist.
POOL.m: There is always something to hear if you stop and listen. Try a few minutes of simply noticing the sounds around you.

POOL.t: The ballet that caused an uproar
POOL.h: On 29 May 1913, the premiere of Igor Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring in Paris drew jeers, shouting and scuffles in the audience.
POOL.b: The jagged music and Vaslav Nijinsky’s stamping choreography shocked many listeners. Accounts of a full riot are probably exaggerated, but the uproar was real. The score is now considered one of the most important of the 20th century.
POOL.m: New ideas often meet loud resistance at first. Early outrage is not a reliable judge of lasting value.

POOL.h: When Johann Sebastian Bach died in 1750, his music was known mostly among musicians and soon went out of fashion.
POOL.b: On 11 March 1829, 20-year-old Felix Mendelssohn conducted Bach’s St Matthew Passion in Berlin, its first performance since Bach’s death. The concert sparked a revival that made Bach one of the most famous composers of all.
POOL.m: Reputations can be rescued by one champion. Sharing forgotten work you love can change how the world sees it.

POOL.h: Antonio Stradivari made instruments in Cremona, Italy, until his death in 1737, and around 650 survive.
POOL.b: In blind tests published in 2012 and 2014, led by researcher Claudia Fritz, experienced soloists often preferred new, high-quality violins. They could not reliably tell the old masterpieces from new ones.
POOL.m: Reputation and price shape what we think we perceive. When you can, judge things blind.

POOL.t: A stage cannon burned the Globe
POOL.h: On 29 June 1613, during a performance of Shakespeare and John Fletcher’s Henry VIII, a stage cannon was fired for dramatic effect.
POOL.b: Sparks lit the thatched roof of the Globe Theatre in London, and it burned to the ground in about an hour. No one died, though one man’s breeches caught fire and were reportedly put out with a bottle of ale. The rebuilt Globe had a tiled roof.
POOL.m: A special effect can become the main event. Fire safety matters most when things are exciting.

POOL.h: Scrabble was invented in the 1930s by Alfred Mosher Butts, an American architect out of work during the Great Depression.
POOL.b: To decide how many tiles each letter should get, he counted letters on the front pages of newspapers, including The New York Times. Rare letters like Q and Z got fewer tiles and higher scores. The game was renamed Scrabble in 1948.
POOL.m: Good design often starts with careful counting. Data about how things are actually used beats guessing.

POOL.h: In 1978 NASA scientists Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais warned that collisions in orbit could create debris that causes more collisions, a runaway chain now called the Kessler syndrome.
POOL.b: In 2009 a working Iridium satellite and a dead Russian satellite collided over Siberia, creating thousands of trackable fragments. Tens of thousands of pieces of debris are now tracked around Earth.
POOL.m: Small messes can compound into big ones. Cleaning up early is cheaper than dealing with a cascade later.

POOL.h: In February 2017 astronomers announced that a small, cool star called TRAPPIST-1, about 40 light-years away, has seven Earth-sized planets.
POOL.b: All of them orbit closer to their star than Mercury does to the Sun, and the innermost takes only about a day and a half to go around. Several lie in the zone where liquid water might exist.
POOL.m: Our solar system is just one way to build a planetary family. The universe is more varied than our own backyard suggests.

POOL.t: Why is the night sky dark?
POOL.h: If the universe were infinite, eternal and evenly filled with stars, every line of sight would end on a star and the night sky would blaze.
POOL.b: This puzzle is called Olbers’ paradox, after German astronomer Heinrich Olbers, who wrote about it in 1823. The answer is that the universe has a finite age, about 13.8 billion years, so light from very distant stars has not reached us yet, and cosmic expansion dims what does arrive.
POOL.m: Ordinary things can hold deep clues. Even darkness at night tells us the universe had a beginning.

POOL.h: Comet Shoemaker-Levy 9, discovered in 1993, had already been torn into more than 20 pieces by Jupiter’s gravity.
POOL.b: In July 1994 the fragments slammed into Jupiter over about six days, leaving dark scars larger than Earth. It was the first collision between two solar system bodies that people watched as it happened.
POOL.m: Space is not static; big impacts still happen. It is one reason astronomers keep watch for asteroids near Earth.

POOL.h: On 14 September 2015, the LIGO detectors in the United States picked up ripples in space itself from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away.
POOL.b: The signal stretched the detectors by far less than the width of a proton. Albert Einstein had predicted such gravitational waves about a century earlier, and the discovery won a Nobel Prize in 2017.
POOL.m: Patient, precise work can confirm ideas decades after they were proposed. Some predictions just need better tools.

POOL.h: Edwin Hubble is usually credited with discovering that the universe is expanding, in 1929.
POOL.b: But in 1927 Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaître had already published the idea, along with the link between a galaxy’s distance and its speed. His paper appeared in French in a little-read journal. In 2018 the International Astronomical Union recommended calling it the Hubble–Lemaître law.
POOL.m: Credit does not always go to whoever was first. Where and how you share an idea can matter as much as the idea.

POOL.t: The fastest thing we have built
POOL.h: On 24 December 2024, NASA’s Parker Solar Probe swept about 6.1 million kilometres from the Sun’s surface at roughly 690,000 km/h, the fastest speed of any human-made object.
POOL.b: At that pace you could fly from Sydney to Perth in under 20 seconds. It was the first NASA spacecraft named after a living person, solar physicist Eugene Parker.
POOL.m: Getting close to the Sun is a speed problem, not just a heat problem. Big engineering goals often hide surprising challenges.

POOL.h: Without gravity loading their skeletons, astronauts can lose roughly 1% or more of the bone density in their hips and spine each month.
