POOL.b: To fight this, crews on the International Space Station exercise for about two hours a day. Some bone loss can take years to recover after returning to Earth.
POOL.m: Bones stay strong because they carry loads. On Earth, walking and weight-bearing exercise do the same job.

POOL.h: In 1963 palaeontologist John Wells counted daily growth ridges on fossil corals about 380 million years old.
POOL.b: He found around 400 ridges per yearly band, suggesting a year then had about 400 days. Earth’s orbit was much the same, so each day must have been shorter, roughly 22 hours. The Moon’s tides have been slowly braking Earth’s spin ever since.
POOL.m: Clues about the deep past can hide in everyday objects. Tiny, steady changes add up over enormous spans of time.

POOL.t: Sunlight is older than it looks
POOL.h: Light leaving the Sun’s surface reaches Earth in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
POOL.b: But the energy in that light was made in the Sun’s core long before. It is absorbed and re-emitted countless times on its way out, a journey estimated to take tens of thousands of years or more.
POOL.m: The sunshine on your skin began its journey before farming existed. Some things are worth pausing to appreciate.

POOL.h: American farmer Charles Osborne began hiccupping in 1922 and did not stop until 1990, about 68 years later, a world record.
POOL.b: A hiccup is a sudden spasm of the diaphragm, followed by the vocal cords snapping shut, which makes the “hic” sound. Most bouts last only minutes and stop on their own.
POOL.m: Hiccups are almost always harmless and brief. Ones that last more than a couple of days are worth checking with a doctor.

POOL.h: In 2009 Japanese researchers used ultra-sensitive cameras to show that the human body gives off visible light.
POOL.b: The glow is about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see. It was brightest around the face and changed through the day, and is thought to come from chemical reactions in the body’s cells.
POOL.m: Your body is constantly busy at a chemical level, even when you are still. Life is a process, not a thing.

POOL.t: Why our eyes show so much white
POOL.h: Humans show much more of the white of the eye than most other primates, making it easy to see where someone is looking.
POOL.b: A 2007 study found human infants tend to follow a person’s gaze, while chimpanzees mostly follow head direction. Some researchers think visible eye whites evolved to help cooperation, though recent work shows some apes have lighter eyes than once assumed.
POOL.m: Where you look sends a signal. Eye contact is one of the oldest tools for working together.

POOL.t: Feeling a limb that is gone
POOL.h: Most people who lose a limb still feel it afterwards, and many feel pain in it.
POOL.b: In the 1990s neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran used a simple mirror box so a patient saw the reflection of their remaining arm where the missing one had been. Moving the reflected arm eased some patients’ phantom cramps. Evidence for mirror therapy is mixed, but it showed how much the brain’s body map shapes feeling.
POOL.m: Sensation is built by the brain, not just by the body part. What we feel is the brain’s best guess.

POOL.t: Why crying makes your nose run
POOL.h: Your eyes make tears all day to keep them moist, not just when you cry.
POOL.b: Extra tears flow when something irritates the eye, like onion fumes, and when you feel strong emotion. Tears drain through tiny holes in the inner corners of your eyelids into your nose, which is why a good cry leaves you reaching for a tissue.
POOL.m: Tears are routine maintenance as well as emotion. Crying is a normal body process, nothing to be embarrassed about.

POOL.h: In 1952 American anaesthetist Virginia Apgar designed a quick check for newborn babies.
POOL.b: At one and five minutes after birth, staff score colour, heart rate, reflex response, muscle tone and breathing from 0 to 2 each, for a total out of 10. The memorable APGAR acronym was added a decade later. Her score is still used in hospitals worldwide.
POOL.m: A simple, standard checklist can save lives. Clear routines help people act well under pressure.

POOL.h: People blink about 15 to 20 times a minute during normal conversation.
POOL.b: When concentrating on a screen or reading, the rate can drop by half or more. Each blink spreads a fresh layer of tears across the eye, which is why long screen sessions can leave eyes dry and tired.
POOL.m: Tired eyes after screen time are common. Regular breaks to look into the distance and blink help.

POOL.h: The air you breathe in is about 21% oxygen, and the air you breathe out still contains about 16%.
POOL.b: Your body only takes a portion of the oxygen from each breath. That leftover oxygen is why rescue breaths during CPR can still help someone who has stopped breathing.
POOL.m: Your exhaled breath can support someone else’s life. It is one reason learning CPR is so valuable.

POOL.t: Hair grows about a centimetre a month
POOL.h: Scalp hair grows roughly one centimetre a month, and a typical scalp has around 100,000 hairs.
POOL.b: Each follicle cycles through growing, resting and shedding phases, and losing 50 to 100 hairs a day is normal. The growing phase lasts years, and its length helps explain why some people can grow much longer hair than others.
POOL.m: Finding hairs on your pillow is usually just the normal cycle. Changes in growth take months to show.

POOL.t: About one in ten are left-handed
POOL.h: Roughly 10% of people are left-handed, and evidence from ancient tools, teeth and cave art suggests a right-handed majority has existed for a very long time.
POOL.b: Handedness is only partly genetic, shaped by many genes with small effects. Even identical twins can have different dominant hands.
POOL.m: Most traits are not decided by a single gene. Small differences between people often have complex, shared causes.

POOL.h: In the 1600s Sweden used copper as money, and its largest plate coins weighed up to about 20 kg.
POOL.b: In 1661 Stockholms Banco began issuing paper notes, the first banknotes in Europe. The bank printed too many and failed within a few years. Its replacement, the Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the world’s oldest central bank still operating.
POOL.m: Convenience made paper money popular, but trust kept it alive. Money only works while people believe in it.

POOL.h: For centuries, cowrie shells were used as money across parts of Africa, South Asia and China.
POOL.b: Many came from the Maldives. They were durable, hard to fake, easy to count and could not be grown at will. In Chinese writing, the character for shell forms part of many words linked to money and value.
POOL.m: Money does not have to be metal or paper. Anything scarce, durable and widely accepted can do the job.

POOL.h: In 1626 Dutch settlers acquired Manhattan from the Lenape people for trade goods valued at 60 guilders, according to a Dutch letter from that year.
POOL.b: In the 1800s a writer converted that to about $24, and the figure stuck. The comparison with modern prices is misleading, and the Lenape likely saw the deal as sharing the land, not selling it forever.
POOL.m: Old prices rarely convert neatly into today’s money. Be wary of any story that makes history sound too simple.

POOL.t: A Coke cost five cents for 70 years
POOL.h: From 1886 until the late 1950s, a standard bottle of Coca-Cola in the United States usually cost five cents.
POOL.b: Economists have traced the reasons, including long-term bottling contracts and vending machines built to accept a single nickel. Changing the price would have meant a much bigger jump, since there was no convenient coin between 5 and 10 cents.
POOL.m: Prices can stick for practical reasons, not just economic ones. Small frictions shape big markets.

POOL.t: The card that began with a dinner
POOL.h: In 1950 Frank McNamara and Ralph Schneider launched Diners Club in New York, one of the first general charge cards.
POOL.b: Company lore says McNamara came up with the idea after forgetting his wallet at a restaurant, though that story was later admitted to be at least partly a marketing tale. The first cards were made of cardboard and worked at a small number of New York restaurants.
POOL.m: Paying later is a modern invention, and a powerful one. Knowing how it changes spending helps you use it wisely.

POOL.t: Big notes are harder to break
POOL.h: In 2009 researchers Priya Raghubir and Joydeep Srivastava found people were less likely to spend money held as a single large note than the same amount in smaller notes or coins.
POOL.b: Breaking a big note seems to feel like a bigger decision. They called this the denomination effect.
POOL.m: The form money takes can change how freely you spend it. Carrying cash as one larger note can act as a small brake.

POOL.h: The most widely accepted theory is that the $ sign grew out of “ps”, a handwritten abbreviation for pesos, the Spanish silver dollars used widely in the Americas.
POOL.b: In 18th-century writing, the p and s gradually merged, with the s written over the p. The sign was in use before the United States minted its first dollar coins in the 1790s.
POOL.m: Everyday symbols often carry hidden history. Money’s language records old trade routes and empires.

POOL.h: In a 2017 study, Ashley Whillans, Elizabeth Dunn, Michael Norton and colleagues surveyed more than 6,000 people in the United States, Canada, Denmark and the Netherlands.
POOL.b: Those who paid for time-saving services, like cleaning or takeaway, reported greater life satisfaction. In a follow-up experiment in Vancouver, working adults felt happier and less time-stressed after spending $40 to save time than after spending it on a material purchase.
POOL.m: If a chore drains you, paying to hand it off can be money well spent. Time is worth budgeting for too.

POOL.t: A pound was once a pound of silver
POOL.h: In Anglo-Saxon England, a pound weight of silver was divided into 240 silver pennies.
POOL.b: That is why British money long had 240 pence to the pound, with 12 pence to the shilling and 20 shillings to the pound. The £ sign is a stylised L for libra, the Latin word for pound. Britain switched to decimal currency in 1971.
POOL.m: Many currency names began as weights of metal. The shekel, lira and pound all started on a scale.

POOL.h: The euro began on 1 January 1999 as a currency for banks and markets only.
POOL.b: On 1 January 2002, euro notes and coins arrived in 12 countries at once, the largest cash changeover in history. Each euro coin has a common side and a national side, so coins from many countries mix in every purse. Bulgaria became the 21st euro-area country on 1 January 2026.
POOL.m: Money is ultimately an agreement, and even huge agreements can change. Big transitions work best with long, careful preparation.

POOL.h: The Great Wall of China is visible from space with the naked eye.
POOL.e: It is long but only a few metres wide. Astronauts, including China’s Yang Liwei, have said they could not see it unaided from orbit.

POOL.h: Goldfish have a three-second memory.
POOL.e: Goldfish have been trained to respond to sounds and cues and remember them for months.

POOL.h: Ninety percent of your brain is just sitting there idle.
POOL.e: Scans light up almost every region over a normal day. Your brain is only about 2 percent of your body weight but burns roughly 20 percent of your energy, far too costly to leave mostly unused.

POOL.h: Once lightning hits a spot, that spot is safe forever.
POOL.e: Tall structures get hit over and over, some many times a year. US park ranger Roy Sullivan was struck by lightning seven separate times and survived them all.

POOL.h: Bulls charge because the colour red enrages them.
POOL.e: Cattle are red-green colour blind. The bull reacts to the cape’s movement, not its colour.

POOL.h: Napoleon was a tiny man by the standards of his day.
POOL.e: At around 170 cm he was average or a bit above for a Frenchman of his era. French inches were longer than English ones, and British cartoonists happily drew him as a pint-sized tantrum thrower.

POOL.h: Humans have more than five senses.
POOL.e: Beyond sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, we sense balance, body position, temperature, pain and internal signals like hunger.

POOL.h: Hair and nails keep growing after death.
POOL.e: The skin dries and pulls back after death, which makes hair and nails look longer.

POOL.h: Keep cracking your knuckles and you'll end up with arthritis.
POOL.e: Research hasn't found a connection. Dr Donald Unger cracked only his left hand's knuckles for about 60 years, found no arthritis in either hand, and won an Ig Nobel Prize for it.

POOL.h: Vikings wore horned helmets into battle.
POOL.e: No horned Viking battle helmet has ever been found. The image comes largely from 19th-century costume design, including for Wagner’s operas.

POOL.h: A sugary treat sends kids bouncing off the walls.
POOL.e: Controlled trials where nobody knows who got sugar find no change in behaviour. The twist: parents told their child had sugar judge them as wilder, even when the drink was sugar-free.

POOL.h: Chameleons change colour mainly to blend in.
POOL.e: Their colour shifts are mostly about mood, signalling to other chameleons and regulating temperature.

POOL.h: Honey stored properly can stay edible for an extremely long time.
POOL.e: Honey is low in water and acidic, which makes it very hard for bacteria to grow. Sealed honey can last for many years.

POOL.h: Toilets flush the opposite way in the Southern Hemisphere.
POOL.e: The Coriolis effect is far too weak at that scale. The shape of the bowl and the water jets decide the direction.

POOL.h: Mount Everest is not the tallest mountain from base to peak.
POOL.e: Mauna Kea in Hawaii rises over 10,000 m from its base on the ocean floor, though most of it is underwater. Everest has the highest summit above sea level.

POOL.h: Bats are blind.
POOL.e: All bats can see. Many use echolocation too, and some fruit bats have excellent eyesight.

POOL.h: Forget your beanie and most of your body heat escapes out the top.
POOL.e: Your head sheds heat in line with its share of your skin, around 10 percent. The myth is often traced to old US Army cold-weather tests where volunteers were bundled in Arctic suits but left bareheaded.

POOL.h: Shave it off and it comes back thicker and darker.
POOL.e: A razor only cuts the dead shaft, so it can't reach the follicle that decides thickness or colour. Stubble just feels coarse because it has a blunt tip instead of a natural tapered one.

POOL.h: The blood in your veins is blue until it meets oxygen.
POOL.e: Human blood is always red: bright red when rich in oxygen, darker red when not. Veins look blue because of the way light passes through skin and is absorbed.

POOL.h: An Australian mammal lays eggs and the males have venomous spurs.
POOL.e: The platypus lays eggs, and males carry a spur on each hind leg that delivers venom painful enough to disable a dog. It’s one of very few venomous mammals.

POOL.h: Going outside with wet hair gives you a cold.
POOL.e: Colds are caused by viruses, so you need to catch one to get sick. Colds are more common in winter mainly because people crowd indoors and some viruses survive better in cool, dry air.

POOL.h: Some turtles can breathe through their bottoms.
POOL.e: Australia’s Fitzroy River turtle absorbs oxygen from water through its cloaca, the rear opening. This lets it stay underwater for very long periods.

POOL.h: Taking vitamin C every day stops most people catching colds.
POOL.e: Large reviews found regular vitamin C does not reduce how often most people catch colds, though it may slightly shorten them. It only cut cold risk in people under heavy physical stress, such as marathon runners.

POOL.h: Dogs see the world only in black and white.
POOL.e: Dogs do see colour, but fewer shades than we do. With two types of colour receptors instead of our three, they mainly see blues and yellows and struggle to separate red from green.

POOL.h: A duck’s quack doesn’t echo.
POOL.e: Acoustics researchers at the University of Salford tested this in 2003 and found a quack echoes like any other sound. The echo is just hard to notice because a quack fades gradually.

POOL.h: Earth's trees outnumber the stars in our galaxy.
POOL.e: Earth has around three trillion trees against a few hundred billion stars in the Milky Way. The same 2015 study estimated the number of trees has nearly halved since humans started farming.

POOL.h: Handle a chick and its parents will abandon it because of your scent.
POOL.e: Most birds barely notice smells and won't ditch a chick over a human touch. Feathered fledglings hopping on the ground are often fine anyway, since their parents keep feeding them there for days.

POOL.h: Camels store water in their humps.
POOL.e: A camel’s hump is mostly fat, an energy reserve for lean times. Camels survive without water thanks to efficient kidneys and blood cells that cope with dehydration.

POOL.h: Humans glow in the dark.
POOL.e: Your body gives off a faint visible light, about 1,000 times too weak for your eyes to see. Japanese researchers filmed it with ultra-sensitive cameras in 2009 and found it was brightest on the face in the late afternoon.

POOL.h: A coin dropped from a skyscraper could kill someone below.
POOL.e: A small, flat coin tumbles and quickly reaches a low top speed because of air resistance. It might sting, but it would not be deadly.

POOL.h: Hippos can’t swim.
POOL.e: Hippos are too dense to float, so instead of swimming they walk or bounce along the riverbed, pushing off the bottom to reach the surface and breathe.

POOL.h: Ostriches bury their heads in the sand when they’re scared.
POOL.e: They don’t. A threatened ostrich may lie flat with its head and neck along the ground, and parents turn their eggs in shallow ground nests with their beaks, which from a distance can look like head-burying.

POOL.h: Walt Disney’s body was frozen so he could be revived in the future.
POOL.e: Disney died in December 1966 and was cremated; his ashes are at Forest Lawn cemetery in Glendale, California. The first person ever cryonically frozen, psychology professor James Bedford, was preserved about a month later, which may have fuelled the rumour.

POOL.h: The inventor of the Pringles can was buried in one.
POOL.e: Fredric Baur, the chemist who designed the stackable can, died in 2008. At his request, his family placed some of his ashes in a Pringles can before burying them.

POOL.h: Australia’s 1932 Emu War was a victory for the soldiers.
POOL.e: Soldiers with machine guns were sent to cull emus in Western Australia’s wheatbelt. The fast, scattered birds were so hard to hit that the operation was withdrawn after a few weeks.

POOL.h: Crows can remember and recognise individual human faces.
POOL.e: In University of Washington studies, crows scolded people wearing a mask that had been worn while trapping them, years later. They even seemed to pass the warning to other crows.

POOL.h: Albert Einstein failed maths at school.
POOL.e: He excelled at it and had mastered calculus before he was 15. The myth spread after a 1935 “Ripley’s Believe It or Not!” item, and Einstein replied that he had never failed in mathematics.

POOL.h: Woolly mammoths were still alive when the Great Pyramid was built.
POOL.e: A small population survived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia, until roughly 4,000 years ago. The Great Pyramid of Giza was finished around 4,500 years ago.

POOL.h: Meteorites are red-hot when they hit the ground.
POOL.e: Only a thin outer layer melts during the fall, and it streams away as it forms. The inside keeps the deep cold of space, so meteorites found soon after landing are usually just warm, or even cool, to the touch.

POOL.h: Nintendo was founded in the 1800s.
POOL.e: Nintendo began in Kyoto in 1889, making handmade hanafuda playing cards. It moved into electronic games only in the 1970s.

POOL.h: Lemmings leap off cliffs in mass suicides.
POOL.e: Lemming numbers boom and bust, and some drown when migrating across water, but they don’t deliberately kill themselves. The myth was cemented by Disney’s 1958 documentary White Wilderness, whose filmmakers herded lemmings off a ledge into a river.

POOL.h: Diamonds are formed from squashed coal.
POOL.e: Most diamonds form about 150 kilometres or more down in Earth’s mantle, far below any coal. Many are over a billion years old, older than land plants, which coal comes from.

POOL.h: An ancient Roman emperor taxed urine.
POOL.e: Emperor Vespasian taxed the collection of urine from public toilets, which was used for laundry and tanning. The phrase “pecunia non olet” (money doesn’t stink) grew from his reply to critics.

POOL.h: Humans evolved from chimpanzees.
POOL.e: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor that lived millions of years ago. Both species have been evolving separately ever since, so chimps are cousins, not ancestors.

POOL.h: In Columbus’s time, educated people believed the Earth was flat.
POOL.e: Educated Europeans had known Earth was round since ancient Greek times. The real debate was about its size, and Columbus badly underestimated it.

POOL.h: Marie Antoinette said “Let them eat cake.”
POOL.e: There’s no evidence she said it. A version of the line appears in Rousseau’s Confessions, written when she was a child in Austria.

POOL.h: The first cultivated carrots were not orange.
POOL.e: Early cultivated carrots, from around Central Asia, were mostly purple or yellow. Orange carrots became common later, especially thanks to Dutch growers in the 1600s.

POOL.h: Emperor Nero played the fiddle while Rome burned.
POOL.e: The fiddle wasn’t invented for another 1,500 years or so. The historian Tacitus says Nero was away at Antium when the fire of 64 CE began and returned to organise relief.

POOL.h: Fresh pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein.
POOL.e: Pineapple contains bromelain, which digests proteins and can make your mouth tingle. It’s also why fresh pineapple stops jelly from setting.

POOL.h: Thomas Edison invented the first electric light bulb.
POOL.e: Inventors including Joseph Swan made working incandescent bulbs before Edison. His achievement, from 1879, was a practical, long-lasting bulb and the system to power it.

POOL.h: Just reading about yawning can make you yawn.
POOL.e: Contagious yawning is triggered by seeing, hearing or even reading about yawns, as psychologist Robert Provine showed. Are you yawning yet?

POOL.h: James Cook was the first European to reach Australia.
POOL.e: Dutch navigator Willem Janszoon charted part of Cape York in 1606, over 160 years before Cook. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had lived there for more than 50,000 years.

POOL.h: Octopuses can taste with their arms.
POOL.e: Their suckers are packed with chemical receptors, so an octopus tastes whatever it touches. Most of its neurons are in its arms, which lets each arm explore and react partly on its own.

POOL.h: “Kangaroo” means “I don’t understand” in an Aboriginal language.
POOL.e: The word comes from “gangurru”, the Guugu Yimithirr word for a type of kangaroo, recorded by Cook’s expedition in 1770. Linguists confirmed the original meaning in the 1970s.

POOL.h: Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus.
POOL.e: Stegosaurus lived about 150 million years ago, while T. rex lived about 68 to 66 million years ago. That puts over 80 million years between them, but only 66 million between T. rex and us.

POOL.h: Peanuts are nuts.
POOL.e: Peanuts are legumes, relatives of peas and beans, and their pods grow underground. Botanically they’re closer to a lentil than a walnut.

POOL.h: One species of jellyfish can reverse its life cycle and become young again.
POOL.e: When stressed or injured, the jellyfish Turritopsis dohrnii can turn back into its early polyp stage and grow up again. It still dies from predators and disease, but not necessarily from old age.

POOL.h: Searing meat seals in the juices.
POOL.e: Seared meat loses about as much moisture as unseared meat. Searing is still worth doing because browning creates rich flavour.

POOL.h: Australia has the world’s largest population of wild camels.
POOL.e: Camels were brought over in the 1800s to carry supplies across the outback. When railways and trucks took over, many were set free, and hundreds of thousands now roam the arid interior.

POOL.h: Swallow your gum and it'll sit in your gut for seven years.
POOL.e: Gum base can't be broken down, but your gut simply pushes it along and out within days. The only real trouble comes from swallowing big wads often, which has occasionally caused blockages in kids.

POOL.h: A giraffe has the same number of neck bones as you.
POOL.e: Both have seven neck vertebrae, like almost all mammals. A giraffe’s are simply enormous, each around 25 cm long.

POOL.h: You must wait 24 hours before reporting someone missing.
POOL.e: Australian police say there is no waiting period. If you’re worried about someone, contact police straight away, and call 000 if you think they’re in danger.

POOL.h: The dot on a lowercase “i” has its own name.
POOL.e: It’s called a tittle, from the medieval Latin titulus, a small mark. The word survives in the King James Bible’s phrase “one jot or one tittle”.

POOL.h: A drink of alcohol warms you up in the cold.
POOL.e: Alcohol widens blood vessels near your skin, so you feel warmer while actually losing heat faster. It can raise the risk of hypothermia.

POOL.h: The Leaning Tower of Pisa started leaning while it was still being built.
POOL.e: The tower began tilting in the 1170s, after the third floor was added on soft ground. Builders later made upper floors taller on one side to compensate, giving it a slight curve.

POOL.h: Caesar salad is named after Julius Caesar.
POOL.e: It’s usually credited to Caesar Cardini, an Italian-born restaurateur in Tijuana, Mexico, in the 1920s.

POOL.h: The Moon has quakes, just like Earth.
POOL.e: Seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded thousands of moonquakes between 1969 and 1977. Some shallow ones reached about magnitude 5 and shook for over ten minutes, because the Moon’s dry, rigid rock rings like a bell.

POOL.h: People are either left-brained (logical) or right-brained (creative).
POOL.e: Some tasks rely more on one side of the brain, but a large study of over 1,000 brain scans found no evidence people favour one side overall. Logic and creativity both use networks across both hemispheres.

POOL.h: Horses can’t vomit.
POOL.e: A strong valve at the base of a horse’s oesophagus, and the angle it joins the stomach, stops food coming back up. It’s one reason colic in horses can be so serious.

POOL.h: You learn best when taught in your preferred learning style, like visual or auditory.
POOL.e: Many people have preferences, but studies find that matching teaching to a person’s preferred style doesn’t improve learning. Matching the method to the material works better.

POOL.h: A “jiffy” is a real unit of time.
POOL.e: Scientists have defined it several ways. In physics it can mean the time light takes to travel one centimetre, about 33 trillionths of a second, while electrical engineers use it for one cycle of mains power: 1/50 of a second in Australia.

POOL.h: Venting anger, like hitting a pillow, helps you let it go.
POOL.e: Studies show venting tends to keep anger going or increase it. Calming activities and time are more effective at cooling down.

POOL.h: “OK” started as a joke abbreviation of a misspelling.
POOL.e: In 1839, a Boston newspaper used “o.k.” for “oll korrect”, part of a fad for comic abbreviations. It spread widely and became one of the world’s most used words.

POOL.h: In relationships, opposites attract.
POOL.e: Research consistently finds that people are drawn to partners who share their values, interests and background. Similarity predicts attraction and lasting relationships much better than difference.

POOL.h: Bumblebees shouldn’t be able to fly, according to science.
POOL.e: The idea came from a 1930s calculation that treated a bee’s wing like a fixed aeroplane wing. Bees actually flap about 200 times a second, sweeping their wings to create swirling air vortices that give plenty of lift.

POOL.h: With practice, you can do two demanding tasks at once as well as one.
POOL.e: For tasks that need attention, the brain switches rapidly between them rather than doing both at once. Each switch costs time and accuracy.

POOL.h: “Irregardless” is listed in major dictionaries.
POOL.e: Merriam-Webster and others include it, labelled as nonstandard. It’s a real word in use since at least the early 1900s, but “regardless” is the safer choice.

POOL.h: You should never end a sentence with a preposition.
POOL.e: This “rule” dates from the late 1600s, when writers such as John Dryden wanted English to follow Latin grammar. Great writers have always broken it, and modern style guides accept it.

POOL.h: SOS stands for “Save Our Souls”.
POOL.e: SOS was chosen in the early 1900s because its Morse code, three dots, three dashes, three dots, is simple and unmistakable. “Save Our Souls” was invented afterwards to fit the letters.

POOL.h: “Ring a Ring o’ Roses” is about the plague.
POOL.e: The rhyme first appeared in print in 1881, and the plague theory wasn’t recorded until the mid-1900s. Folklorists find no evidence linking them.

POOL.h: Food dropped on the floor is safe if you pick it up within five seconds.
POOL.e: Rutgers University researchers found bacteria can transfer in under a second. Moist foods pick up more, and time on the floor only increases it.

POOL.h: Antibiotics will help you get over a cold or flu faster.
POOL.e: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and antibiotics only work on bacteria. Taking them when they’re not needed can cause side effects and helps resistant bacteria spread.

POOL.h: You should put butter on a burn.
POOL.e: Butter holds heat in and can raise infection risk. Australian first-aid advice is to cool the burn under running water for 20 minutes and call 000 for serious burns.

POOL.h: Tilt your head back to stop a nosebleed.
POOL.e: Tilting back can send blood down your throat. First-aid groups advise sitting, leaning forward and pinching the soft part of the nose for about 10 minutes.

POOL.h: Sucking out the venom is good first aid for a snakebite.
POOL.e: It doesn’t remove venom and can cause harm. In Australia, call 000, keep the person still, and apply a pressure immobilisation bandage.

POOL.h: Early humans lived alongside dinosaurs.
POOL.e: The non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. Our species appeared only around 300,000 years ago.

POOL.h: Eating carrots helps you see in the dark.
POOL.e: Vitamin A from carrots prevents night blindness caused by a deficiency, but extra carrots won’t sharpen normal night vision. Britain spread the idea in World War II, partly to explain its night-fighter pilots’ success without revealing its new radar.

POOL.h: More people are alive today than have ever died.
POOL.e: Demographers estimate around 117 billion people have ever been born. The roughly 8 billion alive now are only about 7% of them.

POOL.h: Roman soldiers were paid in salt, which gave us the word “salary”.
POOL.e: “Salary” comes from Latin “salarium”, which is linked to “sal” (salt), but no ancient source says soldiers were paid in salt. The exact connection remains unclear.

POOL.h: 93% of communication is non-verbal.
POOL.e: This figure comes from 1960s experiments on how people judge feelings from single words, tone of voice and facial expressions. The researcher, Albert Mehrabian, has said it doesn’t apply to communication in general.

POOL.h: The seeds are the hottest part of a chilli.
POOL.e: The heat compound capsaicin is concentrated in the white pith that holds the seeds. Seeds taste hot mainly because they touch it.

POOL.h: Spicy food causes stomach ulcers.
POOL.e: Most ulcers are caused by Helicobacter pylori bacteria or by some pain-relief medicines. Australians Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize for discovering the bacterial link.

POOL.h: The North Star is the brightest star in the night sky.
POOL.e: Polaris is only around the 48th brightest star; Sirius is the brightest. Polaris is useful for navigation because it sits almost directly above the North Pole, and it can’t be seen from Australia.

POOL.h: Private or incognito browsing hides what you do online.
POOL.e: Private mode only stops your device saving history and cookies. Websites, your employer or school, and your internet provider can still see your activity.

POOL.h: Force-closing apps on an iPhone saves battery.
POOL.e: Apple says background apps are paused and use little or no power. Relaunching them from scratch can use more battery, so only close an app if it’s frozen.

POOL.h: Microwave ovens cook food from the inside out.
POOL.e: Microwaves only reach the outer couple of centimetres of food. The centre heats up as that warmth spreads inwards, which is why thick dishes need stirring or standing time.

POOL.h: Sea otters sometimes hold hands while they sleep.
POOL.e: Sea otters rest floating on their backs and may link paws or wrap themselves in kelp. This keeps them from drifting apart or away on the current.

POOL.h: You swallow several spiders a year in your sleep.
POOL.e: There’s no evidence for it. A sleeping person’s breathing, heartbeat and snoring create vibrations that spiders tend to avoid, and a mouth is not an inviting place for one.

POOL.h: Frankenstein is the name of the monster.
POOL.e: In Mary Shelley’s 1818 novel, Victor Frankenstein is the scientist. The creature he makes is never given a name.

POOL.h: Different parts of your tongue detect different tastes, like sweet at the tip.
POOL.e: Every area of the tongue with taste buds can detect all the basic tastes. The famous ‘tongue map’ came from a misread German study from 1901.

POOL.h: Everyone needs to drink exactly eight glasses of water a day.
POOL.e: There’s no scientific basis for the eight-glass rule. Food, tea, coffee and other drinks all count, and needs vary with size, activity and weather.

POOL.h: Waking a sleepwalker can harm them.
POOL.e: A woken sleepwalker may be confused or startled, but it won’t hurt them. Gently guiding them back to bed is usually the safest option.

POOL.h: Quit the gym and your muscles will turn to fat.
POOL.e: Muscle and fat are separate tissues made of different cells, so neither can transform into the other. Unused muscle shrinks, and if eating habits stay the same, fat builds up alongside it, which creates the illusion.

POOL.h: Doing sit-ups will burn the fat on your belly specifically.
POOL.e: You can’t choose where your body burns fat from. Sit-ups strengthen the muscles underneath, but fat loss happens across the whole body.

POOL.h: Babies have more bones than adults.
POOL.e: Newborns have around 270 to 300 bones. Many fuse together as we grow, leaving adults with 206.

POOL.h: Identical twins have different fingerprints.
POOL.e: Fingerprints form in the womb, shaped by pressure, position and blood flow as well as genes, so even identical twins end up with distinct patterns.

POOL.h: Your brain itself can’t feel pain.
POOL.e: Brain tissue has no pain receptors, which is why some brain surgery is done while the patient is awake. Headaches come from surrounding tissues and blood vessels.

POOL.h: Brushing your teeth harder cleans them better.
POOL.e: Scrubbing hard can wear away enamel and damage gums. Dentists recommend a soft brush and gentle, thorough strokes.

POOL.h: Dentists often advise spitting out toothpaste instead of rinsing your mouth with water.
POOL.e: Skipping the rinse leaves a thin layer of fluoride on your teeth, giving it more time to strengthen enamel.

POOL.h: Grey skies mean you can skip the sunscreen.
POOL.e: Up to around 80 percent of UV can get through thin cloud. UV isn't linked to temperature either, so a mild, overcast Aussie day can still burn you.

POOL.h: Turkey makes you sleepy because it’s packed with tryptophan.
POOL.e: Turkey has about the same tryptophan as chicken or beef. The drowsiness after a big feast comes from the size of the meal, not the bird.

POOL.h: Play Mozart to your baby and you'll raise a genius.
POOL.e: The original study used university students and found a slight spatial boost lasting minutes. The idea still spread so far that a US governor proposed giving every newborn in Georgia a classical music CD.

POOL.h: Microwaving food destroys most of its nutrients.
POOL.e: Microwaving often keeps nutrients well because cooking times are short and little water is used. Boiling tends to leach out more vitamins.

POOL.h: Fresh vegetables are always more nutritious than frozen ones.
POOL.e: Frozen vegetables are usually picked ripe and frozen within hours, locking in nutrients. Fresh produce can lose vitamins during days of transport and storage.

POOL.h: Bananas are picked from trees.
POOL.e: The banana plant is the world's largest herb, with a stem made of tightly wrapped leaf stalks rather than wood. Botanically, the banana itself counts as a berry.

POOL.h: Cashew nuts grow on the outside of a fruit.
POOL.e: Each cashew hangs from the bottom of a fleshy ‘cashew apple’. The nut’s shell contains an irritating oil, so cashews are always heat-treated before sale.

POOL.h: Your vanilla ice cream owes its flavour to an orchid.
POOL.e: Vanilla beans are the seed pods of a vining orchid. The quick hand-pollination method farmers still use was worked out in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on the island of Réunion.

POOL.h: White chocolate contains none of the brown cocoa solids found in dark chocolate.
POOL.e: White chocolate is made from cocoa butter, sugar and milk. Its only cocoa ingredient is the pale fat, which is why it lacks the rich chocolate flavour of dark and milk chocolate.

POOL.h: Alcohol all cooks off when you add it to a hot dish.
POOL.e: Plenty can remain. Tests found about a quarter of the alcohol still present after an hour of simmering, and far more after a quick flambé.

POOL.h: You should rinse raw chicken before cooking it.
POOL.e: Rinsing doesn’t remove bacteria. It splashes them around your sink and bench. Cooking chicken thoroughly is what kills them.

POOL.h: The green wasabi served with most sushi is real wasabi.
POOL.e: Most of it is horseradish mixed with mustard and green colouring. Real wasabi is a costly, hard-to-grow plant whose flavour fades within minutes of grating.

POOL.h: Bread goes stale faster in the fridge than on the bench.
POOL.e: Staling is mostly starch molecules recrystallising, and that happens fastest at fridge temperatures. Freezing bread slows it right down.

POOL.h: Cut an earthworm in half and you get two worms.
POOL.e: At best, in some species the head end can survive and regrow a tail. The back half usually dies because it lacks the vital organs.

POOL.h: A dog’s mouth is cleaner than a human’s.
POOL.e: Both mouths are full of bacteria, just different kinds. A dog’s mouth is certainly not cleaner, and dog bites can cause nasty infections.

POOL.h: Multiply your dog's age by seven to get its human age.
POOL.e: A one-year-old dog is more like a 15-year-old human, and ageing then slows down. Size matters too, with big breeds like Great Danes getting old much sooner than small dogs.

POOL.h: Cats always land on their feet.
POOL.e: Cats have a remarkable righting reflex, but they don’t always manage it and can still be badly hurt in falls.

POOL.h: Owls can turn their heads all the way around.
POOL.e: Owls can rotate their heads about 270 degrees, not 360. Special blood vessels keep blood flowing to the brain while they twist.

POOL.h: Flamingos come out of the egg already pink.
POOL.e: Chicks hatch fluffy and grey, and it takes a couple of years of eating pigment-rich algae and shrimp to turn pink. Parents feeding chicks can even fade, as they pass those pigments on in a special crop milk.

POOL.h: Koalas are bears.
POOL.e: Koalas are marsupials, like kangaroos and wombats. Their young grow in a pouch, and early European settlers called them ‘bears’ only because of how they looked.

POOL.h: Phar Lap’s heart is on display in Canberra.
POOL.e: The champion racehorse’s heart, about 6.2 kg, is at the National Museum of Australia. His hide is in Melbourne Museum and his skeleton in New Zealand’s Te Papa.

POOL.h: In seahorses, it’s the males that give birth.
POOL.e: The female deposits her eggs in the male’s pouch, where he fertilises and carries them until he gives birth to live young.

POOL.h: Your stomach renews its inner lining every few days.
POOL.e: The surface cells lining the stomach are replaced roughly every three to five days, which helps protect it from its own acid.

POOL.h: If you touch a baby bird, its parents will abandon it.
POOL.e: Most birds have a poor sense of smell and won’t reject a chick because of human scent. It’s still best to leave fledglings alone unless they’re injured.

POOL.h: Snakes dislocate their jaws to swallow large prey.
POOL.e: Nothing is dislocated. A snake’s lower jaw halves aren’t fused at the chin and are joined by a stretchy ligament, and its skull bones are unusually flexible.

POOL.h: Every mosquito bite you've ever had came from a female.
POOL.e: Females need blood protein to make eggs, while males stick to nectar. Males find mates by sound, using feathery antennae to pick up the whine of a female's wingbeats.

POOL.h: Pigs roll in mud because they’re dirty animals.
POOL.e: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so mud helps them cool down and protects their skin from sunburn and insects. Given space, they keep toilet areas separate.

POOL.h: A rhino’s horn is made of the same material as your fingernails.
POOL.e: Rhino horn is keratin, the protein in hair and nails, not bone. That’s why it has no medical value despite being heavily poached.

POOL.h: Polar bears have black skin.
POOL.e: Under their fur, polar bears have black skin that soaks up heat. Their hairs are actually transparent and only look white.

POOL.h: Butterflies taste with their feet.
POOL.e: Taste sensors on their feet tell a butterfly whether a leaf is right for laying eggs or a flower has nectar, just by landing on it.

POOL.h: Sugar makes children hyperactive.
POOL.e: In controlled studies where nobody knew who had sugar, it made no difference to behaviour. Parents who were told their child had sugar rated them as more hyperactive anyway.

POOL.h: The Sun is yellow.
POOL.e: The Sun gives off light across all colours and looks white from space. Our atmosphere scatters some blue light, which makes it look yellowish from the ground.

POOL.h: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
POOL.e: Tall structures are hit again and again. The Empire State Building is struck about 20 to 25 times a year.

POOL.h: The far side of the Moon is always dark.
POOL.e: The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side. It’s only ‘dark’ in the sense that we never see it from Earth.

POOL.h: Black holes hoover up everything in their neighbourhood.
POOL.e: Far away, a black hole pulls just like any other object of the same mass. Squash the Sun into one and it would be only about 6 km across, yet Earth would keep orbiting as normal (just in the dark).

POOL.h: Drop a heavy thing and a light thing together, and the heavy one wins.
POOL.e: Take away air resistance and all objects fall at the same rate. In 1971 astronaut David Scott proved it on the airless Moon, dropping a hammer and a falcon feather that hit the ground together.

POOL.h: The sky is blue because it reflects the ocean.
POOL.e: Air molecules scatter blue light from the Sun far more than red light, so blue light reaches our eyes from all over the sky.

POOL.h: Rubber tyres are what protect you from lightning in a car.
POOL.e: A few centimetres of rubber can’t stop a bolt that has crossed kilometres of air. The metal body carries the current around you and into the ground.

POOL.h: Thunder is the sound of clouds bumping into each other.
POOL.e: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius in a split second. The air expands explosively, and that shockwave is thunder.

POOL.h: Days on Earth are slowly getting longer.
POOL.e: The Moon’s tidal pull acts as a brake on Earth’s spin, adding a couple of milliseconds to the day every century. Hundreds of millions of years ago, a day was only about 22 hours.

POOL.h: Big Ben is the name of the bell, not the clock tower.
POOL.e: Big Ben is the 13.7-tonne great bell inside. The tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 for Queen Elizabeth II’s Diamond Jubilee.

POOL.h: The sunlight reaching you left the Sun about eight minutes earlier.
POOL.e: Light travels about 150 million kilometres from the Sun to Earth, which takes roughly 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

POOL.h: Kakadu National Park is about half the size of Switzerland.
POOL.e: At roughly 20,000 square kilometres, it is Australia’s largest land-based national park and is World Heritage listed for both its nature and its culture.

POOL.h: Daddy long-legs spiders are deadly, but their fangs are too small to bite you.
POOL.e: There’s no evidence their venom is dangerous to people. Their fangs can pierce skin, but a bite causes little more than a brief sting.

POOL.h: Pure water is a poor conductor of electricity.
POOL.e: It’s the dissolved salts and minerals in everyday water that carry current. That’s why tap water and pool water are still dangerous around electricity.

POOL.h: Charles Darwin coined the phrase ‘survival of the fittest’.
POOL.e: Philosopher Herbert Spencer coined it in 1864 after reading Darwin. Darwin later borrowed it for a revised edition of On the Origin of Species.

POOL.h: Your memories are perfect recordings you can replay.
POOL.e: Your brain reconstructs a memory every time you recall it, so it can change. In one famous study, people asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other were more likely to later remember broken glass that was never there.

POOL.h: A polygraph can tell when you're lying.
POOL.e: The machine only tracks stress signals like pulse, breathing and sweat, which honest but anxious people show too. That's a big reason polygraph results are generally not accepted as evidence in Australian courts.

POOL.h: A 1950s cinema experiment proved that flashing ‘Eat popcorn’ on screen boosted sales.
POOL.e: The researcher behind it, James Vicary, later admitted the results were made up. Attempts to repeat it failed.

POOL.h: It takes 21 days to form a new habit.
POOL.e: A University College London study found it took an average of 66 days for a behaviour to become automatic, with a range from 18 days to over 250.

POOL.h: Emergency departments go wild when the moon is full.
POOL.e: Big reviews of hospital and psychiatric data show no consistent full moon effect. The belief is old enough to be baked into language: 'lunatic' comes from 'luna', Latin for moon.

POOL.h: Moving into a higher tax bracket can leave you with less take-home pay.
POOL.e: In a marginal system like Australia’s, the higher rate only applies to the dollars above each threshold. Earning more never lowers your overall after-tax pay from income tax alone.

POOL.h: Lottery numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are less likely to win than random-looking numbers.
POOL.e: Every combination has exactly the same chance. The catch is that many people pick sequences like that, so if they came up, the prize would be split many ways.

POOL.h: After a coin lands heads five times in a row, tails is more likely next.
POOL.e: A fair coin has no memory, so each toss is still 50-50. Believing otherwise is called the gambler’s fallacy.

POOL.h: Albert Einstein called compound interest the eighth wonder of the world.
POOL.e: There’s no record of Einstein saying it. The quote only started being linked to him decades after his death.

POOL.h: Peeking at your own credit score will drag it down.
POOL.e: Checking your own file doesn't count against you; it's credit applications that lenders see. In Australia you can get your credit report free from each credit reporting body every three months.

POOL.h: Australia was the first country to issue a full series of polymer banknotes.
POOL.e: It began with a commemorative $10 note in 1988 for the bicentenary, and every denomination was polymer by 1996. Polymer notes last longer and are much harder to forge, and many countries have since followed.

POOL.h: An Australian Prime Minister vanished while swimming.
POOL.e: Harold Holt disappeared in rough surf at Cheviot Beach, Victoria, in December 1967. His body was never found.

POOL.h: ‘Goodbye’ comes from the phrase ‘God be with ye’.
POOL.e: Over centuries ‘God be with ye’ was squashed down to ‘godbwye’, and ‘God’ shifted to ‘good’ under the influence of greetings like ‘good day’.

POOL.h: Calling someone 'nice' used to be an insult.
POOL.e: 'Nice' traces back to Latin 'nescius', meaning not knowing, and in medieval English it meant silly or foolish. Words can flip the other way too: 'silly' once meant blessed or happy.

POOL.h: ‘Sincere’ comes from the Latin for ‘without wax’.
POOL.e: The story about honest sculptors not hiding cracks with wax is a folk tale. The word comes from the Latin ‘sincerus’, meaning clean or pure.

POOL.h: ‘Posh’ comes from ‘Port Out, Starboard Home’, the shady cabins on voyages to India.
POOL.e: No tickets stamped ‘POSH’ have ever been found, and the phrase appeared long after the word. Its true origin is unknown.

POOL.h: The Hills Hoist was the world’s first rotary clothesline.
POOL.e: Lance Hill began making his in Adelaide in 1945, but Gilbert Toyne had already patented rotary clotheslines in Australia decades earlier.

POOL.h: Your biceps are named after a tiny rodent.
POOL.e: 'Muscle' comes from Latin 'musculus', little mouse, because a rippling muscle looked like a mouse scurrying under the skin. The shellfish 'mussel' comes from the very same word.

POOL.h: ‘Quarantine’ comes from the Italian for forty days.
POOL.e: During plague outbreaks, Venice made arriving ships wait ‘quaranta giorni’, forty days, before anyone could come ashore.

POOL.h: English has more native speakers than any other language.
POOL.e: Mandarin Chinese has by far the most native speakers, and Spanish has more too. English leads only when you count people who learned it as a second language.

POOL.h: The word ‘emoji’ comes from the English word ‘emotion’.
POOL.e: It’s Japanese: ‘e’ means picture and ‘moji’ means character. The resemblance to ‘emotion’ is a happy coincidence.

POOL.h: You should fully drain your phone battery before recharging it.
POOL.e: That advice applied to old nickel-based batteries. Modern lithium-ion batteries wear faster with deep drains and prefer to stay partly charged.

POOL.h: A fridge magnet can wipe the data on your phone.
POOL.e: Phones store data on flash memory, which isn’t magnetic. A strong magnet might briefly confuse the compass, but your photos are safe.

POOL.h: The term ‘computer bug’ was coined when a moth was found in a computer.
POOL.e: Engineers, including Thomas Edison, were calling faults ‘bugs’ by the 1870s. The famous 1947 moth was taped in a logbook as the ‘first actual case of bug being found’, which was a joke.

POOL.h: 'The internet' and 'the web' are just two names for one thing.
POOL.e: The internet is the network of linked computers, with roots in the late 1960s ARPANET. The web is a system of linked pages running on top of it, and the very first website went live at CERN in 1991.

POOL.h: Wi-Fi stands for ‘Wireless Fidelity’.
POOL.e: Wi-Fi isn’t short for anything. A branding agency invented the name in 1999 as a catchy play on ‘hi-fi’.

POOL.h: Bluetooth is named after a Viking-age king.
POOL.e: It honours Harald ‘Bluetooth’ Gormsson, a 10th-century Danish king who united rival tribes. The logo combines his initials in runes.

POOL.h: We call junk email 'spam' thanks to Monty Python.
POOL.e: In a 1970 sketch, singing Vikings chant 'Spam' until nobody can talk, much like junk messages flooding a chat. Early online users borrowed the joke to describe repetitive posts long before email spam was common.

POOL.h: A modern smartphone has far more computing power than the computers that guided Apollo to the Moon.
POOL.e: The Apollo Guidance Computer had about 4 kilobytes of working memory. A typical phone today has millions of times more.

POOL.h: Putting a wet phone in a bag of rice helps it dry out.
POOL.e: Tests have found rice is no better than leaving the phone in open air, and grains or dust can get into the ports. Apple advises against it.

POOL.h: Daylight saving time was introduced to help farmers.
POOL.e: It was first widely adopted during World War I to save fuel. Many farmers opposed it, as cows and crops don’t follow the clock.

POOL.h: Water is a good way to put out a burning pan of oil.
POOL.e: Water sinks into the hot oil, flashes into steam and can throw a fireball. Turn off the heat and smother it with a lid or fire blanket.

POOL.h: The Egyptian pyramids were built by slaves.
POOL.e: Workers’ villages and tombs found near Giza show a paid, fed and respected workforce, likely including farmers working in rotation.

POOL.h: Roman gladiator fights almost always ended in death.
POOL.e: Gladiators were expensive to train and keep, so many bouts ended when one fighter gave up. Most fights were not to the death.

POOL.h: People accused at the Salem witch trials were burned at the stake.
POOL.e: None of the Salem victims were burned. Nineteen people were hanged in 1692, and one man was pressed to death under heavy stones. Burning witches was a practice in parts of Europe, not colonial Massachusetts.

POOL.h: America's first president wore wooden dentures.
POOL.e: Washington's dentures used ivory, metal springs, and human and animal teeth, but no wood. By the time he became president in 1789 he had just one of his own teeth left.

POOL.h: Galileo came up with the first telescope.
POOL.e: Dutch lens makers got there first, with Hans Lippershey applying for a patent in 1608. Galileo improved the design to magnify about 20 times, enough to spot Jupiter's four largest moons.

POOL.h: An apple fell on Isaac Newton’s head and inspired his ideas about gravity.
POOL.e: Newton said he watched an apple fall in his garden, which got him thinking. The bonk on the head was added by later storytellers.

POOL.h: Most people in the Middle Ages died around age 30.
POOL.e: Average lifespans were low mainly because so many children died young. People who reached adulthood often lived into their 50s, 60s or beyond.

POOL.h: Ferdinand Magellan was the first person to sail around the world.
POOL.e: Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521, partway through the voyage. Juan Sebastián Elcano led the surviving crew home to Spain in 1522.

POOL.h: Einstein won his Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity.
POOL.e: His 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics was for explaining the photoelectric effect, work that helped lay the foundations of quantum physics.

POOL.h: The Hundred Years’ War lasted a hundred years.
POOL.e: It ran from 1337 to 1453, which is 116 years, and included long periods of truce.

POOL.h: Italy only got pasta because Marco Polo carried it home from China.
POOL.e: Italians were eating pasta before Polo got back in 1295; a Genoese record from 1279 lists a basket of macaroni. The legend was largely spread by a 1929 article in an American trade magazine called The Macaroni Journal.

POOL.h: Darth Vader says ‘Luke, I am your father.’
POOL.e: The actual line in The Empire Strikes Back is ‘No, I am your father.’ It’s one of the most misquoted lines in film.

POOL.h: Stonehenge was built by the druids.
POOL.e: Stonehenge was begun about 5,000 years ago. Druids don’t appear in the historical record until more than 2,000 years after that.

POOL.h: The Moon’s phases are caused by Earth’s shadow falling on it.
POOL.e: Phases come from our changing view of the Moon’s sunlit half as it circles Earth, a cycle of about 29.5 days. Earth’s shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse.

POOL.h: ‘Mortgage’ comes from Old French words meaning ‘death pledge’.
POOL.e: ‘Mort’ means dead and ‘gage’ means pledge. The pledge ‘dies’ either when the loan is paid off or when the borrower fails to pay and loses the property.

POOL.h: Every bee dies after it stings.
POOL.e: Usually only worker honeybees die, and mainly after stinging mammals, because their barbed sting lodges in thick skin and tears away. Bumblebees and most other bees can sting again and again.

POOL.h: The South Pole is much colder than the North Pole.
POOL.e: The South Pole sits on a continent, on an ice sheet about 2,800 metres high. The North Pole is at sea level on floating ice warmed from below by the ocean, so it averages roughly 30 °C warmer.

POOL.h: Porcupines can shoot their quills at attackers.
POOL.e: Porcupines can’t fire their quills. The quills come loose easily when touched, and a porcupine may back into an attacker or swing its tail to drive them in.

POOL.h: Denim is named after a town in France.
POOL.e: The name comes from ‘serge de Nîmes’, a sturdy twill fabric from Nîmes in southern France. English speakers shortened ‘de Nîmes’ to ‘denim’.

POOL.h: Elephants drink by sucking water up their trunks like a straw.
POOL.e: An elephant draws water partway up its trunk, then curls the trunk and squirts the water into its mouth. The trunk is a nose, so drinking straight through it would be like drinking through your nostrils.

POOL.h: Tomatoes and potatoes belong to the same plant family.
POOL.e: Both are nightshades, and even share a genus, Solanum, with eggplants. The leaves of both plants contain toxic compounds, which is also why potatoes that have turned green should be avoided.

POOL.h: The iron maiden was a common medieval torture device.
POOL.e: There’s no reliable evidence one was used in the Middle Ages. The famous examples were put together in the 1700s and 1800s, apparently inspired by legends and built for display.

POOL.h: The word ‘clue’ originally meant a ball of thread.
POOL.e: It comes from ‘clew’, a ball of yarn. In Greek myth, Theseus followed a thread out of the Minotaur’s labyrinth, so a clew came to mean anything that guides you to an answer.

POOL.h: People once pronounced “Ye Olde Shoppe” with a “yee” sound.
POOL.e: The “Y” stood in for an old English letter called thorn (þ), which made a “th” sound. Early printers lacked the letter and used a similar-looking “y”, so “Ye” was said “the”.

POOL.h: Albert Einstein was offered the presidency of Israel.
POOL.e: When Israel’s first president, Chaim Weizmann, died in 1952, the government offered Einstein the largely ceremonial role. He declined, saying he lacked the aptitude and experience to deal with people.

POOL.h: “Rule of thumb” comes from an old law letting men beat their wives with a stick no thicker than a thumb.
POOL.e: No such law has ever been found in English legal history. The phrase most likely comes from using the thumb as a rough measuring tool, about an inch wide.

POOL.h: Brown eggs are more nutritious than white eggs.
POOL.e: Shell colour depends on the breed of hen, not the quality of the egg. The hen’s diet affects an egg’s nutrition far more than the colour of its shell.

POOL.h: The earliest known printed use of ‘nerd’ is in a Dr Seuss book.
POOL.e: In ‘If I Ran the Zoo’ (1950), a nerd is one of the imaginary creatures the narrator would collect. By the next year the word was appearing as slang for a dull or unfashionable person.

POOL.h: Sea salt contains much less sodium than table salt.
POOL.e: Gram for gram, sea salt and table salt have about the same sodium, roughly 40% by weight. Sea salt’s bigger crystals can mean slightly less per teaspoon, but the difference is small.

POOL.h: Touching a toad can give you warts.
POOL.e: Human warts are caused by the human papillomavirus, which spreads between people. A toad’s bumps are just skin glands, though some, like the cane toad, release toxins, so wash your hands after handling one.

POOL.h: Mars looks red because its surface is rusty.
POOL.e: Martian dust and rock are rich in iron oxide, the same compound as rust. Fine dust blown into the thin atmosphere gives the daytime sky a pinkish, butterscotch tint as well.

POOL.h: All sharks must keep swimming or they will die.
POOL.e: Some sharks, such as great whites, rely on swimming to push water over their gills. Many others, including Port Jackson and wobbegong sharks, can pump water over their gills while resting on the sea floor.

POOL.h: Male lions do most of the hunting for their pride.
POOL.e: Lionesses do most of the hunting, often working as a team. Males hunt less often and spend much of their energy defending the pride’s territory, though they may join in to bring down big prey like buffalo.

POOL.h: ‘Decimate’ originally meant killing one in every ten.
POOL.e: It comes from a Roman army punishment: a unit guilty of mutiny or cowardice drew lots, and one soldier in ten was put to death by his comrades. The Latin ‘decimus’ means tenth.

POOL.h: A housefly lives for only about 24 hours.
POOL.e: Adult houseflies usually live around two to four weeks. The one-day idea may come from mayflies, some of which live as adults for a day or less.

POOL.h: Australia’s $2 coin is smaller than its $1 coin.
POOL.e: The $2 coin is about 20.5 mm across, while the $1 coin is 25 mm. Both replaced notes: the $1 coin arrived in 1984 and the $2 coin in 1988.

POOL.h: Without a spacesuit in space, you would freeze solid instantly.
POOL.e: A vacuum loses heat slowly because there’s no air to carry it away. The real danger is the lack of oxygen and pressure: you would lose consciousness in about 15 seconds.

POOL.h: Ancient Greek statues were meant to be plain white marble.
POOL.e: Many were brightly painted. Traces of pigment survive on statues and temples, and researchers using ultraviolet light have mapped their original patterns. The colours wore away over the centuries.

POOL.h: An ‘apron’ was once called a ‘napron’.
POOL.e: People heard ‘a napron’ as ‘an apron’, and the n moved across. The word comes from Old French ‘naperon’, a small tablecloth, related to ‘napkin’.

POOL.h: Knights in armour were so heavy they had to be winched onto their horses.
POOL.e: A full suit of battlefield plate armour typically weighed about 15 to 25 kg, spread across the whole body. Trained knights could mount, run and get up from the ground without help.

POOL.h: The summit of Mount Everest is made of rock that formed on the sea floor.
POOL.e: The top layer is limestone holding fossils of sea creatures such as trilobites, laid down more than 400 million years ago. The collision of India with Asia later pushed it up to the top of the world.

POOL.h: The dollar sign ($) began as the letters U and S laid over each other.
POOL.e: The sign was already in use in the 1770s, before the United States had its own currency. It most likely grew out of “ps”, a handwritten abbreviation for the Spanish peso, widely used in the Americas.

POOL.h: Your heart stops for a moment when you sneeze.
POOL.e: A sneeze changes the pressure in your chest, which can briefly change the rhythm of your heartbeat. It doesn’t stop your heart, which keeps beating the whole time.

POOL.h: Africa is the only continent crossed by both the equator and the prime meridian.
POOL.e: That gives Africa land north, south, east and west of the two lines. They cross in the Gulf of Guinea, off the West African coast. Other continents are crossed by one line or the other, but not both.

POOL.h: Your blood type reveals your personality.
POOL.e: The idea took off in Japan through popular books in the 1970s and is still widely believed there. Large studies have found no meaningful link between blood type and personality.

POOL.h: Decaf coffee contains no caffeine.
POOL.e: Decaffeination removes most of the caffeine, usually around 97% or more, but not all. A cup of decaf typically has a few milligrams, compared with roughly 80 to 100 mg in a regular cup.

POOL.h: Australia’s newer banknotes have raised bumps to help people with low vision tell them apart.
POOL.e: Starting with the $5 note in 2016, the new series has tactile bumps along the long edges: one for the $5, two for the $10, and so on up to five for the $100.

POOL.h: Ancient Romans had special rooms called vomitoriums for throwing up during feasts.
POOL.e: A vomitorium was a passageway in an amphitheatre or stadium that let crowds pour out quickly. The name comes from the Latin for ‘spew forth’, describing the people, not their dinners.

POOL.h: ‘Hippopotamus’ means ‘river horse’.
POOL.e: It comes from ancient Greek ‘hippos’, horse, and ‘potamos’, river. Despite the name, hippos are more closely related to whales than to horses.

POOL.h: On a clear, dark night you can see millions of stars with the naked eye.
POOL.e: Even under ideal dark skies, the whole sky holds only about 5,000 to 9,000 stars bright enough to see unaided, and less than half are above the horizon at once. From a city it may be just a few hundred.

POOL.h: Rhubarb leaves are poisonous, even though the stalks are safe to eat.
POOL.e: The leaves hold high levels of oxalic acid, which can make you seriously ill. Cut the leaves off and throw them away, and cook only the stalks.

POOL.h: The Sun is a giant ball of fire.
POOL.e: Fire is a chemical reaction that needs oxygen. The Sun shines because of nuclear fusion in its core, where hydrogen is squeezed into helium, releasing enormous amounts of energy.

POOL.h: An ostrich’s eye is bigger than its brain.
POOL.e: Each ostrich eye is about 5 cm across, the largest of any land animal. That makes a single eye bigger than the bird’s brain.

POOL.h: Dogs can’t sweat at all.
POOL.e: Dogs have sweat glands in their paw pads, which is why they can leave damp footprints on a hot day. Paw sweat does little for cooling, so they rely mainly on panting.

POOL.h: Cats can’t taste sweetness.
POOL.e: In 2005, researchers found that a gene needed for the sweet taste receptor is broken in cats, including tigers and cheetahs. As strict meat eaters, they lose little by it.

POOL.h: Cats purr only when they’re happy.
POOL.e: Cats also purr when stressed, injured, giving birth or close to death. Purring seems to be a signal and possibly a way to soothe themselves, not just a sign of contentment.

POOL.h: The Pacific Ocean is bigger than all of Earth’s land put together.
POOL.e: The Pacific covers about 165 million km², while all the land on Earth adds up to about 149 million km². It holds roughly half of the world’s ocean water.

POOL.h: Penguins live only in Antarctica.
POOL.e: Only a handful of the roughly 18 penguin species breed on Antarctica. Others live in South America, southern Africa, New Zealand and southern Australia, and Galápagos penguins live right on the equator.

POOL.h: The rule “i before e except after c” is a reliable spelling guide.
POOL.e: It has many exceptions, such as “weird”, “seize”, “their” and “science”. It works for some words like “receive”, but it breaks down too often to rely on.

POOL.h: The word ‘disaster’ literally means ‘bad star’.
POOL.e: It comes from the Italian ‘disastro’, from ‘dis-’, meaning ill, and ‘astro’, star. It reflects the old belief that misfortune came from an unlucky position of the stars and planets.

POOL.h: Adult clothes moths chew holes in your clothes.
POOL.e: The damage is done by the larvae, which feed on wool, silk and other animal fibres. Adult clothes moths don’t eat at all and live only to breed.

POOL.h: Earwigs crawl into people’s ears to lay eggs.
POOL.e: Earwigs don’t seek out human ears. They prefer damp, dark places under bark, leaves and rocks, and females lay and guard their eggs in soil. One in an ear is a rare accident.

POOL.h: You should wait 30 minutes after eating before you swim.
POOL.e: There’s no evidence that swimming on a full stomach causes dangerous cramps or drowning. A 2011 review by the American Red Cross Scientific Advisory Council found that swimming within an hour of eating does not increase the risk of drowning.

POOL.h: A short promotional description of a book, film or product.
POOL.ex: The blurb promised a gripping thriller, but the book was a slog.
POOL.o: Coined in 1907 by American humorist Gelett Burgess, whose mock book jacket showed a gushing young woman he named Miss Belinda Blurb.

POOL.h: Grimly mocking or cynical.
POOL.ex: Her sardonic “Well, that went well” summed up the meeting.
POOL.o: From Greek sardonios, later linked to a plant from Sardinia said to twist the faces of those who ate it into a deathly grin.

POOL.h: Calm and evenness of mind, especially under pressure.
POOL.ex: She took the bad news with an equanimity that steadied everyone else.
POOL.o: Latin aequus (even) + animus (mind). A core Stoic ideal.

POOL.h: A life of flourishing and fulfilment, not just passing pleasure.
POOL.ex: For Aristotle, eudaimonia came from living well and acting with virtue.
POOL.o: Greek eu (good) + daimon (spirit).

POOL.h: A state of serene calm, free from worry and disturbance.
POOL.ex: The Epicureans prized ataraxia above wealth or fame.
POOL.o: Greek, literally “not being troubled”.

POOL.h: A lucky find you stumble on when you weren't even trying.
POOL.ex: Taking a wrong turn in Hobart led us, by pure serendipity, to the best fish and chips of the trip.
POOL.o: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, after a fairy tale, The Three Princes of Serendip.

POOL.h: Lasting a very short time.
POOL.ex: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.
POOL.o: Greek ephemeros, “lasting only a day”.

POOL.h: Optimistic, especially in a difficult situation.
POOL.ex: Despite the setbacks, the coach remained sanguine about the season.
POOL.o: From Latin sanguis, blood; blood was once thought to cause a cheerful temperament.

POOL.h: Quick to notice and understand things others miss.
POOL.ex: A perspicacious editor spotted the flaw in the argument at once.
POOL.o: Latin perspicere, “to see through”.

POOL.h: Sweet and smooth to hear, like a flowing voice.
POOL.ex: The narrator’s mellifluous voice made the audiobook a pleasure.
POOL.o: Latin mel (honey) + fluere (to flow).

POOL.h: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to a downfall.
POOL.ex: It was hubris to launch without testing.
POOL.o: In Greek tragedy, hubris provoked the gods’ punishment.

POOL.h: Idealistic in a way that is noble but unrealistic.
POOL.ex: His quixotic plan was to reply personally to every email he had ever received.
POOL.o: From Don Quixote, Cervantes’ knight who tilted at windmills.

POOL.h: The inability to remember the word you want.
POOL.ex: A bout of lethologica left her pointing at the “thing” on the shelf.
POOL.o: Greek lethe (forgetfulness) + logos (word).

POOL.h: Buying books and letting them pile up unread.
POOL.ex: His bedside table was a monument to tsundoku.
POOL.o: Japanese, combining words for “piling up” and “reading”.

POOL.h: The intense, obsessive early stage of romantic infatuation.
POOL.ex: In the grip of limerence, he reread every message she sent.
POOL.o: Coined by psychologist Dorothy Tennov in 1979.

POOL.h: A soft whispering or rustling sound.
POOL.ex: The susurrus of the gum trees filled the evening.
POOL.o: Latin, “a whisper”.

POOL.h: Denoting a past time that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
POOL.ex: They talked about the halcyon days of university.
POOL.o: From a Greek myth of a bird that calmed the sea to nest.

POOL.h: A change of fortune, usually an unwelcome one.
POOL.ex: The business survived the vicissitudes of three recessions.
POOL.o: Latin vicis, “change, turn”.

POOL.h: The warmth of the sun on a cold winter’s day.
POOL.ex: They sat on the step, enjoying the apricity of a July afternoon.
POOL.o: A rare word from Latin apricus, “warmed by the sun”.

POOL.h: Too eager to please or obey.
POOL.ex: The obsequious waiter refilled their glasses every thirty seconds.
POOL.o: Latin obsequi, “to comply with”.

POOL.h: The act of throwing someone out of a window.
POOL.ex: The 1618 Defenestration of Prague helped spark the Thirty Years’ War.
POOL.o: Latin de (out of) + fenestra (window).

POOL.h: Given to using long words; or, a long word itself.
POOL.ex: The lecture was so sesquipedalian that half the room reached for a dictionary.
POOL.o: From Horace’s joke about words “a foot and a half long”.

POOL.h: Too great or intense to be expressed in words.
POOL.ex: Standing under the night sky in the outback gave her an ineffable sense of calm.
POOL.o: From Latin ineffabilis, “unutterable”, from in- “not” and effari “to speak out”.

POOL.h: A misheard word or phrase, especially a song lyric, that creates a new meaning.
POOL.ex: For years he sang a mondegreen of the chorus and nobody had the heart to correct him.
POOL.o: Coined by American writer Sylvia Wright in 1954, who as a child misheard the ballad line “and laid him on the green” as “and Lady Mondegreen”.

POOL.h: So common it seems to turn up absolutely everywhere you look.
POOL.ex: On bin night, those yellow-lidded recycling bins are ubiquitous, lined up along every kerb in the suburb.
POOL.o: From Latin ubique, “everywhere”.

POOL.h: Physical beauty.
POOL.ex: The poet praised her pulchritude, which is ironic, because the word itself is rather ugly.
POOL.o: From Latin pulchritudo, from pulcher, “beautiful”.

POOL.h: To make something deliberately unclear or hard to understand.
POOL.ex: The contract seemed designed to obfuscate the real fees.
POOL.o: From Latin obfuscare, “to darken”, from ob- “over” and fuscus “dark”.

POOL.h: A person who flatters powerful people to gain an advantage.
POOL.ex: The manager surrounded himself with sycophants and never heard bad news until it was too late.
POOL.o: From Greek sykophantes, literally “fig-shower”, originally meaning an informer or slanderer; exactly why figs were involved is unknown.

POOL.h: Honest and open, saying what you really think without softening it.
POOL.ex: My hairdresser was candid: the fringe I wanted would never sit right with my cowlick.
POOL.o: From Latin candidus, “shining white”; “candidate” shares the root because Roman office seekers wore whitened togas.

POOL.h: A sentimental longing for a period in the past.
POOL.ex: The smell of sunscreen fills him with nostalgia for childhood summers.
POOL.o: Coined in 1688 by Swiss medical student Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos “homecoming” and algos “pain”, to describe severe homesickness as an illness.

POOL.h: A deep, lingering and often thoughtful sadness.
POOL.ex: A gentle melancholy settled over the town once the tourists had gone.
POOL.o: From Greek melankholia, “black bile”, one of the four bodily humours once thought to cause gloom.

POOL.h: To delay or put off something that should be done.
POOL.ex: I procrastinate most on the tasks that matter most.
POOL.o: From Latin procrastinare, from pro- “forward” and crastinus “belonging to tomorrow”.

POOL.h: Acting against your own better judgement; weakness of will.
POOL.ex: Knowing I should sleep but watching one more episode is pure akrasia.
POOL.o: From Greek akrasia, “lack of command over oneself”, from a- “without” and kratos “power”; Socrates and Aristotle both debated how it is possible.

POOL.h: Calm, unemotional and not easily excited.
POOL.ex: Her phlegmatic reaction to the flat tyre calmed everyone else in the car.
POOL.o: From Greek phlegma, “phlegm”, the bodily humour once believed to make people sluggish and calm.

POOL.h: Kind, friendly and supportive towards someone younger, like a favourite uncle.
POOL.ex: The avuncular coach knew the name of every junior player.
POOL.o: From Latin avunculus, “mother’s brother”, literally “little grandfather”, from avus, “grandfather”.

POOL.h: A person who believes people are motivated mainly by self-interest.
POOL.ex: Even the cynics in the office were moved by her farewell speech.
POOL.o: From Greek kynikos, “dog-like”; Diogenes, the most famous of the ancient Cynic philosophers, was nicknamed “the Dog” for living shamelessly in public.

POOL.h: Very large; bigger than usual.
POOL.ex: We ordered a kilo of jumbo prawns for the barbecue.
POOL.o: From Jumbo, a huge African elephant at London Zoo who became a celebrity and was sold to American showman P. T. Barnum in 1882.

POOL.h: An experienced and trusted adviser.
POOL.ex: A good mentor tells you what you need to hear, not what you want to hear.
POOL.o: From Mentor, the friend of Odysseus in Homer’s Odyssey, whose form the goddess Athena takes to guide his son Telemachus.

POOL.h: A long-standing rival or enemy, or something that causes someone’s downfall.
POOL.ex: Maths was my nemesis all through high school.
POOL.o: Named after Nemesis, the Greek goddess of retribution who punished arrogance.

POOL.h: Sudden, overwhelming fear that often causes unthinking behaviour.
POOL.ex: When the alarm went off, the trained staff calmly prevented a panic.
POOL.o: From Greek panikos, “of Pan”, the god of the wild whose sudden shouts were said to fill people and animals with terror.

POOL.h: To tease or torment with the sight of something desirable that is out of reach.
POOL.ex: The smell from the bakery tantalised us all the way to work.
POOL.o: From Tantalus, who in Greek myth was punished by standing in water beneath fruit trees, with the water and fruit always retreating as he reached for them.

POOL.h: An independent-minded person who refuses to follow the crowd.
POOL.ex: The company needed a maverick to challenge how things had always been done.
POOL.o: From Samuel Maverick, a 19th-century Texas landowner who did not brand his cattle, so unbranded strays came to be called mavericks.

POOL.h: To refuse to deal with a person, business or country as a form of protest.
POOL.ex: Shoppers vowed to boycott the brand after the scandal.
POOL.o: From Captain Charles Boycott, an estate manager in County Mayo, Ireland, who was ostracised by the local community in 1880 during a dispute over rents.

POOL.h: A period of isolation to stop a disease from spreading.
POOL.ex: The new puppy spent ten days in quarantine before arriving in Australia.
POOL.o: From Venetian Italian quarantena, “a period of forty days”, the time ships were made to wait before landing during late medieval plague outbreaks.

POOL.h: Body tissue that contracts to produce movement.
POOL.ex: Regular strength training helps you keep muscle as you age.
POOL.o: From Latin musculus, “little mouse”, perhaps because a flexing muscle looked like a mouse moving under the skin.

POOL.h: A person you spend time with or travel with.
POOL.ex: On a long hike, the right companion matters more than the right boots.
POOL.o: From Late Latin companio, literally “one who shares bread with you”, from com- “together” and panis “bread”.

POOL.h: A sudden event that causes great damage or loss.
POOL.ex: Good planning turned what could have been a disaster into a minor delay.
POOL.o: From Italian disastro, “ill-starred”, from dis- “bad” and astro “star”, reflecting the old belief that misfortune came from unlucky positions of the stars.

POOL.h: A piece of evidence or information that helps solve a problem or mystery.
POOL.ex: The muddy footprints were the first real clue.
POOL.o: From “clew”, a ball of thread, recalling the Greek myth in which Theseus used a thread to find his way out of the Minotaur’s labyrinth.

POOL.h: Pleasant, agreeable or kind.
POOL.ex: It was nice of you to remember my birthday.
POOL.o: From Latin nescius, “ignorant”; in Middle English it meant “foolish”, and only gradually drifted over centuries to mean “pleasant”.

POOL.h: Lacking good sense; foolish, often in a harmless way.
