POOL.ex: It seems silly now, but I was terrified of that dog as a kid.
POOL.o: From Old English gesælig, “happy, blessed”; the meaning slid over centuries through “innocent” and “pitiable” to “foolish”.

POOL.h: Full of frantic, busy activity.
POOL.ex: The week before school holidays is always hectic.
POOL.o: From Greek hektikos, “habitual, continuous”, first used in English for a persistent fever, then for anything feverishly busy.

POOL.h: Giving the impression that something harmful or evil is happening.
POOL.ex: There was something sinister about the empty house at the end of the street.
POOL.o: From Latin sinister, “left”, because the left side was traditionally considered unlucky.

POOL.h: A frightening dream, or a very unpleasant experience.
POOL.ex: Moving house in the middle of exams was a nightmare.
POOL.o: From Old English mære, an evil spirit believed to sit on sleepers’ chests and bring bad dreams; it has nothing to do with horses.

POOL.h: Excessively harsh or severe, especially of laws or rules.
POOL.ex: The school’s draconian phone policy banned devices even at lunch.
POOL.o: From Draco, an Athenian lawmaker of around 621 BC whose code prescribed death for many minor offences.

POOL.h: A person who is hostile or indifferent to art and culture.
POOL.ex: Only a philistine would paint over that mural.
POOL.o: From German student slang Philister for townspeople outside the university, after the biblical Philistines; popularised in English by Matthew Arnold in the 1860s.

POOL.h: Describing a victory won at such great cost that it is hardly worth it.
POOL.ex: Winning the argument was a Pyrrhic victory: he lost the friendship.
POOL.o: From Pyrrhus, King of Epirus, whose victories over Rome in 280 and 279 BC cost him so many of his best soldiers that further wins like them would have ruined him.

POOL.h: To follow a winding course, or to wander aimlessly.
POOL.ex: We meandered through the laneways with no plan at all.
POOL.o: From the Maeander, a famously winding river in ancient Asia Minor, now the Büyük Menderes in Turkey.

POOL.h: A cosy, contented feeling of comfort and togetherness.
POOL.ex: Candles, soup and a good book: that’s my idea of winter hygge.
POOL.o: A Danish word, borrowed from Norwegian hygge, “wellbeing”.

POOL.h: Pleasure felt at someone else’s misfortune.
POOL.ex: He felt a pang of schadenfreude when his know-it-all colleague got the answer wrong.
POOL.o: German, from Schaden “harm” and Freude “joy”.

POOL.h: The defining spirit or mood of a particular period of history.
POOL.ex: The film captured the zeitgeist of the early internet years.
POOL.o: German, from Zeit “time” and Geist “spirit”.

POOL.h: A feeling of listless boredom and dissatisfaction.
POOL.ex: By the third wet week of holidays, a heavy ennui had settled over the house.
POOL.o: French, from Latin in odio, as in the phrase “to be in hatred”, the same root that gave English the word “annoy”.

POOL.h: Quiet, stubborn determination to keep going against the odds.
POOL.ex: Finishing the marathon after cramping at 30 kilometres took real sisu.
POOL.o: A Finnish word central to national identity, from sisus, “insides” or “guts”.

POOL.h: A sense of purpose; the thing that makes life feel worth living.
POOL.ex: Since retiring, gardening and grandchildren have become her ikigai.
POOL.o: Japanese, from iki “life” and kai (softened to gai) “worth” or “benefit”.

POOL.h: The Japanese art of repairing broken pottery with gold, making the cracks part of its beauty.
POOL.ex: He treats his old failures like kintsugi: the repairs are part of who he is.
POOL.o: Japanese, from kin “gold” and tsugi “joining”.

POOL.h: A deep, bittersweet longing for someone or something absent or lost.
POOL.ex: Old photos of her grandparents’ village filled her with saudade.
POOL.o: Portuguese, from Latin solitas, “solitude” or “loneliness”.

POOL.h: A person who strolls around a city, unhurried, simply observing its life.
POOL.ex: On Sunday mornings he plays the flâneur, wandering the markets with no shopping list.
POOL.o: French, from flâner, “to stroll” or “to saunter”; made famous by the poet Charles Baudelaire in 19th-century Paris.

POOL.h: Studied carelessness; making something difficult look effortless.
POOL.ex: The pianist played with such sprezzatura that nobody guessed the hours of practice behind it.
POOL.o: Italian, coined by Baldassare Castiglione in The Book of the Courtier, published in 1528.

POOL.h: A longing to travel to distant places; the opposite of homesickness.
POOL.ex: Scrolling through photos of Iceland gave her a bad case of fernweh.
POOL.o: German, from fern “far” and Weh “ache”, modelled on Heimweh, “homesickness”.

POOL.h: To understand something thoroughly and intuitively.
POOL.ex: It took a week of practice before I really grokked how the software worked.
POOL.o: Invented by science-fiction author Robert Heinlein in his 1961 novel Stranger in a Strange Land, as a Martian word.

POOL.h: A liquid soap for washing hair.
POOL.ex: After a week of camping, the first shampoo felt like pure luxury.
POOL.o: From Hindi chāmpo, “press” or “knead”, first meaning a head massage; Sake Dean Mahomed popularised “shampooing” baths in Brighton, England, from 1814.

POOL.h: To laugh in a breathy, gleeful way.
POOL.ex: Grandad chortled at his own joke before he reached the punchline.
POOL.o: Coined by Lewis Carroll in Through the Looking-Glass (1871), probably blending “chuckle” and “snort”.

POOL.h: Wild and noisy disorder or confusion.
POOL.ex: Pandemonium broke out when the dog got loose at the wedding.
POOL.o: Coined by John Milton in Paradise Lost (1667) as the capital of Hell, from Greek pan “all” and daimon “spirit”, meaning “place of all demons”.

POOL.h: An imagined place or state in which everything is perfect.
POOL.ex: A four-day work week sounds like utopia to most people.
POOL.o: Coined by Thomas More for his 1516 book, from Greek ou “not” and topos “place”, so literally “nowhere”, with a pun on eu-topos, “good place”.

POOL.h: A huge, powerful force or organisation that seems unstoppable.
POOL.ex: The small café couldn’t compete once the coffee juggernaut opened next door.
POOL.o: From Jagannath, a form of the Hindu god Vishnu whose image is pulled through Puri, India, each year on enormous chariots.

POOL.h: An official who investigates complaints against organisations or government.
POOL.ex: When the telco ignored her complaint, she took it to the ombudsman.
POOL.o: From Swedish ombudsman, “representative”; Sweden created the first parliamentary ombudsman in 1809.

POOL.h: A wide range of different things; originally a buffet of many dishes.
POOL.ex: The festival offered a smorgasbord of music, food and art.
POOL.o: From Swedish smörgåsbord, from smörgås “open sandwich” and bord “table”.

POOL.h: To be excessively submissive or obedient to someone.
POOL.ex: She refused to kowtow to the loudest person in the meeting.
POOL.o: From Chinese kòutóu, “knock the head”, describing the act of kneeling and touching the forehead to the ground as a sign of respect.

POOL.h: A wealthy, powerful person in business or industry.
POOL.ex: The shipping tycoon started out with a single second-hand truck.
POOL.o: From Japanese taikun, “great lord”, a title used for the shogun in dealings with foreigners.

POOL.h: Representing the most perfect or typical example of something.
POOL.ex: A backyard barbecue on a hot afternoon is the quintessential Australian summer scene.
POOL.o: From medieval Latin quinta essentia, “fifth essence”, a substance beyond earth, air, fire and water that was thought to make up the heavens.

POOL.h: A harsh, jarring mixture of sounds.
POOL.ex: At dawn the cockatoos created a cacophony outside the window.
POOL.o: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos “bad” and phone “sound”.

POOL.h: Active or appearing at dawn and dusk.
POOL.ex: Many kangaroos and wallabies are crepuscular, so drive with extra care at dawn and dusk.
POOL.o: From Latin crepusculum, “twilight”.

POOL.h: Relating to a transitional stage, between one state and the next.
POOL.ex: The weeks between finishing uni and starting work felt strangely liminal.
POOL.o: From Latin limen, “threshold”.

POOL.h: Generous and forgiving, especially towards a rival or someone less powerful.
POOL.ex: She was magnanimous in victory and thanked her opponent first.
POOL.o: From Latin magnanimus, from magnus “great” and animus “soul” or “mind”.

POOL.h: Lacking courage or determination; timid.
POOL.ex: The board’s pusillanimous response let the problem grow for years.
POOL.o: From Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus “very small” and animus “soul”: literally “small-souled”, the opposite of magnanimous.

POOL.h: Showing great care, persistence and attention.
POOL.ex: Her assiduous note-taking paid off at exam time.
POOL.o: From Latin assiduus, from assidere, “to sit beside”, suggesting someone who stays at a task.

POOL.h: Extremely careful about every little detail, leaving nothing to chance.
POOL.ex: He's meticulous about packing his tackle box, with every lure sorted by size and colour.
POOL.o: From Latin meticulosus, “fearful” or “timid”, from metus “fear”; the sense shifted to being careful out of fear of making mistakes.

POOL.h: Very careful to do what is honest and morally right; thorough.
POOL.ex: A scrupulous tradie will tell you when you don’t need the expensive repair.
POOL.o: From Latin scrupulus, “small sharp stone”, like a pebble in the shoe that nags at you, just as a conscience does.

POOL.h: Stubbornly uncooperative towards authority or control.
POOL.ex: Even the most recalcitrant printer eventually gives in to being turned off and on again.
POOL.o: From Latin recalcitrare, “to kick back with the heel”, from calx “heel”, as a stubborn horse or mule does.

POOL.h: Behaving as though you think you are superior to others.
POOL.ex: The waiter gave a supercilious glance at our choice of wine.
POOL.o: From Latin supercilium, “eyebrow”, evoking the raised eyebrow of disdain.

POOL.h: Lacking enthusiasm and effort; careless.
POOL.ex: His lackadaisical approach to the budget caught up with him at tax time.
POOL.o: From the old exclamation “lackaday”, short for “alack the day”, an expression of regret or weary sighing.

POOL.h: To think deeply and repeatedly about something.
POOL.ex: Instead of ruminating over the mistake, write down one lesson and move on.
POOL.o: From Latin ruminari, “to chew the cud”, as cows do, bringing food back up to chew again.

POOL.h: To avoid telling the truth by speaking evasively.
POOL.ex: When asked where the money went, he began to prevaricate.
POOL.o: From Latin praevaricari, “to walk crookedly”, from prae “before” and varicare “to straddle”.

POOL.h: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
POOL.ex: Scrolling late at night can exacerbate poor sleep.
POOL.o: From Latin exacerbare, “to make harsh”, from acerbus “harsh” or “bitter”.

POOL.h: To make something bad or unsatisfactory better.
POOL.ex: Planting trees along the street helped ameliorate the summer heat.
POOL.o: From French améliorer, from Latin melior, “better”.

POOL.h: A mental shortcut or rule of thumb that helps you make decisions quickly.
POOL.ex: “If in doubt, leave it out” is a useful heuristic for packing.
POOL.o: From Greek heuriskein, “to find”, the same root as “eureka”, “I have found it”.

POOL.h: A sudden and striking realisation.
POOL.ex: She had an epiphany in the shower: the problem wasn’t the job, it was the commute.
POOL.o: From Greek epiphaneia, “appearance” or “manifestation”.

POOL.h: The release of strong emotions, bringing relief.
POOL.ex: Writing the angry letter and then deleting it was pure catharsis.
POOL.o: From Greek katharsis, “cleansing” or “purging”; Aristotle used it in his Poetics for the emotional release an audience feels at a tragedy.

POOL.h: The lowest point of something.
POOL.ex: Losing the grand final by one point was the nadir of the club’s season.
POOL.o: From Arabic nazir, “opposite”, originally the point in the sky directly opposite the zenith.

POOL.h: A set of step-by-step rules for solving a problem, especially by a computer.
POOL.ex: The app’s algorithm learns what you like and shows you more of it.
POOL.o: From the name of al-Khwarizmi, a 9th-century Persian mathematician in Baghdad whose name was Latinised as Algoritmi.

POOL.h: Something reused or altered but still bearing visible traces of its earlier form.
POOL.ex: The old city is a palimpsest, with colonial buildings layered over far older streets.
POOL.o: From Greek palimpsestos, “scraped again”, describing parchment scraped clean so it could be written on once more.

POOL.h: The tendency to see meaningful patterns or connections in random information.
POOL.ex: Believing your lucky socks win matches is a textbook case of apophenia.
POOL.o: Coined in 1958 by German psychiatrist Klaus Conrad, from Greek roots meaning “to make visible”.

POOL.h: Seeing faces or familiar shapes in random things, like clouds or power sockets.
POOL.ex: Thanks to pareidolia, the front of every car seems to have a facial expression.
POOL.o: From Greek para “beside” or “faulty” and eidolon “image” or “form”.

POOL.h: Joy felt at another person’s good fortune; the opposite of envy.
POOL.ex: Instead of envy, she felt mudita when her friend got the promotion.
POOL.o: A Pali and Sanskrit word meaning “joy”, one of the four virtues cultivated in Buddhist meditation.

POOL.h: Practical wisdom: knowing how to act well in real situations.
POOL.ex: Rules only get you so far; phronesis is knowing when to bend them.
POOL.o: Greek for “practical wisdom”, a central virtue in Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics.

POOL.h: The appearance of being true or real.
POOL.ex: The novel’s verisimilitude came from years the author spent working in hospitals.
POOL.o: From Latin verisimilitudo, from verus “true” and similis “like”.

POOL.h: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things.
POOL.ex: The garrulous taxi driver told us his entire life story before we reached the airport.
POOL.o: From Latin garrulus, from garrire, “to chatter”.

POOL.h: Saying very little; reserved in speech.
POOL.ex: My taciturn uncle speaks rarely, but when he does, everyone listens.
POOL.o: From Latin taciturnus, from tacere, “to be silent”.

POOL.h: Appearing relaxed and unconcerned.
POOL.ex: She was nonchalant about the job interview, but she had prepared for days.
POOL.o: From Old French nonchaloir, “to not be concerned”, ultimately from Latin calere, “to be warm”, so literally “not getting heated”.

POOL.h: A solution or remedy for all problems or diseases.
POOL.ex: A new app is not a panacea for a disorganised team.
POOL.o: From Panacea, the Greek goddess of universal remedy, from pan “all” and akos “cure”.

POOL.h: To manipulate electoral boundaries to favour one party.
POOL.ex: Independent commissions help stop politicians from gerrymandering their seats.
POOL.o: From Elbridge Gerry, governor of Massachusetts in 1812, whose party drew a district that critics said looked like a salamander.

POOL.h: A commotion or fuss, especially over something minor.
POOL.ex: There was quite a kerfuffle over who had eaten the last Tim Tam.
POOL.o: From Scots curfuffle, based on fuffle, “to throw into disorder”.

POOL.h: Thinking of the perfect reply only after the moment has passed.
POOL.ex: Hours after the argument, esprit de l’escalier struck and I finally knew what to say.
POOL.o: French for “staircase wit”, from Denis Diderot, who described being unable to reply in company and thinking of the answer only at the bottom of the stairs.

POOL.h: A choice that is really no choice at all: take what is offered or nothing.
POOL.ex: With one flight left that day, it was Hobson’s choice.
POOL.o: From Thomas Hobson, a 17th-century Cambridge stable owner who made customers take the horse nearest the door or none at all.

POOL.h: A pattern, phrase or rhyme that helps you remember something.
POOL.ex: “Never Eat Soggy Weet-Bix” is a classic mnemonic for the compass points.
POOL.o: From Greek mnemonikos, “relating to memory”, from mneme “memory”; Mnemosyne was the Greek goddess of memory.

POOL.h: A phrase that combines contradictory terms, such as “deafening silence”.
POOL.ex: “Working holiday” sounds like an oxymoron, but it can be the best kind of trip.
POOL.o: From Greek oxys “sharp” and moros “dull” or “foolish”, so the word is itself an oxymoron.

POOL.h: A perfect example of a quality or type.
POOL.ex: The old lighthouse keeper was the epitome of patience.
POOL.o: From Greek epitome, “abridgement”, from epitemnein, “to cut short”; the idea shifted from a summary to something that sums up a quality.

POOL.h: To manipulate someone into doubting their own memory, perception or sanity.
POOL.ex: He tried to gaslight her into believing she had imagined the conversation.
POOL.o: From Patrick Hamilton’s 1938 play Gas Light, in which a husband’s secret night-time searching makes the gas lamps dim, and he then insists his wife is imagining it.

POOL.h: A person who looks strikingly like someone else; a double.
POOL.ex: I met my doppelgänger at the airport and we both did a double take.
POOL.o: German, “double-goer”, coined by the novelist Jean Paul in 1796.

POOL.h: Very loud and powerful, especially of a voice.
POOL.ex: The coach’s stentorian voice carried across three footy ovals.
POOL.o: From Stentor, a herald in Homer’s Iliad whose voice was as loud as fifty men.

POOL.h: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood.
POOL.ex: Working for a mercurial boss means never knowing which version will turn up.
POOL.o: From the planet Mercury: astrologers believed people born under it were quick-witted and changeable.

POOL.h: Gloomy, serious and brooding in temperament.
POOL.ex: Behind his saturnine expression was a surprisingly dry sense of humour.
POOL.o: From the planet Saturn, which astrologers linked with a cold, gloomy and sluggish temperament.

POOL.h: A lack of energy and enthusiasm.
POOL.ex: A short walk outside is often the best cure for afternoon lethargy.
POOL.o: From Greek lethargia, from lethe “forgetfulness” and argos “idle”; Lethe was the river of forgetting in the Greek underworld.

POOL.h: The capacity to recover quickly from difficulties.
POOL.ex: Resilience isn’t never falling down; it’s getting back up a little faster each time.
POOL.o: From Latin resilire, “to leap back” or “rebound”.

POOL.h: Outstandingly bad; shocking.
POOL.ex: Charging $12 for tap water is an egregious rip-off.
POOL.o: From Latin egregius, from e grege, “out of the flock”; it originally meant “outstanding” in a good sense before turning ironic.

POOL.h: An opening in a wall, usually fitted with glass, to let in light and air.
POOL.ex: Open a window for ten minutes a day to freshen the air in winter.
POOL.o: From Old Norse vindauga, literally “wind eye”, from vindr “wind” and auga “eye”.

POOL.h: Attractive and exciting qualities that make something seem special.
POOL.ex: The glamour of the film industry hides a lot of very long days.
POOL.o: A Scots alteration of “grammar”: learning was linked with the occult, so “glamour” came to mean a magic spell before it meant allure.

POOL.h: A loan to buy property, with the property itself as security.
POOL.ex: Paying a little extra off the mortgage each month can save years of interest.
POOL.o: From Old French mort gage, “dead pledge”, because the agreement dies either when the debt is paid or when payment fails and the property is lost.

POOL.h: Casual talk about other people’s private lives.
POOL.ex: A good rule: if you wouldn’t say it in front of them, it’s probably gossip.
POOL.o: From Old English godsibb, “godparent”; it came to mean a close friend, then someone who chatters, then the chatter itself.

POOL.h: Someone who gives opinions on matters beyond their knowledge or expertise.
POOL.ex: Social media is full of ultracrepidarians who became experts overnight.
POOL.o: From Latin ultra crepidam, “beyond the sandal”, after the painter Apelles told a cobbler not to judge above the shoe; popularised by essayist William Hazlitt in 1819.

POOL.h: The act of stretching and yawning at the same time, especially on waking.
POOL.ex: The cat’s long morning pandiculation was a masterclass in not rushing.
POOL.o: From Latin pandiculari, “to stretch oneself”.

POOL.h: Rough and prickly in how you deal with people, so you rub them up the wrong way.
POOL.ex: The new neighbour's abrasive notes about our parking made the whole street wary of her.
POOL.o: From Latin abradere, ‘to scrape off’, from ab- ‘away’ and radere ‘to scrape’.

POOL.h: To hold yourself back from doing something, like voting or treating yourself.
POOL.ex: I'm abstaining from chocolate until Easter, which is tough with a pantry full of it.
POOL.o: From Latin abstinere, ‘to hold back’, from ab- ‘from’ and tenere ‘to hold’.

POOL.h: About ideas and qualities rather than things you can see or touch.
POOL.ex: Freedom felt like an abstract idea until the day I got my own car keys.
POOL.o: From Latin abstractus, ‘drawn away’, from abs- ‘away’ and trahere ‘to draw’.

POOL.h: A mark of praise or an honour someone earns for doing something well.
POOL.ex: The pie shop hung its latest accolade, a gold ribbon from the Royal Show, right above the till.
POOL.o: From French accolade, originally the ceremonial embrace or touch of a sword used to confer knighthood.

POOL.h: To go along with something you'd rather not, without making a fuss.
POOL.ex: Tired of arguing, Mum acquiesced and let us put the Christmas tree up in November.
POOL.o: From Latin acquiescere, ‘to rest, find contentment’, from ad- ‘to’ and quiescere ‘to rest’.

POOL.h: Something you've obtained or bought, or the act of getting it.
POOL.ex: The footy club's biggest acquisition this off-season was a tall key forward from interstate.
POOL.o: From Latin acquisitio, from acquirere, ‘to acquire’, from ad- ‘to’ and quaerere ‘to seek’.

POOL.h: A court's official ruling that someone charged with a crime is not guilty.
POOL.ex: Reporters crowded the courthouse steps as news of the acquittal spread.
POOL.o: From Old French aquiter, ‘to pay a debt, clear’, related to Latin quietus, ‘at rest, free’.

POOL.h: Full of bitter anger and resentment, especially during an argument.
POOL.ex: What began as a friendly book club ended in an acrimonious split over who picked the next novel.
POOL.o: From Latin acrimonia, ‘sharpness, pungency’, from acer, ‘sharp, bitter’.

POOL.h: A sharp knack for making smart calls, usually in a particular area.
POOL.ex: Her acumen for spotting bargains meant she furnished the whole flat from garage sales.
POOL.o: From Latin acumen, ‘sharpness, point’, from acuere, ‘to sharpen’.

POOL.h: Totally firm about something and not budging, no matter what.
POOL.ex: Grandpa is adamant that cricket was better before the players wore coloured uniforms.
POOL.o: From Greek adamas, ‘unbreakable stone’, the root also behind the word ‘diamond’.

POOL.h: A change that helps a living thing or system cope with its surroundings.
POOL.ex: The echidna's long, sticky tongue is an adaptation for slurping up ants.
POOL.o: From Latin adaptare, ‘to fit to’, from ad- ‘to’ and aptare, ‘to fit’.

POOL.h: To stop a meeting or hearing for now and pick it up again later.
POOL.ex: The P&C decided to adjourn at nine and finish planning the school fete next week.
POOL.o: From Old French ajourner, ‘to appoint a day’, from a- ‘to’ and jour, ‘day’.

POOL.h: To act as the official judge who decides a dispute or contest.
POOL.ex: The school debating final will be adjudicated by a panel of local barristers.
POOL.o: From Latin adjudicare, ‘to award judicially’, from ad- ‘to’ and judicare, ‘to judge’.

POOL.h: Skilful and quick-thinking, especially when things get tricky.
POOL.ex: With some adroit steering, she guided the overloaded trolley through the packed car park without a scratch.
POOL.o: From French adroit, ‘skilful’, from à droit, ‘according to right, properly’.

POOL.h: Warm, easygoing and pleasant to chat with.
POOL.ex: The affable tour guide had the whole bus laughing before we'd even left Cairns.
POOL.o: From Latin affabilis, ‘easy to speak to’, from ad-, ‘to’, and fari, ‘to speak’.

POOL.h: A written statement someone swears is true, which can be used in court.
POOL.ex: The landlord swore an affidavit describing the damage before the tribunal hearing.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin affidavit, literally ‘he has stated on oath’, from affidare, ‘to pledge’.

POOL.h: Well-off and wealthy, with plenty of money to spare.
POOL.ex: The op shop in that affluent suburb is full of barely worn designer jackets.
POOL.o: From Latin affluere, ‘to flow towards’, from ad- ‘to’ and fluere, ‘to flow’.

POOL.h: To bring lots of separate bits together into one combined total.
POOL.ex: My fitness tracker aggregates the week's steps into a single score every Sunday.
POOL.o: From Latin aggregare, ‘to add to a flock’, from ad- ‘to’ and grex, ‘flock’.

POOL.h: Used to add a small catch or limit, meaning 'though' or 'even if'.
POOL.ex: We finally got the tent up, albeit a bit lopsided, just as the rain started.
POOL.o: A contraction of the Middle English phrase ‘al be it’, meaning ‘although it be’.

POOL.h: Having a pH above 7, which puts it on the opposite side of the scale from acids.
POOL.ex: The pool shop said our water was too alkaline and sold us something to bring the pH down.
POOL.o: From Arabic al-qaly, ‘the ashes’, referring to the alkaline ash of certain burnt plants.

POOL.h: A claim that someone did something wrong, before it's been proven.
POOL.ex: The cafe owner laughed off the allegation that her 'homemade' muffins came from the supermarket.
POOL.o: From Latin allegare, ‘to bring forward, cite’, from ad- ‘to’ and legare, ‘to depute, charge’.

POOL.h: To hand out or set aside a portion of something for a specific use.
POOL.ex: We allocate one shelf of the fridge to each housemate to avoid arguments.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin allocare, ‘to place, allot’, from ad- ‘to’ and locare, ‘to place’.

POOL.h: A loud, heated clash between people that can turn physical.
POOL.ex: A fight over a parking spot at the shopping centre sparked an altercation between two drivers.
POOL.o: From Latin altercatio, ‘a dispute’, from altercari, ‘to dispute, wrangle’.

POOL.h: Putting other people's needs first, with nothing in it for yourself.
POOL.ex: In an altruistic move, she spent her holidays teaching older neighbours how to use their phones.
POOL.o: From French altruisme, from Italian altrui, ‘somebody else’.

POOL.h: Unclear because it could mean more than one thing.
POOL.ex: The sign saying 'No parking after 6' was ambiguous: did it mean 6 am or 6 pm?
POOL.o: From Latin ambiguus, ‘doubtful’, from ambigere, ‘to waver’ (literally ‘to drive both ways’).

POOL.h: Feeling torn, with both good and bad feelings about the same thing.
POOL.ex: She's ambivalent about the new puppy: it's adorable, but it chewed through her favourite thongs.
POOL.o: From Latin ambi-, ‘both’, and valentia, ‘strength’. Coined by the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler around 1910.

POOL.h: Open to going along with a suggestion or being talked round.
POOL.ex: The coach was amenable to moving training to Thursday so the players could watch the final.
POOL.o: From French amener, ‘to lead’, from Latin minare, ‘to drive animals’.

POOL.h: To change the wording of something official, usually to fix or improve it.
POOL.ex: The club amended its rules so junior members could vote at the annual meeting.
POOL.o: From Latin emendare, ‘to free from faults’.

POOL.h: Good-natured and pleasant, the kind of person people warm to.
POOL.ex: Our amiable postie always stops for a quick yarn about the weather.
POOL.o: From Latin amicabilis, ‘friendly’, from amicus, ‘friend’.

POOL.h: An official offer to let people off for certain wrongdoings, usually for a limited time.
POOL.ex: The library's fine amnesty brought back books that had been overdue since the nineties.
POOL.o: From Greek amnestia, ‘forgetfulness’, from a- ‘without’ and mnesis, ‘memory’.

POOL.h: To pay off a debt, or spread out a big cost, bit by bit over time.
POOL.ex: The farm amortised the cost of its new harvester over eight seasons.
POOL.o: From Old French amortir, ‘to deaden, extinguish a debt’, from Latin mortuus, ‘dead’.

POOL.h: A cold-blooded animal, like a frog, that lives partly in water and partly on land.
POOL.ex: After the storm, a fat green tree frog, our favourite local amphibian, was stuck to the bathroom window.
POOL.o: From Greek amphibios, ‘living a double life’, from amphi- ‘both’ and bios, ‘life’.

POOL.h: Alike enough in some way to make a helpful comparison.
POOL.ex: Learning to surf is analogous to learning to ride a bike: lots of falling, then suddenly it clicks.
POOL.o: From Greek analogos, ‘proportionate’, from ana- ‘according to’ and logos, ‘ratio, reckoning’.

POOL.h: How a living thing's body is built, or the science that studies it.
POOL.ex: The butcher gave us a quick lesson in cow anatomy while pointing out where each cut comes from.
POOL.o: From Greek anatome, ‘dissection’, from ana- ‘up’ and temnein, ‘to cut’.

POOL.h: Based on people's personal stories, not on proper testing or data.
POOL.ex: The claim that the new roundabout causes more crashes is purely anecdotal so far.
POOL.o: From Greek anekdota, ‘things unpublished’.

POOL.h: Something that doesn't fit the usual pattern or what you'd expect.
POOL.ex: A $900 water bill was such an anomaly that we checked the garden for a burst pipe.
POOL.o: From Greek anomalia, ‘unevenness’, from an-, ‘not’, and homalos, ‘even’.

POOL.h: The complete opposite of something, or a striking contrast between two ideas.
POOL.ex: Our loud, messy Sunday roast is the antithesis of my in-laws' silent formal dinners.
POOL.o: From Greek antithesis, ‘opposition’, from anti- ‘against’ and thesis, ‘placing’.

POOL.h: To calm someone's anger or annoyance, often by giving in to them.
POOL.ex: To appease the crying toddler, the checkout operator handed over a free sticker.
POOL.o: From Old French apaisier, ‘to bring to peace’, from a- ‘to’ and pais, ‘peace’.

POOL.h: The person who takes a court decision to a higher court to challenge it.
POOL.ex: The appellant's lawyers claimed the trial judge had misread a key piece of evidence.
POOL.o: From Latin appellare, ‘to address, call upon’, the same root as ‘appeal’.

POOL.h: An official judgement of what something is worth or how well someone is doing.
POOL.ex: The jeweller's appraisal valued Nan's old brooch at far more than we expected.
POOL.o: From Old French apreisier, ‘to set a price on’, from Latin ad- ‘to’ and pretium, ‘price’.

POOL.h: Uneasy or nervous about what might be coming.
POOL.ex: I was apprehensive about the dentist until the receptionist said it was just a clean.
POOL.o: From Latin apprehendere, ‘to seize, grasp’, which also gives us ‘apprehend’.

POOL.h: A natural knack for picking up or doing a certain thing.
POOL.ex: My nephew has an aptitude for languages and was chatting in Italian after one holiday.
POOL.o: From Latin aptitudo, ‘fitness, suitability’, from aptus, ‘fitted, suited’.

POOL.h: A layer of rock or soil underground that stores water and lets it move through.
POOL.ex: The town's bore draws its drinking water from an aquifer deep beneath the paddocks.
POOL.o: From Latin aqua, ‘water’, and ferre, ‘to carry’.

POOL.h: Decided on a whim or at random, with no real reason behind it.
POOL.ex: The gym's rule that you can only use a treadmill for 22 minutes feels completely arbitrary.
POOL.o: From Latin arbitrarius, from arbiter, ‘judge’: left to a judge’s discretion.

POOL.h: To step in as a neutral judge and settle a disagreement between two sides.
POOL.ex: When my brothers fought over the last sausage on the barbie, Dad had to arbitrate.
POOL.o: From Latin arbitrari, ‘to give judgement’, from arbiter, ‘judge’.

POOL.h: The court session where someone hears the charges against them and pleads guilty or not guilty.
POOL.ex: The arraignment lasted barely ten minutes, but the courtroom was packed with journalists.
POOL.o: From Old French araisnier, ‘to call to account’, from Latin ad- ‘to’ and ratio, ‘reckoning’.

POOL.h: Money you owe that is already overdue.
POOL.ex: Once his phone bill slipped into arrears, the provider cut off his service until he paid.
POOL.o: From Old French arere, ‘behind’, from Latin ad retro, ‘to the back’.

POOL.h: Acting as if you're far more important or talented than you really are.
POOL.ex: The arrogant contestant laughed at the other cooks, then burnt his own dessert.
POOL.o: From Latin arrogare, ‘to claim for oneself’, from ad- ‘to’ and rogare, ‘to ask’.

POOL.h: Good at putting thoughts into clear, well-chosen words when speaking.
POOL.ex: My eight-year-old is surprisingly articulate when she's arguing for a later bedtime.
POOL.o: From Latin articulare, ‘to divide into joints, utter distinctly’, from articulus, ‘joint’.

POOL.h: To find out for sure, usually by checking the facts.
POOL.ex: Before booking, I rang the campground to ascertain whether dogs were allowed.
POOL.o: From Old French acertener, ‘to make certain’, from certain, ‘sure’.

POOL.h: A damaging remark about someone's character or reputation, often in 'cast aspersions'.
POOL.ex: At the family reunion, Uncle Ray cast aspersions on everyone's cooking except his own.
POOL.o: From Latin aspergere, ‘to sprinkle on’, originally used in the sense of splashing someone with dirt.

POOL.h: Confident enough to speak up for what you want, without being pushy.
POOL.ex: She got more assertive at the mechanic's and finally asked for a proper quote upfront.
POOL.o: From Latin asserere, ‘to claim, declare’, from ad- ‘to’ and serere, ‘to join’.

POOL.h: To take in and absorb new information, or to blend into a new group or culture.
POOL.ex: It took me a whole semester to assimilate all the jargon in my accounting course.
POOL.o: From Latin assimilare, ‘to make similar to’, from ad- ‘to’ and similis, ‘like’.

POOL.h: Sharp and shrewd, especially at reading a situation and acting on it.
POOL.ex: An astute shopper, he waited until the market was closing to haggle for cheaper mangoes.
POOL.o: From Latin astutus, ‘crafty’, from astus, ‘craft, skill’.

POOL.h: Protection a country gives to someone escaping danger or persecution back home.
POOL.ex: The journalist was granted asylum after her reporting made it unsafe to return home.
POOL.o: From Greek asylon, ‘refuge’, from a- ‘without’ and sylon, ‘right of seizure’.

POOL.h: To shrink or weaken over time, usually from not being used.
POOL.ex: Astronauts' leg muscles can atrophy after months of floating in zero gravity.
POOL.o: From Greek atrophia, ‘lack of food, wasting’, from a- ‘without’ and trophe, ‘nourishment’.

POOL.h: A slow wearing down in numbers or strength as things are gradually lost.
POOL.ex: The marathon saw steady attrition, with runners dropping out at every drinks station.
POOL.o: From Latin attritio, ‘a rubbing against’, from atterere, ‘to rub against, wear down’.

POOL.h: Daring and bold, willing to take big risks that surprise people.
POOL.ex: The rookie tried an audacious snap from the boundary line, and it sailed straight through.
POOL.o: From Latin audax, ‘bold’, from audere, ‘to dare’.

POOL.h: A formal check of an organisation's books or the way it runs things.
POOL.ex: The school canteen passed its food safety audit with flying colours.
POOL.o: From Latin audire, ‘to hear’, as early audits were literally read aloud to officials.

POOL.h: Very plain and bare, with no comforts or frills; also stern and serious.
POOL.ex: The shearers' quarters were austere: a tin roof, a cold shower and a row of narrow bunks.
POOL.o: From Greek austeros, ‘harsh, bitter, severe’.

POOL.h: The freedom to make your own decisions and run your own affairs.
POOL.ex: Getting her P-plates gave my daughter a whole new sense of autonomy.
POOL.o: From Greek autonomia, ‘independence’, from autos, ‘self’, and nomos, ‘law’.

POOL.h: A basic idea everyone accepts as true without needing it proved.
POOL.ex: It's an axiom in our house that whoever cooks doesn't wash up.
POOL.o: From Greek axioma, ‘that which is thought worthy’, from axios, ‘worthy’.

POOL.h: The long, thread-like arm of a nerve cell that sends signals onward.
POOL.ex: When you stub your toe, the pain message races along an axon towards your spinal cord.
POOL.o: From Greek axon, ‘axle’.

POOL.h: The setting or situation that events play out against; also a painted stage background.
POOL.ex: The school play's backdrop was a bedsheet painted to look like the outback.
POOL.o: A theatrical term from ‘back’ and ‘drop’, the painted cloth dropped behind a stage set.

POOL.h: A pile-up of work or jobs that still need doing.
POOL.ex: After two weeks off, I came back to a backlog of 300 unread emails.
POOL.o: From ‘back’ plus ‘log’, originally a large log kept burning at the back of a fire, later meaning stored-up work.

POOL.h: To keep pestering someone until they give in.
POOL.ex: My flatmate badgered me for weeks until I finally signed up for the fun run.
POOL.o: From the animal ‘badger’, likening the persistence of the behaviour to baiting one in old blood sports.

POOL.h: Money handed over to save a struggling business, industry or country from going under.
POOL.ex: Without a last-minute bailout from its members, the local footy club would have folded.
POOL.o: From ‘bail out’, originally meaning to remove water from a sinking boat.

POOL.h: Dull and unoriginal because it's been said or done so many times.
POOL.ex: The pop song's lyrics were so banal that I could guess every next line.
POOL.o: From French banal, originally meaning ‘compulsory’ or ‘communal’, later ‘commonplace’.

POOL.h: Light, friendly teasing and joking back and forth.
POOL.ex: The banter between the two radio hosts is the best part of my morning drive.
POOL.o: Origin uncertain; recorded in English since the 1600s as light, playful talk.

POOL.h: A flood of things, like questions or complaints, coming at you all at once.
POOL.ex: After posting her holiday photos, she got a barrage of messages asking where the beach was.
POOL.o: From French barrer, ‘to bar’, originally a military term for concentrated artillery fire.

POOL.h: Arriving or happening later than it was meant to.
POOL.ex: The council finally installed a belated pedestrian crossing, years after locals first asked for one.
POOL.o: From ‘be-’ plus ‘lated’, from Middle English laten, ‘to delay’.

POOL.h: To hit someone with a steady stream of problems that won't let up.
POOL.ex: Months of roadworks have beleaguered the shopkeepers on the main street.
POOL.o: From Dutch belegeren, ‘to besiege’, from be- and leger, ‘camp’.

POOL.h: Aggressive and hostile, spoiling for a fight or argument.
POOL.ex: The belligerent seagull refused to let go of my chip and squawked at anyone who came near.
POOL.o: From Latin belligerare, ‘to wage war’, from bellum, ‘war’, and gerere, ‘to carry on’.

POOL.h: Mildly puzzled, like you can't quite work out what's going on.
POOL.ex: The cat looked bemused when the robot vacuum bumped into her tail.
POOL.o: From ‘be-’ plus ‘muse’, originally meaning ‘to be lost in thought’.

POOL.h: A standard you use to measure or compare other things against.
POOL.ex: Mum's lamingtons are the benchmark every other cake at the fete gets judged against.
POOL.o: A surveyor’s mark cut into stone to rest a levelling rod on, like a bench.

POOL.h: Kind-hearted and generous, wanting good things for others.
POOL.ex: The benevolent farmer left boxes of free oranges at his gate for anyone passing by.
POOL.o: From Latin bene ‘well’ + volens ‘wishing’.

POOL.h: Harmless and mild, not likely to hurt anyone or anything.
POOL.ex: The huntsman spider looks terrifying but is fairly benign to humans.
POOL.o: From Latin benignus, ‘kind, well-born’, from bene- ‘well’ and gignere, ‘to beget’.

POOL.h: To leave someone completely baffled and unsure what to do.
POOL.ex: The self-checkout's endless warnings bewildered my grandad so much that he queued for a person instead.
POOL.o: From ‘be-’ plus ‘wilder’, an old word meaning ‘to lead astray into wild country’.

POOL.h: A list of all the books and sources a writer used or mentions.
POOL.ex: I spent longer formatting the bibliography than writing the actual history assignment.
POOL.o: From Greek biblion, ‘book’, and graphein, ‘to write’.

POOL.h: Having two separate houses in a parliament, like an upper and a lower house.
POOL.ex: Queensland is the only Australian state without a bicameral parliament, having abolished its upper house in 1922.
POOL.o: From Latin bi- ‘two’ and camera, ‘chamber, room’.

POOL.h: To split into two separate paths, branches or parts.
POOL.ex: The creek bifurcates just past the old bridge, so take the left arm for the swimming hole.
POOL.o: From Latin bifurcus, ‘two-pronged’, from bi- ‘two’ and furca, ‘fork’.

POOL.h: Involving two sides, especially an agreement between two countries.
POOL.ex: The sister cities set up a bilateral student exchange, sending ten teenagers each way every year.
POOL.o: From Latin bi- ‘two’ and latus, ‘side’.

POOL.h: Having only two options, or using a counting system of just 0 and 1.
POOL.ex: The pub quiz's final round was binary: every question was simply true or false.
POOL.o: From Latin bini, ‘two together’, from bis, ‘twice’.

POOL.h: Made up of two terms or names, as in algebra or scientific species names.
POOL.ex: The koala's binomial name, Phascolarctos cinereus, is far harder to spell than its common one.
POOL.o: From Latin bi- ‘two’ and nomen, ‘name’.

POOL.h: Able to break down naturally with help from bacteria and other tiny organisms.
POOL.ex: We served the sausage sizzle on biodegradable plates that went straight into the compost.
POOL.o: From Greek bios, ‘life’, and ‘degradable’, from Latin degradare, ‘to lower in rank’.

POOL.h: Backed by, or involving, both sides of politics rather than just one.
POOL.ex: The push to protect the reef earned bipartisan support in state parliament.
POOL.o: From Latin bi- ‘two’ and partisan, from parte, ‘part, side’.

POOL.h: Dull and flat, missing any real flavour or personality.
POOL.ex: The airline pasta was so bland that I'd have swapped it for a packet of chips.
POOL.o: From Latin blandus, ‘smooth, flattering, mild’.

POOL.h: Glaringly obvious and done without any shame.
POOL.ex: Parking across two spaces outside the chemist was a blatant bit of selfishness.
POOL.o: Possibly coined by the poet Edmund Spenser, from a word suggesting loud, bellowing noise.

POOL.h: A clumsy mistake, often an embarrassing one.
POOL.ex: Sending the joke meant for my sister to the whole work group chat was a serious blunder.
POOL.o: From Middle English blunderen, ‘to stumble about blindly’.

POOL.h: Stock wording that gets reused in contracts or documents with little change.
POOL.ex: The gym membership form was mostly boilerplate, so I skimmed straight to the cancellation fees.
POOL.o: From the metal plates once used to print standardised newspaper content, resembling boiler plating.

POOL.h: Loud, lively and full of energy, sometimes a bit rowdy.
POOL.ex: A boisterous hens party took over the back of the ferry, singing all the way to Manly.
POOL.o: From Middle English boistous, ‘rough, coarse’.

POOL.h: To prop up or strengthen something, like confidence, support or an argument.
POOL.ex: Glowing customer reviews bolstered her case for opening a second food truck.
POOL.o: From Old English bolster, ‘a long pillow’, used metaphorically to mean ‘to prop up’.

POOL.h: To hit someone with a relentless stream of something, like questions or attacks.
POOL.ex: Every spring, magpies bombard cyclists who ride too close to their nests.
POOL.o: From French bombarder, from bombe, ‘bomb’, ultimately from Greek bombos, ‘a deep, hollow sound’.

POOL.h: A spot where things get squeezed and slowed down, holding everything up.
POOL.ex: The single lane over the bridge becomes a bottleneck every long weekend.
POOL.o: From the physical shape of a bottle’s narrow neck, where flow is restricted.

POOL.h: Middle-class, often in a way that suggests conventional or material-minded tastes.
POOL.ex: His bandmates teased him about his bourgeois love of matching cushions and scented candles.
POOL.o: From French bourgeois, ‘town-dweller’, from bourg, ‘town’.

POOL.h: Describing the point where money coming in exactly covers costs, with no profit or loss.
POOL.ex: The band needs to sell 200 tickets just to reach the break-even mark for the tour.
POOL.o: From ‘break’, meaning to divide evenly, and ‘even’, meaning balanced.

POOL.h: Upbeat and lively, or able to stay afloat easily.
POOL.ex: Shoppers were in a buoyant mood as the doors opened for the Boxing Day sales.
POOL.o: From Spanish boyar, ‘to float’, related to boya, ‘buoy’.

POOL.h: A system run by lots of officials, forms and strict procedures.
POOL.ex: Updating my licence photo meant a whole morning lost to bureaucracy and three different forms.
POOL.o: From French bureau, ‘office, desk’, and Greek kratos, ‘power, rule’.

POOL.h: To grow or spread quickly and strongly.
POOL.ex: Since the new primary school opened, the number of young families in our street has burgeoned.
POOL.o: From Old French borjoner, ‘to bud’, from borjon, ‘a bud’.

POOL.h: To back up or reinforce something, like a wall or an argument.
POOL.ex: She buttressed her case for a pay rise with a spreadsheet of every extra task she'd taken on.
POOL.o: From Old French bouterez, ‘thrusting’, from bouter, ‘to push’.

POOL.h: Grumpy and argumentative, and hard to get along with.
POOL.ex: The cantankerous ferry captain barked at anyone who leaned on the rails.
POOL.o: Possibly a blend of ‘contentious’ and ‘rancorous’, first recorded in the 18th century.

POOL.h: To make the most of a chance, or to put money into a business.
POOL.ex: The umbrella seller outside the station capitalised on the sudden downpour.
POOL.o: From ‘capital’, ultimately Latin caput, ‘head’, which came to mean wealth or a principal sum.

POOL.h: Prone to changing suddenly and unpredictably, for no clear reason.
POOL.ex: Our capricious cat adores you one minute and swipes at your ankles the next.
POOL.o: From Italian capriccio, possibly linked to ‘capra’, ‘goat’, evoking a goat’s sudden leaps.

POOL.h: To grab someone's attention and keep them hooked.
POOL.ex: The magician captivated the kids at the birthday party for a full forty minutes.
POOL.o: From Latin captivare, ‘to take captive’, from captus, ‘caught’.

POOL.h: Relaxed and happy, with nothing weighing on your mind.
POOL.ex: Newly retired, they spent a carefree month driving across the Nullarbor with no fixed plans.
POOL.o: A straightforward compound of ‘care’ and ‘free’, in use since the 16th century.

POOL.h: Something that speeds up a chemical reaction, or that sparks a change.
POOL.ex: Losing his wallet was the catalyst for finally setting up payments on his phone.
POOL.o: From Greek katalysis, ‘dissolution’. The chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined ‘catalysis’ in 1835.

POOL.h: Too casual and offhand about something that deserves to be taken seriously.
POOL.ex: Leaving the pool gate propped open with toddlers around was a cavalier thing to do.
POOL.o: From Old French cavalier, ‘horseman, knight’, which came to suggest a haughty, casual manner.

POOL.h: A warning or condition that puts a limit on what's been said.
POOL.ex: The rental looks perfect, with one caveat: the only toilet is out the back.
POOL.o: Latin for ‘let him beware’, as in caveat emptor, ‘let the buyer beware’.

POOL.h: To do with living cells, or made up of them.
POOL.ex: Under the school microscope, the onion skin showed a neat cellular pattern like tiny bricks.
POOL.o: From Latin cellula, ‘small chamber’, diminutive of cella, ‘cell’.

POOL.h: Pushing or moving outward, away from the centre of a spin.
POOL.ex: A salad spinner uses centrifugal force to fling the water off the lettuce.
POOL.o: From Latin centrum, ‘centre’, and fugere, ‘to flee’.

POOL.h: Completely messy and out of control.
POOL.ex: School drop-off is chaotic when it rains and every parent tries to park at the gate.
POOL.o: From Greek khaos, meaning ‘vast chasm’ or ‘formless void’, via the noun ‘chaos’.

POOL.h: Having a magnetic charm that draws people in.
POOL.ex: The charismatic stallholder drew a crowd at the farmers market just by talking about her honey.
POOL.o: From Greek kharisma, ‘favour, gift’, from kharis, ‘grace’.

POOL.h: Liking to talk a lot, in a friendly, casual way.
POOL.ex: The chatty taxi driver told me his whole life story before we reached the airport.
POOL.o: From ‘chat’, a shortened form of ‘chatter’, imitative of the sound of talk.

POOL.h: Playfully rude or bold in a way that's more funny than offensive.
POOL.ex: My cheeky nephew asked if he could have my bedroom once I move out.
POOL.o: From ‘cheek’, long used to mean impudence, as in ‘to give someone cheek’.

POOL.h: The green substance in plants that captures sunlight to make food.
POOL.ex: The grass under the forgotten paddling pool had lost its chlorophyll and turned a sickly yellow.
POOL.o: From Greek khloros, ‘pale green’, and phyllon, ‘leaf’.

POOL.h: A tightly coiled strand of DNA that carries a cell's genetic instructions.
POOL.ex: In science class, we used pipe cleaners to show how each chromosome copies itself before a cell divides.
POOL.o: From Greek khroma, ‘colour’, and soma, ‘body’, since they stain visibly under a microscope.

POOL.h: Lasting a long time or constantly coming back.
POOL.ex: Our street has a chronic parking shortage whenever there's a game at the oval.
POOL.o: From Greek khronikos, ‘of time’, from khronos, ‘time’.

POOL.h: Rude, grumpy and unwilling to be gracious.
POOL.ex: He gave a churlish shrug instead of thanking the volunteers who'd cleaned up after his party.
POOL.o: From Old English ceorlisc, ‘of a churl’, a peasant or low-ranking freeman.

POOL.h: To do with the body's natural daily rhythm of roughly 24 hours.
POOL.ex: After flying home from London, my circadian rhythm had me wide awake at 3 am.
POOL.o: From Latin circa, ‘about’, and dies, ‘day’.

POOL.h: To pass something around, or to keep moving through a system.
POOL.ex: A ceiling fan helps circulate cool air around the bedroom on sticky nights.
POOL.o: From Latin circulare, ‘to form a circle’, from circulus, ‘small ring’.

POOL.h: A reference to a source you've used, or an official notice like a fine.
POOL.ex: The online encyclopedia flagged the dodgy claim with a note saying 'citation needed'.
POOL.o: From Latin citatio, from citare, ‘to summon’.

POOL.h: To point to a source or example to back up what you're saying.
POOL.ex: When asked why she quit, she cited the two-hour commute each way.
POOL.o: From Latin citare, ‘to summon, call forth’.

POOL.h: To sort things into groups based on what they have in common.
POOL.ex: The council's recycling app helps you classify each item as paper, plastic or general waste.
POOL.o: From Latin classis, ‘a class or division’, combined with -fy, ‘to make’.

POOL.h: A specific section or condition in a legal document.
POOL.ex: A clause in my phone contract lets them raise the price once a year.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin clausa, ‘conclusion’, from claudere, ‘to close’.

POOL.h: The regular customers a business serves, taken as a group.
POOL.ex: The wine bar's clientele wears suits, while the pub next door fills up with tradies in hi-vis.
POOL.o: From French clientèle, from Latin clientela, ‘the clients of a patron’.

POOL.h: Awkward and prone to dropping or bumping into things.
POOL.ex: I'm so clumsy that I tripped over the dog on my way to the fridge.
POOL.o: From an old dialect word ‘clumse’, meaning numbed with cold, related to being stiff and unable to move well.

POOL.h: A messy jumble of stuff lying around.
POOL.ex: The spare room's clutter meant our guests had to sleep on a blow-up mattress in the lounge.
POOL.o: Probably related to ‘clot’, originally meaning a clotted mass, later a confused heap.

POOL.h: To turn rules or habits into a clear, written system.
POOL.ex: After one too many arguments, the share house codified its cleaning roster on a whiteboard.
POOL.o: From French codifier, from ‘code’, ultimately from Latin codex, ‘book of laws’.

POOL.h: Getting someone to act by using threats or pressure rather than their free choice.
POOL.ex: Threatening to cancel the beach trip unless the kids tidied up was mild coercion, but it worked.
POOL.o: From Latin coercere, ‘to restrain, compel’, from arcere, ‘to shut in’.

POOL.h: Clear, logical and persuasive.
POOL.ex: The tenant wrote a cogent letter explaining exactly why the rent increase was unfair.
POOL.o: From Latin cogere, ‘to compel, drive together’.

POOL.h: The brain's ways of thinking, learning, remembering and understanding.
POOL.ex: Crows show impressive cognition, bending sticks into hooks to fish out grubs.
POOL.o: From Latin cognitio, ‘a getting to know’, from cognoscere, ‘to know’.

POOL.h: Making sense, with ideas that connect logically.
POOL.ex: His late-night text wasn't very coherent, just three emojis and half a sentence.
POOL.o: From Latin cohaerere, ‘to stick together’.

POOL.h: Holding together well as one united whole.
POOL.ex: The community choir sounded far more cohesive after a weekend retreat together.
POOL.o: From Latin cohaerere, ‘to stick together’, from haerere, ‘to stick’.

POOL.h: To team up with others to work on something together.
POOL.ex: Two local bakeries collaborated on a hot cross bun with a chocolate and chilli twist.
POOL.o: From Latin com- ‘together’ plus laborare, ‘to work’.

POOL.h: Something you offer as a guarantee on a loan, which the lender can take if you don't repay.
POOL.ex: He put up his boat as collateral to borrow money for the new fishing charter business.
POOL.o: From Latin collateralis, ‘side by side’, so something standing alongside the loan.

POOL.h: Quick to argue or pick a fight.
POOL.ex: The combative contestant argued with the judges over every single score.
POOL.o: From Latin combattere, ‘to fight together’, from com- and battere, ‘to beat’.

POOL.h: The process of burning, which gives off heat and light.
POOL.ex: The rocket launch was a spectacular show of combustion, with flames lighting up the night sky.
POOL.o: From Latin combustio, from comburere, ‘to burn up’.

POOL.h: A fee earned as a cut of sales, or an official body set up to do a job.
POOL.ex: The art gallery takes a 30 per cent commission on every painting it sells.
POOL.o: From Latin commissio, ‘a joining or entrusting’, from committere.

POOL.h: A basic raw product, like wheat or oil, that's traded in bulk.
POOL.ex: Wool was once Australia's most important commodity, hence the saying that the nation rode on the sheep's back.
POOL.o: From Latin commoditas, ‘suitableness, advantage’, from commodus, ‘convenient’.

POOL.h: So ordinary and frequent that nobody notices it any more.
POOL.ex: Paying by phone is so commonplace now that some cafes won't even take cash.
POOL.o: From a Latin phrase locus communis, ‘common place’, originally a stock literary theme.

POOL.h: To travel back and forth between home and work, or to reduce a sentence.
POOL.ex: He commutes by ferry across the harbour, which beats sitting in traffic.
POOL.o: From Latin commutare, ‘to change altogether’, from mutare, ‘to change’.

POOL.h: Caring and understanding towards people who are hurting.
POOL.ex: A compassionate stranger sat with the lost child until her parents turned up.
POOL.o: From Latin compassio, ‘suffering together with’, from pati, ‘to suffer’.

POOL.h: So gripping or convincing that you can't ignore it.
POOL.ex: The podcast was so compelling that I sat in the driveway to hear the last ten minutes.
POOL.o: From Latin compellere, ‘to drive together, force’, from pellere, ‘to drive’.

POOL.h: A handy collection of information packed into one place.
POOL.ex: Grandma's recipe folder is a compendium of fifty years of family dinners.
POOL.o: From Latin compendium, ‘a shortening, saving’, from pendere, ‘to weigh’.

POOL.h: Involving a fight to be the best, or priced well against others.
POOL.ex: Rentals in our town are so competitive that twenty people turn up to every inspection.
POOL.o: From Latin competere, ‘to strive together, be suitable’, from petere, ‘to seek’.

POOL.h: To gather bits of information from different places into one collection.
POOL.ex: I compiled a playlist of everyone's favourite songs for the road trip.
POOL.o: From Latin compilare, ‘to plunder or pile up’, from pilare, ‘to plunder’.

POOL.h: So comfortable with how things are that you stop being careful or trying.
POOL.ex: After ten quiet years, we got complacent about locking the back door.
POOL.o: From Latin complacere, ‘to please greatly’.

POOL.h: The person who makes a formal complaint or brings a case against someone.
POOL.ex: The complainant told the ombudsman her internet had dropped out every day for a month.
POOL.o: From Latin complangere, ‘to lament loudly’, via ‘complain’.

POOL.h: Covering pretty much everything, leaving little out.
POOL.ex: Before the road trip, we booked the car in for a comprehensive service, from tyres to wipers.
POOL.o: From Latin comprehendere, ‘to grasp fully’, from prehendere, ‘to seize’.

POOL.h: A deal where each side gives up a bit of what they wanted.
POOL.ex: Our compromise was pizza on Friday and Thai on Saturday, so everyone got a turn.
POOL.o: From Latin compromissum, a mutual promise to abide by an arbiter’s decision.

POOL.h: Far too impressed with yourself, your looks or your talents.
POOL.ex: The conceited influencer spent the whole wedding photographing himself instead of the couple.
POOL.o: From ‘conceit’, originally meaning ‘a thought or idea’, which shifted to mean an overly favourable idea of oneself.

POOL.h: About ideas and concepts rather than solid, real things.
POOL.ex: The conceptual artwork was just a chair in an empty room, and people argued about it for hours.
POOL.o: From Latin conceptus, ‘a thing conceived’, from concipere, ‘to conceive’.

POOL.h: When vapour cools and turns back into liquid water.
POOL.ex: Beads of condensation ran down the outside of my icy can of lemonade.
POOL.o: From Latin condensare, ‘to make dense’, from densus, ‘thick’.

POOL.h: Treating others as if they're less clever or important than you.
POOL.ex: The car salesman was condescending, explaining every feature to my husband and ignoring me.
POOL.o: From Latin condescendere, ‘to stoop’.

POOL.h: How easily a material lets heat or electricity pass through it.
POOL.ex: Cast iron has lower conductivity than copper, so a cast iron pan takes longer to heat up.
POOL.o: From Latin conducere, ‘to lead together’, via ‘conduct’.

POOL.h: Friendly and pleasant, or nicely suited to your tastes.
POOL.ex: The quiet country town proved a congenial place to finish her novel.
POOL.o: From Latin com- ‘together’ plus genialis, ‘of birth, genial’, from genius.

POOL.h: A huge company made up of many different, often unrelated, businesses.
POOL.ex: The conglomerate that owns our supermarket also runs petrol stations, hardware stores and a liquor chain.
POOL.o: From Latin conglomerare, ‘to roll together’, from glomus, ‘a ball of thread’.

POOL.h: A guess or theory put forward without solid proof.
POOL.ex: Talk that the star midfielder is moving interstate is just conjecture until he signs.
POOL.o: From Latin conjectura, ‘a putting together’, from conicere, ‘to throw together’.

POOL.h: The extra feeling or idea a word carries on top of its basic meaning.
POOL.ex: Calling the flat 'cosy' in the ad had a connotation of 'tiny' that renters saw straight through.
POOL.o: From Latin connotare, ‘to mark along with’, from notare, ‘to note’.

POOL.h: Careful and dutiful, taking real care to do things properly.
POOL.ex: The conscientious house-sitter left a note listing every plant she'd watered.
POOL.o: From Latin conscientia, ‘knowledge within oneself, conscience’.

POOL.h: Broad agreement shared by most of a group.
POOL.ex: The group chat's consensus was that the beach was too windy, so we went bowling instead.
POOL.o: From Latin consentire, ‘to agree’, from con-, ‘together’, and sentire, ‘to feel’.

POOL.h: Thoughtful about how your actions affect other people.
POOL.ex: Our considerate neighbours always warn us before they fire up the chainsaw.
POOL.o: From Latin considerare, ‘to examine closely’, from sidus, ‘star’, originally about careful observation.

POOL.h: To merge separate things into one stronger or neater whole.
POOL.ex: I consolidated all my old super accounts into one fund to save on fees.
POOL.o: From Latin consolidare, ‘to make solid’, from solidus, ‘solid’.

POOL.h: A group of companies or organisations teaming up on a shared project.
POOL.ex: A consortium of local wineries pooled their money to run a joint food and wine festival.
POOL.o: From Latin consortium, ‘fellowship, partnership’, from consors, ‘sharing’.

POOL.h: Easily spread from person to person, like a germ or a mood.
POOL.ex: The toddler's giggling was so contagious that the whole train carriage started laughing.
POOL.o: From Latin contagio, ‘a touching, contact’, from tangere, ‘to touch’.

POOL.h: Scorn for someone or something, or, in law, defying a court's authority.
POOL.ex: She stared at the rubbish-strewn beach with open contempt for whoever had left it.
POOL.o: From Latin contemptus, ‘a despising’, from contemnere, ‘to scorn’.

POOL.h: Something that might happen, or a backup plan in case it does.
POOL.ex: As a contingency, we packed a second esky in case the ice ran out.
POOL.o: From Latin contingere, ‘to touch, to happen’.

POOL.h: A person or company hired under a contract to do a job, often building work.
POOL.ex: The contractor laying our new driveway said the concrete would need a week to cure.
POOL.o: From Latin contractus, ‘a drawing together, an agreement’, from contrahere.

POOL.h: Truly sorry for something you did wrong.
POOL.ex: Looking contrite, my son handed over the cricket ball that had smashed the neighbour's window.
POOL.o: From Latin contritus, ‘ground down, worn out’, from conterere, ‘to crush’.

POOL.h: A puzzling problem that's hard to solve.
POOL.ex: Fitting a surfboard, two kids and a dog into a hatchback was a real conundrum.
POOL.o: Origin uncertain; it appeared in 16th century English, possibly a humorous, mock-Latin invention.

POOL.h: Handy and easy, fitting in well with what you need.
POOL.ex: The bus stop right outside our gate is very convenient on rainy mornings.
POOL.o: From Latin convenire, ‘to come together, agree, be suitable’.

POOL.h: Friendly and polite, though a little on the formal side.
POOL.ex: The rival coaches shared a cordial handshake before the grand final.
POOL.o: From Latin cordialis, ‘of the heart’, from cor, ‘heart’.

POOL.h: A result that naturally follows from something else.
POOL.ex: A corollary of living near the beach is sand in absolutely everything you own.
POOL.o: From Latin corollarium, originally ‘money paid for a garland’, later ‘something extra, a deduction’.

POOL.h: To do with big businesses or companies in general.
POOL.ex: The corporate box at the stadium came with free food and a perfect view of the try line.
POOL.o: From Latin corpus, ‘body’, via corporare, ‘to form into a body’.

POOL.h: To be linked, so that when one thing changes the other tends to as well.
POOL.ex: Ice cream sales correlate with shark sightings, but that doesn't mean one causes the other.
POOL.o: From Latin com- ‘together’ plus relatus, ‘related’.

POOL.h: To back up someone's claim with supporting evidence.
POOL.ex: The dashcam footage corroborated her version of how the crash happened.
POOL.o: From Latin corroborare, ‘to strengthen’, from robur, ‘strength’ (and ‘oak’).

POOL.h: Able to eat away at materials, or causing slow, steady damage.
POOL.ex: Constant gossip had a corrosive effect on the trust within the team.
POOL.o: From Latin corrodere, ‘to gnaw away’, from rodere, ‘to gnaw’.

POOL.h: Snug, warm and comfortable.
POOL.ex: The corner armchair at our local cafe is my cosy spot on wet winter afternoons.
POOL.o: Possibly from Scandinavian roots meaning sheltered or comfortable, first recorded in Scots English.

POOL.h: Advice, especially legal advice, or the lawyer who gives it.
POOL.ex: Following her father's counsel, she saved half of every pay packet from her first job.
POOL.o: From Old French conseil, from Latin consilium, ‘plan, advice’.

POOL.h: Polite and respectful towards others.
POOL.ex: The courteous driver stopped and waved the kids across the zebra crossing.
POOL.o: From Old French corteis, ‘having courtly manners’, from ‘court’.

POOL.h: A formal, binding promise or agreement between parties.
POOL.ex: Members of the garden co-op signed a covenant to share tools and help with each other's harvests.
POOL.o: From Old French covenant, from Latin convenire, ‘to come together, agree’.

POOL.h: Eagerly wanting something that belongs to someone else.
POOL.ex: I cast a covetous glance at the next table's giant seafood platter.
POOL.o: From Old French coveitous, from Latin cupiditas, ‘desire, eagerness’.

POOL.h: Tight and uncomfortable, without enough room to move.
POOL.ex: Twelve hours in a cramped economy seat left my knees aching.
POOL.o: From ‘cramp’, originally a metal clasp for holding things tightly together.

POOL.h: To want something badly and intensely.
POOL.ex: On frosty mornings I crave a hot meat pie with sauce.
POOL.o: From Old English crafian, ‘to demand or ask’.

POOL.h: A qualification or document that proves you're qualified or authorised.
POOL.ex: Her most useful credential for the lifeguard job was a current first aid certificate.
POOL.o: From Latin credere, ‘to believe or trust’.

POOL.h: Too quick to believe things, so easily taken in.
POOL.ex: My credulous little brother believed me when I said drop bears lived in the backyard gum tree.
POOL.o: From Latin credulus, ‘believing easily’, from credere, ‘to believe’.

POOL.h: To wince or feel a hot wave of embarrassment.
POOL.ex: I cringe every time Dad hits the dance floor at weddings.
POOL.o: From Old English cringan, ‘to bend, yield or fall in battle’.

POOL.h: The standards used to judge or decide something.
POOL.ex: The scholarship's criteria include community work as well as good marks.
POOL.o: From Greek kriterion, ‘a means for judging’, from krites, ‘judge’.

POOL.h: A careful review that weighs up a piece of work's strengths and weaknesses.
POOL.ex: The chef's critique of my pavlova was harsh but useful: too sweet and not crisp enough.
POOL.o: From French critique, from Greek kritikos, ‘able to judge’.

POOL.h: An animal with a hard outer shell and jointed legs, like a crab or prawn.
POOL.ex: The yabby my son pulled from the dam was the biggest crustacean he'd ever held.
POOL.o: From Latin crusta, ‘shell, rind, crust’.

POOL.h: The central, deciding point of an issue.
POOL.ex: The crux of the problem is that nobody wants to be the one to cancel the trip.
POOL.o: From Latin crux, meaning ‘cross’, later used figuratively for a difficult or crucial point.

POOL.h: To do with producing or working with extremely low temperatures.
POOL.ex: The dessert bar uses cryogenic liquid nitrogen to freeze ice cream in seconds.
POOL.o: From Greek kryos, ‘frost, cold’, and genes, ‘produced’.

POOL.h: Made of crystals, or clear and sparkling like them.
POOL.ex: We swam in a crystalline rock pool so clear we could count the pebbles on the bottom.
POOL.o: From Greek krystallos, ‘ice, clear crystal’.

POOL.h: Clunky and awkward because it's big, heavy or complicated.
POOL.ex: The old pram was so cumbersome that it wouldn't fit through the bus doors.
POOL.o: From Middle English combren, ‘to hinder or block’, related to ‘encumber’.

POOL.h: Building up bit by bit as more is added.
POOL.ex: Our cumulative driving time across the whole road trip came to nearly forty hours.
POOL.o: From Latin cumulare, ‘to heap up’, from cumulus, ‘a heap’.

POOL.h: Keen to find out about things; also, odd or unusual.
POOL.ex: The curious puppy stuck his nose into every shopping bag we carried inside.
POOL.o: From Latin curiosus, ‘careful, inquisitive’, from cura, ‘care’.

POOL.h: A grumpy, stubborn person, often an older one.
POOL.ex: Even the local curmudgeon cracked a smile when the kids sang carols at his door.
POOL.o: Origin uncertain; recorded in English since the 16th century, meaning a churlish or miserly fellow.

POOL.h: The set of subjects and topics a school or course teaches.
POOL.ex: Swimming lessons are part of the primary school curriculum in many states.
POOL.o: From Latin curriculum, ‘a running, a course’, from currere, ‘to run’.

POOL.h: To cut something back or cut it short.
POOL.ex: Bad light curtailed the cricket match after only thirty overs.
POOL.o: From Old French courtault, ‘shortened’, related to ‘curt’ and ‘tail’.

POOL.h: Legal responsibility for looking after someone, or being held by police.
POOL.ex: Nan was given custody of her two grandsons while their parents worked overseas.
POOL.o: From Latin custodia, ‘guarding, watching’, from custos, ‘guard’.

POOL.h: Normal or traditional for a certain place or occasion.
POOL.ex: In Japan, it's customary to take your shoes off before stepping into someone's home.
POOL.o: From ‘custom’, from Old French costume, ultimately from Latin consuetudo, ‘habit’.

POOL.h: Wary and careful to consider all the consequences before acting.
POOL.ex: Be circumspect about giving your address to online sellers you don’t know.
POOL.o: From Latin circumspicere, ‘to look around’, from circum, ‘around’, and specere, ‘to look’.

POOL.h: Seeming so hard or big that it's a bit off-putting.
POOL.ex: Staring up at the 800 steps to the lookout was daunting after a big lunch.
POOL.o: From Old French danter, ‘to tame or subdue’.

POOL.h: A sudden, embarrassing failure or collapse.
POOL.ex: The school concert became a debacle when the microphone died and the curtain fell down.
POOL.o: From French debacler, ‘to unbar’, originally describing ice breaking up on a river.

POOL.h: Charming, confident and stylish.
POOL.ex: The debonair waiter charmed every table with his smooth manner and perfect bow tie.
POOL.o: From Old French de bon aire, ‘of good disposition’.

POOL.h: Able to make firm choices quickly and confidently.
POOL.ex: When the fire alarm went off, the decisive manager had everyone out of the restaurant in under a minute.
POOL.o: From Latin decidere, ‘to cut off, decide’.

POOL.h: To rot and break down into simpler parts over time.
POOL.ex: The pumpkin we forgot in the pantry had started to decompose into a sticky orange mess.
POOL.o: From Latin com-, ‘together’, and ponere, ‘to put’, with the prefix de- reversing it.

POOL.h: Polite, proper and fitting for the occasion.
POOL.ex: The usually rowdy uncles were surprisingly decorous at the christening.
POOL.o: From Latin decorus, ‘seemly, becoming’, from decor, ‘beauty, grace’.

POOL.h: To work something out by reasoning from the clues you have.
POOL.ex: From the crumbs on his shirt, I deduced who had eaten the last Tim Tam.
POOL.o: From Latin deducere, ‘to lead down or away’.

POOL.h: Harming someone's reputation by spreading false claims about them.
POOL.ex: The restaurant owner sued for defamation over a fake review claiming he served rat.
POOL.o: From Latin diffamare, ‘to spread abroad by ill report’.

POOL.h: The person being accused or sued in a court case.
POOL.ex: The defendant arrived at court in a borrowed suit that was two sizes too big.
POOL.o: From Latin defendere, ‘to defend’, via Old French defendant.

POOL.h: Boldly refusing to obey or give in.
POOL.ex: With a defiant grin, the teenager dyed his hair blue the day before school photos.
POOL.o: From Old French defiant, from defier, ‘to challenge’.

POOL.h: The shortfall when you have less of something than you need.
POOL.ex: After all the Christmas shopping, our household budget was running a deficit.
POOL.o: From Latin deficit, ‘it is lacking’, from deficere, ‘to fail’.

POOL.h: Quick, neat and skilful, especially with the hands.
POOL.ex: With a deft flick, the fisherman unhooked the flathead and slid it back into the water.
POOL.o: A variant of daft, which once meant ‘gentle, meek’ before shifting to its modern sense.

POOL.h: To lose water, or to dry something out by removing it.
POOL.ex: Long-haul flights can dehydrate you, so keep sipping water.
POOL.o: From de-, ‘removing’, and Greek hydor, ‘water’.

POOL.h: So tasty that every bite feels like a real treat.
POOL.ex: The mango sorbet from the Mindil Beach stall was delectable in the sticky Darwin heat.
POOL.o: From Latin delectare, ‘to delight’.

POOL.h: To hand off part of your workload for someone else to take care of.
POOL.ex: Mum delegated the washing up to the kids so she could finally sit down.
POOL.o: From Latin delegare, ‘to send on a commission’.

POOL.h: A defined piece of work you must hand over at a set point in a project.
POOL.ex: The first deliverable for the website redesign is a clickable homepage mock-up.
POOL.o: From deliver, from Old French delivrer, ‘to set free, hand over’.

POOL.h: A group of people sorted by shared traits like age, income or location.
POOL.ex: The breakfast radio show is pitched at the school-run demographic.
POOL.o: From Greek demos, ‘people’, and graphein, ‘to write, describe’.

POOL.h: Quiet and modest, with a touch of shyness.
POOL.ex: The usually loud toddler turned demure the moment Grandma's friends arrived.
POOL.o: From Old French meur, ‘ripe, mature’, later blended with demurer, ‘to linger’.

POOL.h: To unfairly run someone down so others think less of them.
POOL.ex: The coach warned players not to denigrate the umpires on social media.
POOL.o: From Latin denigrare, ‘to blacken’, from nigrare, ‘to blacken’, from niger, ‘black’.

POOL.h: How tightly packed the stuff in a given space is.
POOL.ex: Ice floats in your drink because its density is lower than that of liquid water.
POOL.o: From Latin densus, ‘thick, dense’.

POOL.h: To drain the supply of something until it runs low.
POOL.ex: Streaming videos on the train depleted my monthly data allowance by Wednesday.
POOL.o: From Latin deplere, ‘to empty out’.

POOL.h: To send people, gear or tools out to where they're needed for a job.
POOL.ex: The council deployed extra rangers to the beach over the Easter long weekend.
POOL.o: From French deployer, ‘to unfold’, from Latin displicare.

POOL.h: A sworn account of evidence, recorded outside court for use in a case.
POOL.ex: The retired engineer gave his deposition by video link from his home in Perth.
POOL.o: From Latin deponere, ‘to put down, set aside’.

POOL.h: To be worth less and less as time goes by.
POOL.ex: That laptop will depreciate the minute you walk out of the shop.
POOL.o: From Latin depretiare, ‘to lower the price of’.

POOL.h: Left empty and neglected until it's crumbling.
POOL.ex: A derelict petrol station sat beside the highway, its pumps rusted solid.
POOL.o: From Latin derelinquere, ‘to abandon completely’.

POOL.h: Unoriginal, because it borrows too heavily from work that already exists.
POOL.ex: The new cafe's menu felt derivative, like a copy of every brunch spot in Fitzroy.
POOL.o: From Latin derivare, ‘to draw off’, from de- and rivus, ‘stream’.

POOL.h: To dry something out completely, or very nearly.
POOL.ex: Gran likes to desiccate apple slices in a low oven for crunchy snacks.
POOL.o: From Latin desiccare, ‘to dry up thoroughly’.

POOL.h: Bleak and empty, with nothing lively or welcoming about it.
POOL.ex: The caravan park was desolate in the middle of winter, with every site empty.
POOL.o: From Latin desolare, ‘to abandon completely’.

POOL.h: Low, disheartened and close to giving up hope.
POOL.ex: He was despondent when the rain washed out his long-planned camping trip.
POOL.o: From Latin despondere, ‘to give up, lose heart’.

POOL.h: An all-powerful ruler who treats people harshly.
POOL.ex: In the video game, you overthrow a despot who taxes villagers into starvation.
POOL.o: From Greek despotes, ‘master, lord’.

POOL.h: To officially keep someone from leaving, often for questioning.
POOL.ex: Airport security detained a passenger after finding a knife in his carry-on bag.
POOL.o: From Latin detinere, ‘to hold back’.

POOL.h: Anything that makes people think twice before doing something.
POOL.ex: The hefty late fee is a deterrent to returning library books late.
POOL.o: From Latin deterrere, ‘to frighten away’.

POOL.h: Sneaky and dishonest in how you go about getting your way.
POOL.ex: My devious little brother hid the TV remote so he could pick the show.
POOL.o: From Latin devius, ‘off the beaten track’, from de- and via, ‘way’.

POOL.h: A sharp split or contrast between two opposite things.
POOL.ex: There's a funny dichotomy between his spotless desk and his chaotic car.
POOL.o: From Greek dikhotomia, ‘a cutting in two’.

POOL.h: Designed to teach, often in a preachy, lecturing way.
POOL.ex: The picture book was so didactic that my kids got bored of its lecture on sharing.
POOL.o: From Greek didaktikos, ‘apt at teaching’, from didaskein, ‘to teach’.

POOL.h: Run-down and falling to bits from age or neglect.
POOL.ex: We stayed in a dilapidated beach shack with a sagging verandah and a leaky roof.
POOL.o: From Latin dilapidare, ‘to scatter like stones, squander’.

POOL.h: To stretch open wider, or to make something open wider.
POOL.ex: Blood vessels near your skin dilate on hot days to help your body cool down.
POOL.o: From Latin dilatare, ‘to spread out’.

POOL.h: Hard-working and thorough about getting things right.
POOL.ex: The diligent volunteer checked every life jacket before the kayaks went out.
POOL.o: From Latin diligere, ‘to value highly’.

POOL.h: To shrink or fade, or to make something lose size, strength or importance.
POOL.ex: The roar of the home crowd diminished as the away team scored again.
POOL.o: From Latin diminuere, ‘to break into small pieces’.

POOL.h: A statement saying you're not responsible for something, or that a claim isn't true.
POOL.ex: The fitness video opens with a disclaimer telling viewers to check with a doctor first.
POOL.o: From disclaim, from Old French desclamer, ‘to renounce a claim’.

POOL.h: To let people know something that had been kept secret.
POOL.ex: The real estate agent had to disclose that the house had flooded before.
POOL.o: From Old French desclos, ‘unclosed’, from Latin claudere, ‘to close’.

POOL.h: Serious discussion or debate about a subject, spoken or written.
POOL.ex: The podcast aims to lift the level of discourse about Australian history.
POOL.o: From Latin discursus, ‘a running about’, from discurrere.

POOL.h: Careful and tactful, so you don't cause embarrassment or draw attention.
POOL.ex: The waiter was discreet, slipping the bill to him so his date wouldn't see.
POOL.o: From Latin discretus, ‘separated, distinct’, later ‘wise, discerning’.

POOL.h: A gap or mismatch between two things that ought to agree.
POOL.ex: I noticed a discrepancy between the shelf price and the one at the checkout.
POOL.o: From Latin discrepare, ‘to sound differently, disagree’.

POOL.h: Messy-looking, with hair or clothes all over the place.
POOL.ex: She stepped off the overnight bus dishevelled, her hair squashed flat on one side.
POOL.o: From Old French deschevele, ‘with hair uncovered or disordered’.

POOL.h: To get information or ideas out to lots of people.
POOL.ex: Volunteers disseminated bushfire safety flyers to every letterbox in town.
POOL.o: From Latin disseminare, ‘to scatter seed’, from dis- and semen, ‘seed’.

POOL.h: Disagreement with an official view or with what most people think.
POOL.ex: When the club voted to raise fees, there was loud dissent from the older members.
POOL.o: From Latin dissentire, ‘to differ in feeling’.

POOL.h: To boil something down to its most important points.
POOL.ex: Could you distil your three-page email into a two-line text?
