POOL.o: From Latin distillare, ‘to drip down’, from de- and stillare, ‘to drip’.

POOL.h: Splitting off in different directions after starting in the same place.
POOL.ex: The twins went to the same school but took divergent careers, one in nursing and one in music.
POOL.o: From Latin divergere, ‘to turn apart’, from dis- and vergere, ‘to bend’.

POOL.h: To spread into more kinds of products or activities so you're not relying on just one.
POOL.ex: The fish and chip shop diversified by adding gelato and coffee to its menu.
POOL.o: From Latin diversus, ‘turned different ways’.

POOL.h: To offload a business, asset or investment by selling it or cutting ties.
POOL.ex: The university voted to divest its shares in tobacco companies.
POOL.o: From Latin devestire, ‘to undress’, from de- and vestire, ‘to clothe’.

POOL.h: Bossy and overbearing, always trying to control others.
POOL.ex: Her domineering older sister decided who sat where at every family dinner.
POOL.o: From dominate, from Latin dominari, ‘to rule, be lord over’.

POOL.h: Asleep or switched off for now, but able to spring back to life.
POOL.ex: The bulbs lie dormant under the soil all winter, then flower in spring.
POOL.o: From Old French dormant, ‘sleeping’, from Latin dormire, ‘to sleep’.

POOL.h: On or near the back, especially of an animal.
POOL.ex: The lizard had a row of dorsal spikes running down its spine.
POOL.o: From Latin dorsum, ‘back’.

POOL.h: A drop in business, the economy or how well something is going.
POOL.ex: The tourism downturn during the wet season hits Cairns tour operators hard.
POOL.o: From down and turn, describing a shift downward on a graph.

POOL.h: Being made of two sides, often ones that clash or contrast.
POOL.ex: The duality of the song is striking, with cheerful music behind heartbreaking lyrics.
POOL.o: From Latin dualis, ‘of two’, from duo, ‘two’.

POOL.h: Doubtful, either unsure yourself or seeming a bit dodgy.
POOL.ex: I was dubious when the online shop promised next-day delivery to Broome.
POOL.o: From Latin dubius, ‘wavering, uncertain’.

POOL.h: A pipe or channel that moves air, liquid or other stuff from place to place.
POOL.ex: The builder ran a new duct from the rangehood up through the roof.
POOL.o: From Latin ductus, ‘a leading, conducting’, from ducere, ‘to lead’.

POOL.h: To shrink little by little until there's not much left.
POOL.ex: Our pile of firewood dwindled as the cold snap dragged on.
POOL.o: From Old English dwinan, ‘to waste away, vanish’.

POOL.h: An imagined world where life is grim, harsh or tightly controlled.
POOL.ex: The board game drops players into a dystopia where robots ration the water.
POOL.o: From Greek dys-, ‘bad’, and topos, ‘place’, coined as the opposite of utopia.

POOL.h: Genuinely serious and heartfelt in what you say or do.
POOL.ex: The little boy wrote an earnest letter asking the council for a skate park.
POOL.o: From Old English eornoste, ‘seriousness, zeal’.

POOL.h: Bubbling over with energy, excitement and good cheer.
POOL.ex: The ebullient tour guide cracked jokes the whole way along the Blue Mountains track.
POOL.o: From Latin ebullire, ‘to boil up, bubble out’.

POOL.h: Quirky and a bit odd in how you behave or live.
POOL.ex: Our eccentric neighbour mows his lawn in a tuxedo every Sunday morning.
POOL.o: From Greek ekkentros, ‘out of the centre’, from ek- and kentron, ‘centre’.

POOL.h: A web of plants, animals and their surroundings, all depending on each other.
POOL.ex: A single rock pool is a tiny ecosystem of crabs, snails and seaweed.
POOL.o: From eco- (Greek oikos, ‘house’) and system.

POOL.h: Pouring out praise or thanks without holding back.
POOL.ex: My aunt was effusive about the scarf I knitted her, showing it to everyone at lunch.
POOL.o: From Latin effusus, ‘poured out’, from effundere.

POOL.h: Full of yourself and convinced you matter more than others.
POOL.ex: The egotistical contestant spent every episode talking about his own talent.
POOL.o: From ego, Latin for ‘I’, with -tistical added by analogy with egoistic.

POOL.h: Detailed and intricate, with lots of carefully planned parts.
POOL.ex: The kids built an elaborate sandcastle with moats, bridges and towers.
POOL.o: From Latin elaborare, ‘to work out thoroughly’.

POOL.h: Stretchy, and able to spring back to its original shape.
POOL.ex: The hair tie was so elastic it still held a ponytail after months of use.
POOL.o: From Greek elastikos, ‘propulsive’, from elaunein, ‘to drive’.

POOL.h: Over the moon, usually after something goes your way.
POOL.ex: He was elated to get the text saying he'd passed his driving test.
POOL.o: From Latin elatus, ‘raised, lifted up’, from efferre.

POOL.h: A salt or mineral that splits into charged particles in water, letting it carry electricity.
POOL.ex: The doctor said a bad stomach bug can throw your electrolytes out of balance.
POOL.o: From electro- and Greek lytos, ‘able to be loosed, dissolved’.

POOL.h: To explain something clearly so it finally makes sense.
POOL.ex: The pharmacist elucidated how to space the tablets out across the day.
POOL.o: From Latin elucidare, ‘to make light, clarify’, from e- and lucidus, ‘clear’.

POOL.h: Tricky to catch, track down, achieve or get your head around.
POOL.ex: A decent night's sleep has been elusive since the new puppy arrived.
POOL.o: From Latin eludere, ‘to escape from, evade’, from e- and ludere, ‘to play’.

POOL.h: A government ban that blocks trade or dealings with a particular country or group.
POOL.ex: During the embargo, the island couldn't import fuel or spare parts.
POOL.o: From Spanish embargar, ‘to seize, impede’.

POOL.h: To dress something up with decoration, or to add fake details to a story.
POOL.ex: The kids embellished their birthday cards with glitter and stickers.
POOL.o: From Old French embellir, ‘to make beautiful’, from bel, ‘beautiful’.

POOL.h: To release something like light, noise, heat or fumes.
POOL.ex: The smoke alarm emits a short chirp when its battery is running low.
POOL.o: From Latin emittere, ‘to send out’.

POOL.h: Being able to sense and share what someone else is feeling.
POOL.ex: The bus driver showed real empathy, waiting patiently while a flustered mum found her card.
POOL.o: From Greek empatheia: en- ‘in’ + pathos ‘feeling’. Coined in English in 1908.

POOL.h: Based on what you can observe or measure, not just on theory.
POOL.ex: I gathered empirical evidence that toast lands butter-side down by dropping it twenty times.
POOL.o: From Greek empeirikos, ‘experienced’, from empeiria, ‘experience’.

POOL.h: A determined try at achieving something worthwhile.
POOL.ex: Learning to surf at fifty was a bold endeavour, but she loved every wipeout.
POOL.o: From Old French en devoir, ‘to do one’s duty’.

POOL.h: Public backing or approval for a person, plan or product.
POOL.ex: The local bakery's pies got a glowing endorsement from a famous chef.
POOL.o: From endorse, from Latin indorsare, ‘to write on the back of’.

POOL.h: A mystery, whether a person or a thing, that nobody can quite work out.
POOL.ex: How the cat gets onto the roof is an enigma to the whole household.
POOL.o: From Greek ainigma, ‘riddle’, from ainissesthai, ‘to speak in riddles’.

POOL.h: A company, or a big, gutsy project that takes real effort.
POOL.ex: Running a food truck is a demanding enterprise with very long hours.
POOL.o: From Old French entreprise, ‘something undertaken’.

POOL.h: Acting as though you deserve special treatment or perks.
POOL.ex: The entitled passenger demanded an upgrade because he'd flown with the airline once before.
POOL.o: From title, from Latin titulus, via Old French entiteler.

POOL.h: Disorder, and the way things naturally drift from neat to messy over time.
POOL.ex: Within an hour of tidying, entropy had returned the kids' playroom to chaos.
POOL.o: Coined by the German physicist Rudolf Clausius in 1865, from Greek tropē, ‘transformation’.

POOL.h: To do with knowledge, and how we know what we think we know.
POOL.ex: The science teacher posed an epistemic puzzle: how can you prove the sun will rise tomorrow?
POOL.o: From Greek episteme, ‘knowledge’, from epistasthai, ‘to know’.

POOL.h: A distinct stretch of history, marked by big events or changes.
POOL.ex: The arrival of smartphones opened a new epoch in how we communicate.
POOL.o: From Greek epokhe, ‘a stopping point, fixed point in time’.

POOL.h: A steady balance between forces or influences pulling opposite ways.
POOL.ex: The fish tank took weeks to reach a healthy equilibrium after we added new plants.
POOL.o: From Latin aequilibrium, from aequus, ‘equal’, and libra, ‘balance, scales’.

POOL.h: What you actually own of something once the loans on it are paid off; also, fairness.
POOL.ex: After paying off half the ute loan, he finally had some equity in the vehicle.
POOL.o: From Latin aequitas, ‘fairness, equality’, from aequus, ‘equal’.

POOL.h: When water, wind or ice slowly wears land away, or anything gets gradually worn down.
POOL.ex: Walkers are asked to stay on the track to prevent erosion of the sand dunes.
POOL.o: From Latin erodere, ‘to gnaw away’.

POOL.h: All over the place, never steady or predictable.
POOL.ex: The wifi has been erratic all week, dropping out every few minutes.
POOL.o: From Latin errare, ‘to wander, stray’.

POOL.h: Seriously well read and knowledgeable across many subjects.
POOL.ex: The erudite quiz host knew every answer long before the contestants did.
POOL.o: From Latin eruditus, ‘instructed, polished’, from erudire, ‘to educate’.

POOL.h: Cash or paperwork parked with a neutral party until both sides meet the deal's terms.
POOL.ex: The online marketplace keeps your payment in escrow until the seller ships the item.
POOL.o: From Old French escroe, ‘a scroll or roll of parchment’.

POOL.h: Doing the right thing, or concerned with questions of right and wrong.
POOL.ex: He only buys from ethical fashion brands that pay their workers fairly.
POOL.o: From Greek ethikos, ‘relating to character’, from ethos, ‘character’.

POOL.h: To heat up and drift into the air as vapour, turning from liquid to gas.
POOL.ex: Sweat evaporated from his skin almost instantly in the dry desert air.
POOL.o: From Latin evaporare, ‘to disperse in vapour’.

POOL.h: To make a feeling or trait plain for others to see.
POOL.ex: His shaky voice evinced how nervous he was about the speech.
POOL.o: From Latin evincere, ‘to conquer, prove conclusively’.

POOL.h: To stir up a feeling or memory, or conjure a picture in your mind.
POOL.ex: The smell of eucalyptus always evokes camping trips with Dad.
POOL.o: From Latin evocare, ‘to call out, summon’, from e- and vocare, ‘to call’.

POOL.h: To show exactly what something is like by being a textbook example of it.
POOL.ex: The volunteer firefighters exemplify the country town's community spirit.
POOL.o: From Latin exemplum, ‘example, sample’.

POOL.h: Thrilling in a way that leaves you buzzing with energy.
POOL.ex: Riding the rollercoaster at Dreamworld for the first time was exhilarating.
POOL.o: From Latin exhilarare, ‘to make cheerful’, from ex- and hilaris, ‘cheerful’.

POOL.h: The total you pay out on something.
POOL.ex: Our weekly expenditure on takeaway coffee added up to a shocking amount.
POOL.o: From Latin expendere, ‘to weigh out, pay out’.

POOL.h: A thorough, easy-to-follow explanation of a topic or idea.
POOL.ex: The museum guide gave a fascinating exposition of how the old steam engine worked.
POOL.o: From Latin expositio, ‘a setting forth’, from exponere, ‘to put out, explain’.

POOL.h: So finely made and delicate it takes your breath away.
POOL.ex: The Japanese garden was lined with exquisite little bonsai trees.
POOL.o: From Latin exquisitus, ‘sought out, choice’, from exquirere.

POOL.h: To predict beyond what you know by assuming a current trend will keep going.
POOL.ex: If I extrapolate from how fast the puppy is growing, he'll be enormous by Christmas.
POOL.o: Coined in the late 1800s from extra-, ‘outside’, modelled on interpolate (estimating between known points).

POOL.h: A single side of something that has lots of different sides to it.
POOL.ex: Learning the rules is just one facet of becoming a good umpire.
POOL.o: From French facette, ‘little face’, a diminutive of face, originally describing the cut surfaces of a gemstone.

POOL.h: Joking about something serious in a way that doesn't suit the moment.
POOL.ex: When the boss asked about the missed deadline, his facetious reply made things worse.
POOL.o: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, ‘jest, witty remark’.

POOL.h: To smooth the way so something happens more easily.
POOL.ex: The new ramp facilitates access for prams and wheelchairs at the library.
POOL.o: From Latin facilis, ‘easy’, via French faciliter.

POOL.h: A smaller organised group inside a bigger one, often with its own agenda.
POOL.ex: A faction within the book club wanted to read nothing but crime novels.
POOL.o: From Latin factio, ‘a group acting together’, from facere, ‘to do’.

POOL.h: A popular belief that's wrong, often because the thinking behind it is flawed.
POOL.ex: It's a fallacy that you lose most of your body heat through your head.
POOL.o: From Latin fallacia, ‘deception’, from fallere, ‘to deceive’.

POOL.h: Not perfect, so you can slip up and get things wrong.
POOL.ex: Weather apps are fallible, so pack a raincoat anyway.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin fallibilis, from Latin fallere, ‘to deceive, fail’.

POOL.h: Extremely careful and particular about getting every detail right.
POOL.ex: The fastidious baker weighs every ingredient to the gram.
POOL.o: From Latin fastidiosus, ‘disdainful, squeamish’, from fastidium, ‘loathing, distaste’.

POOL.h: To get your head around something, often after thinking hard about it.
POOL.ex: I can't fathom how anyone finishes a family-size pizza on their own.
POOL.o: Originally a unit for measuring the depth of water (six feet), from Old English faedm, meaning ‘outstretched arms’. To fathom something was first to measure its depth.

POOL.h: Realistic and practical enough to actually be done.
POOL.ex: Cycling to work is feasible now that there's a bike lane along the river.
POOL.o: From Old French faisable, from faire, ‘to do’.

POOL.h: To put on a fake show of a feeling or condition.
POOL.ex: The kid feigned a tummy ache to get out of swimming lessons.
POOL.o: From Old French feindre, ‘to shape, fashion, pretend’, ultimately from Latin fingere, ‘to touch, handle, or devise’.

POOL.h: Well suited to the moment; just right.
POOL.ex: Playing a Paul Kelly song at the farewell was a felicitous touch.
POOL.o: From Latin felicitas, ‘happiness, good fortune’, from felix, ‘lucky, fruitful’.

POOL.h: Deeply and passionately felt, or showing that feeling.
POOL.ex: He's a fervent believer that pineapple belongs on pizza.
POOL.o: From Latin fervere, ‘to boil, glow’, originally describing heat.

POOL.h: Always changing your mind about what or who you like.
POOL.ex: Our fickle cat abandons her favourite bed as soon as we buy her a new one.
POOL.o: From Old English ficol, ‘deceitful, tricky’, related to ‘befool’.

POOL.h: Using words in a non-literal way, like a metaphor.
POOL.ex: When Dad said he'd kill for a cuppa, he was speaking in figurative terms.
POOL.o: From Latin figurativus, from figura, ‘shape, figure’.

POOL.h: Smooth, subtle skill in handling something tricky or delicate.
POOL.ex: The barista poured the latte art with real finesse.
POOL.o: From French finesse, ‘fineness, subtlety’, from fin, ‘fine’.

POOL.h: About how a government raises and spends its money.
POOL.ex: The state treasurer promised fiscal restraint after years of big spending.
POOL.o: From Latin fiscalis, from fiscus, ‘the state treasury’ (literally ‘basket’).

POOL.h: Blatant and shameless, especially in breaking the rules.
POOL.ex: Parking across three accessible bays was a flagrant disregard of the rules.
POOL.o: From Latin flagrare, ‘to blaze, burn’, originally describing a crime ‘still blazing’ or fresh.

POOL.h: Too casual or cheeky about something that deserves respect.
POOL.ex: She gave a flippant shrug when her mum asked about her failed maths test.
POOL.o: Probably imitative of the sound ‘flip’, suggesting a quick, careless movement of the tongue.

POOL.h: To grow strongly and do really well.
POOL.ex: The community choir has flourished since it moved into the town hall.
POOL.o: From Old French florir, ‘to blossom’, from Latin flos, ‘flower’.

POOL.h: To keep shifting higher and lower with no steady pattern.
POOL.ex: My energy levels fluctuate wildly when I'm working night shifts.
POOL.o: From Latin fluctuare, ‘to undulate, waver’, from fluctus, ‘a wave’.

POOL.h: A creeping sense that something bad is coming.
POOL.ex: He opened the email from his landlord with a feeling of foreboding.
POOL.o: From Old English forebodian, ‘to announce beforehand’, from fore- (‘before’) and bodian (‘to proclaim’).

POOL.h: Using science to investigate crimes.
POOL.ex: A forensic expert matched the fibres on the jacket to the car's seats.
POOL.o: From Latin forensis, ‘of the forum’, where legal proceedings were held in ancient Rome.

POOL.h: To lose something as a penalty for breaking a rule or failing to act.
POOL.ex: If you don't claim your raffle prize within 30 days, you forfeit it.
POOL.o: From Old French forfait, ‘crime, penalty’, from forfaire, ‘to transgress’.

POOL.h: Looking abandoned and miserable, as if nobody cares.
POOL.ex: A forlorn teddy bear sat on the train seat after everyone had got off.
POOL.o: From Old English forloren, past participle of forleosan, ‘to lose utterly’.

POOL.h: So big, strong or skilled that people respect or fear it.
POOL.ex: The chess champion was a formidable opponent, even at the age of twelve.
POOL.o: From Latin formidabilis, ‘causing fear’, from formido, ‘dread’.

POOL.h: Down to luck rather than planning, usually in a good way.
POOL.ex: Finding a parking spot right outside the concert was fortuitous.
POOL.o: From Latin fortuitus, ‘happening by chance’, from fors, ‘chance’.

POOL.h: A licence to run a business under a company's brand in a certain area.
POOL.ex: She owns the gym franchise in her town and pays a monthly fee to head office.
POOL.o: From Old French franchise, ‘freedom, exemption’, from franc, ‘free’.

POOL.h: Dishonest and meant to deceive, often for money.
POOL.ex: The fraudulent website sold concert tickets that never existed.
POOL.o: From Latin fraudulentus, from fraus, ‘deceit, fraud’.

POOL.h: Tense and stressful, or loaded with problems.
POOL.ex: Moving house with two dogs and a newborn made for a fraught weekend.
POOL.o: From Middle English fraught, the past participle of freighten, ‘to load a ship’, related to ‘freight’. It came to mean ‘loaded with’ trouble or danger.

POOL.h: Wildly fast and energetic, almost out of control.
POOL.ex: The frenetic final minutes of the netball game had everyone on their feet.
POOL.o: From Old French frenetique, ultimately from Greek phrenitis, ‘delirium’, from phren, ‘mind’.

POOL.h: The resistance you get when one surface rubs or slides against another.
POOL.ex: Rub your hands together and the friction will warm them up.
POOL.o: From Latin frictio, from fricare, ‘to rub’.

POOL.h: The outer edge of a group or subject, far from the mainstream.
POOL.ex: The band started out on the fringe of the music scene before hitting the charts.
POOL.o: From Old French frenge, ultimately from Latin fimbria, ‘a border, edge’.

POOL.h: Lacking any serious purpose, especially said of a legal claim.
POOL.ex: The tribunal dismissed his frivolous complaint about the neighbour's wind chimes.
POOL.o: From Latin frivolus, ‘silly, trifling’.

POOL.h: The furthest edge of what we know or can do in a field.
POOL.ex: Deep-sea exploration remains a frontier where new species turn up every year.
POOL.o: From Old French frontiere, ‘border area’, from front, ‘forehead, front’.

POOL.h: Good at making money and supplies go a long way, without waste.
POOL.ex: My frugal grandad reuses every bread bag and rubber band.
POOL.o: From Latin frugalis, from frux, ‘fruit’ or ‘value’.

POOL.h: Basic and essential, forming the core of something.
POOL.ex: Knowing how to swim is a fundamental skill for kids growing up near the coast.
POOL.o: From Late Latin fundamentalis, from fundamentum, ‘foundation’, from fundare, ‘to found’.

POOL.h: Swappable for any other identical unit of the same thing.
POOL.ex: Litres of petrol are fungible, so it doesn't matter which bowser you fill up from.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin fungibilis, from fungi, ‘to perform, discharge’, used of goods that could fulfil an obligation interchangeably.

POOL.h: Sneaky and secretive, trying not to be noticed.
POOL.ex: The dog took a furtive bite of sausage while nobody was watching the barbecue.
POOL.o: From Latin furtivus, ‘stolen, secret’, from furtum, ‘theft’.

POOL.h: Two or more things merged or mixed into something new.
POOL.ex: Their wedding music was a fusion of jazz and traditional Greek songs.
POOL.o: From Latin fusio, from fundere, ‘to pour, melt’.

POOL.h: Pointless, because it can't achieve anything.
POOL.ex: Trying to keep sand out of the car after a beach day is futile.
POOL.o: From Latin futilis, ‘leaky, worthless’, originally describing a vessel that easily spilled its contents.

POOL.h: To jolt people into taking action.
POOL.ex: The closure of the local pool galvanised parents into starting a petition.
POOL.o: Named after Luigi Galvani, whose 18th-century experiments showed electric currents could make a dead frog’s muscles twitch.

POOL.h: To take money straight from someone's pay or bank account, by legal order, to settle a debt.
POOL.ex: The revenue office warned it would garnish his wages if the toll debts stayed unpaid.
POOL.o: From Old French garnir, ‘to warn, equip’, a legal sense that developed alongside the more familiar culinary one.

POOL.h: Flashy and over the top in a tacky way.
POOL.ex: The hotel lobby was gaudy, with gold statues and neon pink carpet.
POOL.o: Possibly from Latin gaudium, ‘joy’, via the earlier sense of a showy trinket or ‘gaud’.

POOL.h: Not brand-name or specific; typical of a whole type.
POOL.ex: The supermarket's generic cornflakes taste just like the famous brand.
POOL.o: From Latin genus, ‘kind, class’.

POOL.h: Where something first came from and how it got started.
POOL.ex: The genesis of the festival was a single backyard jam session in 1998.
POOL.o: From Greek genesis, ‘origin, creation’, from gignesthai, ‘to be born’.

POOL.h: An organism's full set of genetic instructions.
POOL.ex: Researchers mapped the wheat genome to breed crops that survive drought.
POOL.o: A blend of ‘gene’ and ‘chromosome’, coined in the early 20th century.

POOL.h: A category of art, music or writing with its own style.
POOL.ex: Country is his go-to genre for long drives.
POOL.o: From French genre, ‘kind, sort’, from Latin genus.

POOL.h: To do with the heat stored deep inside the earth.
POOL.ex: Rotorua's bubbling mud pools are powered by geothermal heat.
POOL.o: From Greek geo, ‘earth’, and thermos, ‘heat’.

POOL.h: The time a baby develops before birth, or the time an idea takes to take shape.
POOL.ex: An elephant's gestation lasts nearly two years.
POOL.o: From Latin gestatio, from gestare, ‘to carry’.

POOL.h: Awful enough to make you shudder.
POOL.ex: The hostel bathroom was ghastly, with mould creeping up every wall.
POOL.o: From Old English gæstlic, ‘terrifying’, related to gast, ‘spirit, ghost’.

POOL.h: The main point or overall meaning of something.
POOL.ex: The podcast was two hours long, but my mate gave me the gist in two minutes.
POOL.o: From Anglo-French gist, ‘it lies’, from Old French gesir, ‘to lie’, originally a legal term for where a case ‘lay’ or rested.

POOL.h: To gather information bit by bit from different sources.
POOL.ex: I gleaned the plot of the show from overhearing my flatmates.
POOL.o: From Old French glener, originally meaning to gather leftover grain after a harvest.

POOL.h: Smooth and slick with words, but shallow or insincere.
POOL.ex: The salesman's glib patter made us trust the car even less.
POOL.o: Probably related to Low German glibberig, ‘slippery’.

POOL.h: Far more of something than anyone needs.
POOL.ex: A glut of zucchinis from the garden meant zucchini slice every night.
POOL.o: From Old French gloutir, ‘to swallow’, related to ‘glutton’.

POOL.h: Friendly feelings, or a business's good reputation valued as an asset.
POOL.ex: The cafe built up plenty of goodwill by giving free coffee to firefighters.
POOL.o: A compound of ‘good’ and ‘will’, originally meaning simple benevolence before it took on its accounting sense.

POOL.h: Kind, polite and warm, even to people you don't need to impress.
POOL.ex: The famous author was gracious to every fan in the long signing queue.
POOL.o: From Latin gratiosus, ‘agreeable, obliging’, from gratia, ‘grace, favour’.

POOL.h: Made of grains, or broken down into very fine detail.
POOL.ex: The fitness app gives granular stats, right down to the pace of each kilometre.
POOL.o: From Latin granum, ‘grain’.

POOL.h: To leave someone feeling pleased or rewarded.
POOL.ex: It gratified the old gardener to see kids picking strawberries from his patch.
POOL.o: From Latin gratificari, ‘to do a favour to’, from gratus, ‘pleasing’.

POOL.h: An extra amount paid on top of the bill for good service; a tip.
POOL.ex: The cruise added a daily gratuity for the cabin staff to our bill.
POOL.o: From Medieval Latin gratuitas, ‘freely given’, from gratus, ‘pleasing, grateful’.

POOL.h: Loving company and happiest around other people.
POOL.ex: Gregarious by nature, she made three new friends on the first day of her TAFE course.
POOL.o: From Latin gregarius, from grex, ‘flock, herd’.

POOL.h: A formal complaint about being treated unfairly.
POOL.ex: The cleaners filed a grievance after their shifts were cut without notice.
POOL.o: From Old French grever, ‘to burden, harm’, from Latin gravare, ‘to weigh down’.

POOL.h: Bleak and depressing, or stern and forbidding in manner.
POOL.ex: The waiting room was grim, with flickering lights and no windows.
POOL.o: From Old English grimm, ‘fierce, cruel’.

POOL.h: The early work that sets up something bigger.
POOL.ex: Weeks of practice sessions laid the groundwork for the choir's big performance.
POOL.o: A compound of ‘ground’ and ‘work’, from the literal sense of the base or foundation of a building.

POOL.h: Given reluctantly, without much goodwill.
POOL.ex: My brother gave a grudging nod when I beat him at Mario Kart.
POOL.o: From ‘grudge’, from Old French grouchier, ‘to grumble, murmur’.

POOL.h: So tough and draining it wears you right out.
POOL.ex: Harvest season means gruelling twelve-hour days on the farm.
POOL.o: From the verb gruel, ‘to exhaust’, related to the earlier phrase ‘to get one’s gruel’, meaning to be punished.

POOL.h: The legal duty to care for someone who can't manage their own affairs.
POOL.ex: After Grandpa's stroke, Mum applied for guardianship so she could make decisions for him.
POOL.o: From ‘guardian’, from Old French garder, ‘to guard, keep’.

POOL.h: Quick to fall for tricks and tall tales.
POOL.ex: My gullible cousin believed me when I said drop bears were real.
POOL.o: From ‘gull’, an old word for a person easily cheated, itself possibly from a dialect word for a young, unfledged bird.

POOL.h: Loads of zest and enjoyment in how you do something.
POOL.ex: The kids tucked into the pavlova with gusto.
POOL.o: From Italian gusto, ‘taste’, ultimately from Latin gustus.

POOL.h: Done without much effort or enthusiasm.
POOL.ex: The cat gave a halfhearted swipe at the toy mouse and went back to sleep.
POOL.o: A compound of ‘half’ and ‘heart’, suggesting only part of one’s heart is in the effort.

POOL.h: The formal passing of responsibility or information to someone else.
POOL.ex: The nurses do a bedside handover at 7am so nothing gets missed.
POOL.o: A compound of ‘hand’ and ‘over’, from the literal act of handing something across.

POOL.h: A strong craving or longing for something.
POOL.ex: Every winter I get a hankering for Mum's lamb roast.
POOL.o: Possibly related to ‘hanker’, from Dutch hunkeren, ‘to long for’.

POOL.h: Random and unplanned, with no real order.
POOL.ex: The bookshelf was stacked in a haphazard way, cookbooks mixed in with comics.
POOL.o: From ‘hap’, an old word for chance or luck, and ‘hazard’, from Old French hasard, ‘a game of dice’.

POOL.h: Unlucky, often in a way that isn't their fault.
POOL.ex: The hapless goalkeeper slipped on the wet grass just as the ball arrived.
POOL.o: From ‘hap’, an old word for luck or chance, plus ‘-less’.

POOL.h: Frazzled and rushed because there's too much to do.
POOL.ex: A harried teacher tried to count thirty kids onto the bus.
POOL.o: From ‘harry’, from Old English hergian, ‘to lay waste, plunder’.

POOL.h: Done too quickly, without enough thought.
POOL.ex: Her hasty packing meant she arrived in Hobart without a jumper.
POOL.o: From Old French haste, related to Old High German heisti, ‘violent’.

POOL.h: Snobbish and acting superior to others.
POOL.ex: The haughty shop assistant ignored us because we were in thongs and boardies.
POOL.o: From Old French haut, ‘high’, from Latin altus.

POOL.h: To try to lure someone away from their current job to work for you.
POOL.ex: A tech startup tried to headhunt the hospital's best software engineer.
POOL.o: A 20th-century business coinage borrowing the vivid image of a literal headhunter tracking a target.

POOL.h: Stubbornly set on doing things your own way.
POOL.ex: The headstrong pup ignored every command and dragged me into the surf.
POOL.o: A compound suggesting the ‘head’ leads too ‘strongly’, ignoring caution or advice.

POOL.h: Something that holds back progress, like wind blowing against you.
POOL.ex: A shortage of builders has been a headwind for the new housing estate.
POOL.o: From the literal meaning, wind blowing directly against the direction of travel of a plane or ship.

POOL.h: Warm and wholehearted, or filling and satisfying when it's food.
POOL.ex: Grandma gave me a hearty hug the moment I walked through the door.
POOL.o: From ‘heart’, reflecting the idea of feeling that comes ‘from the heart’.

POOL.h: Someone who sees pleasure as the most important thing in life.
POOL.ex: A true hedonist, he booked a week of spa days and long lunches in the Barossa.
POOL.o: From Greek hedone, ‘pleasure’.

POOL.h: The dominance of one group, nation or idea over the rest.
POOL.ex: The streaming giant's hegemony over home entertainment is starting to slip.
POOL.o: From Greek hegemonia, ‘leadership’, from hegemon, ‘leader’.

POOL.h: Made up of lots of different kinds of things.
POOL.ex: The op shop's stock is heterogeneous, from vinyl records to wedding dresses.
POOL.o: From Greek heteros, ‘other, different’, and genos, ‘kind, race’.

POOL.h: A system that ranks people or things from top to bottom.
POOL.ex: The chooks have a clear hierarchy, with the oldest hen always eating first.
POOL.o: From Greek hierarkhia, ‘rule of a high priest’, from hieros, ‘sacred’, and arkhein, ‘to rule’.

POOL.h: Understanding something only once it's already happened.
POOL.ex: With hindsight, buying white carpet with three kids wasn't smart.
POOL.o: From hind, ‘behind’, + sight.

POOL.h: Looking at the whole picture rather than just the separate parts.
POOL.ex: The school takes a holistic view of students, caring about wellbeing as much as grades.
POOL.o: From Greek holos, ‘whole’, with the suffix -istic.

POOL.h: The way a living thing or system keeps its internal conditions steady.
POOL.ex: Shivering is one way your body fights to keep homeostasis when you're cold.
POOL.o: From Greek homeo, ‘similar’, and stasis, ‘standing still’.

POOL.h: Uniform throughout, with every part the same kind.
POOL.ex: The new estate looks homogeneous, with rows of identical grey houses.
POOL.o: From Greek homos, ‘same’, and genos, ‘kind, race’.

POOL.h: Linking businesses at the same stage of an industry, such as rivals merging.
POOL.ex: Buying up two rival bakeries was a horizontal move that gave the chain control of the town's bread market.
POOL.o: From Greek horizon, ‘boundary, horizon’, via Latin horizontalis.

POOL.h: Dull and routine, with nothing exciting going on.
POOL.ex: Her humdrum commute changed when she started learning Italian on the train.
POOL.o: Probably a reduplication of ‘hum’, imitating a dull, droning sound.

POOL.h: What you get when two different species, or two different things, are combined.
POOL.ex: The pluot is a hybrid of a plum and an apricot.
POOL.o: From Latin hybrida, referring to the offspring of a tame sow and a wild boar.

POOL.h: Powered by liquid being pushed through pipes or cylinders.
POOL.ex: The mechanic used a hydraulic jack to lift the car off the ground.
POOL.o: From Greek hydor, ‘water’, and aulos, ‘pipe’.

POOL.h: The science of where water is, how it moves and how it behaves.
POOL.ex: Understanding the hydrology of the wetland helped rangers protect its birdlife.
POOL.o: From Greek hydor, ‘water’, and -logia, ‘study of’.

POOL.h: Deliberate exaggeration that isn't meant literally.
POOL.ex: Saying she'd waited a million years for the bus was pure hyperbole.
POOL.o: From Greek hyperbole, ‘excess’, from hyper, ‘beyond’, and ballein, ‘to throw’.

POOL.h: An idea put forward to explain something, which can then be tested.
POOL.ex: The kids tested their hypothesis that ants prefer honey to sugar.
POOL.o: From Greek hypothesis, ‘foundation, supposition’: hypo ‘under’ + thesis ‘placing’.

POOL.h: Just around the corner and likely to happen any moment.
POOL.ex: With the baby's arrival imminent, they packed the hospital bag.
POOL.o: From Latin imminere, ‘to overhang or threaten’.

POOL.h: Fair to all sides, without favouring anyone.
POOL.ex: Judges at the pumpkin show must stay impartial, even when their friends have entries.
POOL.o: From im-, ‘not’, and partial, ‘taking a part or side’.

POOL.h: A standstill where neither side can move forward.
POOL.ex: The flatmates reached an impasse over whose turn it was to clean the bathroom.
POOL.o: From French impasse, literally ‘no passage’.

POOL.h: So perfect you can't find a single fault.
POOL.ex: The choir's timing was impeccable from the first note to the last.
POOL.o: From Latin impeccabilis, ‘not liable to sin’, from peccare, ‘to sin’.

POOL.h: To hold something back or get in its way.
POOL.ex: Fallen trees impeded the road crews trying to reach the town.
POOL.o: From Latin impedire, ‘to entangle the feet’, from pes, ‘foot’.

POOL.h: Rushing into things without thinking them through.
POOL.ex: In an impetuous moment, he bought a puppy on the drive home.
POOL.o: From Latin impetus, ‘an attack or force’, suggesting sudden force of action.

POOL.h: Understood without being spelled out.
POOL.ex: There's an implicit rule in our house: whoever cooks doesn't wash up.
POOL.o: From Latin implicare, ‘to enfold or entangle’.

POOL.h: To get an idea across by hinting rather than spelling it out.
POOL.ex: By leaving the gym brochure on my desk, was he implying I should join?
POOL.o: From Latin implicare, ‘to involve or enfold’.

POOL.h: Unplanned and done on the spur of the moment.
POOL.ex: The buskers started an impromptu dance-off in Rundle Mall.
POOL.o: From Latin in promptu, ‘in readiness, at hand’.

POOL.h: Happening by mistake, without anyone meaning it to.
POOL.ex: An inadvertent reply-all sent her holiday photos to the whole office.
POOL.o: From Latin advertere, ‘to turn towards’, with the negative prefix in-.

POOL.h: To officially launch or open something, often with a ceremony.
POOL.ex: The school inaugurated its new library with a ribbon-cutting and a sausage sizzle.
POOL.o: From Latin inaugurare, ‘to install under good omens’, linked to Roman augury.

POOL.h: To lock someone up in prison or jail.
POOL.ex: Fremantle Prison once incarcerated convicts shipped out from Britain.
POOL.o: From Latin incarcerare, ‘to put in prison’, from carcer, ‘prison’.

POOL.h: Designed to start fires, or likely to stir up anger.
POOL.ex: Ancient armies hurled incendiary pots of burning oil over city walls.
POOL.o: From Latin incendium, ‘a fire’, from incendere, ‘to set alight’.

POOL.h: A reward or reason that nudges you to do something.
POOL.ex: Free pizza was the incentive that got everyone to the working bee.
POOL.o: From Latin incentivus, ‘setting the tune’, from incinere, ‘to sing’.

POOL.h: Sharp, clear and quick to get to the heart of something.
POOL.ex: The editor's incisive notes trimmed my rambling story down to its best parts.
POOL.o: From Latin incidere, ‘to cut into’.

POOL.h: Hiding who you really are.
POOL.ex: The restaurant critic dined incognito so the chef wouldn't know she was there.
POOL.o: From Italian incognito, ‘unknown’, from Latin incognitus.

POOL.h: Out of place and not matching its surroundings.
POOL.ex: A lone surfboard looked incongruous in the middle of the snowy car park.
POOL.o: From Latin incongruus, from congruere, ‘to agree or come together’.

POOL.h: Too set in bad habits to ever be changed.
POOL.ex: Our incorrigible kelpie still chases every ute that drives past.
POOL.o: From Latin incorrigibilis, from corrigere, ‘to correct’.

POOL.h: Currently in the role, or required as a duty.
POOL.ex: The incumbent mayor is running for a third term.
POOL.o: From Latin incumbere, ‘to lie or lean upon’.

POOL.h: Protection against loss or damage, or payment to cover it.
POOL.ex: The hire company's indemnity covered the cost when the kayak was damaged.
POOL.o: From Latin indemnis, ‘unhurt’, from damnum, ‘damage’.

POOL.h: To officially accuse someone of a crime so they face trial.
POOL.ex: Prosecutors indicted the fake charity's organisers for pocketing donations.
POOL.o: From Old French enditer, ultimately from Latin indicere, ‘to declare’.

POOL.h: Angry about something that feels unfair.
POOL.ex: The kids were indignant when the pool closed early on the hottest day of the year.
POOL.o: From Latin indignari, ‘to be displeased at’, from dignus, ‘worthy’.

POOL.h: So important you can't do without it.
POOL.ex: A good hat is indispensable for a day at the cricket.
POOL.o: From Latin dispensare, ‘to weigh out’, with the negative prefix in-.

POOL.h: Happy to laze about and dodge any hard work.
POOL.ex: After a week of indolent mornings, getting up for work felt brutal.
POOL.o: From Latin indolentia, ‘freedom from pain’, which shifted in meaning towards a lack of effort.

POOL.h: Clumsy and unskilled at doing something.
POOL.ex: I'm so inept at parallel parking that I'll walk an extra block instead.
POOL.o: From Latin ineptus, ‘unsuitable’, from aptus, ‘fit or apt’.

POOL.h: Motionless and lifeless, or in chemistry, unwilling to react with other substances.
POOL.ex: Argon is inert, so it's used inside light bulbs to stop the filament burning up.
POOL.o: From Latin iners, ‘unskilled, idle’, from in-, ‘without’, and ars, ‘skill’.

POOL.h: Bound to happen, with no way of avoiding it.
POOL.ex: A bit of squabbling is inevitable on a ten-hour family road trip.
POOL.o: From Latin inevitabilis: in- ‘not’ + evitare ‘to avoid’.

POOL.h: So reliable it simply can't get things wrong.
POOL.ex: Dad treats his old street directory as infallible, even though half the roads have changed.
POOL.o: From Latin fallere, ‘to deceive’, with the negative prefix in-.

POOL.h: Known far and wide, but for all the wrong reasons.
POOL.ex: The cafe is infamous for its forty-minute wait on Sunday mornings.
POOL.o: From Latin infamis, ‘of ill repute’, from fama, ‘reputation’.

POOL.h: A conclusion you work out from clues rather than being told directly.
POOL.ex: Crumbs on the couch led to the obvious inference that the kids had found the biscuits.
POOL.o: From Latin inferre, ‘to bring in’.

POOL.h: Clever and inventive in an original way.
POOL.ex: He came up with an ingenious way to water his plants with old bottles while on holiday.
POOL.o: From Latin ingenium, ‘natural talent’.

POOL.h: Innocent and trusting, with no hidden motives.
POOL.ex: The new recruit's ingenuous enthusiasm made the jaded staff smile.
POOL.o: From Latin ingenuus, ‘native, freeborn’, later ‘noble in character’.

POOL.h: Built into something as a natural part of it.
POOL.ex: Rock climbing comes with inherent dangers, no matter how good your gear is.
POOL.o: From Latin inhaerere, ‘to stick in’, from haerere, ‘to stick’.

POOL.h: Deep unfairness or outright wickedness.
POOL.ex: The documentary exposed the iniquity of paying farm workers a few dollars an hour.
POOL.o: From Latin iniquitas, from iniquus, ‘unequal, unjust’.

POOL.h: Present from birth, not picked up along the way.
POOL.ex: Baby turtles have an innate urge to head for the ocean after hatching.
POOL.o: From Latin innatus, ‘born in’, from nasci, ‘to be born’.

POOL.h: Harmless and unlikely to upset or hurt anyone.
POOL.ex: The innocuous-looking chilli turned out to be fiercely hot.
POOL.o: From Latin innocuus, ‘harmless’, from nocere, ‘to harm’.

POOL.h: To come up with fresh ways of doing things, or new stuff nobody has tried before.
POOL.ex: The local bakery innovated by selling day-old bread from a vending machine at the train station.
POOL.o: From Latin innovare, ‘to renew’, from novus, ‘new’.

POOL.h: Doing damage slowly and quietly, so you barely notice until it's serious.
POOL.ex: Mould is insidious; it spreads behind the wardrobe for months before anyone smells it.
POOL.o: From Latin insidiae, ‘an ambush’, from insidere, ‘to sit in wait’.

POOL.h: So short of money that you can't cover what you owe.
POOL.ex: The builder went insolvent halfway through, leaving the family with a house that had no roof.
POOL.o: From Latin solvere, ‘to loosen or pay’, with the negative prefix in-.

POOL.h: Ongoing trouble falling asleep or staying asleep.
POOL.ex: His insomnia had him watching cricket replays at three in the morning.
POOL.o: From Latin insomnis, ‘sleepless’, from somnus, ‘sleep’.

POOL.h: To get something started, often trouble, by pushing for it.
POOL.ex: My little brother instigated the water fight at the barbecue, then pretended he was innocent.
POOL.o: From Latin instigare, ‘to urge on’.

POOL.h: Openly defying the people you're meant to take orders from.
POOL.ex: The insubordinate apprentice told the head chef he'd plate the dish however he liked.
POOL.o: From Latin subordinare, ‘to place under’, with the negative prefix in-.
