Police matter that isn’t urgent, like a past break-in: call 131 444.
Storm or flood damage to your home: call the SES on 132 500.
Health question and not sure what to do: call healthdirect on 1800 022 222.
POOL.n: Using the right line keeps 000 free for people whose lives are at risk.

steps: Store bottled water for at least three days and some non-perishable food.
Add a torch, a battery radio, spare batteries and a power bank.
Include a first aid kit, any medicines you need and copies of important documents.
Check it once a year and replace anything expired.
POOL.n: Power, water and phone networks can fail for days after storms or fires, and a ready kit means you don’t have to shop in a crisis.

steps: Don’t switch lights or appliances on or off, and don’t light anything.
Turn off the gas at the meter if it’s safe to do so.
Open doors and windows, then get everyone outside.
Once outside, call your gas distributor’s fault line, or 000 if it’s serious.
POOL.n: Gas is odourless, so suppliers add a strong smell to it, and a single spark from a switch can ignite a leak.

POOL.t: Fall into cold water? Float first
steps: Fight the urge to thrash or swim hard.
Lean back, spread your arms and legs, and float.
Keep your airway clear while your breathing settles, which takes about a minute or so.
Once calm, call for help or swim to safety.
POOL.n: The first gasping shock of cold water passes fairly quickly, and panicking during it is when people breathe in water.

POOL.t: Save a phone that got wet
steps: Unplug any cables and don’t try to charge it.
Tap it gently with the charging port facing down to drain water.
Leave it somewhere dry with good airflow.
Skip the bag of rice and the hair dryer.
POOL.n: Apple advises against rice because small particles can get inside, and heat can damage the phone further.

steps: Put the router somewhere central and high, not in a cupboard or on the floor.
Keep it away from thick walls, mirrors and the microwave.
Restart it now and then, and install firmware updates.
In a larger home, add a mesh system rather than a basic extender.
POOL.n: Wi-Fi signals weaken through walls and water, so the router’s position often matters more than its speed.

POOL.t: Name files so they sort themselves
steps: Start each name with the date as YYYY-MM-DD.
Add a few clear words about what it is.
Use hyphens instead of spaces.
Add a version number like v01 instead of calling it “final”.
POOL.n: The year-month-day order follows the ISO 8601 standard, so files automatically sort by date.

steps: Open a separate savings account.
Set up an automatic transfer for the day your pay arrives.
Start with an amount you won’t miss, even if it’s small.
Raise it each time your pay goes up.
POOL.n: Saving before you can spend takes willpower out of the process, which is why automatic saving works so well.

POOL.t: Track your spending for a month
steps: Record every purchase for 30 days, including small ones.
Group them into categories like groceries, transport and eating out.
Compare the totals with what you expected.
Pick one category to cut back next month.
POOL.n: Small regular purchases are easy to underestimate until you see them added up.

POOL.t: Compare loans by the comparison rate
steps: Look at the comparison rate, not just the advertised interest rate.
Compare loans with the same amount and term.
Ask about costs it leaves out, like early repayment or break fees.
Read the key fact sheet before you sign.
POOL.n: In Australia, lenders must show a comparison rate that combines interest with most fees, making loans easier to compare.

steps: When the renewal notice arrives, compare the new premium with last year’s.
Get at least two quotes for the same level of cover.
Check the excess, limits and exclusions, not just the price.
Call your insurer, mention the better quote and ask them to match it.
POOL.n: Australian regulators have found long-standing customers often pay more than new ones for the same cover.

steps: Before negotiating, write down what you’ll do if there’s no deal.
Use that to set the point where you’ll walk away.
Work to improve your alternative, like getting another offer.
Think about what the other side will do without a deal, too.
POOL.n: This is the BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) from the 1981 book Getting to Yes by Roger Fisher and William Ury.

steps: Research the fair range for what you’re negotiating.
Open with an ambitious offer you can justify.
Give a clear reason for your number.
If they go first with an extreme number, don’t haggle from it. Reset with your own.
POOL.n: The first number tends to anchor the whole discussion, an effect described by psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman.

steps: List things that cost you little but matter to the other side.
Never give a concession without asking for something back.
Frame it as, “If you can do this, then I can do that.”
Make each concession smaller than the last.
POOL.n: Trading keeps the deal balanced, and shrinking concessions signal you’re nearing your limit.

steps: Start with “what”, “how” or “tell me about”.
Avoid questions that can be answered with yes or no.
Go easy on “why”, which can sound like an accusation.
Follow up on their answer before changing the subject.
POOL.n: Open questions invite people to explain in their own words, so you learn more and they feel listened to.

POOL.t: Leave a voicemail that gets a call back
steps: Say your name and number at the start.
Give the reason for your call in one sentence.
Say what you need and by when.
Repeat your number slowly at the end.
POOL.n: People often play voicemails while not near a pen, so repeating the number saves them replaying the whole thing.

steps: Say both names clearly.
Add one short detail about each person.
Mention something they have in common or why they should talk.
Stay for a moment until the conversation gets going.
POOL.n: A shared starting point takes the awkward first step out of the conversation for both people.

steps: Admit plainly that you don’t know.
Share what you do know that’s relevant.
Say how and by when you’ll find out.
Follow up with the answer when you said you would.
POOL.n: Guessing and being wrong costs more trust than admitting a gap and then closing it.

steps: List what you need to get done.
Estimate how long each task will take.
Give each one a block in your calendar, hardest work in your best hours.
Leave buffer time between blocks for overruns and messages.
POOL.n: Work tends to expand to fill the time available, so a fixed block gives each task a clear finish line.

steps: Look at each vague item on your list, like “car”.
Ask, “What’s the very next physical step?”
Rewrite it starting with a verb, like “Call mechanic to book service”.
Break large projects into their first small action.
POOL.n: This comes from David Allen’s Getting Things Done: a clear next step is easier to start than a fuzzy goal.

steps: Check email and messages one last time for anything urgent.
Write down every unfinished task so nothing lives only in your head.
Glance at tomorrow and note your first task.
Say a set phrase or close the laptop to mark the end.
POOL.n: Cal Newport describes this ritual in Deep Work as a way to stop work thoughts following you into the evening.

steps: Park on level ground, turn the engine off and wait a few minutes.
Pull out the dipstick, wipe it clean and push it all the way back in.
Pull it out again and check the oil sits between the two marks.
If it’s low, top up slowly with the oil grade in your manual. Don’t overfill.
POOL.n: Low oil lets engine parts wear against each other, so a monthly check can prevent expensive damage.

steps: Find the small raised bars inside the tyre’s main grooves.
If the tread is level with those bars, the tyre is worn out.
Check across the whole width, as tyres can wear unevenly.
Replace tyres before they reach the legal minimum of 1.5 mm.
POOL.n: Worn tread can’t clear water from under the tyre, so grip in the wet drops sharply.

steps: Red means stop safely as soon as you can, such as for oil pressure or engine temperature.
Amber or yellow means get it checked soon.
Green or blue is information, like headlights or cruise control being on.
A flashing engine light is serious: slow down and get it seen quickly.
POOL.n: Most cars use this traffic-light colour code, but your owner’s manual explains each symbol.

steps: Stop somewhere safe, turn on your hazard lights and check for injuries.
Call 000 if anyone is hurt or the road is blocked or dangerous.
Swap names, addresses, registration numbers and insurer details with the other driver.
Take photos of the scene and damage, then contact your insurer.
POOL.n: Australian law requires drivers to stop and exchange details after a crash, and each state has its own rules about reporting to police.

steps: Indicate and pull over as far to the left as you safely can.
Turn on your hazard lights.
If it’s safe to get out, leave by the side away from traffic and wait well back, behind a barrier if there is one.
If it isn’t safe, stay in with seatbelts on, then call your roadside assistance provider.
POOL.n: Passing traffic is the real danger at a breakdown, so keeping well away from it matters more than the car.

steps: Sit where there’s least movement: the front of a car, over the wing on a plane, the middle of a boat.
Look at the horizon, not a book or screen.
Get fresh air where you can.
Recline and close your eyes if you start to feel queasy.
POOL.n: Motion sickness comes from a mismatch between what your eyes see and what your inner ear feels.

steps: Keep it to 10 to 20 minutes and set an alarm.
Nap before mid-afternoon so it doesn’t affect your night’s sleep.
Find somewhere dark and quiet, or use an eye mask.
Get up straight away when the alarm goes.
POOL.n: Longer naps can drop you into deep sleep, and waking from it leaves you groggy rather than refreshed.

POOL.h: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. How much is the ball?
POOL.a: 5 cents. If the ball were 10 cents, the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20. Most people blurt out 10 cents first.

POOL.h: A patch of lily pads doubles in size every day. It covers the whole lake on day 48. On which day did it cover half?
POOL.a: Day 47. It doubles each day, so it was half the size the day before.

POOL.h: Five machines working together turn out five widgets in five minutes. Scale up to 100 machines making 100 widgets. How many minutes does it take?
POOL.a: Still 5 minutes. Every machine needs 5 minutes to build a single widget, so 100 machines working side by side finish 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.

POOL.h: Mary’s father has five daughters: Nana, Nene, Nini, Nono. What is the fifth daughter’s name?
POOL.a: Mary. The question tells you in the first two words.

POOL.h: You’re in a race and you overtake the person in second place. What place are you in now?
POOL.a: Second. You took their place, you didn’t pass first.

POOL.h: There are 17 sheep in a paddock. Every one of them except 9 escapes through a hole in the fence. How many sheep are still in the paddock?
POOL.a: 9. 'Every one except 9' escaped, so the 9 left out of that group are the ones still there. The 17 is just a distraction.

POOL.h: Some months have 31 days, some have 30. How many have 28?
POOL.a: All 12. Every month has at least 28 days.

POOL.h: Four cards show A, K, 4 and 7. Each has a letter on one side and a number on the other. Rule: “If a card has a vowel on one side, it has an even number on the other.” Which cards must you turn over to test it?
POOL.a: A and 7. The A must hide an even number, and the 7 must not hide a vowel. Turning the 4 tells you nothing. This is the Wason selection task, which most people get wrong.

POOL.h: Try to memorise this in five seconds: FBICIAUSANASA
POOL.a: Split it into chunks: FBI · CIA · USA · NASA. Thirteen letters become four familiar units, well within working memory.

POOL.h: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 3:15?
POOL.a: 7.5 degrees. The hour hand has moved a quarter of the way from 3 to 4, which is 30° ÷ 4.

POOL.h: Find the next number in this pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, ?
POOL.a: 13, because 5 + 8 = 13. Every term is made by adding the previous two, a pattern known as the Fibonacci sequence that shows up in pinecones and sunflower seed spirals.

POOL.h: Rearrange the letters of LISTEN to make a word that means the opposite of noise.
POOL.a: SILENT.

POOL.h: You have two ropes. Each takes exactly 60 minutes to burn, but unevenly. How do you measure 45 minutes?
POOL.a: Light rope A at both ends and rope B at one end. A burns out in 30 minutes. Then light B’s other end. It finishes 15 minutes later: 45 in total.

POOL.h: Two Australian coins add up to 30 cents. One of them is not a 10-cent coin. What are the two coins?
POOL.a: A 20-cent coin and a 10-cent coin. The 20-cent coin is the one that is not a 10-cent coin. The wording tricks you into thinking neither is.

POOL.h: A snail sits at the bottom of a 10-metre well. Each day it climbs 3 metres, and each night it slips back 2 metres. On which day does it reach the top?
POOL.a: Day 8. It gains 1 metre net per full day, so after 7 days and nights it is at 7 metres. On day 8 it climbs 3 metres to reach 10 and is out before it can slip back.

POOL.h: A drawer holds 10 black socks and 10 white socks, all mixed up. In the dark, how many socks must you take out to be certain of a matching pair?
POOL.a: Three. With only two colours, the first two could be different, but the third must match one of them.

POOL.h: Sally has three brothers. Each of her brothers has two sisters. How many sisters does Sally have?
POOL.a: One. The brothers’ two sisters are Sally and one other girl.

POOL.h: A brick weighs 1 kilogram plus half a brick. How much does the whole brick weigh?
POOL.a: 2 kilograms. If the brick is 1 kg plus half itself, then the other half must be 1 kg, so the whole is 2 kg.

POOL.h: A wooden cube is painted red on the outside, then cut into 27 equal small cubes. How many of the small cubes have no paint on them at all?
POOL.a: Just 1, the one in the very centre. The 8 corners have three painted faces, the 12 edge pieces have two, and the 6 face centres have one: 8 + 12 + 6 + 1 = 27.

POOL.h: You take a spoonful of wine from a glass of wine and stir it into a glass of water. Then you take a spoonful of the mixture back into the wine. Is there more wine in the water, or more water in the wine?
POOL.a: They’re exactly equal. Both glasses end up with the same volume they started with, so whatever wine is missing from the wine glass has been replaced by the same amount of water.

POOL.h: Ten people meet, and every person shakes hands once with every other person. How many handshakes happen?
POOL.a: 45. Each person shakes 9 hands, giving 10 × 9 = 90, but that counts every handshake twice, so halve it.

POOL.h: How much soil is in a hole that is 1 metre long, 1 metre wide and 2 metres deep?
POOL.a: None. It is a hole, so the soil has been removed. The numbers invite you to calculate when you should just think.

POOL.h: A straight fence is 30 metres long, with a post every 3 metres, including one at each end. How many posts are there?
POOL.a: 11. There are 10 gaps of 3 metres, and you need one more post than gaps. This “off by one” error trips up builders and programmers alike.

POOL.h: It takes 10 minutes to saw a log into 2 pieces. At the same rate, how long does it take to saw it into 4 pieces?
POOL.a: 30 minutes. Four pieces need only three cuts, not four, and each cut takes 10 minutes.

POOL.h: How many digits do you need to print the page numbers 1 to 100?
POOL.a: 192. Pages 1 to 9 use 9 digits, pages 10 to 99 use 90 × 2 = 180, and page 100 uses 3.

POOL.h: You drive 60 km to a town at 60 km/h, then drive the same 60 km home at 30 km/h. What was your average speed for the whole trip?
POOL.a: 40 km/h, not 45. You covered 120 km in 3 hours (1 hour there, 2 hours back). The slow leg takes longer, so it counts for more.

POOL.h: A $100 jacket’s price rises by 10%. Later, the new price is cut by 10%. What does the jacket cost now?
POOL.a: $99. The rise takes it to $110, and 10% of $110 is $11, bringing it to $99. The same percentage up and down does not cancel out.

POOL.h: A father is 30 years older than his son. In 5 years, he will be exactly three times his son’s age. How old are they now?
POOL.a: The son is 10 and the father is 40. In 5 years they will be 15 and 45, and 45 is three times 15.

POOL.h: You are driving a bus. At the first stop, 4 people get on. At the second, 2 get off and 5 get on. At the third, 3 get off. What colour are the bus driver’s eyes?
POOL.a: The same colour as yours. You are the driver. The numbers are there to distract you from the first sentence.

POOL.h: How many animals of each kind did Moses take on the ark?
POOL.a: None. In the story it was Noah, not Moses. Most people miss this, a quirk psychologists call the “Moses illusion”: we skim past words that fit the general meaning.

POOL.h: A farmyard has only chickens and cows. Together they have 10 heads and 28 legs. How many cows are there?
POOL.a: 4 cows (and 6 chickens). If all 10 were chickens there would be 20 legs. Each cow adds 2 extra legs, and 8 extra legs means 4 cows.

POOL.h: You have nine identical-looking coins. One is slightly heavier. Using a balance scale, what is the fewest number of weighings that guarantees you find it?
POOL.a: Two. Split the coins into three groups of three and weigh two groups: the heavier side, or the group left off if they balance, holds the coin. Then weigh two coins from that group the same way.

POOL.h: Two doors: one leads out, one does not. Each has a guard. One guard always lies and one always tells the truth, but you don’t know which. You may ask one guard one question. What do you ask?
POOL.a: Ask: “Which door would the other guard say leads out?” Then take the opposite door. Either way the answer passes through exactly one lie, so it always points to the wrong door.

POOL.h: A farmer must cross a river with a wolf, a goat and a cabbage. His boat carries him and one item. Left alone, the wolf eats the goat and the goat eats the cabbage. What must he take across first?
POOL.a: The goat. Taking the wolf leaves the goat with the cabbage, and taking the cabbage leaves the wolf with the goat. The goat is the only safe first trip.

POOL.h: Three switches outside a closed room control one old-style incandescent bulb inside. You can flip switches as you like, but may enter the room only once. How do you find the right switch?
POOL.a: Turn on switch 1 for a few minutes, then turn it off and turn on switch 2. Walk in: if the bulb is lit, it is switch 2. If it is off but warm, switch 1. If off and cold, switch 3.

POOL.h: You have a 5-litre jug and a 3-litre jug, and a tap. How do you measure exactly 4 litres?
POOL.a: Fill the 5 L jug and pour into the 3 L jug, leaving 2 L. Empty the 3 L jug and pour the 2 L into it. Fill the 5 L jug again and top up the 3 L jug, which takes 1 L. Exactly 4 L remain.

POOL.h: You have a 7-minute hourglass and a 4-minute hourglass. How do you time exactly 9 minutes?
POOL.a: Start both. When the 4-minute one runs out, flip it. When the 7-minute one runs out, flip it. When the 4-minute one runs out again (at 8 minutes), the 7-minute glass has 1 minute of sand at the bottom. Flip it, and it runs out at exactly 9 minutes.

POOL.h: The day before yesterday I was 25. Next year I will turn 28. How is that possible?
POOL.a: Today is 1 January and your birthday is 31 December. Two days ago (30 Dec) you were 25, yesterday you turned 26, this year you turn 27, and next year 28.

POOL.h: A man pushes his car up to a hotel and immediately knows he is bankrupt. What is going on?
POOL.a: He is playing Monopoly. His car is his playing piece, and he has landed on a hotel he cannot afford.

POOL.h: Two fathers and two sons go fishing. They catch three fish and each takes home exactly one. How?
POOL.a: There are only three people: a grandfather, his son and his grandson. The middle man is both a father and a son.

POOL.h: Mia has just turned 20, yet she has had only five birthdays on her actual date of birth. How?
POOL.a: She was born on 29 February. That date only comes around in leap years, roughly once every four years.

POOL.h: When does 11 plus 2 equal 1?
POOL.a: On a clock. Two hours after 11 o’clock is 1 o’clock.

POOL.h: Starting at noon and stopping just before midnight, how many times do a clock’s hour and minute hands overlap?
POOL.a: 11 times, not 12. The hands overlap about every 1 hour 5.5 minutes, so there is no overlap between 11 and 1 other than at 12 itself.

POOL.h: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. A says: “We are both knaves.” What are A and B?
POOL.a: A is a knave and B is a knight. A knight could never say that, so A is a knave. Then the statement is false, so they are not both knaves: B must be a knight.

POOL.h: Three boxes are labelled “Apples”, “Oranges” and “Mixed”. Every label is wrong. You may take out one fruit from one box without looking inside. Which box do you choose to fix all the labels?
POOL.a: The box labelled “Mixed”. It must hold only one kind. If you draw an apple, it is the apple box. The box labelled “Oranges” can’t be oranges or apples, so it is mixed, and the last box is oranges.

POOL.h: In a race, Ava beat Ben. Cal finished behind Dee. Ben beat Dee. Who came last?
POOL.a: Cal. Putting the clues in order gives Ava, Ben, Dee, Cal.

POOL.h: In a family, each daughter has as many brothers as sisters. Each son has twice as many sisters as brothers. How many sons and daughters are there?
POOL.a: Four daughters and three sons. Each girl has 3 sisters and 3 brothers. Each boy has 2 brothers and 4 sisters, which is twice as many.

POOL.h: A clock takes 6 seconds to strike 6 o’clock, from the first chime to the last. How long does it take to strike 12 o’clock?
POOL.a: 13.2 seconds, not 12. Six chimes have only 5 gaps, so each gap is 1.2 seconds. Twelve chimes have 11 gaps: 11 × 1.2 = 13.2.

POOL.h: Two trains start 100 km apart and head towards each other, each at 50 km/h. A fly zips back and forth between them at 75 km/h until they meet. How far does the fly travel?
POOL.a: 75 km. The trains close the gap at 100 km/h, so they meet in 1 hour. The fly flies for 1 hour at 75 km/h. No need to add up the zigzags.

POOL.h: Four people must cross a narrow bridge at night with one torch. At most two can cross at once, and anyone crossing needs the torch. They take 1, 2, 5 and 10 minutes, and a pair moves at the slower pace. What is the shortest total time?
POOL.a: 17 minutes. 1 and 2 cross (2), 1 returns (1), 5 and 10 cross together (10), 2 returns (2), 1 and 2 cross (2). The trick is sending the two slowest together.

POOL.h: Three friends pay $30 for a room, $10 each. The manager realises it costs $25 and sends $5 back with a porter, who keeps $2 and returns $1 to each friend. Each friend paid $9, so $27, plus the porter’s $2 makes $29. Where is the missing dollar?
POOL.a: There isn’t one. The $27 the friends paid already includes the porter’s $2 ($25 room + $2 porter). Adding the $2 again is a meaningless sum. The correct check is $27 + $3 returned = $30.

POOL.h: A man points at a portrait and says: “Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man’s father is my father’s son.” Who is in the portrait?
POOL.a: His son. With no brothers, “my father’s son” is the speaker himself. So the portrait shows a man whose father is the speaker.

POOL.h: A cowboy rides into town on Friday, stays for three days, then leaves on Friday. How?
POOL.a: His horse is named Friday.

POOL.h: Linda is 31, outspoken and very bright. She studied philosophy and cares deeply about social justice. Which is more likely: (A) Linda is a bank teller, or (B) Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement?
POOL.a: A. Every feminist bank teller is also a bank teller, so B can never be more likely than A. Most people pick B because it fits the story, a trap called the conjunction fallacy.

POOL.h: You roll two ordinary dice and add them up. Which total is most likely?
POOL.a: 7. Six of the 36 possible combinations make 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4 and the reverse), more than any other total. Totals of 2 and 12 each have only one way to happen.

POOL.h: A disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test always detects it, but also wrongly flags 1% of healthy people. You test positive. Roughly what is the chance you have the disease?
POOL.a: About 9%. In 1,000 people, 1 has the disease and about 10 healthy people also test positive. So only about 1 of every 11 positives is real. Rare conditions make false alarms common.

POOL.h: Jar A holds 10 marbles, 1 of them red. Jar B holds 100 marbles, 8 of them red. You win if you draw a red marble. Which jar should you pick?
POOL.a: Jar A: a 10% chance versus 8%. Many people feel drawn to Jar B because 8 red marbles seems like more, a bias called denominator neglect.

POOL.h: In the carol, “my true love” gives 1 gift on day one, 2 + 1 on day two, 3 + 2 + 1 on day three, and so on. How many gifts are given over all twelve days?
POOL.a: 364, one for almost every day of the year. Each day’s total grows (1, 3, 6, 10…), and adding all twelve of those day totals gives 364.

POOL.h: A rope is wrapped snugly around the Earth’s equator. You add just 1 metre to its length and lift it evenly all the way around. Roughly how high above the ground is it now?
POOL.a: About 16 cm, enough to slide a cat under. Circumference is 2π times the radius, so adding 1 metre raises the radius by 1 ÷ 2π, whatever the size of the circle.

POOL.h: On days when ice cream sales go up, drownings go up too. Does ice cream cause drowning?
POOL.a: No. Hot weather drives both: people buy more ice cream and swim more. When two things rise together, look for a hidden third factor before assuming one causes the other.

POOL.h: Would you rather have $1 million today, or 1 cent on day 1 that doubles every day, keeping whatever it has grown to on day 30?
POOL.a: Take the cent. On day 30 it is worth 2 to the power of 29 cents, about $5.37 million. Doubling looks tiny at first and enormous at the end.

POOL.h: All roses are flowers. Some flowers fade quickly. Does it follow that some roses fade quickly?
POOL.a: No. The flowers that fade quickly might all be other kinds of flowers. The conclusion sounds sensible, but the logic does not guarantee it.

POOL.h: What is 43 × 11, worked out in your head?
POOL.a: 473. For a two-digit number, add its digits (4 + 3 = 7) and put the result in the middle: 4, 7, 3. If the sum is 10 or more, carry the 1: 78 × 11 = 858.

POOL.h: What is 65 × 65?
POOL.a: 4,225. For a number ending in 5, multiply the first digit by the next number up (6 × 7 = 42), then write 25 on the end.
100. Adding the first few odd numbers always gives a square: 1, 4, 9, 16 and so on. There are ten odd numbers here, so the total is 10 × 10.

POOL.h: What is 468 × 5?
POOL.a: 2,340. Multiplying by 5 is the same as halving and multiplying by 10: half of 468 is 234, then add a zero.

POOL.h: In a year that is not a leap year, 1 January falls on a Monday. What day of the week is 31 December?
POOL.a: Monday. A normal year has 365 days, which is 52 weeks plus one day, so the year ends on the same weekday it began. That extra day is also why your birthday shifts one weekday later each year.

POOL.h: What is the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 100?
POOL.a: 5,050. Pair them from the ends: 1 + 100, 2 + 99, 3 + 98 and so on. That is 50 pairs, each adding up to 101, and 50 × 101 = 5,050.

POOL.h: Is 123,456,789 divisible by 3?
POOL.a: Yes. A number is divisible by 3 if its digits add up to a multiple of 3. These digits sum to 45, so it is divisible by 3 (and by 9 as well).

POOL.h: What is 97 × 96?
POOL.a: 9,312. Both are just below 100: 3 short and 4 short. Take either number minus the other’s shortfall (97 − 4 = 93), then multiply the shortfalls (3 × 4 = 12). Join them: 9,312.

POOL.h: How many squares of any size are there on a standard 8 × 8 chessboard?
POOL.a: 204. There are 64 small squares, 49 of size 2 × 2, 36 of size 3 × 3, and so on down to one 8 × 8. Adding 64 + 49 + 36 + 25 + 16 + 9 + 4 + 1 gives 204.
42. The gaps grow by 2 each time (4, 6, 8, 10, 12). Each term is also n × (n + 1): 6 × 7 = 42.

POOL.h: O, T, T, F, F, S, S, E, …
POOL.a: N. They are the first letters of One, Two, Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, so next is Nine.

POOL.h: J, F, M, A, M, J, J, …
POOL.a: A. They are the first letters of the months, January to July, so next is August.
65. Each number is double the previous one minus 1 (33 × 2 − 1 = 65). The gaps also double: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.
312211. Each line describes the one before out loud: 111221 is “three 1s, two 2s, one 1”, written 31 22 11.

POOL.h: A, C, F, J, O, …
POOL.a: U. The gaps between letters grow by one each time: skip 1, 2, 3, 4, then 5. In number terms: 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, then 21, which is U.

POOL.h: What occurs once in a minute, twice in a moment, but never in a thousand years?
POOL.a: The letter M.

POOL.h: Which word is spelled incorrectly in every dictionary?
POOL.a: “Incorrectly”. It is spelled i-n-c-o-r-r-e-c-t-l-y in every dictionary.

POOL.h: Which common English word has three pairs of double letters in a row?
POOL.a: Bookkeeper (or bookkeeping): b-OO-KK-EE-per.

POOL.h: Count the letters in each word of this sentence: “How I wish I could calculate pi.” What number do you get?
POOL.a: 3.141592, the first seven digits of pi. Sentences like this, where word lengths encode digits, are called “piems” and are an old memory trick.

POOL.h: Without a calendar, how can you tell which months have 31 days using only your fists?
POOL.a: Put your fists together and count months across the knuckles and the dips between them. Knuckles are 31-day months, dips are shorter months. January is a knuckle, February a dip, and July and August fall on two knuckles side by side.

POOL.h: Stalactites and stalagmites form in caves. Which one hangs from the ceiling, and how can you remember?
POOL.a: Stalactites hang from the ceiling. Stalactites have a “c” for ceiling, and stalagmites have a “g” for ground.

POOL.h: On a ship, facing forward, which side is port?
POOL.a: The left. “Port” and “left” both have four letters. Port side navigation lights are also red, like port wine.

POOL.h: How can you work out 9 × 7 using only your ten fingers?
POOL.a: 63. Hold up all ten fingers and fold down the 7th from the left. There are 6 fingers to the left of it (tens) and 3 to the right (ones). It works for 9 × 1 up to 9 × 10.

POOL.h: When daylight saving starts, do clocks go forward or back an hour? How can you remember?
POOL.a: Forward. “Spring forward, fall back”: clocks spring ahead an hour in spring and fall back in autumn. In the states that use it, that means forward in October and back in April.

POOL.h: Read once and count the letter F: “FINISHED FILES ARE THE RESULT OF YEARS OF SCIENTIFIC STUDY COMBINED WITH THE EXPERIENCE OF YEARS.”
POOL.a: Six. Most people count three because the brain skims over “OF”, where the F sounds like a V. There are three “OF”s plus FINISHED, FILES and SCIENTIFIC.

POOL.h: Using Australian coins, what is the fewest coins you need to make exactly 95 cents?
POOL.a: Four: 50c + 20c + 20c + 5c. Three coins can reach at most 90c without going over, using 50c + 20c + 20c.

POOL.h: What has keys but can’t open a single lock?
POOL.a: A piano (or a computer keyboard). Its keys play notes or type letters, not open doors.

POOL.h: The more of these you take, the more you leave behind. What are they?
POOL.a: Footsteps. Every step you take leaves another one behind you.

POOL.h: What gets bigger the more you take away from it?
POOL.a: A hole. The more soil you dig out, the larger it grows.

POOL.h: I speak without a mouth and hear without ears. I have no body, but I come alive with sound. What am I?
POOL.a: An echo. It’s just sound bouncing back to you off a surface such as a cliff or a wall.

POOL.h: I’m tall when I’m young and short when I’m old. What am I?
POOL.a: A candle. It burns down as it gets older.

POOL.h: What has to be broken before you can use it?
POOL.a: An egg. You have to crack it before you can cook with it.

POOL.h: What belongs to you, but other people use it far more than you do?
POOL.a: Your name. Others say it all the time; you rarely need to.

POOL.h: What has an eye but can’t see?
POOL.a: A needle. (A potato and a cyclone have ‘eyes’ too.)

POOL.h: I have cities but no houses, forests but no trees, and water but no fish. What am I?
POOL.a: A map. It shows all those things without actually containing them.

POOL.h: If you have me, you want to share me. If you share me, you no longer have me. What am I?
POOL.a: A secret. Once you’ve told it, it isn’t a secret any more.

POOL.h: What breaks as soon as you say its name?
POOL.a: Silence. Speaking the word ends it.

POOL.h: What can travel all around the world while staying in one corner?
POOL.a: A postage stamp. It rides in the corner of an envelope.

POOL.h: What starts with E, ends with E, and usually holds just one letter?
POOL.a: An envelope. The ‘letter’ is the kind you post, not one of the alphabet.

POOL.h: What runs but never walks, has a mouth but never talks, and has a bed but never sleeps?
POOL.a: A river. It runs downhill, flows out through its mouth and lies in a riverbed.

POOL.h: Forwards I’m heavy, backwards I’m not. What am I?
POOL.a: The word TON. Spelled backwards, it’s NOT.

POOL.h: I’m light as a feather, but even the strongest person can’t hold me for more than a few minutes. What am I?
POOL.a: Your breath. It weighs almost nothing, yet no one can hold it for long.

POOL.h: Which five-letter word gets shorter when you add two letters to it?
POOL.a: SHORT. Add E and R and it becomes SHORTER.

POOL.h: Which English word still sounds exactly the same after you remove its last four letters?
POOL.a: QUEUE. Take away U, E, U and E and you’re left with Q, which is pronounced the same way.

POOL.h: Which English word could jokingly claim to be the longest?
POOL.a: SMILES, because there’s a ‘mile’ between its first and last letters.

POOL.h: How can you take one away from seven and leave it even?
POOL.a: Take the letter S away from SEVEN and you’re left with EVEN.

POOL.h: Which number, written as an English word, has all its letters in alphabetical order?
POOL.a: FORTY: F, O, R, T, Y. No other English number word does this.

POOL.h: Rearrange the letters of DORMITORY into two words that describe one.
POOL.a: DIRTY ROOM. Both use exactly the same nine letters.

POOL.h: ELEVEN PLUS TWO is an anagram of another sum that means the same thing. What is it?
POOL.a: TWELVE PLUS ONE. Both use the same 13 letters, and both equal 13.

POOL.h: Change CAT into DOG by changing one letter at a time, making a real word at every step. What’s the shortest way?
POOL.a: CAT, COT, COG, DOG. Three steps is the minimum, since all three letters need to change.

POOL.h: STARTLING stays a real word as you remove one letter at a time, all the way down to a single letter. Can you find the chain?
POOL.a: STARTLING, STARTING, STARING, STRING, STING, SING, SIN, IN, I. Remove L, T, A, R, T, G, S, then N.

POOL.h: What single word can go in front of BALL, FALL, FLAKE and MAN?
POOL.a: SNOW: snowball, snowfall, snowflake and snowman.

POOL.h: What single word can go after BUTTER, FIRE, HOUSE and DRAGON?
POOL.a: FLY: butterfly, firefly, housefly and dragonfly.

POOL.h: A man lives on the 10th floor. Each morning he takes the lift down. Each evening he rides to the 7th floor and walks the rest, unless it’s raining or someone else is in the lift. Why?
POOL.a: He’s too short to reach the button for 10. He can reach 7, and on rainy days he presses 10 with his umbrella (or asks another passenger).

POOL.h: A boy breaks his arm and his father drives him to hospital. The surgeon on duty says, ‘I can’t operate on this boy. He’s my son.’ The surgeon isn’t his father. How?
POOL.a: The surgeon is his mother. (Or, just as fairly, his other dad.) The puzzle works because many people automatically picture a surgeon as a man.

POOL.h: A man walks for an hour in heavy rain with no umbrella, hat or hood. His clothes are soaked, but not a single hair on his head gets wet. How?
POOL.a: He’s bald. There’s no hair on his head to get wet.

POOL.h: Twins Ella and Max were born minutes apart, but in different years. How?
POOL.a: One was born just before midnight on 31 December and the other just after midnight on 1 January.

POOL.h: A small town has two barbers. One has a neat haircut; the other’s hair is a mess. Each can only get his hair cut by the other. Which one should you visit?
POOL.a: The one with the messy hair. He’s the one who gave the other barber that neat cut.

POOL.h: A man walks into a cafe and asks for a glass of water. The waiter suddenly shouts ‘Boo!’ at him. The man says thanks and leaves happy. Why?
POOL.a: He had hiccups. The fright cured them, so he no longer needed the water.

POOL.h: A window cleaner slips off a 20-metre ladder onto concrete, but isn’t hurt at all. How?
POOL.a: He slipped off the bottom rung. It’s a long ladder, but he only fell a few centimetres.

POOL.h: You see a boat full of people, yet there isn’t a single person on board. How?
POOL.a: Everyone on board is married, so not one of them is single.

POOL.h: A truck driver goes the wrong way down a one-way street. Two police officers watch, but do nothing. Why?
POOL.a: He’s walking, not driving. Nothing says a truck driver has to be in his truck.

POOL.h: A black dog sits in the middle of a country road with no street lights. A car with its headlights off comes along and stops in time. How did the driver see the dog?
POOL.a: It was daytime. Nothing in the puzzle says it was night.

POOL.h: A man in a small town has married more than 20 women. None of them has died, he’s never been divorced, and he’s broken no law. How?
POOL.a: He’s a marriage celebrant. He married them to their husbands, not to himself.

POOL.h: How far can a dog run into a forest?
POOL.a: Halfway. After that, it’s running out of the forest.

POOL.h: A truck gets wedged under a low bridge, just a few centimetres too tall. It can’t go forward or back. What’s a simple fix?
POOL.a: Let some air out of the tyres. The truck sinks a little, which is enough to drive it free.

POOL.h: A rooster lays an egg right on the peak of a sloping roof. Which side does the egg roll down?
POOL.a: Neither. Roosters are male, so they don’t lay eggs.

POOL.h: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. Tom says: ‘At least one of us two is a knave.’ What are Tom and his friend Jim?
POOL.a: Tom is a knight and Jim is a knave. If Tom were a knave, his statement would be true, which a knave can’t say. So Tom tells the truth, and Jim must be the knave.

POOL.h: Amy, Ben and Cara each own one pet: a cat, a dog or a goldfish, all different. Amy’s pet has no fur. Ben’s pet barks. Who owns the cat?
POOL.a: Cara. Amy has the furless goldfish and Ben has the barking dog, which leaves the cat for Cara.

POOL.h: If the day before yesterday was Thursday, what day will the day after tomorrow be?
POOL.a: Monday. If the day before yesterday was Thursday, today is Saturday, and two days on is Monday.

POOL.h: You roll a fair die twice. What’s the chance of getting at least one six?
POOL.a: 11 in 36, about 31%, not 1 in 3. The chance of no six is 5/6 × 5/6 = 25/36, so at least one six is the other 11/36.

POOL.h: How many people need to be in a room for there to be a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday?
POOL.a: Just 23. That many people make 253 different pairs, each a chance for a match. Ignoring leap days, the chance is about 51%.

POOL.h: A game show has three doors: a car behind one, goats behind the others. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, always opens another door to show a goat, then lets you switch. Should you?
POOL.a: Yes. Switching wins 2 times in 3. Your first pick is right only 1 time in 3, so the other closed door hides the car the remaining 2 times in 3.

POOL.h: You toss three fair coins. What’s the chance they all land the same way, all heads or all tails?
POOL.a: 1 in 4. Of the 8 equally likely outcomes, only HHH and TTT match. Many people guess 1 in 2.

POOL.h: 128 players enter a knockout tennis tournament. How many matches are needed to find the champion?
POOL.a: 127. Every match knocks out exactly one player, and all but one of the 128 must be knocked out.

POOL.h: Is it certain that at least two people in Sydney have exactly the same number of hairs on their head?
POOL.a: Yes. People have far fewer than a million hairs on their head, but Sydney has over 5 million people. There are more people than possible counts, so some must share one. This is the pigeonhole principle.

POOL.h: Writing out the numbers from 1 to 100, how many times do you write the digit 9?
POOL.a: 20. Ten times in the units place (9, 19, 29 ... 99) and ten times in the tens place (90 to 99). 99 counts twice.

POOL.h: If a hen and a half lays an egg and a half in a day and a half, how many eggs does one hen lay in 3 days?
POOL.a: 2 eggs. One and a half hens lay one and a half eggs in a day and a half, so one hen lays 1 egg in a day and a half. In 3 days, that’s 2.

POOL.h: Three whole numbers in a row add up to 72. What are they?
POOL.a: 23, 24 and 25. The middle number is always the total divided by 3: 72 divided by 3 is 24.

POOL.h: Volumes 1, 2 and 3 stand in order, left to right, on a shelf, spines facing you. Each has 4 cm of pages plus a 0.5 cm cover on each side. A bookworm chews from the first page of volume 1 to the last page of volume 3. How far does it go?
POOL.a: 6 cm. With the spine facing you, a book’s first page is on its right and its last page on its left. So the worm crosses just volume 1’s front cover (0.5 cm), all of volume 2 (5 cm) and volume 3’s back cover (0.5 cm).

POOL.h: I’m a two-digit number. My digits add up to 9. Swap my digits and you get a number 27 bigger than me. What am I?
POOL.a: 36. Swapped, it’s 63, and 63 minus 36 is 27. Its digits, 3 and 6, add up to 9.

POOL.h: Sam buys a bike for $60 and sells it for $70. He buys it back for $80 and sells it again for $90. How much profit did he make?
POOL.a: $20. He made $10 on each sale. In total he paid out $140 and took in $160.

POOL.h: Grandpa is as many years old as his grandson is months old. Together, their ages add up to 65 years. How old is each?
POOL.a: Grandpa is 60 and his grandson is 5. Five years is 60 months, and 60 plus 5 is 65.

POOL.h: A 100-metre train travels at 36 km/h. How long does it take to pass completely through a 200-metre tunnel, from its front going in to its back coming out?
POOL.a: 30 seconds. 36 km/h is 10 metres a second, and the train must travel 300 metres: the tunnel plus its own length.

POOL.h: At a hardware shop, 1 costs $3, 10 costs $6 and 100 costs $9. What is being sold?
POOL.a: House numbers. Each digit costs $3, so 1 has one digit, 10 has two and 100 has three.

POOL.h: Pick a three-digit number whose first and last digits differ by 2 or more, say 732. Reverse it and subtract the smaller from the larger. Reverse that answer and add the two. What do you get?
POOL.a: 1089, every time. With 732: 732 minus 237 is 495, and 495 plus 594 is 1089. Try any other starting number and see.

POOL.h: Leap years usually come every four years. So was 1900 a leap year?
POOL.a: No. A century year is only a leap year if it divides evenly by 400, so 2000 was a leap year but 1900 wasn’t.

POOL.h: You have 100 kg of potatoes that are 99% water. You leave them out until they are 98% water. How much do they weigh now?
POOL.a: 50 kg. The dry part weighs 1 kg and never changes. At 98% water, that 1 kg is 2% of the total, so the total must be 50 kg.

POOL.h: A bag holds 3 red, 4 blue and 5 green balls. Without looking, how many must you take out to be certain of getting three balls of the same colour?
POOL.a: 7. In the worst case you draw two of each colour first, which is 6 balls. The 7th must make three of one colour.

POOL.h: A says: “B is lying.” B says: “C is lying.” C says: “A and B are both lying.” Each person either always lies or always tells the truth. Who is telling the truth?
POOL.a: Only B. If C were truthful, A and B would both be liars, but then B’s claim that C lies would be true, a contradiction. So C lies, B is truthful, and A, who calls B a liar, is lying.

POOL.h: A lion lies on Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays, and tells the truth on every other day. One day he says: “Yesterday I was lying.” What day could it be?
POOL.a: Monday or Thursday. On a truthful day the claim must be true, which only works on Thursday. On a lying day it must be false, which only works on Monday, since Sunday was a truthful day.

POOL.h: In a 100-metre race, Ana beats Bec by 10 metres. For a rematch, Ana starts 10 metres behind the start line. Both run at the same speeds as before. Who wins?
POOL.a: Ana. When she has run 100 metres, Bec has run 90, so they are level with 10 metres to go. Ana is faster, so she wins the last stretch.

POOL.h: A drawer holds 2 red socks and 2 blue socks. You pull out two at random. What is the chance they match?
POOL.a: 1 in 3, not 1 in 2. Whatever the first sock is, only 1 of the 3 socks left is the same colour.

POOL.h: You have 10 bags of coins. Real coins weigh 10 g, but one whole bag is full of fakes weighing 11 g each. With one reading on a digital scale, how do you find the fake bag?
POOL.a: Take 1 coin from bag 1, 2 from bag 2, and so on up to 10 from bag 10. Real coins would weigh 550 g in total, so the number of extra grams tells you the fake bag’s number.

POOL.h: A fair coin lands heads five times in a row. What is the chance the next toss is heads?
POOL.a: Still 1 in 2. The coin has no memory, so past tosses don’t change the next one. Expecting tails to be “due” is called the gambler’s fallacy.

POOL.h: A man shaves many times a day, yet he still has a full beard. How?
POOL.a: He’s a barber. He shaves other people, not himself.

POOL.h: A woman shoots her husband, then holds him under water for five minutes, then hangs him up. Later they go out to dinner together. How?
POOL.a: She’s a photographer. She took his photo, developed it in a tray of liquid and hung it up to dry.

POOL.h: A plane crashes exactly on the border between two countries. In which country do they bury the survivors?
POOL.a: Neither. Survivors are alive, so nobody buries them.

POOL.h: Is it legal for a man to marry his widow’s sister?
POOL.a: No, because he’s dead. If he has a widow, he is no longer alive to marry anyone.

POOL.h: A butcher’s assistant is 1.8 metres tall and wears size 11 shoes. What does he weigh?
POOL.a: Meat. Weighing meat is his job.

POOL.h: Before Mount Everest was discovered, what was the highest mountain in the world?
POOL.a: Mount Everest. It was always the highest, whether anyone had measured it or not.

POOL.h: An electric train heads north while the wind blows from the west. Which way does the smoke go?
POOL.a: There is no smoke. Electric trains don’t burn fuel on board.

POOL.h: A man builds a house where every wall faces south. A bear walks past. What colour is it?
POOL.a: White. The only place where every wall faces south is the North Pole, so it’s a polar bear.

POOL.h: A basket holds five apples. You give one apple each to five friends, yet one apple stays in the basket. How?
POOL.a: The last friend gets their apple still in the basket.

POOL.h: Which is heavier: a kilogram of feathers or a kilogram of bricks?
POOL.a: Neither. They both weigh one kilogram. The feathers just take up far more space.

POOL.h: A rope ladder hangs over a ship’s side, its bottom rung just touching the water. The rungs are 30 cm apart. The tide rises 1 metre. How many rungs are now under water?
POOL.a: None. The ship floats, so it rises with the tide, and the ladder rises with it.

POOL.h: How many times can you subtract 5 from 25?
POOL.a: Once. After that you are subtracting 5 from 20, not from 25.

POOL.h: How can half of 12 be 7?
POOL.a: Write 12 as the Roman numeral XII and cut it across the middle. The top half reads VII.

POOL.h: Add one symbol to the Roman numeral IX to turn it into six.
POOL.a: Put an S in front: SIX.

POOL.h: What can you hold in your left hand but never in your right?
POOL.a: Your right elbow. Try it. Your right hand works too: your left can hold it, but it can’t hold itself.

POOL.h: What gets wetter the more it dries?
POOL.a: A towel. As it dries you, it soaks up the water.

POOL.h: What starts with T, ends with T, and has T in it?
POOL.a: A teapot. It begins and ends with the letter T, and you put tea in it.

POOL.h: What kind of room has no doors and no windows?
POOL.a: A mushroom.

POOL.h: I have branches, but no fruit, no trunk and no leaves. What am I?
POOL.a: A bank. Its branches are its offices in different towns.

POOL.h: What has a thumb and four fingers but isn’t alive?
POOL.a: A glove. It has the shape of a hand without being one.

POOL.h: What word contains 26 letters but has only three syllables?
POOL.a: Alphabet. It holds all 26 letters, and the word itself has three syllables: al-pha-bet.

POOL.h: What has 13 hearts but no other organs?
POOL.a: A standard deck of playing cards. The hearts suit has 13 cards.

POOL.h: Which common English word contains the vowels A, E, I, O and U, each exactly once and in alphabetical order?
POOL.a: Facetious (abstemious works too). F-A-c-E-t-I-O-U-s.

POOL.h: Rearrange the letters of THE EYES into two words that describe what they do.
POOL.a: THEY SEE. Both phrases use the same seven letters.

POOL.t: M, V, E, M, J, S, U
POOL.h: What letter comes next: M, V, E, M, J, S, U, …?
POOL.a: N. They are the planets in order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.

POOL.h: What is 36 × 25, worked out in your head?
POOL.a: 900. Multiplying by 25 is the same as dividing by 4 and multiplying by 100: 36 ÷ 4 is 9, and 9 × 100 is 900.

POOL.h: Quick: what is 8% of 50?
POOL.a: 4. Percentages can be flipped: 8% of 50 is the same as 50% of 8, which is easy.

POOL.h: Kim can paint a fence in 3 hours. Lee takes 6 hours to paint the same fence. Working together, how long do they take?
POOL.a: 2 hours. Kim paints a third of the fence each hour and Lee a sixth, so together they do half each hour.

POOL.h: A shop takes 20% off an item, then takes a further 20% off the sale price. What is the total discount?
POOL.a: 36%, not 40%. The second 20% comes off a smaller price: 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, so you pay 64% of the original.

POOL.h: Your car’s odometer reads 15951 km, a palindrome. Exactly two hours later it shows the next palindrome. What was your average speed?
POOL.a: 55 km/h. The next palindrome is 16061, which is 110 km further on. 110 km in 2 hours is 55 km/h.

POOL.h: How many times a day do the hour and minute hands of a clock form a right angle?
POOL.a: 44. The minute hand laps the hour hand 22 times a day, and they are at right angles twice in each lap.

POOL.h: What comes next: 61, 52, 63, 94, 46, …?
POOL.a: 18. Reverse each number: 16, 25, 36, 49, 64 are the squares of 4 to 8. The next square is 81, and reversed that’s 18.

POOL.h: What comes next: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, …?
POOL.a: 720. Each term is the one before multiplied by the next whole number: × 2, × 3, × 4, × 5, then 120 × 6.

POOL.h: A sheet of paper is 0.1 mm thick. If you could fold it in half 42 times, roughly how thick would it be?
POOL.a: About 440,000 km, further than the Moon, which is about 384,000 km away. Each fold doubles the thickness, and 2 to the power of 42 is over 4 trillion. In practice paper can’t be folded that many times.

POOL.h: Roughly how long is a million seconds? And a billion seconds?
POOL.a: A million seconds is about 11.5 days. A billion seconds is about 32 years. The gap between a million and a billion is far bigger than it sounds.

POOL.h: A car with a spare tyre rotates all five tyres evenly and drives 50,000 km. How many kilometres does each tyre travel?
POOL.a: 40,000 km. Four tyres are on the road at any time, giving 200,000 tyre-kilometres, shared equally among five tyres.

POOL.h: Climbing from level 1 to level 4 of a building takes 30 seconds. At the same pace, how long does it take to climb from level 1 to level 8?
POOL.a: 70 seconds, not 80. Level 1 to 4 is only 3 flights, so each flight takes 10 seconds, and level 1 to 8 is 7 flights.

POOL.h: Multiply together every digit on a phone keypad. What do you get?
POOL.a: 0. The keypad includes 0, and anything multiplied by 0 is 0.

POOL.h: Split 45 into four numbers so that adding 2 to the first, subtracting 2 from the second, multiplying the third by 2 and dividing the fourth by 2 all give the same answer.
POOL.a: 8, 12, 5 and 20. Each one becomes 10, and 8 + 12 + 5 + 20 = 45.

POOL.h: Using exactly eight 8s and only addition, make 1,000.
POOL.a: 888 + 88 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 1,000. The big numbers do most of the work, and three single 8s finish it.

POOL.h: You have 25 candles. When five candles burn down, their leftover stubs can be melted into one new candle. How many candles can you burn in total?
POOL.a: 31. The 25 stubs make 5 new candles. Their 5 stubs make 1 more. That’s 25 + 5 + 1.

POOL.h: For the same price, would you rather have one 45 cm pizza or two 30 cm pizzas?
POOL.a: The single 45 cm pizza. Area grows with the square of the width: 45 × 45 is 2,025, while two 30 cm pizzas give 2 × 900 = 1,800. That’s about 12.5% more pizza.

POOL.h: An ice cube floats in a glass filled with water right to the brim. When the ice melts, does the glass overflow?
POOL.a: No. The level stays the same. Floating ice pushes aside exactly its own weight of water, and when it melts it turns into that same amount of water.
